### 5.2.14 Templating engines and view rendering
🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** · Prerequisites: 5.2.5

**Definition:** A template engine turns a template plus a data object into HTML. Express's `res.render` locates a file in `views/`, runs it through a registered engine, and sends the result. The security property that matters is **escaping by default** — because server-rendered HTML is the number-one XSS delivery path for a Node service.

**The engines you will be asked about**

| Engine | Syntax | Escapes by default | Compile step | Verdict today |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **EJS** | `<%= %>` (escaped), `<%- %>` (raw), `<% %>` (logic) | Yes | No | Still the default choice for small apps; easy to get wrong with `<%- %>` |
| **Pug / Jade** | Indentation | Yes (attributes too) | No | Compact and hard to read; the indentation means a stray space changes semantics |
| **Handlebars** | `{{ }}` escaped, `{{{ }}}` raw | Yes | No | The safest pleasant default; great for partial-heavy apps |
| **Nunjucks** | Jinja-style `{{ }}`, `{% %}` | Yes | No | Jinja users' favourite; powerful inheritance |
| **Eta** | `<%= %>` (escaped), `<%~ %>` (raw) | Yes | Configurable | Modern, fast, TS-first |
| **React / Vue SSR** | JSX/template | By default (no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`) | Yes | The right answer for anything with real interactivity |

**A working setup, both engines**

```js
// EJS
app.set('view engine', 'ejs');
app.set('views', path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'views'));
app.set('view cache', process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production');   // ON in production
// app.engine('html', require('ejs').renderFile);
```

```js
// Nunjucks
import nunjucks from 'nunjucks';
const env = new nunjucks.Environment(
  new nunjucks.FileSystemLoader('views', { watch: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' }),
  { autoescape: true, express: app, noCache: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' },
);
app.set('view engine', 'njk');
app.set('views', 'views');
```

```js
// Handlebars
import { engine } from 'express-handlebars';
app.engine('hbs', engine({ extname: '.hbs', defaultLayout: 'main' }));
app.set('view engine', '.hbs');
```

**Rendering, with the layout and locals that actually get used**

```js
app.get('/orders/:id', asyncHandler(async (req, res) => {
  const order = await orders.findByIdOrThrow(req.params.id);
  res.render('order', {
    title: `Order ${order.number}`,
    order,
    user: req.user,
    helpers: { money: (cents) => (cents / 100).toFixed(2) },
    layout: 'main',
  });
}));
```

**XSS: the rules, and the exact mechanism**

```js
// EJS: <%= %> escapes. <%- %> does NOT.
<p><%= user.bio %></p>              ✅ escapes < > & " '
<p><%- user.bio %></p>              ❌ RAW — a bio of <script>...</script> executes

// Handlebars: {{ }} escapes. {{{ }}} does not.
<p>{{ user.bio }}</p>               ✅
<p>{{{ user.bio }}}</p>             ❌

// Pug: | escapes, != does not.
p!= user.bio                       ❌

// THE SAFEST OPTION: do not build HTML strings at all.
res.json({ bio: user.bio });        // ✅ JSON is not executed as HTML
```

The deeper version, which interviewers push on: **escaping at render time is not a complete defence for rich text.** A user-authored `<b>` and a user-authored `<script>` are the same string to an escaper; you either escape everything (losing formatting) or you sanitise with an allowlist parser (`sanitize-html`, DOMPurify on the client). The correct pipeline is: store raw → sanitise on write with a strict allowlist → escape on render. Never sanitise on render only, because the stored value is then still dangerous for the next consumer.

```js
// Rich text: sanitise on WRITE with an allowlist, escape on RENDER.
import sanitizeHtml from 'sanitize-html';
const SAFE = { allowedTags: ['b','i','em','strong','a','p','ul','ol','li'],
               allowedAttributes: { a: ['href','title'] },
               allowedSchemes: ['http','https','mailto'],
               transformTags: { a: sanitizeHtml.simpleTransform('a', { rel: 'noopener noreferrer' }, true) } };
user.bioHtml = sanitizeHtml(input.bio, SAFE);      // write time
// template: <%= user.bioHtml %>                    // escapes the RESULT on render
```

**Performance, and the production settings that matter**

```js
app.set('view cache', true);   // production: cache compiled templates in memory
app.disable('x-powered-by');
// EJS: cache is on by default in production
// Pug: `cache: true` unless NODE_ENV is development
// Nunjucks: `noCache: false` in production
// Eta: `cache: true` in production, and `views` pointing at a precompiled dir
```

- `res.render` is **synchronous** in the template engine's execution (after the async file read when cache is off). A heavy template on a hot path is a main-thread block. Templates are usually cheap; a loop over 10,000 rows in a template is not.
- With `view cache` off (development), every render reads the file. That is the point in dev and a throughput problem in production.
- Precompile at build time (EJS: `ejs --compile` into a directory; Eta has a `precompile` API) and point the engine at the output. This removes both the file read and the runtime compile from the request path.

**When to use templates at all — the question that gets the modern answer**

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Marketing site, docs, admin UI, any content with real interactivity | A frontend framework with SSR or static generation (**PHASE 4**) |
| Email templates | A template engine, with **no** request data in them (no CSRF tokens to leak) |
| 4 KB HTML fragment inserted into a page | `res.send('<div>…</div>')` is fine |
| Server-rendered JSON API | Never a template — `res.json` |
| Legacy app you are maintaining | EJS/Handlebars, and invest in the escaping discipline |

**The architectural point worth making out loud:** a template engine is a *server-rendered* answer, and the industry has largely moved to a JSON API plus a client framework (**PHASE 4**) because interactivity, code splitting, and component reuse beat server rendering past a certain complexity. Interviewers are not looking for you to abandon templates — they are looking for whether you can say *which* problem each solves.

**Trade-offs**

- Templates keep everything in one language and one deploy, and the first paint needs no JavaScript. They lose on interactivity, on asset pipelines, and on reuse.
- A template engine is not a security boundary on its own; it is a set of defaults. A single `<%-` in a codebase disables the protection for that value, and no linter you have will reliably catch it.
- Layouts and partials are the engine's real ergonomic story. EJS's `include` is a synchronous file read per render unless the file is cached.
- SSR with a framework gives you the same one-language story with a component model, at the cost of a build step, a hydration cost, and a much larger dependency surface.

**Production considerations**

- `view cache` on in production, always. A missing cache is the single most common template performance bug.
- Never put secrets in a template-rendered page. A server-rendered HTML page can end up in a browser cache, a proxy cache, or a `view-source`.
- Set `Cache-Control: no-store` on any authenticated HTML page. HTML is cacheable by default heuristics and an authenticated page in a shared cache is a data leak.
- Add `autoescape` explicitly (`nunjucks`, `eta`, `handlebars`) rather than relying on the default, so a future config change cannot turn it off silently.
- Lint for the raw-output tags: `rg '<%-' views/` and `rg '\{\{\{' views/` in CI. It is a crude check and it catches the mistake.
- Precompile templates in the build stage; do not ship the template source if you do not need to.

**Common mistakes**

- `<%- %>` / `{{{ }}}` on user input → stored XSS.
- `view cache` off in production → a file read per render.
- `res.render` on an API endpoint, returning HTML where the client expects JSON.
- `res.send('<html>…' + userInput + '…</html>')` with no escaping at all.
- Caching authenticated HTML.
- Escaping a value twice (`&amp;amp;`) because both the template and a sanitiser escaped it.

**What an interviewer probes**

- "How do you prevent XSS in a template?" — escape-by-default syntax, never the raw tag on user input, sanitise rich text with an allowlist on write, encode at the output context.
- "When would you not use a template engine?" — anything interactive; a JSON API plus a client framework.
- "Templates are slow in production." — `view cache`, precompilation, and the synchronous-render point.
- "How do you review a template for XSS?" — grep for the raw-output tags, and a rule that user input never reaches a raw tag.

---
### 5.2.15 Fastify and Hono awareness, and the framework comparison
🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** · Prerequisites: 5.2.1, 5.2.2, 5.3.1

**Definition:** Fastify is a Node HTTP framework built around **encapsulation** and **schema-driven serialisation**. Hono is a tiny, Web-standard router that runs on Node, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers, and edge platforms. Both exist for the same underlying reason: Express's global middleware stack and untyped request/response are hard to reason about and hard to make fast.

**Fastify, and the three ideas that are actually different**

```js
import Fastify from 'fastify';

const app = Fastify({
  logger: { level: 'info' },          // Pino, BUILT IN. No pino-http needed.
  trustProxy: true,
  bodyLimit: 1_048_576,
  disableRequestLogging: false,
});

// 1. ENCAPSULATION: hooks and decorators registered inside a plugin are
//    invisible outside it. No accidental global state, no ordering surprises.
async function authPlugin(app) {
  app.decorateRequest('user', null);          // must be DECLARED, and it is a prototype change
  app.addHook('onRequest', async (req) => {   // runs before routing
    const t = req.headers.authorization;
    if (!t) throw app.httpErrors.unauthorized();
    req.user = await verify(t);
  });
  app.get('/me', async () => req.user);        // ← correct scoping: this is 5.2.11's onion,
}                                              //    but guaranteed by the plugin boundary
```

```js
// 2. SCHEMA: validation AND serialisation from one definition.
app.post('/orders', {
  schema: {
    body: { type: 'object', required: ['customerId', 'items'],
            properties: { customerId: { type: 'string', format: 'uuid' },
                          items: { type: 'array', minItems: 1,
                                   items: { type: 'object', required: ['sku','qty'],
                                            properties: { sku: { type: 'string' },
                                                          qty: { type: 'integer', minimum: 1 } } } },
                          total: { type: 'number' } },          // ← NOT in body: stripped
            additionalProperties: false },
    params: { type: 'object', properties: { id: { type: 'string', format: 'uuid' } } },
    querystring: { type: 'object', properties: { page: { type: 'integer', minimum: 1, default: 1 } } },
    response: {                                              // ← SERIALISATION, the big one
      201: { type: 'object', properties: { data: { type: 'object',
        properties: { id: { type: 'string' }, total: { type: 'number' } } } } },
      400: { type: 'object', properties: { code: { type: 'string' }, message: { type: 'string' } } },
    },
  },
}, async (req, reply) => {
  // req.body is validated. `total` from the client is GONE (additionalProperties:false).
  const order = await orders.create(req.body);
  return reply.code(201).header('location', `/api/orders/${order.id}`).send({ data: order });
});
```

The `response` schema is the reason Fastify is fast: it **pre-compiles a serialiser** for the shape, so `JSON.stringify` is replaced by a generated function that writes only the declared fields. That is not a 5% win; on JSON-heavy APIs it is routinely 2-3× faster on throughput and meaningfully lower on p99, and it is a *security* property as well — a field you forget to declare cannot leak.

```js
// 3. HOOKS, in a named, documented order.
app.addHook('onRequest', ...)       // raw request, before parsing
     .addHook('preParsing', ...)    // transform the incoming stream
     .addHook('preValidation', ...)
     .addHook('preHandler', ...)
     .addHook('preSerialization', (req, reply, payload) => payload)   // wrap the payload
     .addHook('onSend', ...)        // modify the serialized string/stream
     .addHook('onResponse', ...)    // headers sent
     .addHook('onTimeout', ...)
     .addHook('onError', ...)
     .addHook('onReady', ...)       // boot complete

// Errors: throw, do not next(err). A thrown error becomes a reply via setErrorHandler.
app.setErrorHandler((err, req, reply) => {
  req.log.error({ err }, 'request failed');
  const status = err.statusCode ?? 500;
  reply.code(status).type('application/problem+json').send({
    type: `https://errors.example.com/${err.code ?? 'internal_error'}`,
    status, code: err.code ?? 'internal_error', traceId: req.id,
  });
});
app.setNotFoundHandler((req, reply) => reply.code(404).send({ code: 'not_found' }));

await app.listen({ port: 3000, host: '0.0.0.0' });
await app.close();     // drains; part of the graceful shutdown in 5.1.11
```

**Fastify plugins, and the encapsulation payoff**

```js
// Encapsulation means two sibling plugins CANNOT see each other's decorators.
// This is the structural fix for every ordering bug from 5.2.3.
app.register(async (a) => {
  a.decorate('db', makePool());
  a.addHook('onClose', async () => a.db.end());
}, { prefix: '/api/orders' });        // a.db is invisible to /api/users

app.register(require('@fastify/helmet'), { global: false });   // opt in per plugin
app.register(require('@fastify/cors'), { origin: ALLOWED_LIST, credentials: true });
app.register(require('@fastify/rate-limit'), { max: 300, timeWindow: '1 minute' });
app.register(require('@fastify/sensible'));   // httpErrors — the ergonomic win
```

**Hono, and the thing it optimises for**

```ts
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { cors } from 'hono/cors';
import { logger } from 'hono/logger';
import { secureHeaders } from 'hono/secure-headers';
import { zValidator } from '@hono/zod-validator';
import { z } from 'zod';

const app = new Hono();
app.use('*', logger());
app.use('*', secureHeaders());
app.use('/api/*', cors({ origin: (o) => ALLOWED.has(o) ? o : null, credentials: true }));

// Hono's middleware is the Web-standard (Request, Context) shape, and the
// same code runs on Cloudflare Workers, Deno Deploy, Bun and Node.
app.get('/api/orders/:id', zValidator('param', z.object({ id: z.string().uuid() })),
  async (c) => {
    const { id } = c.req.valid('param');
    const order = await orders.findById(id);
    if (!order) return c.json({ code: 'not_found' }, 404);
    return c.json({ data: order });
  });

export default app;                       // a fetch handler
// Node adapter:  import { serve } from '@hono/node-server'; serve(app);
```

Hono's real proposition: **one codebase, Web-standard APIs, deployable to a Node server, a Bun server, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge, and Deno Deploy.** Its Express-equivalents (`c.req.param`, `c.req.query`, `c.req.json()`) are a thin layer over the standard, which is exactly why it ports. The cost: a smaller ecosystem of middleware, fewer of the Node-specific integrations you rely on, and no streaming in the same shape.

**The honest comparison table**

| | Express 5 | Fastify 5 | Hono | NestJS (5.3) | Koa |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Paradigm | Global middleware stack | Plugin encapsulation | Web-standard fetch | Decorators + DI | Minimal middleware |
| Validation | `zod`/`joi` middleware | **JSON Schema, in the route** | Zod/Valibot middleware | class-validator pipes | none built in |
| Serialisation | `res.json` (stringify) | **Pre-compiled from the schema** | `c.json` | class-serializer | `ctx.body` |
| Async errors | Automatic (5.x) | Throw | Throw | Automatic | — |
| Logging | pino/morgan | **Pino built in** | middleware | built in | middleware |
| Raw throughput | Baseline | **2-3× on JSON** | Fast (very low overhead) | Below Express | Middle |
| Ecosystem | The largest | Large, modern | Small, growing | Large | Small |
| Typing | `@types/express` | First-class TS generics | First-class TS | Decorator metadata | Weak |
| Edge runtime | No (with effort) | No | **Yes, natively** | No | Partially |
| Learning curve | Lowest | Medium | Low | Highest | Low |
| Best when | You already know it, or the team does | You want speed + type safety, at scale | Multi-runtime or edge | Large teams, many domains | You want the raw `ctx` |

**How to choose, in one sentence each**

- **Express** — the default, and the right answer unless you have a specific reason. The largest middleware ecosystem, the most documentation, the most hireable skill. If your team knows it, the cost of anything else is real.
- **Fastify** — when JSON throughput, typed handlers, or *structural* correctness (encapsulation removes a whole bug class) justify a migration. The strongest "why not Express" answer, because it names mechanisms rather than benchmarks.
- **Hono** — when you must run the same API on more than one runtime, including the edge, or when you want Web-standard types.
- **NestJS** — when the coordination cost of many engineers and many modules exceeds the framework's tax (5.3.1).

**Trade-offs and migration cost, honestly**

- Express → Fastify is a rewrite, not a refactor: handlers, middleware, error handling, and every plugin. The `#fastify/express` compatibility layer exists and it gets you started, but it is a first step, not a destination.
- Fastify's JSON Schema validation and serialisation require writing schemas. That is a real cost on a codebase with dynamic shapes, and it is *also* the thing that makes it fast and type-safe. Teams that hate duplication love it; teams with a fast-moving internal API hate it.
- Fastify's encapsulation is a feature and a constraint: a "global" middleware is a plugin with `fastify-plugin`, and a decorator declared in the wrong scope is a runtime error. It is learnable in an hour and it eliminates the ordering bugs of 5.2.3 permanently.
- Hono's middleware ecosystem is a fraction of Express's, and several Node-specific integrations (heavy APM instrumentation, some pino transports) are less battle-tested.
- NestJS is a layer above all of this; you can run it on Fastify. Choosing NestJS *and* Express *and* Hono is three runtimes in one codebase.

**Production considerations**

- Fastify: `trustProxy: true` means *all* proxies, which is only correct if nothing can reach the app directly. Use `trustProxy: 'loopback'` or a hop count.
- Fastify: `app.close()` is the graceful shutdown entry point; it stops accepting, waits for in-flight requests, and runs `onClose` hooks. Wire it to `SIGTERM` exactly as in 5.1.11.
- Fastify: `decorateRequest('user', null)` declares a property on the prototype; use `decorate` for functions and `decorateRequest` for request properties, or you get a deprecation or a subtle bug.
- Hono: on the edge, there is no long-lived process, so 5.1.11 does not apply; instead every request is billed cold, and the design constraints are bundle size and no Node built-ins.
- Whichever you pick: put the request-id/logging/error-shaping logic in one module so it is portable, and keep the domain layer runtime-agnostic.

**Common mistakes**

- Migrating "for performance" with no benchmark of *your* workload. Fastify's win is on JSON serialisation and routing; if your bottleneck is a database, the framework change buys you nothing.
- Assuming Fastify's `response` schema is optional. Without it you get none of the performance benefit and none of the leak protection.
- Hono on Node with a `fetch`-shaped handler and then reaching for `req`/`res` Node objects — the whole point is that you do not.
- Treating a benchmark from the framework's README as a result for your service.
- Believing Fastify encapsulation lets you register a "global" middleware anywhere; it does not, and that is the point.

**What an interviewer probes**

- "Why would you choose Fastify over Express?" — named mechanisms (pre-compiled serialisation from the response schema, schema validation on the route, encapsulation) plus the migration cost, and the honest note that the cost is usually not worth it without a specific reason.
- "What problem does encapsulation solve?" — the ordering and accidental-global-state bugs of a flat middleware stack; a decorator or hook registered in one plugin cannot leak into a sibling.
- "What is Hono for?" — one Web-standard codebase across Node, Bun, Deno and the edge; smallest overhead.
- "How do you compare frameworks fairly?" — the same workload, the same payload shapes, p50/p99, CPU per request, and the ecosystem/team-skills cost included in the answer.

# 5.1-5.2 MUST-IMPLEMENT-FROM-SCRATCH (10 Problems)

**How to practice:** write each from memory on a blank file, then test against the edge cases listed. In an interview, state your assumptions out loud, implement the main path, then *say* which edge cases you would handle next — reasoning about edges is what separates a mid-level from a senior.

These ten are the highest-leverage exercises in this part. Each fits in 20-35 minutes and each has a specific thing it proves.

---

### 1. A correct `EventEmitter` with leak detection, `once` semantics, and a disposable subscription

**The contract:** listeners fire in registration order; `once` fires exactly once even if the emit is re-entrant; `off` removes by identity; a bound listener count is reported; subscriptions are cancellable.

```js
export class TypedBus {
  #listeners = new Map();     // event -> array of {fn, once, ctx}
  #max = 10;

  constructor({ maxListeners = 10 } = {}) { this.#max = maxListeners; }

  on(event, fn, ctx = null) { return this.#add(event, fn, false, ctx); }
  once(event, fn, ctx = null) { return this.#add(event, fn, true, ctx); }
  prependListener(event, fn) { return this.#add(event, fn, false, null, true); }

  #add(event, fn, once, ctx, front = false) {
    if (typeof fn !== 'function') throw new TypeError('listener must be a function');
    const arr = this.#listeners.get(event) ?? [];
    if (arr.length >= this.#max) {
      // The real EventEmitter PRINTS A WARNING here rather than throwing.
      // Making it throw is a defensible choice for an internal bus: a leak
      // should be a hard failure in tests, not a line in a log file.
      console.warn(`[TypedBus] possible leak: ${arr.length + 1} listeners for "${event}"`);
    }
    const rec = { fn, once, ctx, off: null };
    rec.off = (e) => { if (e !== event) return; this.#off(event, rec); };
    front ? arr.unshift(rec) : arr.push(rec);
    this.#listeners.set(event, arr);
    return rec.off;                       // a disposer, which is the whole API design
  }

  off(event, fn) {                        // removes the LAST matching registration
    const arr = this.#listeners.get(event);
    if (!arr) return this;
    for (let i = arr.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) if (arr[i].fn === fn) { this.#off(event, arr[i]); break; }
    return this;
  }

  #off(event, rec) {
    const arr = this.#listeners.get(event);
    if (!arr) return;
    const i = arr.indexOf(rec);
    if (i >= 0) arr.splice(i, 1);
    if (arr.length === 0) this.#listeners.delete(event);
  }

  emit(event, ...args) {
    const arr = this.#listeners.get(event);
    if (!arr || arr.length === 0) {
      // THE special rule: 'error' with zero listeners THROWS. Everything else
      // is a no-op. This is the behaviour every Node API depends on.
      if (event === 'error') throw args[0] instanceof Error ? args[0] : new Error(String(args[0]));
      return false;
    }
    // Snapshot: listeners added during this emit do NOT run for this emit,
    // and listeners removed during it are still invoked (Express relies on
    // this for once-semantics under re-entrancy).
    for (const rec of [...arr]) {
      if (rec.once) this.#off(event, rec);
      rec.fn.apply(rec.ctx, args);          // a throw propagates out of emit
    }
    return true;
  }

  listenerCount(event) { return this.#listeners.get(event)?.length ?? 0; }
  eventNames() { return [...this.#listeners.keys()]; }
  removeAll(event) { event ? this.#listeners.delete(event) : this.#listeners.clear(); return this; }
}

/** Promise-shaped subscription with a disposer — the leak-free interface. */
export function subscribe(bus, event) {
  let resolve;
  const promise = new Promise((r) => { resolve = r; });
  const off = bus.on(event, (...args) => resolve(args));
  return { promise, dispose: off, get settled() { return false; } };
}
```

*Edge cases:* `once` under a re-entrant emit; `off` removing the last duplicate; emitting `'error'` with no listeners (throws) versus with one; a listener that throws (propagates synchronously, later listeners do not run); a listener removed during the emit still running; the disposer returned by `on` being called twice (idempotent); `prependListener` order.

*Follow-ups:* why the real `EventEmitter` warns at 10 rather than throwing; how `events.once` differs (it also listens for `'error'` so a stream error rejects the promise); how you would implement `AsyncIterator` support on top.

---

### 2. A Readable/Writable pipeline with real backpressure and a byte-counting cap

**The contract:** a producer that can outrun a consumer never buffers more than one `highWaterMark` at a time; exceeding a byte cap errors the stream and destroys everything; a source error propagates and the destination is closed.

```js
import { Readable, Writable, Transform, pipeline } from 'node:stream';
import { createReadStream, createWriteStream } from 'node:fs';

// --- a Transform that caps total bytes and counts newlines, incrementally ---
export function makeCounter({ maxBytes = 1 << 20, onDone = () => {} } = {}) {
  let bytes = 0, lines = 0, last = 0;
  return new Transform({
    transform(chunk, _enc, cb) {
      bytes += chunk.length;
      if (bytes > maxBytes) { const e = new Error('limit exceeded'); e.code = 'ELIMIT'; return cb(e); }
      for (let i = 0; i < chunk.length; i++) if (chunk[i] === 0x0a) lines++;
      last = chunk[chunk.length - 1];
      cb(null, chunk);            // cb(err) is the ONLY way to fail synchronously
    },
    flush(cb) {                  // forgetting this is how a stream never ends
      onDone({ bytes, lines: lines + (last === 0x0a ? 0 : 1) });
      cb();
    },
  });
}

// --- a Readable from any async source, object mode ---
export function fromAsync(fn) {
  let i = 0;
  return new Readable({
    objectMode: true,
    async read() {
      if (i >= 10) return this.push(null);          // push(null) == end of stream
      const v = await fn(i++);
      this.push(v);
    },
    destroy(err, cb) { /* release resources here; cb(err) forwards the error */ },
  });
}

// --- manual backpressure, shown so you can explain why pipeline() is better ---
export async function manualPipe(src, dst) {
  for await (const chunk of src) {      // async iteration handles backpressure for you
    if (!dst.write(chunk)) await new Promise((r) => dst.once('drain', r));
    if (dst.destroyed) break;
  }
  if (!dst.destroyed) dst.end();
}

// --- the production shape ---
export async function processFile(srcPath, destPath, maxBytes) {
  const stats = {};
  try {
    await pipeline(
      createReadStream(srcPath, { highWaterMark: 64 * 1024 }),
      makeCounter({ maxBytes, onDone: (s) => Object.assign(stats, s) }),
      createWriteStream(destPath),
      { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(30_000) },
    );
    return stats;
  } catch (e) {
    if (e.code === 'ELIMIT') { const w = new Error('payload too large'); w.status = 413; throw w; }
    throw e;
  }
}
```

*Edge cases:* an empty file (zero lines, `flush` still called); a file ending in a newline (do not count a phantom line); a chunk boundary splitting a multi-byte character (use `StringDecoder`); the cap exceeded exactly at the boundary; `AbortSignal` aborting mid-pipeline; the destination erroring with `ENOSPC` and the source being destroyed; `push()` after `push(null)`.

*Follow-ups:* why `pipe()` is not enough (no error forwarding, no teardown); how `objectMode` changes the `highWaterMark` unit; how you would implement a `split2`-style line splitter with a partial-line tail.

---

### 3. `process.nextTick` / microtask / timer ordering, demonstrated and asserted

**The contract:** given a program with a known mix of scheduling primitives, print the exact order — and be able to say which orderings are guaranteed and which are a race.

```js
export function traceOrder({ fromIO = false } = {}) {
  const out = [];
  const log = (label) => out.push(label);

  log('sync:1');
  setTimeout(() => { log('timer:1'); setTimeout(() => log('timer:2'), 0); }, 0);
  setImmediate(() => { log('immediate:1'); setImmediate(() => log('immediate:2')); });
  process.nextTick(() => { log('tick:1'); process.nextTick(() => log('tick:2')); });
  Promise.resolve().then(() => log('microtask:1'));
  queueMicrotask(() => log('microtask:2'));
  log('sync:2');

  if (fromIO) {
    // Inside an I/O cycle the race is decided: we are already past the timers
    // phase, so a 0ms timer cannot fire until the NEXT tick, while an
    // immediate scheduled right here runs in THIS tick's check phase.
    setTimeout(() => {
      const inner = [];
      setTimeout(() => inner.push('timer'), 0);
      setImmediate(() => inner.push('immediate'));
      inner.push('sync');
      setTimeout(() => { log('fromIO:' + inner.join(',')); process.nextTick(() => log('afterTick:' + inner.join(','))); });
    }, 5);
  }
  return out;
}
```

**The guaranteed output of the top-level program (deterministic on every platform):**

```
sync:1  sync:2  tick:1  tick:2  microtask:1  microtask:2   ← then a RACE for timer vs immediate
```

**The `fromIO` part is fully deterministic:**

```
fromIO:sync,immediate     ← immediate always wins from inside an I/O callback
afterIO:sync,immediate    ← nextTick sees the already-completed array
```

*Edge cases:* `nextTick` scheduled from inside a microtask still runs before the next microtask (the nextTick queue drains first at every boundary); a `setTimeout` registered from inside a `setImmediate` runs on the next tick, not this one; `unref()`'d timers do not keep the process alive; a throwing `nextTick` becomes an uncaught exception at the top of the tick; a long microtask chain starves timers entirely.

*Follow-ups:* why the top-level `setTimeout(0)` vs `setImmediate` order is unspecified (you are inside a tick that already passed its timers phase); what the "deprecation" of recursive `nextTick` was about; how `queueMicrotask` differs from `process.nextTick` in ordering.

---

### 4. A thread-pool-aware `fs` workload with a diagnostic mode

**The contract:** saturate the libuv thread pool deterministically, show the queueing, and make the diagnosis reproducible from the command line.

```js
import fsp from 'node:fs/promises';
import os from 'node:os';
import { performance } from 'node:perf_hooks';

const POOL = Number(process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE ?? 4);
const N = 16;

async function one(i) {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  // `stat` is a pool operation. Nothing in this function blocks the loop,
  // and nothing is parallel except POOL at a time.
  await fsp.stat('./package.json');
  return { i, ms: Math.round(performance.now() - t0) };
}

export async function diagnose() {
  console.log(`cpus=${os.availableParallelism()} pool=${POOL} cpus().length=${os.cpus().length}`);
  const t0 = performance.now();
  const results = await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: N }, (_, i) => one(i)));
  const wall = performance.now() - t0;
  const batches = Math.ceil(N / POOL);
  console.table(results);
  console.log({
    wallMs: Math.round(wall),
    expectedIfPoolBound: Math.round(batches * results[0].ms),
    verdict: wall > results[0].ms * 2 * 1.2 ? 'POOL BOUND' : 'not pool bound',
  });
  // The same script with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1 and =16 tells you which it is.
}
```

```bash
node pool-probe.js                      # pool=4 → two waves
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1 node pool-probe.js # pool=1 → sixteen waves
UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 node pool-probe.js# pool=16 → one wave
```

The teaching point: **latency is a step function of concurrency / pool size, not a smooth curve.** Every operation that touches the pool — `fs`, `zlib`, `crypto.scrypt`, `dns.lookup` — inherits that step function, and a diagnostic that only runs the default is a diagnostic that cannot see the problem.

*Edge cases:* the env var must be set **before** the process starts (assigning it in code is a no-op); `fs.createReadStream` holds a pool slot per in-flight chunk, so the effective concurrency is lower than the pool size implies; `zlib` and `crypto` share the same pool, so a compressing route can starve an unrelated `fs` route; `dns.lookup` is in the pool and `dns.resolve4` is not.

*Follow-ups:* which ten of your dependencies' operations use the pool; what you would change about a service that saturates it; the difference between "raise the pool" and "move the work".

---

### 5. A bounded worker-thread pool with transferables, timeouts, and a queue cap

**The contract:** `run()` never exceeds `size` concurrent jobs; a job that exceeds its timeout kills the worker and rejects; large buffers are transferred, not cloned; `close()` terminates everything.

```js
// pool.js
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';

export class Pool extends EventEmitter {
  #workers; #idle = []; #queue = []; #jobs = new Map(); #size; #closed = false;

  constructor(size, url, { maxQueue = 0 } = {}) {
    super();
    if (size < 1) throw new RangeError('size must be >= 1');
    this.#size = size; this.maxQueue = maxQueue;
    this.#workers = Array.from({ length: size }, (_, id) => this.#spawn(url, id));
  }

  #spawn(url, id) {
    const w = new Worker(url, { workerData: { id } });
    w.__job = null;
    w.on('message', (r) => this.#finish(w, null, r));
    w.on('error',   (e) => this.#finish(w, e));
    w.on('exit',    (c) => { if (c !== 0 && this.#jobs.has(w)) this.#finish(w, new Error(`worker exited ${c}`)); });
    w.unref();                                 // never hold the process open on its own
    return w;
  }

  #finish(w, err, result) {
    const job = w.__job;
    w.__job = null;
    if (job) { clearTimeout(job.timer); err ? job.reject(err) : job.resolve(result); }
    else if (err) this.emit('error', err);     // idle worker failed: surface it anyway
    if (this.#closed || !this.#queue.length) { this.#idle.push(w); return; }
    this.#dispatch(w, this.#queue.shift());
  }

  #dispatch(w, job) {
    w.__job = job;
    job.timer = setTimeout(() => { w.terminate(); job.reject(new Error('job timeout')); }, job.timeoutMs);
    job.timer.unref();
    const transfer = job.transfer ?? [];
    w.postMessage(job.payload, transfer);       // transfer = zero copy; sender is detached
  }

  run(payload, { timeoutMs = 30_000, transfer = [] } = {}) {
    if (this.#closed) return Promise.reject(new Error('pool closed'));
    if (this.maxQueue && this.#queue.length >= this.maxQueue) {
      return Promise.reject(Object.assign(new Error('pool saturated'), { status: 503 }));
    }
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const job = { payload, transfer, timeoutMs, resolve, reject, timer: null };
      const w = this.#idle.pop();
      if (w) this.#dispatch(w, job);
      else this.#queue.push(job);
    });
  }

  get stats() { return { size: this.#size, idle: this.#idle.length, queued: this.#queue.length }; }

  async close() {
    this.#closed = true;
    for (const j of this.#queue.splice(0)) j.reject(new Error('pool closing'));
    await Promise.all(this.#workers.map((w) => w.terminate()));
  }
}
```

```js
// worker.js
import { parentPort, workerData } from 'node:worker_threads';
if (!workerData?.id && !parentPort) throw new Error('not a worker');
parentPort.on('message', ({ buf }) => {
  // Own V8 isolate: this is genuinely parallel CPU work.
  const view = new Uint8Array(buf);
  let acc = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < view.length; i++) acc = (acc + view[i] * 31) >>> 0;
  parentPort.postMessage(acc);
});
```

*Edge cases:* a worker dying while a job is queued; `w.terminate()` rejecting the in-flight job; the sender's `ArrayBuffer` being detached after transfer; `unref()` so a pool does not keep a CLI alive; backpressure from `maxQueue` (overload → 503, not OOM); sizing with `os.availableParallelism()` in a container, never `os.cpus().length`.

*Follow-ups:* `SharedArrayBuffer` plus `Atomics.wait` for a shared counter; when to use `child_process.fork` instead (native crash isolation); the cost of a 100 µs job at ~50 µs of message overhead.

### 6. A line-delimited JSON parser as a Transform, correct across chunk boundaries

**The contract:** split on `\n`; handle records that straddle chunk boundaries; handle multi-byte UTF-8 characters split across chunks; emit parsed objects; report a parse error with the line number; never lose the final record.

```js
import { Transform } from 'node:stream';
import { StringDecoder } from 'node:string_decoder';

export function ndjson({ maxLine = 1 << 20, skipEmpty = true } = {}) {
  const decoder = new StringDecoder('utf8');   // buffers partial multi-byte sequences
  let buf = '';
  let lineNo = 0;

  return new Transform({
    readableObjectMode: true,                   // push objects, not strings
    transform(chunk, _enc, cb) {
      try {
        buf += decoder.write(chunk);
        if (buf.length > maxLine) { const e = new Error('line too long'); e.code = 'ELINETOOLONG'; return cb(e); }
        let i;
        while ((i = buf.indexOf('\n')) >= 0) {
          const raw = buf.slice(0, i);
          buf = buf.slice(i + 1);
          lineNo++;
          const line = raw.endsWith('\r') ? raw.slice(0, -1) : raw;   // CRLF
          if (skipEmpty && line.trim() === '') continue;
          try { this.push(JSON.parse(line)); }
          catch { const e = new Error(`invalid JSON on line ${lineNo}`); e.line = lineNo; return cb(e); }
        }
        cb();
      } catch (e) { cb(e); }
    },
    flush(cb) {
      // The tail: called once, at end of stream. Skipping it drops the last record.
      const rest = (buf + decoder.end()).trim();
      if (rest !== '') {
        lineNo++;
        try { this.push(JSON.parse(rest)); }
        catch { const e = new Error(`invalid JSON on line ${lineNo}`); e.line = lineNo; return cb(e); }
      }
      cb();
    },
  });
}
```

```js
// The property test that proves it, including the byte-splitting case.
import { Readable } from 'node:stream';
import { randomBytes } from 'node:crypto';

const records = Array.from({ length: 500 }, (_, i) => ({ i, s: 'héllo😀'.repeat(3), n: i * 1.5 }));
const text = records.map((r) => JSON.stringify(r)).join('\n') + '\n';
const bytes = Buffer.from(text, 'utf8');

for (const size of [1, 2, 3, 7, 64, 1024, bytes.length]) {
  const chunks = [];
  for (let o = 0; o < bytes.length; o += size) chunks.push(bytes.subarray(o, o + size));
  const got = [];
  for await (const r of Readable.from(chunks).pipe(ndjson())) got.push(r);
  console.assert(JSON.stringify(got) === JSON.stringify(records), `FAILED at chunk size ${size}`);
}
console.log('all chunk sizes reconstruct exactly');
```

*Edge cases:* a record split across every possible byte boundary (the property test above); a `\r\n` line ending; a final line with no newline; blank lines; a JSON array spread over lines (not valid NDJSON — document that); a line longer than `maxLine`; `decoder.end()` in `flush`; a `Transform` that pushes after `push(null)`.

*Follow-ups:* replacing this with `split2`; NDJSON vs a length-prefixed binary framing; validating each record with Zod inside the transform and mapping the failure to a 422 with a line number.

### 7. An `AsyncLocalStorage` request context with a correlation id and safe cleanup

**The contract:** a request id is available synchronously anywhere in the async chain; it is returned in the response header and in error bodies; it appears in every log line; it does not leak into a subsequent request on the same socket.

```js
// context.js
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from 'node:async_hooks';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

const als = new AsyncLocalStorage();
export const ctx = () => als.getStore() ?? {};
export const reqId = () => ctx().id;

export function runWithContext(store, fn) { return als.run(store, fn); }

export function requestContext({ idHeader = 'x-request-id', allowInbound = true } = {}) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    // Only accept an inbound id from a trusted proxy. Accepting it from the
    // public internet lets a client poison every log line and collide ids.
    const inbound = allowInbound && req.headers[idHeader];
    const id = (typeof inbound === 'string' && /^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{8,64}$/.test(inbound))
      ? inbound : randomUUID();
    res.setHeader('X-Request-Id', id);
    const started = process.hrtime.bigint();
    runWithContext({ id, startedAt: Date.now(), tenantId: req.headers['x-tenant-id'] ?? null },
      () => next());
  };
}

// Interop: a stream callback may run outside the ALS chain, so bind explicitly.
import { AsyncResource } from 'node:async_hooks';
export function bindEmitter<T extends { on: Function; off: Function }>(emitter: T): T {
  for (const ev of (emitter as any).eventNames?.() ?? []) {
    for (const fn of (emitter as any).listeners?.(ev) ?? []) {
      emitter.off(ev, fn);
      emitter.on(ev, AsyncResource.bind(fn));
    }
  }
  return emitter;
}
```

```js
// server.js
app.use(requestContext());
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  const start = process.hrtime.bigint();
  res.on('finish', () => {
    logger[res.statusCode >= 500 ? 'error' : res.statusCode >= 400 ? 'warn' : 'info'](
      { reqId: reqId(), method: req.method, url: req.originalUrl,
        status: res.statusCode, ms: Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1e6 },
      'request');
  });
  next();
});

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  if (res.headersSent) return next(err);
  logger.error({ reqId: reqId(), err }, 'unhandled');
  res.status(500).type('application/problem+json')
     .json({ code: 'internal_error', traceId: reqId() });
});
```

*Edge cases:* two concurrent requests on the same keep-alive socket (this is the test that matters — a module-level variable would fail it); a request id containing characters that break log parsing (the regex); `enterWith` leaking context into a later request (never use it at this boundary); a callback from a third-party emitter running outside the chain (`AsyncResource.bind` or `bindEmitter`); a worker thread, where ALS state does not cross the boundary and must be sent in the message.

*Follow-ups:* `pino-http` with `mixin` instead of hand-rolled; propagating the id to downstream services; why the id must be validated before being trusted.

### 8. An Express mini-framework: router, onion middleware, typed validation, and a single error pipeline

**The contract:** `createApp()` returns a configured app with a documented middleware order, a Zod-validated boundary, domain errors mapped once to `application/problem+json`, and an async handler wrapper — and a test proves each property.

```js
// mini.js — the pieces Express gives you, written out so you know what they do.
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';

const LAYER = Symbol('layer');

export function Router() {
  const stack = [];
  const router = (req, res, next) => {
    let idx = 0;
    const step = (err) => {
      if (err) return next(err);
      const layer = stack[idx++];
      if (!layer) return next();               // fell off the end → 404 in the app
      const m = layer.match(req);
      if (!m) return step();
      req.params = { ...req.params, ...(m.params ?? {}) };
      if (layer.arity === 4) return void layer.fn(err, req, res, step);
      const ret = layer.fn(req, res, step);
      if (ret && typeof ret.then === 'function') ret.catch(step);   // Express 5 behaviour
    };
    step();
  };
  router.stack = stack;
  router[LAYER] = true;
  const add = (method, path, ...fns) => {
    stack.push({ method, ...compile(path), fn: fns[0],
                 arity: fns[0].length, match: matcher(path) });
    return router;
  };
  router.use = (path, fn) => {
    const prefix = path === '/' ? '' : path.replace(/\/$/, '');
    stack.push({ method: null, prefix, fn, arity: fn.length,
                 match: (req) => req.url === prefix || req.url.startsWith(prefix + '/') });
    return router;
  };
  for (const m of ['get','post','put','patch','delete','all']) router[m] = (p, ...f) => add(m, p, ...f);
  return router;
}

function compile(path) {
  const keys = [];
  const rx = new RegExp('^' + path.replace(/\/:([A-Za-z_]\w*)(\([^)]*\))?/g,
    (_, k, pat) => { keys.push(k); return pat ?? '[^/]+'; }).replace(/\//g, '\\/') + '/?$');
  return { keys, rx };
}
function matcher(path) {
  const { keys, rx } = compile(path);
  return (req) => {
    const m = rx.exec(req.path);
    if (!m) return false;
    const params = {}; keys.forEach((k, i) => { params[k] = m[i + 1]; });
    return { params };
  };
}

export const ah = (fn) => (req, res, next) =>
  Promise.resolve(fn(req, res, next)).catch(next);      // the Express 4 fix
```

```js
// app.js — the whole pipeline, in the order the rules in 5.2.3 demand.
import express from 'express';
import helmet from 'helmet';
import cors from 'cors';
import { z } from 'zod';
import { HttpError, errorHandler, notFound } from './errors.js';

export function createApp(deps) {
  const app = express();
  app.disable('x-powered-by');
  app.set('trust proxy', deps.trustProxy);
  app.set('query parser', 'simple');
  app.set('etag', false);

  app.use(deps.requestId);                  // 1
  app.use(deps.logger);                     // 2
  app.use(helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: false }));  // 3 (API: nosniff + HSTS)
  app.use(cors(deps.corsOptions));          // 4 — before routes AND auth
  app.use(express.json({ limit: deps.bodyLimit, strict: true }));  // 5
  app.use('/api', deps.rateLimiter);        // 6
  app.use(deps.authenticate);               // 7
  app.use('/api', deps.apiRouter);          // 8
  app.get('/healthz', (_q, r) => r.send('ok'));
  app.use(notFound);                        // 9
  app.use(errorHandler);                    // 10
  return app;
}

export const validate = (schemas) => (req, _res, next) => {
  for (const [src, schema] of Object.entries(schemas)) {
    const r = schema.safeParse(req[src]);
    if (!r.success) {
      return next(new HttpError(422, 'validation_failed', 'Invalid request', {
        details: r.error.issues.map((i) => ({ path: '/' + i.path.join('/'), code: i.code, message: i.message })),
      }));
    }
    req[src] = r.data;                      // the PARSED value flows inward
  }
  next();
};
```

```js
// The tests that prove the order is a correctness property.
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import request from 'supertest';

const app = createApp(buildTestDeps());

test('preflight for a protected route is answered by cors, not by auth', async () => {
  const res = await request(app).options('/api/orders')
    .set('Origin', 'https://app.example.com')
    .set('Access-Control-Request-Method', 'POST');
  assert.equal(res.status, 204);
  assert.equal(res.headers['access-control-allow-origin'], 'https://app.example.com');
});

test('a rejected promise becomes a 500 problem+json, not a hang', async () => {
  const res = await request(app).get('/api/boom');
  assert.equal(res.status, 500);
  assert.equal(res.headers['content-type'].split(';')[0], 'application/problem+json');
  assert.ok(res.body.traceId);
});

test('an unknown route is JSON, never HTML', async () => {
  const res = await request(app).get('/api/nope');
  assert.equal(res.status, 404);
  assert.equal(res.headers['content-type'].split(';')[0], 'application/problem+json');
});

test('unknown body keys are rejected (no mass assignment)', async () => {
  const res = await request(app).post('/api/orders').send({ customerId: 'not-a-uuid', role: 'admin' });
  assert.equal(res.status, 422);
  assert.ok(res.body.errors.some((e) => e.code === 'unrecognized_keys'));
});
```

*Edge cases:* a 3-arity "error handler" registered by mistake; `res.headersSent` when a second send happens; a `next(err)` after the response started; `additionalProperties: false` rejecting a client that sends an extra field (mobile clients always do); a validation failure on `query` where the default was not applied; a route shadowed by a parameter route registered earlier; a rate limiter that blocks the preflight.

*Follow-ups:* what Express 5 changes here; how Fastify's encapsulation makes several of these impossible; how you would test the ordering invariants without reaching into `_router.stack`.

### 9. A graceful-shutdown coordinator with draining, a deadline, and idempotency

**The contract:** on the first `SIGTERM`, readiness flips, the listener closes, idle sockets are ended, in-flight requests are awaited up to a deadline, resources flush in order, and the process exits 0. A second signal forces exit 1.

```js
// shutdown.js
export function createShutdown({ server, resources, timeoutMs = 25_000, logger, onDraining }) {
  const sockets = new Set();
  let inFlight = 0, shuttingDown = false, done = false;

  server.on('connection', (s) => {
    sockets.add(s);
    s.once('close', () => sockets.delete(s));
    s.on('error', () => sockets.delete(s));
  });

  // The in-flight counter. Increment on entry, decrement on finish OR close —
  // an aborted request emits 'close' without 'finish', and missing that is how
  // a drain hangs forever.
  const track = (req, res, next) => {
    inFlight++;
    let counted = true;
    const done_ = () => { if (!counted) return; counted = false; inFlight--; };
    res.once('finish', done_);
    res.once('close', done_);
    next();
  };

  async function run(signal) {
    if (shuttingDown) { logger.error({ signal }, 'repeat signal, forcing exit'); process.exit(1); }
    if (done) return;
    shuttingDown = true;
    logger.info({ signal, inFlight, sockets: sockets.size }, 'draining');

    // 1. Readiness flips FIRST; liveness must stay green or we get killed mid-drain.
    onDraining?.();

    // 2. Stop accepting; end idle keep-alives immediately, they will not close on their own.
    server.close();
    for (const s of sockets) if (s.writableLength === 0) s.end();

    // 3. Deadline. unref() so the timer never holds the loop open by itself.
    const deadline = setTimeout(() => {
      logger.error({ inFlight, sockets: sockets.size }, 'drain timeout, forcing exit');
      for (const s of sockets) s.destroy();
      void flush().finally(() => process.exit(1));
    }, timeoutMs);
    deadline.unref();

    // 4. Wait for in-flight work, polling because there is no event for "count is zero".
    while (inFlight > 0) await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 25));
    for (const s of sockets) s.end();
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100));      // let the FINs flush

    clearTimeout(deadline);
    await flush();
    done = true;
    process.exit(0);
  }

  async function flush() {
    // allSettled, not all: one failing pool must not prevent the others closing.
    const results = await Promise.allSettled(resources.map((r) => r.close()));
    for (const [i, r] of results.entries())
      if (r.status === 'rejected') logger.error({ resource: resources[i].name, err: r.reason }, 'flush failed');
  }

  const install = () => {
    process.on('SIGTERM', () => { run('SIGTERM').catch((e) => { logger.fatal({ e }, 'shutdown crashed'); process.exit(1); }); });
    process.on('SIGINT',  () => { run('SIGINT').catch((e)  => { logger.fatal({ e }, 'shutdown crashed'); process.exit(1); }); });
  };
  return { install, track, get inFlight() { return inFlight; }, run };
}
```

```js
// server.js — the whole wiring, with the deadline arithmetic in a comment.
const server = createApp(deps);
const shutdown = createShutdown({
  server, logger,
  // orchestrator grace 30s > code 25s > per-request 20s > socket drain 5s > flush 2s
  timeoutMs: 25_000,
  onDraining: () => { readiness.state = 'draining'; },
  resources: [
    { name: 'pg',        close: () => deps.pool.end() },
    { name: 'queue',     close: () => deps.queue.close() },
    { name: 'producer',  close: () => deps.producer.flush().then(() => deps.producer.disconnect()) },
    { name: 'tracing',   close: () => deps.tracer.shutdown() },
  ],
});
app.use(shutdown.track);            // register the counter middleware
server.listen(env.PORT, env.HOST);
shutdown.install();
```

*Edge cases:* a request that aborts (`close` without `finish`); a keep-alive socket that never closes; a resource whose `close()` hangs (the deadline covers it); a second `SIGTERM` (must force exit); `readiness` flipping but the proxy not noticing in time; a request arriving *after* `server.close()` (it should not, but a `Connection: keep-alive` race can); stdout writes truncated by `process.exit` (use `pino.final`).

*Follow-ups:* why liveness must stay green during a drain; what `Connection: close` + `Retry-After` tells a client using WebSockets; how to make this testable (`kill -TERM` under a load test, and assert the drain duration).

### 10. A leak detector: bounded-cache + listener-count assertions, proven by a create/destroy loop

**The contract:** a bounded LRU cache, a listener-count assertion helper, and a test that runs 10,000 create/destroy cycles, forces GC, and asserts the heap returns to baseline.

```js
// lru.js — a bounded cache is the difference between a cache and a leak.
export class LRU {
  #map = new Map();
  constructor(readonly max = 1000) { if (max < 1) throw new RangeError('max must be >= 1'); }

  get(key) {
    if (!this.#map.has(key)) return undefined;
    const v = this.#map.get(key);
    this.#map.delete(key); this.#map.set(key, v);   // reinsert = most-recently-used
    return v;
  }

  set(key, value) {
    if (this.#map.has(key)) this.#map.delete(key);
    this.#map.set(key, value);
    while (this.#map.size > this.max) this.#map.delete(this.#map.keys().next().value);
    return this;
  }

  get size() { return this.#map.size; }
  clear() { this.#map.clear(); }
}
```

```js
// leak-assert.js — the test that catches 5.1.12's shapes in CI.
import { getEventListeners } from 'node:events';
import { getHeapStatistics } from 'node:v8';

export function assertNoListenerLeak(emitter, event, baseline = 0) {
  const n = getEventListeners(emitter, event).length;
  if (n !== baseline) {
    throw new Error(`listener leak on "${event}": expected ${baseline}, found ${n}`);
  }
}

/** Runs a create/destroy cycle and asserts the heap returns to baseline. */
export async function assertNoHeapGrowth(make, destroy, { cycles = 2_000, tolerance = 0.15 } = {}) {
  global.gc();                                       // requires --expose-gc
  const before = getHeapStatistics().used_heap_size;
  for (let i = 0; i < cycles; i++) await destroy(await make(i));
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { global.gc(); await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50)); }
  const after = getHeapStatistics().used_heap_size;
  const growth = (after - before) / before;
  if (growth > tolerance) {
    throw new Error(`possible heap leak: +${(growth * 100).toFixed(1)}% over ${cycles} cycles ` +
                    `(${Math.round(before / 1e6)}MB → ${Math.round(after / 1e6)}MB)`);
  }
  return { before, after, growth };
}
```

```js
// leak.test.js — run with: node --expose-gc --test leak.test.js
import test from 'node:test';
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';
import { connections, openConnections } from './src/conn-mgr.js';

test('disconnecting removes every listener', async () => {
  const bus = new EventEmitter();
  await assertNoHeapGrowth(
    async () => {                       // make: simulate a WebSocket connection
      const h = () => {};
      bus.on('message', h); bus.on('close', h);
      return { h, off: () => { bus.off('message', h); bus.off('close', h); } };
    },
    async (c) => c.off(),               // destroy: disconnect
    { cycles: 5_000 },
  );
  assertNoListenerLeak(bus, 'message', 0);
  assertNoListenerLeak(bus, 'close', 0);
  assert.equal(openConnections(), 0);
});
```

*Edge cases:* a handler that throws in the destroy path (use try/finally in the harness or the loop stops early and the assertion is meaningless); a cache whose `max` is larger than the working set (no eviction pressure, so a leak would be missed); a Map keyed by objects (retains the key graph); `global.gc()` not being available (skip the test rather than failing); GC not being deterministic across Node versions (tolerance, and 3 forced GCs with pauses); a leak in *external* memory (Buffers), which this test will not catch — for that, assert on `process.memoryUsage().external`.

*Follow-ups:* the production version of the same check (a periodic `listenerCount` sweep, 5.1.10); a heap-snapshot-based test in CI; why a "leak" in a *bounded* cache is a working-as-designed eviction policy.
