# 6.30 Rapid-Fire
Advanced · **Must-know**

| # | Question | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is partition tolerance optional? | No; partitions are routine, so every distributed system is P |
| 2 | What do you actually choose under CAP? | Behaviour per operation during a partition, and the freshness/availability trade |
| 3 | PACELC adds what? | Latency vs consistency in the *healthy* case, which is where you live 99.9% of the time |
| 4 | Linearizable read costs? | A leader or quorum round trip, and 2x the RCU in DynamoDB |
| 5 | Linearizable reads allowed in a MongoDB transaction? | No |
| 6 | What is "eventual" without a bound? | Meaningless; state a convergence SLO and monitor it |
| 7 | Phi accrual detector? | Reports a suspicion level from the distribution of heartbeat intervals |
| 8 | Why must a lease be fenced? | A failure detector can be wrong; a paused client can act after its lease expired |
| 9 | Redlock's known weakness? | Process pauses between acquire and act, so a stale holder can still write |
| 10 | Lock release must check what? | The token, in one atomic Lua call, in a `finally` |
| 11 | `MULTI/EXEC` is ACID? | No; no rollback, no isolation, only no interleaving |
| 12 | `KEYS *` alternative? | `SCAN` with `COUNT`, plus `SSCAN`/`HSCAN`/`ZSCAN` |
| 13 | `MOVED` vs `ASK`? | Permanent relocation vs in-progress migration; never cache `ASK` |
| 14 | `CROSSSLOT` fix? | Hash tags so the keys share a slot: `{user:42}:a` and `{user:42}:b` |
| 15 | `maxmemory-policy` for a limiter? | `noeviction`, so keys are never silently dropped |
| 16 | Why separate limiter and cache instances? | Eviction and growth in one would corrupt the other |
| 17 | RDB vs AOF `everysec`? | Snapshot loses everything since it; AOF loses about a second |
| 18 | `WAIT n timeout`? | Turns async replication into a tunable quorum at the cost of latency |
| 19 | Redis value size guidance? | Keep small; put bulk in object storage |
| 20 | Cache-aside's weakness? | A miss storm on expiry, so add jitter, single-flight, and SWR |
| 21 | TTL jitter size? | About ±20% |
| 22 | Write-around for? | Data unlikely to be re-read, to avoid polluting the cache |
| 23 | Write-back's risk? | Data loss if the process dies before the flush |
| 24 | Pub/Sub as invalidation? | Fire-and-forget; fine as an optimization on top of a TTL, never alone |
| 25 | Fixed window's flaw? | 2x the limit across a boundary; two requests in the same millisecond |
| 26 | Sliding log's cost? | One zset entry per request in the window |
| 27 | Sliding log member id must be unique? | Yes, or same-millisecond writes overwrite each other |
| 28 | Sliding window counter estimate? | `current + previous * (1 - fractionElapsed)` |
| 29 | Token bucket's burst size? | The capacity |
| 30 | Leaky bucket protects what a token bucket does not? | A downstream that cannot absorb bursts at all |
| 31 | Redis Lua float gotcha? | Lua numbers truncate to integers in replies; return `tostring` |
| 32 | Pass the clock in from the app? | Yes, so you control skew and can test |
| 33 | DynamoDB `Query` requires? | An equality on the partition key |
| 34 | `Scan` cost with a filter? | Unchanged: the filter runs after the read |
| 35 | Hot partition hard limit? | 1,000 WCU and 1,000 RCU per second per partition |
| 36 | Unique index rule when sharded? | It must be prefixed by the shard key |
| 37 | LSI vs GSI on consistency? | Both eventually consistent reads only |
| 38 | Sparse GSI purpose? | Keep a GSI containing only the entities that belong in it |
| 39 | `ConsistentRead: false` right after a write? | Can return nothing for that key; retry |
| 40 | Strongly consistent DynamoDB read cost? | 2x the read capacity units |
| 41 | Idempotent DynamoDB write? | A unique idempotency key attribute plus a condition on it |
| 42 | DAX does not do what? | Strongly consistent reads, and it does not speed up writes |
| 43 | Cassandra clustering prefix rule? | Range predicates must follow the clustering order |
| 44 | `ALLOW FILTERING` cost? | Reads and buffers the entire partition |
| 45 | `QUORUM` for N=5? | 3 |
| 46 | The anti-entropy rule? | `R + W > N` |
| 47 | `W > N/2` prevents? | Acknowledged writes that can be "unwritten" by a stale coordinator |
| 48 | `gc_grace` default? | 10 days; bounds hinted handoff and tombstone retention |
| 49 | LWT cost and limit? | About two round trips, and single-partition only |
| 50 | Compaction for time-series? | TWCS, with TTLs and time-windowed buckets |
| 51 | Cassandra write path order? | Client → coordinator → memtable → SSTable, with a row cache and bloom filter |
| 52 | Graph store: when? | Unbounded traversal depth plus relationships that carry data |
| 53 | Cypher traversal control? | Bound the depth, `LIMIT` early, filter inside the relationship pattern |
| 54 | Hyperedge in a property graph? | An intermediate node; edges join exactly two nodes |
| 55 | `DETACH DELETE`? | Deletes incident edges too; without it you get orphans |
| 56 | Hypertable buys you? | Automatic time chunking, compression, cheap retention drops |
| 57 | `end_offset` on a continuous aggregate? | Leaves the newest buckets raw so late data lands correctly |
| 58 | `time_bucket_gapfill`? | Fills missing buckets so an outage is not drawn as zero |
| 59 | Prometheus series definition? | A unique label set; memory scales with the count |
| 60 | Five illegal labels? | `user_id`, `request_id`, `trace_id`, `error_message`, a URL with an id |
| 61 | Prometheus head block? | In memory/WAL, and the OOM risk; the checkpoint controls it |
| 62 | Recording rules vs downsampling? | Rules pre-aggregate cheap series; downsampling keeps long ranges affordable |
| 63 | HNSW knob? | `ef_search` (and `iterative_scan` for filtered recall), with `m` and `ef_construction` at build time |
| 64 | IVFFlat requires what at build time? | A representative dataset, so build after loading |
| 65 | pgvector operator for cosine? | `<=>` for distance, so similarity is `1 - distance` |
| 66 | Operator class must match? | Yes, or the index is silently unused |
| 67 | Quantize-then-rerank? | Cheap ANN candidate retrieval, then a precise rescore |
| 68 | Prisma client lifecycle? | One per process; the `globalThis` cache is only for dev |
| 69 | `migrate dev` vs `deploy`? | Dev creates and may reset; deploy only applies pending files |
| 70 | Prisma's biggest query-API gap? | No `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, windows, CTEs, `LATERAL`, or `DISTINCT ON` |
| 71 | Prisma transaction timeout default? | 5s, with a 2s wait for the connection |
| 72 | The transaction escape bug? | Using the global client inside the `$transaction` callback |
| 73 | `Promise.all` inside a transaction? | No parallelism; everything queues on one connection |
| 74 | Prisma's serialization-failure code? | `P2034`; raw Postgres is SQLSTATE `40001` |
| 75 | Drizzle's defining trait? | SQL-first: the schema is the SQL, and `sql` templates escape the builder |
| 76 | TypeORM's `synchronize`? | Destructive schema sync; never against real data |
| 77 | Sequelize eager-load fix? | `separate: true`, or accept the N+1 |
| 78 | Sequelize `paranoid`? | Soft deletes by default |
| 79 | Mongoose `.lean()`? | Plain objects, no hydration, no getters, no middleware |
| 80 | Mongoose `populate` cost? | A second query per path, one per array in the worst case |
| 81 | Mongoose middleware gap? | `updateMany`/`deleteMany` do not fire document hooks |
| 82 | DataLoader scope? | Request-scoped; a module-level instance caches across users |
| 83 | DataLoader dispatch primitive? | A microtask after the current synchronous block |
| 84 | Elasticsearch NRT? | Refresh interval, default 1s; use `refresh=wait_for` for read-your-writes |
| 85 | `_source` vs doc values? | Original JSON vs a columnar on-disk copy for sort/aggregation |
| 86 | Doc values on a `text` field? | Not available |
| 87 | `dynamic: strict`? | Rejects unmapped fields; the correct default for a typed index |
| 88 | Mapping explosion fix? | `dynamic` templates, `flattened`, or an index per entity type |
| 89 | `ignore_above` gotcha? | Longer values are not indexed but stay in `_source`, silently breaking aggregations |
| 90 | Deep pagination recipe? | A PIT plus `search_after` with a unique sort tuple |
| 91 | `doc_count_error_upper_bound`? | The terms-agg shard skew bound; check it before trusting a facet |
| 92 | ILM phases? | hot, warm, cold, frozen, delete, with rollover/shrink/forcemerge actions |
| 93 | BM25 `k1` and `b`? | Term-frequency saturation and length normalisation |
| 94 | Filters belong in `filter` because? | No scoring and cacheable |
| 95 | Postgres FTS when? | A few million docs, filters, and transactional data in one place |
| 96 | Fact grain? | One sentence; "one row per order line per day" |
| 97 | SCD type 2? | New row with validity dates, so history is preserved |
| 98 | Why partition a fact table by date? | Pruning, cheap retention, small working set |
| 99 | ETL vs ELT? | Land raw, transform in the warehouse: cheaper compute, keeps raw |
| 100 | Exactly once? | At-least-once plus an idempotent sink, achieved by dedupe or merge |
| 101 | Event time vs processing time? | Event time, with a watermark and an allowed lateness |
| 102 | Backfill rule? | Idempotent, resumable, through the same code path as the incremental load |
| 103 | Multipart upload leak? | Aborted uploads are billed forever; add a lifecycle abort rule |
| 104 | Multipart ETag? | Not the MD5 of the object |
| 105 | Presigned URL risk? | A bearer credential; constrain the key prefix per user |
| 106 | Object store rename? | None; it is copy plus delete, and it is not atomic |
| 107 | Exclusion constraint for no-overlap? | `EXCLUDE USING gist (resource WITH =, tstzrange(a, b, '[)') WITH &&)` |
| 108 | Why `[)`? | Half-open intervals: adjacent bookings do not overlap |
| 109 | Prerequisite for a scalar in a GiST exclusion? | `CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist` |
| 110 | Add an exclusion constraint safely on a big table? | `NOT VALID`, then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` |
| 111 | Booking with 10 identical seats? | A counter with `WHERE available >= n` and `RETURNING`, not intervals |
| 112 | Confirming an expired hold? | A conditional update on `status = 'held' AND hold_expires_at > now()`; 0 rows means refund |
| 113 | Fan-out on write vs read? | Push for the following feed; pull for large fan-out authors |
| 114 | Follow-graph read? | A join table with a composite PK plus a reverse index; a recursive CTE for depth |
| 115 | Multi-tenant: leading index column? | `tenant_id`, always |
| 116 | Multi-tenant safety net? | Row-level security, `FORCE`d, with `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id` per transaction |
| 117 | Schema-per-tenant limit? | Migration cost grows with N; connection and catalogue overhead |
| 118 | Database-per-tenant limit? | N pools, N backups, N restores, N migration states |
| 119 | Audit capture: trigger vs CDC? | Complete and synchronous vs decoupled and eventually complete |
| 120 | Tamper-evident audit? | A hash chain with the head stored outside the database |
| 121 | A failed idempotency key? | Store the key with the result and return the stored result, never re-execute |
| 122 | Distributed tracing id as a store? | Yes: it makes "which request caused this write" answerable |

# PHASE 7, PART 1: Network Protocols and the Request Lifecycle

> This part treats the network as a *stack of contracts*. Every layer below HTTP/2 is a protocol with its own state machine, its own failure modes, and its own diagnostic tool. The goal is not to memorise header names; it is to be able to point at a symptom and name the layer that produced it.

---

# 7.1 The Full Request Lifecycle
Advanced · **Must-know**

**Definition:** The complete, ordered sequence of machine work that turns a URL in an address bar into rendered pixels, and back again into a response body, with a measurable amount of time spent at each stage.

**Why interviewers ask:** It is the single best "system thinking" question. A candidate who can say "where does the 400ms go" and then defend the answer with `curl -v`, `dig`, and DevTools timing rows is demonstrating operational maturity, not trivia.

**The chain, and the tool that reveals each hop**

| # | Hop | What actually happens | Tool that reveals it | Typical cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | URL parse + navigation | scheme/host/port/path/query/fragment; HSTS and preload checks; browser cache + service worker interception | DevTools Network, `Application` panel | 0–1 ms |
| 2 | DNS resolution | browser cache → OS cache/resolver → hosts file → recursive resolver → root → TLD → authoritative | `dig`, `nslookup`, DevTools "DNS Lookup", `getent hosts` | 0 ms cached, 1–80 ms cold |
| 3 | Routing decision | longest-prefix match on the local routing table, ARP/NDP for the next hop | `ip route`, `traceroute`, `tracepath` | sub-ms locally, 10–40 ms cross-region |
| 4 | TCP/QUIC handshake | SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK, or QUIC Initial with embedded TLS | `ss -tan`, `tcpdump`, Wireshark, `curl -v` | 1 RTT (TCP), 1 RTT (QUIC 1-RTT) |
| 5 | TLS handshake | ClientHello (SNI, ALPN) → ServerHello → cert chain → key exchange → Finished | `openssl s_client`, `curl -v`, Wireshark | 1 RTT (TLS 1.3), 2 RTT (TLS 1.2 ECDHE) |
| 6 | Request sent | HTTP request line + headers + optional body | `curl -v`, server access logs, Wireshark | 1 RTT |
| 7 | CDN / edge | cache lookup, POP selection, TLS termination, WAF, geo rules | `curl -I` + `x-cache`/`cf-cache-status`, `dig` for anycast | 0–20 ms if hit |
| 8 | Load balancer | L4 or L7 decision, health-check filtering, connection reuse | LB metrics, `nginx -T`, HAProxy stats page | 0–5 ms |
| 9 | Reverse proxy | re-terminate TLS, rewrite path, add `X-Forwarded-*`, buffer, compress, cache | access logs with `$request_time`, `$upstream_response_time` | 1–3 ms |
| 10 | Application server | routing, middleware, auth, business logic | app logs / APM traces | 5–500 ms |
| 11 | Database / cache | query planning, execution, lock waits, connection acquisition | `pg_stat_statements`, slow query log, `EXPLAIN` | 1–2000 ms |
| 12 | Response | status line, headers, body streamed back, connection kept alive | `curl -w` timing breakdown, DevTools "Content Download" | bandwidth-bound |
| 13 | Parse + render | HTML → DOM, CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite, then subresources | DevTools Performance panel, `PerformanceObserver` | 100–3000 ms |

**ASCII walkthrough of a cold HTTPS GET**

```
 client                     resolver            edge/LB          app            db
   |                            |                   |              |             |
   |--1. dig example.com A--->  |                   |              |             |
   |      (if no cache)         |--2. root -------> |              |             |
   |                            |--3. .com NS -----> |              |             |
   |                            |--4. auth NS ----> |              |             |
   |<--5. A 203.0.113.10, ttl 60|                   |              |             |
   |                            |                   |              |             |
   |---6. SYN ----------------> |                   |              |             |
   |<--7. SYN-ACK ------------- |                   |              |             |
   |---8. ACK ----------------> |                   |              |             |
   |---9. ClientHello(SNI,ALPN)->|                   |              |             |
   |<--10. ServerHello+cert+key |                   |              |             |
   |---11. Finished ----------->|                   |              |             |
   |                            |                   |              |             |
   |--12. GET / HTTP/2 :authority: example.com ------>|              |             |
   |                            |                   |--13. GET --> |             |
   |                            |                   |              |--14. SELECT->|
   |                            |                   |              |<--15. row --|
   |                            |                   |<--16. 200 ---|             |
   |<--17. HEADERS + DATA ------|                   |              |             |
   |                            |                   |              |             |
   |== 18. parse HTML, fetch CSS/JS/images, reuse the same connection ==|
```

**Where latency accumulates — the mental model**

Think of the cold path as a sum of *round trips* plus *serialised work*:

```
cold_cost = DNS(0-1 RTT) + TCP(1 RTT) + TLS(1-2 RTT) + request/response(1 RTT)
            + edge_processing + proxy_processing + app_processing + db_round_trips
            + transfer_time(bytes / effective_bandwidth)

warm_cost = 1 RTT per HTTP/2 stream-set, no DNS, no handshake
```

Rules of thumb that show seniority:
- **Round trips dominate over bytes** on the cold path. A tiny 2 KB response over a 400 ms handshake is slow because of the *handshake*, not the payload.
- **Serialisation dominates on the warm path.** Waterfall charts are the enemy: JS that must load before it can call an API that must load before it can render data costs 3 serialised RTTs.
- **DB round trips multiply.** Ten sequential `await`s on the database is the most common cause of a 300 ms TTFB in a "fast" app.
- **Redirects, middleware, and proxies each add a hop.** A 301 to add a trailing slash costs a full extra connection setup if it crosses an origin.

**Timing fields you must be able to read cold**

| Field | Meaning | Why it lies to you |
|---|---|---|
| DevTools "Stalled" | queueing/blocking on an already-used connection, or priority | large values on HTTP/2 mean client-side contention or proxy coalescing |
| "DNS Lookup" | resolver time | 0 ms means cached, not "instant DNS" |
| "Initial connection" | TCP + TLS for a new socket | if the request is the first on a connection, this also includes queued time |
| "SSL" | TLS handshake only (HTTP/1.1); folded into "Initial connection" in some views | 0 ms on a reused connection |
| "Request sent" | write of request headers/body | large = big headers, cookies, or a slow uplink |
| "Waiting (TTFB)" | first byte of response headers | server think time: app + db + proxy |
| "Content Download" | remaining body bytes | bandwidth and compression |
| `curl` `%{time_namelookup}` | DNS | — |
| `curl` `%{time_connect}` | TCP done | subtract namelookup for pure TCP |
| `curl` `%{time_appconnect}` | TLS done | subtract connect for pure TLS |
| `curl` `%{time_pretransfer}` | request ready to send | — |
| `curl` `%{time_starttransfer}` | first byte | subtract pretransfer for TTFB |
| Nginx `$request_time` | whole request at the edge | — |
| Nginx `$upstream_response_time` | upstream first byte | `-` means the request never reached upstream; multiple values mean a retry |

**Header provenance: who sets what, and who may lie**

```
browser ──Host/:authority──> edge ──X-Forwarded-For: <client>──> proxy ──> app
   │                                                              │
   └──Authorization, Cookie, User-Agent, Accept-Encoding          └──(adds X-Request-ID,
                                                                     X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-Proto)
```

- `Host` / `:authority` is **client-controlled input** and is used for virtual hosting and, if you build absolute URLs, for the `Location` header. Never use it to build file paths or redirect targets without validation.
- `X-Forwarded-For` is **append-only by convention** and trivially spoofable: a client can send `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4` and any proxy that appends produces `1.2.3.4, <real-ip>`. Trust the **right-most** entry that came from a proxy you control, or explicitly set `X-Real-IP` at the edge and overwrite (not append) on ingress.
- `Authorization` and `Cookie` cross every hop; they are the reason a leaked access log is a credential leak. Redact them.
- `Accept-Encoding` is a *hint*. If the server ignores it and sends identity, the client just gets a bigger body; the reverse is a bug.

**Questions**
1. Walk me through `GET https://api.example.com/v1/orders?status=open` from Enter key to first byte of JSON. *(model answer below)*
2. Which of the ten stages can you measure server-side versus client-side only, and why does that matter for attribution?
3. TTFB is 800 ms. Enumerate, in order of likelihood at a typical startup, the causes and how you'd eliminate each one.
4. Why does a 301 redirect cost more than an internal rewrite, and what is the exact extra cost?
5. What is `curl -w` and which format variables would you use to attribute 40 ms to DNS, 60 ms to TLS, and 700 ms to the app?
6. Read this DevTools row and explain every number: `Stalled 12ms, DNS 0ms, Initial connection 143ms, SSL 118ms, Request sent 1ms, Waiting 61ms, Content Download 4ms`.
7. When an `upstream_response_time` field contains `-`, what does that tell you, and what are the other common values you'll see there?
8. Why can adding a CDN make TTFB *look* worse on your origin dashboards while making the user experience better?
9. Explain connection coalescing: which requests share a socket, what the client keys on, and when it silently doubles your server connections.
10. Describe the difference between "the browser waited" and "the server was slow" for a given TTFB, and name the tools that distinguish them.
11. What does `Connection: keep-alive` do in HTTP/1.1, and why was it made the default?
12. A request succeeds from your laptop and fails from a corporate network. Which stage is most likely different, and what single command would you run to check?
13. Why does a service worker change the meaning of "TTFB" entirely, and what should you measure instead?
14. Rank these by how often they are the true root cause of a slow first load: TLS cost, DNS, TCP handshake, server work, serialised waterfalls, and uncompressed assets. Defend your ranking.

**Model answer, Q1 (3-minute version):**
> "I'll go hop by hop. First the browser parses the URL — scheme, host, default port 443, path, query — and checks its own caches: the HTTP cache, HSTS, and any service worker, because a service worker can answer without a network request at all. Then it needs an address, so it resolves `api.example.com`: browser cache, then OS resolver, then a recursive resolver, which if it has no cached answer walks root to the `.com` TLD nameservers to the authoritative servers and gets an A record with a TTL. I can confirm that part with `dig +noall +answer +stats api.example.com`, where the Query time is the authoritative lookup and the first line's Query time is the recursive lookup.
>
> With an IP, the next question is how bytes get there. The kernel matches the destination against its routing table by longest prefix; I can see that with `ip route get 203.0.113.10`. Then the browser opens a TCP connection — a SYN, a SYN-ACK, an ACK, one round trip. `ss -tan state syn-recv` on the server will show it if connections are piling up.
>
> Next, TLS. The client sends a ClientHello carrying the TLS versions it supports, a list of cipher suites, the SNI hostname, the ALPN list — usually `h2,http/1.1` — and in TLS 1.3, a `key_share` for the group it wants to use. The server replies with its own choice of version, cipher, a key share, and its certificate chain. The client validates that chain against its trust store, checks the hostname against the certificate's SANs, checks validity dates, and derives handshake traffic keys. I verify all of that with `openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -alpn h2`, which prints the negotiated protocol, cipher, `Verify return code: 0 (ok)`, the chain, and the stapled OCSP response.
>
> Then the request itself. If ALPN gave us `h2`, the browser opens a stream and sends HEADERS with the pseudo-header `:authority: api.example.com` plus `:method`, `:path`, `:scheme`, and regular headers like `Authorization` and `Accept-Encoding: br, gzip`. That write is the first half of a round trip.
>
> Server side: the request lands on a CDN edge point or a load balancer. If it's a CDN, there's a cache lookup keyed by method, host, path, query, and the `Vary` headers; a hit returns in single-digit milliseconds and never reaches me. On a miss, a load balancer picks a backend by its algorithm after excluding unhealthy targets, and a reverse proxy terminates TLS, adds `X-Forwarded-For`, and forwards to the app server. The app does auth, then hits the database. The single most common cause of a large TTFB is a handful of sequential DB round trips plus an unindexed query, not framework overhead.
>
> The response goes back the same way: status, headers, then the body, possibly gzipped or brotli-compressed because I sent `Accept-Encoding`. The browser decompresses, parses the JSON, and the app renders. If this is the very first request on this connection, the total is roughly DNS plus one RTT for TCP, one to two for TLS, one for the request, and then server think time and transfer. If the connection is warm, all of the first part collapses to zero and TTFB is just the server.
>
> The one thing I'd add is: at every one of those stages there's a different tool, and the discipline is to never guess. DNS with `dig`, transport with `tcpdump` or `ss`, TLS with `openssl s_client`, server with `$request_time` and `$upstream_response_time`, and the client view with the DevTools waterfall. The most common interview mistake is describing this flow without naming the measurement for each step."

**Model answer, Q11 (senior framing: Context → Decision → Reasoning → Trade-offs → Failure scenario → Alternative):**
> "Context: the browser opens one connection and would rather not open another, because a new connection costs DNS (maybe cached), a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, and a fresh congestion window starting at ten packets. On a page with sixty assets, sixty separate connections is sixty handshakes.
>
> Decision: in HTTP/1.1, persistent connections are the default; every request is `Host`-scoped on a single TCP connection, sent one at a time in order, and the connection is closed only when both sides agree, the client closes, or an idle timeout fires. In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 the connection is multiplexed, so reuse is structural rather than negotiated.
>
> Reasoning: the cost model is bytes-per-round-trip. Reuse amortises three to four round trips across every subsequent request, and it also avoids re-growing the congestion window and re-doing TLS work.
>
> Trade-offs: keep-alive holds server resources. A thousand idle sockets is a thousand file descriptors and a thousand state machines in `CLOSE_WAIT` if the client leaks them. So you tune `keepalive_timeout` low — 5 to 15 seconds is typical for proxies — and you set `keepalive_requests` to recycle connections after a few thousand requests so memory and any state you attached get reclaimed. There's also a security angle: connection-level state such as TLS tickets or HTTP/2 stream state is only as isolated as your connection teardown.
>
> Failure scenario: a rolling deploy where old pods are kept alive by long-lived keep-alive connections. Clients keep talking to a version you're about to kill, in-flight requests die at the drain deadline, and you get a spike of `502`s. The fix is coordinated drain: LB marks the target unhealthy, sends `Connection: close` on in-flight responses, and the server stops accepting new connections, waits for existing ones to finish, then exits.
>
> Alternative: if the handshake is the real cost, don't negotiate reuse, remove it. HTTP/3 with 0-RTT resumption, or connection preconnect from the browser, or just fewer requests — bundling and inlining beat any keep-alive tuning."

**Mistakes:** describing "the server" as one machine; saying DNS happens once per request; treating TLS as part of "connecting"; assuming a cached DNS lookup is 0 cost in aggregate; quoting TTFB without saying whether the connection was warm; assuming a `502` means the app crashed; forgetting that redirects and preflights show up as separate rows in the waterfall.

**Mini task:** Pick any site you use daily. In DevTools Network, disable cache, hard-reload, and record `DNS Lookup`, `Initial connection`, `SSL`, `Waiting`, and `Content Download` for the document. Then reproduce the same request with `curl -v -o /dev/null -w` and all the `time_*` variables, and reconcile the two number sets line by line in a short table. Finally, `dig` the hostname with `+stats` and explain the Query time and TTL you see. Write down which of the three sources disagreed and why.

## 7.1.1 Reading `curl -v` and `dig` Like a Second Language
Advanced · **Must-know**

**`curl -v` line-by-line**

```
$ curl -v --http2 https://api.example.com/v1/orders?status=open -o /dev/null
*   Trying 203.0.113.10:443...
* Connected to api.example.com (203.0.113.10) port 443 (#0)
* ALPN: server accepted h2
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Certificate (IN):
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, CertificateRequest (IN):
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, CertificateVerify (IN):
* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Finished (IN):
* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, ClientHello (OUT):
* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Finished (OUT):
* using HTTP/2
* h2h3 [:method: GET] [:scheme: https] [:authority: api.example.com] [:path: /v1/orders?status=open]
* h2h3 [:authority: api.example.com] user-agent: curl/8.5.0
* h2h3 [:method: GET] [:scheme: https] [:path: /v1/orders?status=open]
> GET /v1/orders?status=open HTTP/2
> host: api.example.com
> user-agent: curl/8.5.0
> accept: */*
>
< HTTP/2 200
< content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
< cache-control: private, no-store
< x-request-id: 01JB2Q7W3K9F
<
* Request completely sent off
{ [5 bytes data]
* Connection #0 to host api.example.com left intact
```

Reading it:
- `*` lines are curl's commentary. `Trying`, `Connected to`, `ALPN:`, the TLS handshake names, `using HTTP/2`, and the `h2h3` pseudo-header echoes are all diagnostics.
- `>` lines are what curl **sent**. `>` does not mean "upstream" in any other context, which trips people up when reading proxy logs.
- `<` lines are what curl **received**.
- `* Request completely sent off` confirms the request body left the client. If a `POST` hangs here, the failure is in sending, not waiting.
- `* Connection #0 to host ... left intact` means keep-alive succeeded. `Connection #0 to host ... closed` means the server closed it — a frequent cause of mysterious retries.
- With `--http3` you additionally get `* Connected to ... (3)`, QUIC version reporting, and sometimes `Alt-Svc` behaviour where curl deliberately uses a cached alternative endpoint.
- `--resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.10` pins DNS so you can test one edge while everything else stays identical. `--connect-to` and `--interface` are the next level up.

Flags that change what you learn:
- `-I` / `--head` — HEAD only; fastest way to inspect response headers and cache directives.
- `--http1.1` / `--http2` / `--http3` — force a version. Comparing the same request across the three isolates protocol overhead from server time.
- `-w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_appconnect} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total} %{http_version} %{ssl_verify_result}\n'` — machine-readable timing.
- `--trace-time --trace-ascii -` — full hex/ascii of headers, useful when a header contains characters that `curl` normalises away.
- `--compressed` — adds `Accept-Encoding` and transparently decodes, so your byte counts match what a browser would see.
- `--cert` / `--cacert` / `--insecure` — client certs and custom trust. `--insecure` disables verification and is for debugging only; never ship it.

**`dig` line-by-line**

```
$ dig +noall +answer +stats api.example.com
api.example.com.        60      IN      A       203.0.113.10

;; Query time: 24 msec
;; SERVER: 10.0.0.53#53(10.0.0.53)  (UDP)
;; WHEN: Tue Oct 01 09:14:02 UTC 2026
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 57
```

- `+noall +answer` gives only the answer section, which is what you want in scripts.
- `+stats` shows the resolver you actually used and the round trip. The `SERVER:` line tells you whether you hit your ISP resolver, a local caching resolver, or `127.0.0.53` (systemd-resolved).
- `MSG SIZE rcvd: 57` lets you detect truncation. If you see `rcvd: 512` and a `TC` flag in the header, you must retry over TCP — `dig +tcp`.
- `+trace` walks the delegation from the root. It is the tool for "why is my zone broken".
- `+noall +answer +authority` distinguishes an **authoritative NXDOMAIN** (a real "no such name", from your own zone) from an empty NOERROR with no answer (the name exists but has no record of that type). This distinction matters enormously in deployments.
- `@1.1.1.1` forces a specific resolver; `+short` gives you just the answer for scripting.

Useful invocations:
```
dig +short A     api.example.com            # just the address
dig +short AAAA  api.example.com            # IPv6, empty means no v6
dig +short CNAME www.example.com            # alias target
dig +trace example.com                      # delegation path from root
dig +tcp +dnssec example.com                # force TCP, request DNSSEC records
dig @8.8.8.8 +noall +answer example.com     # bypass local resolver
dig -x 203.0.113.10                         # reverse lookup
dig +noall +comments SOA example.com        # zone serial, refresh, retry, expire
```

**Questions**
1. In the `curl -v` sample above, what is the difference between the `h2h3` echo lines and the `>`/`<` header lines, and why do both exist?
2. `curl` reports `ALPN: server accepted h2`. What would `ALPN: curl offers h2,http/1.1` tell you, and what should you do?
3. You see `Connection #0 to host api.example.com closed`. List four causes in order of likelihood.
4. `dig` returns `status: NOERROR` with zero answer records. Is the domain down? Why does this happen, and what's the deploy implication?
5. What does `MSG SIZE rcvd: 512` hint at, and what's the fix?
6. `+trace` shows the root referring to TLD servers, but the TLD servers return nothing for your zone. Whose problem is it, and what do you change?
7. How would you use `--resolve` to prove that a DNS problem, rather than the origin, is causing an outage?
8. Why does `time_appconnect` minus `time_connect` isolate TLS, and what would a negative or absurd value tell you?
9. Compare and contrast `nslookup` and `dig`. When would you still reach for `nslookup`?
10. Explain `ssl_verify_result` in curl's `-w` output and how it maps to a certificate problem.

**Model answer, Q4:** "No, an empty NOERROR is not the same as NXDOMAIN, and that distinction is the whole point. NOERROR with an empty answer section means the resolver successfully reached an authoritative server for the zone and was told the name exists as a name but has no record of the type I asked for — for example I asked for AAAA and the zone has only A records, or the CNAME target exists but the name itself has no A. NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist at all. A resolver that has a cached negative answer will repeat that empty NOERROR for the SOA's negative-caching TTL, which is why a half-finished deploy where you created the zone but not yet the A record produces a hard failure that persists for minutes. The deploy implication is real: if your target record doesn't exist yet, you must publish it *before* you point the alias at it, and you should verify with `dig +noall +answer` rather than trusting a health check that only tests a hostname which happens to resolve elsewhere."

**Mistakes:** treating `*` lines in `curl -v` as server output; forgetting curl prints `> <` for HTTP/1.1 and pseudo-header echoes for HTTP/2; assuming `dig` failure means DNS is down (it may be a record-type issue); not knowing that `dig` can silently use a different resolver than your browser; using `--insecure` and then believing the result.

**Mini task:** Run `curl -v --http1.1` and `curl -v --http2` against the same HTTPS endpoint and diff the output. Find the exact lines that prove which protocol was used. Then run `dig +trace` for a domain you own or one you can query, and mark each delegation step and its glue. Add `+nocookie` to see how the answer changes when your local resolver holds a negative answer.

## 7.1.2 The Hop-by-Hop Diagnostic Checklist
Advanced · **Nice-to-have**

A disciplined order of operations. Do these in sequence; each is cheap and rules out a layer.

```
1. Is it DNS?          dig +short <host>            (from the client network AND from the server network)
2. Is it the edge?      curl -sI https://<host> | grep -Ei 'server|via|x-cache|cf-|age|alt-svc'
3. Is it TLS?           openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -servername <host> </dev/null
4. Is it routing?       traceroute -T -p 443 <host>        (TCP mode, so ICMP rate limits don't lie)
5. Is it TCP state?     ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l    (on the server)
6. Is it the proxy?     nginx -T | grep -n 'proxy_pass'
7. Is it the app?       look at $request_time vs $upstream_response_time
8. Is it the DB?        pg_stat_statements, slow query log, EXPLAIN ANALYZE
9. Is it the client?    DevTools waterfall, HAR file, throttling profile
```

Two rules that separate experienced from inexperienced debugging:
- **Reproduce from two vantage points.** An outage that only affects one network is almost always a path problem (DNS, routing, MTU, middlebox) rather than an application problem.
- **Change one variable at a time.** `curl --resolve` to move DNS, `curl --http1.1` to change protocol, `curl -H 'Host: ...'` to change vhost, `--interface` to change egress. If you change three things you learn nothing.

**Questions**
1. Why is `traceroute -T -p 443` often more informative than the default ICMP traceroute?
2. You can reach the origin IP directly with `curl --resolve` but the hostname fails. What are the three most likely causes, ordered?
3. `ss -tan` shows 40,000 sockets in `TIME_WAIT`. What is the immediate symptom and what are two structurally different fixes?
4. You have `$request_time: 2.500` and `$upstream_response_time: 0.010`. Where is the time going?
5. You have `$request_time: 0.010` and `$upstream_response_time: 2.400`. What does that combination say about your instrumentation, and how do you fix it?
6. `$upstream_response_time: 0.030, 0.900` — what just happened in your upstream block, and what should you do about it?

**Model answer, Q3:** "The immediate symptom is usually `EADDRNOTAVAIL` or `Cannot assign requested address` on bind, or a proxy that starts refusing new connections, because the client side ran out of ephemeral ports. `TIME_WAIT` sockets are the memory of a connection that closed and must linger for two MSLs so delayed or retransmitted segments can't be mistaken for a new connection's. The two structurally different fixes are: reduce the rate at which you create short-lived connections — keep-alive, connection pooling, HTTP/2 multiplexing, so you make far fewer connections in the first place — or make your sockets reusable and your state smaller, which means `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1`, raising the ephemeral port range, and using `SO_REUSEPORT` so multiple listeners can share a port. A third option is to lower `tcp_fin_timeout`, but I'll be honest that in production that mostly trades a correctness safety margin for memory, and I'd rather not do it. The real fix for a service churn problem is fewer connections: I measured that our p99 `CLOSE_WAIT` came from clients leaking sockets, and we fixed the client."

**Mistakes:** starting at the application when the browser shows `ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED`; using ICMP traceroute and trusting the first hop; changing DNS, protocol, and headers simultaneously; ignoring the difference between the client's view and the server's view.

**Mini task:** Build a `netdiag.sh` that takes a hostname and runs, in order, `dig +short`, `curl -sI` with timing, `openssl s_client` with SNI and ALPN, `traceroute -T -p 443`, and — if you have shell access — `ss -tan` on the target. Print a one-screen summary. Run it against a healthy service and against a deliberately broken one and confirm the summary tells you which layer broke.

# 7.2 Layers and Encapsulation
Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Definition:** The practice of wrapping data in control information at each layer, so that a layer can serve many higher layers while hiding its own mechanics, and so that a router can forward a packet without understanding what is inside it.

**OSI vs TCP/IP**

| # | OSI layer | TCP/IP model name | PDU | Protocols / concepts | Dev relevance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | Application | Application | data/message | HTTP, DNS, TLS(≈6-7), SMTP, gRPC, WebSocket | where your code lives; headers and status codes |
| 6 | Presentation | Application | data | TLS, JSON, Protobuf, gzip/br, ASCII/UTF-8 | encoding, encryption, compression, serialization |
| 5 | Session | Application | data | TLS session tickets, HTTP/2 streams, WebSocket | multiplexing, session state, connection state |
| 4 | Transport | Transport | segment (TCP) / datagram (UDP) | TCP, UDP, QUIC's own reliability | ports, reliability, flow/congestion control |
| 3 | Network | Internet | packet / IP datagram | IP, ICMP, IGMP, routing, NAT | addressing, routing, TTL, MTU |
| 2 | Data link | Network access | frame | Ethernet, Wi-Fi (802.11), PPP, VLAN, ARP | MAC addresses, local delivery, broadcast domains |
| 1 | Physical | Network access | bit | copper, fibre, radio, NIC drivers | latency floor, duplex, packet loss characteristics |

The mapping is a teaching device, not a protocol spec. In real engineering you use the five-layer TCP/IP model, and you should say so if asked, while still being able to place a concept in the seven-layer picture.

**Encapsulation on the way down, decapsulation on the way up**

```
WRITE (client)
 app:  GET /v1/orders HTTP/1.1
       │
 seg:  [TCP hdr | seq=1 ack=1 flags=ACK | payload = HTTP request]
       │
 pkt:  [IP hdr | src=10.0.0.5 dst=203.0.113.10 | TCP segment]
       │
 frm:  [Eth hdr | 00:11:22:33:44:55 -> aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff | 0x0800 | IP packet | FCS]

READ (server, bottom-up)
 frm → strip Eth → pkt → strip IP (check dst == me, decrement TTL) → seg
    → strip TCP (check port 443, verify checksum, reassemble by seq) → HTTP
```

**Why each layer's header exists**

- **Ethernet (14 bytes):** source and destination MAC. Exists because on a shared local medium someone must say who this frame is for. It changes at every hop. That is why MAC addresses are useless for identifying a client across the internet.
- **IP (20 bytes minimum, 60 with options):** source and destination address, protocol, TTL, and the total length. Exists so packets can be routed across heterogeneous networks. TTL also provides a loop-breaker: routers decrement it, and at zero the packet is dropped with an ICMP Time Exceeded.
- **TCP (20 bytes minimum):** ports, sequence and acknowledgement numbers, flags, window, checksum. Everything above is just payload to TCP.
- **UDP (8 bytes):** ports, length, checksum. That's all. Everything else is left to the application or to QUIC.

**Ports**

| Range | Name | Who assigns it | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–1023 | Well-known / registered | IANA | needs privilege to bind; HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SMTP 25, submission 587, IMAP 143/993, POP3 110/995, SSH 22 |
| 1024–49151 | Registered | IANA | applications register here, but collisions are handled by convention |
| 49152–65535 | Dynamic / ephemeral | OS | what your runtime binds for outbound connections; the range is the port-exhaustion budget |

**MTU and MSS — the concept that bites in production**

```
MSS = MTU_of_path − 40 (IPv4 TCP header) − 20 (TCP header) = MTU − 60
IPv6: MSS = MTU − 60 as well (40 IPv6 + 20 TCP)
```

- Common Ethernet MTU is **1500** bytes, so MSS is **1460** for IPv4 and **1440** for IPv6.
- Each router that forwards a packet decrements TTL and, if the outgoing MTU is smaller than the packet, must either fragment it or drop it and send ICMP "Fragmentation needed and DF set" (IPv4) or ICMPv6 "Packet Too Big" (IPv6, which *must* be honoured).
- A router configured to drop instead of fragmenting — common on tunnels, PPPoE, and VPNs — creates an **MTU black hole**: small packets work, large ones vanish, and both endpoints still think `PMTU` discovery succeeded because nobody sends the ICMP error. Diagnose with `ping -M do -s 1472 <host>` and `tracepath <host>`.
- TCP avoids fragmentation entirely with path-MTU discovery: it sets the DF bit and shrinks its own segment size based on ICMP feedback. The cost is complexity: cached PMTU per destination, stale caches after a tunnel change, and the fact that some networks black-hole the ICMP messages.
- QUIC takes a different approach: it does not use IP fragmentation and it does not rely on receiving ICMP. Instead it learns the path MTU from its own congestion controller and packet-count feedback, which is a genuine robustness improvement in mobile and multi-path networks.

**Head-of-line blocking by layer** — this concept threads the whole part:

| Layer | Can one thing block another? | Fixed by |
|---|---|---|
| Ethernet / Wi-Fi | Yes, shared medium, CSMA/CA in Wi-Fi | more airtime, 5 GHz vs 2.4 GHz |
| IP | No, packets are independent | — |
| TCP | Yes: a lost segment blocks all later bytes on that connection | retransmission; removed by QUIC's per-stream model |
| HTTP/1.1 | Yes: responses must be read in order on a connection | pipelining (badly supported) or more connections |
| HTTP/2 | No at the application level, but TCP HOL still applies to the whole connection | QUIC / HTTP/3 |
| Application (e.g. one slow query) | Yes, if you serialise calls | parallelise, cache, prefetch |

**Questions**
1. Give the PDU name at each layer, and say which header holds the destination MAC versus the destination IP.
2. Why does a router not need to understand HTTP to forward a packet, and what breaks when a device is a "middlebox" instead?
3. Explain encapsulation in terms of what a layer treats as payload.
4. What is the MSS on a path with MTU 1500 for IPv4, and what would it be for IPv6? Why is the IPv6 value lower for the same MTU?
5. What is an MTU black hole, what are its symptoms, and how do you confirm one?
6. Why is it a problem that `traceroute` and `ping` sometimes work while TCP fails? What does that tell you about ICMP filtering?
7. What does the TTL field protect against, and why is it often set to 64 or 255 rather than 255 everywhere?
8. Explain why MAC addresses cannot identify a user, and what identifier can.
9. Where does NAT sit, and why is it a layer-3 translation rather than layer-4?
10. What breaks if a middlebox is a stateful firewall and your protocol is UDP with an unusual handshake?

**Model answer, Q5:** "An MTU black hole is when the true path MTU is smaller than what the endpoints think it is, and the intermediate devices that would tell them are dropping the ICMP message that would say so. The endpoints therefore keep sending full-size packets, and those packets are silently discarded, so the symptom is a confusing partial failure: DNS resolves, small requests succeed, TCP establishes because the SYN is small, TLS fails or the request hangs, and any page with large images breaks while the rest of the site works. On a VPN or PPPoE link, 1500-byte assumptions are routinely wrong. I confirm it by setting the DF bit and increasing size until it breaks — `ping -M do -s 1472 <host>` succeeds at 1472 which is exactly 1500 minus 28 bytes of IP plus ICMP, and fails at 1473 — or with `tracepath <host>`, which prints the discovered PMTU per hop. The fix is either to lower the MTU on the tunnel interface, or to clamp MSS at the tunnel endpoints so TCP never emits a segment larger than the path can carry, and to make sure the tunnel actually forwards ICMP Packet Too Big."

**Mistakes:** saying OSI is the protocol the internet runs; mixing up segment and packet and frame; forgetting IPv6's larger header; assuming fragmentation is normal; believing `ping` failing proves the host is down; thinking a NAT box is a "firewall feature" rather than an addressing feature.

**Mini task:** On a machine you control, run `ping -M do -s 1472` and `ping -M do -s 1473` to a public host, then to a host on your VPN if you have one, and note where it breaks. Cross-check with `tracepath`. Then write down the MSS each connection to that host would use, and where you'd put an `clamp-mss-to-pmtu` rule if you owned a router on that path.

# 7.3 IP Addressing, Subnets, NAT, and Routing
Advanced · **Must-know**

**Definition:** The addressing, subdivision, and forwarding rules that let packets find their way across a network, including the private-address-plus-translation scheme that made IPv4 deployable in the 1990s.

**IPv4 address anatomy**

```
203.0.113.42
^          ^   ^
|          |   +-- host part   (variable length)
|          +------ network part (variable length)
+-------------- 32 bits, dotted decimal
```

**Special IPv4 ranges you must know**

| Range / mask | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `0.0.0.0/8` | this network | "any" in some contexts; also `0.0.0.0` as a bind address means all interfaces |
| `10.0.0.0/8` | private, class A | 16,777,216 addresses; used by most cloud VPCs internally |
| `100.64.0.0/10` | CGNAT / shared address space (RFC 6598) | carrier-grade NAT; not routable on the public internet |
| `127.0.0.0/8` | loopback | `127.0.0.1` is localhost; the whole /8 loops |
| `169.254.0.0/16` | link-local | self-assigned when DHCP fails; also used by AWS metadata at `169.254.169.254` |
| `172.16.0.0/12` | private, class B | 1,048,576 addresses |
| `192.168.0.0/16` | private, class C | home and small office networks |
| `192.0.2.0/24`, `198.51.100.0/24`, `203.0.113.0/24` | documentation (RFC 5737) | use these in examples and docs; they are never routable |
| `224.0.0.0/4` | multicast | 224.0.0.1 all hosts, 224.0.0.2 all routers |
| `240.0.0.0/4` | reserved | includes `255.255.255.255` broadcast |
| `192.88.99.0/24` | 6to4 relay anycast | deprecated by RFC 7526 |

The private ranges are not "reserved for home use" in a soft sense; they are the reason a corporate network can use 192.168.1.0/24 internally and another one can use the same range, because neither ever appears on the public internet.

**CIDR, prefix lengths, and VLSM**

| Prefix | Addresses | Usable hosts | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `/24` | 256 | 254 | a small subnet, a rack |
| `/25` | 128 | 126 | two more subnets from a /24 |
| `/26` | 64 | 62 | four more |
| `/27` | 32 | 30 | eight more |
| `/28` | 16 | 14 | 16 more |
| `/29` | 8 | 6 | small point-to-point or a load-balancer VIP range |
| `/30` | 4 | 2 | the classic routed link between two routers |
| `/31` | 2 | 2 | RFC 3021 point-to-point links, both addresses usable |
| `/32` | 1 | 1 | a single host, or a loopback, or a `/32` route pinning one host |
| `/0` | all | — | the default route |

VLSM (variable-length subnet masking) means allocating right-sized blocks instead of a uniform size. The allocation order is: largest requirement first, then align each block to a power-of-two boundary. Example: a site needs `/24` (250 hosts), `/25` (120 hosts), `/27` (28 hosts), and two `/30` links.

```
allocation:  10.0.0.0/24      → 250 hosts        (0-255)
             10.0.1.0/25      → 120 hosts        (0-127)
             10.0.1.128/27    → 28 hosts         (128-159)
             10.0.1.160/30    → p2p link         (160-163)
             10.0.1.164/30    → p2p link         (164-167)
             10.0.1.168/29    → 6 hosts          (168-175)
```

**Subnetting arithmetic you should be able to do in your head**

- Hosts in a `/n` = `2^(32−n) − 2` (the minus two is the network and broadcast addresses).
- Block size = `256 − (last octet of mask)`. For `/26` the block size is 64, so boundaries are 0, 64, 128, 192.
- To find the network address, AND the address with the mask. To find the broadcast, OR it with the inverted mask.
- A `/24` with mask `255.255.255.0`, address `10.1.2.130` → network `10.1.2.0`, broadcast `10.1.2.255`, usable `.1`–`.254`.
- Private range membership: `10.x` always; `172.16–31.x`; `192.168.x`.

**NAT and PAT**

```
inside host                     outside
10.0.0.5:54321  --->  [NAT]  --->  198.51.100.7:61000  --->  203.0.113.10:443
        ^                        ^
   private:port          translated address:port
   (table entry)        (PAT: many hosts share one public IP via distinct ports)
```

- **NAT** (network address translation) rewrites addresses. **PAT** (port address translation, "NAT overload") also rewrites ports and is what lets hundreds of internal hosts share one public address.
- The state lives in a translation table with a timeout. Each new outbound flow from an internal host consumes an entry. That's the second reason port exhaustion happens.
- **Inbound requires explicit port forwarding or a static mapping.** This is why inbound-only apps on a home connection are hard, and why cloud providers use Elastic IPs or 1:1 NAT instead.
- **Hairpin NAT** is the detail that bites in development: a client inside the same network resolving the public IP must be translated back to the internal address, or it just talks to the firewall. If it "works from home but not from the office", hairpinning is a prime suspect.
- **STUN** discovers your public mapping; **TURN** relays when you cannot be mapped (see 7.14).

**Routing tables and longest-prefix match**

```
$ ip route
default via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp src 10.0.0.5 metric 100
10.0.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.0.5
10.10.0.0/16 via 10.0.0.9 dev eth0 proto static metric 50
10.10.4.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.0.5
$ ip route get 10.10.4.7
10.10.4.7 dev eth0 src 10.0.0.5 uid 1000
```

- **Longest prefix wins.** The `/24` beats the `/16` beats the default. This is the only reason overlapping route ranges work at all.
- `metric` breaks ties between equal prefixes. ECMP (equal-cost multi-path) uses identical cost, not a metric.
- The default route `0.0.0.0/0` is the catch-all. Its absence means "no way out", and the resulting error is `ENETUNREACH`.
- ARP resolves the next-hop MAC. Outside the local subnet, the ARP is for the *gateway*, not the destination.

**IPv4 vs IPv6, and the transition**

| Aspect | IPv4 | IPv6 |
|---|---|---|
| Size | 32 bits, ~4.3 billion | 128 bits, 2^128 |
| Notation | dotted decimal | colon hex, with `::` compression and embedded IPv4 notation |
| Header | 20 bytes min, variable via options | fixed 40 bytes, extension headers by chaining |
| Fragmentation | routers may fragment; PMTUD fragile | routers never fragment; sender must use PMTUD via ICMPv6 |
| Broadcast | yes, 255.255.255.255 | none; multicast replaces it |
| Config | DHCP or manual | SLAAC (stateless address autoconfiguration, RFC 4862), DHCPv6, or static |
| Auto-config address | via DHCP | EUI-64 derived link-local `fe80::/10` per interface, always present |
| Loopback | 127.0.0.1 | `::1` |
| Minimum MTU | 68 | 1280 |
| Header checksum | yes | none (rely on lower layers; faster forwarding) |
| NAT | essentially required | designed to be NAT-free (RFC 4864 discusses the problems NAT creates) |

**Transition mechanisms**
- **Dual stack** — run both families; clients and servers pick per connection (the "Happy Eyeballs" algorithm in RFC 8305 races v6 against v4 with a 250 ms fallback delay).
- **Tunnelling** — encapsulate v6 in v4 (6in4, Teredo).
- **Translation** — NAT64/DNS64 (RFC 6052, RFC 6147) synthesises AAAA records from A records so a v6-only client can reach a v4-only server via a translator; and SIIT.
- **6rd**, **CGN** with v4-in-v6.

**Operational consequences of IPv6 preference bugs** — this is the part that gets you hired

Symptoms seen in the wild:
- **AAAA published, v6 broken.** You add AAAA records, packets leave, and something in the path is broken: a router that drops ICMPv6, a middlebox that mangles fragmentation, an ISP with a bad route. Users on v6 get intermittent failures while v4 is fine. Fix is to actually test v6, not to reason about it.
- **Happy Eyeballs not engaged** because the server has a 30-second v6 connect timeout. Users see a 30-second hang instead of a fast v6 connection. RFC 8305 says ~250 ms fallback.
- **A record in `/etc/hosts` overrides only AAAA behaviour inconsistently** — with `getaddrinfo` ordering, some binaries prefer v6 and hang.
- **V6-only environments break v4-only dependencies:** monitoring agents, license servers, hardcoded IPv4 literals, `0.0.0.0` binds where `::` is required, and `X-Forwarded-For`-style logic that only understands 32-bit addresses. Note that IPv6 literals in URLs are bracketed: `http://[2001:db8::1]:8080/`.
- **Bind address mismatch:** a service listening on `0.0.0.0:443` is *not* listening on IPv6. You need `::` or two listeners. This is the single most common "IPv6 doesn't work on my server" bug.
- **Observability blind spots:** dashboards, log parsers, and rate limiters that assume dotted-quad addresses will silently mis-handle `2001:db8::1`. Compressed-notation differences (`::1` vs `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1`) break naive string comparison for rate-limit keys.
- **Privacy extensions** (RFC 4941) rotate the interface identifier, so per-device identification by address is unreliable — a real privacy and also a real observability change.

**Questions**
1. Why is `10.0.0.0/8` considered private while `11.0.0.0/8` is not, and what would break if you used `11.0.0.0/8` internally?
2. Compute the network and broadcast address for `172.19.203.44/26`, and list the usable range.
3. Explain longest-prefix match with two overlapping routes and say which wins and why.
4. What does PAT do that plain NAT cannot, and what is the resource it consumes?
5. Describe hairpin NAT and give a symptom that uniquely suggests it.
6. Why does IPv6 forbid router fragmentation, and how does a sender learn the path MTU?
7. What is SLAAC, and what address does a host always have on an IPv6 interface?
8. Your service binds `0.0.0.0:8080` and works over IPv4 but refuses IPv6 connections. Diagnose.
9. Explain Happy Eyeballs and what user-visible symptom appears when it is absent.
10. Why is a `/31` subnet legal on a point-to-point link but confusing elsewhere?
11. In a Kubernetes cluster, how do packets get from a pod to the internet, and what is CNI's role?
12. A VPC has `10.0.0.0/16` for the VPC and `10.0.1.0/24` for a public subnet. Are they allowed to overlap with a peering connection to another VPC using `10.0.0.0/16`? Why?
13. Your rate limiter keys on client IP. What breaks when the same client alternates between v6 and v4?
14. What is CGNAT and why does it cause "my port forwarding doesn't work"?

**Model answer, Q8 (senior framing: Context → Decision → Reasoning → Trade-offs → Failure scenario → Alternative):**
> "Context: the symptom is that IPv4 works from every client and IPv6 gets connection refused or times out, on a host that has both an A and an AAAA record published.
>
> Decision: the first thing I check is the listener. `ss -ltnp` is the fastest discriminator, because it prints the exact local address each socket is bound to. A socket on `0.0.0.0:8080` is IPv4-only by definition; IPv4-mapped addresses are a different thing and don't cover plain v6 listeners. The fix is to bind the wildcard for the family you need — `::` with `net.ipv6.bindv6only=0` covers both families on Linux, or two explicit listeners — and to make sure the service's config and the container's port declarations include the v6 port.
>
> Reasoning: `0.0.0.0` and `::` are not synonyms. Historically `::` accepted v4-mapped connections, but the kernel flag `bindv6only` and explicit `IPV6_V6ONLY` socket options make behaviour deployment-dependent, which is exactly the kind of ambiguity that produces intermittent bugs. Being explicit is the fix.
>
> Trade-offs: dual-stack doubles the address-management surface and means your logs, metrics labels, and rate-limit keys have to handle two address families, including the compressed-notation problem where the same address can be written several ways. A v6-only deployment is cleaner but breaks any dependency that hardcodes v4.
>
> Failure scenario: the exact case I've seen is a service that binds correctly, but a security group or a Network ACL only allowed the v4 CIDR, so v6 SYN packets were dropped and the client saw a hang rather than a refusal. `tcpdump -i any 'ip6 and tcp port 8080'` on the host shows whether the SYN arrives at all: nothing arriving means a network policy problem, arriving-and-then-nothing means a host firewall, and arriving-with-RST means the listener.
>
> Alternative: if you can't get v6 right end to end today, publish only the A record and add a plan, rather than publishing a broken AAAA. A working v4 path with a tracked v6 backlog beats a v6 record that intermittently fails for a slice of your users."

**Mistakes:** treating classful A/B/C boundaries as relevant in modern routing; thinking broadcast addresses are "reserved forever" without noting `/31`; assuming `ip addr` shows a routable v6 address because a link-local exists; forgetting that `0.0.0.0` is IPv4-only; using a public range internally "because we ran out of private ones" and creating a routability conflict.

**Mini task:** Take a VPC or your home LAN. Compute the network, broadcast, and usable ranges for every subnet. Then, on a Linux box, add a dummy interface with a `/26` and confirm with `ip addr` and `ip route get` that longest-prefix works. Set up a tiny NAT experiment with two namespaces if you have `iproute2` and `iptables` — then delete the hairpin route and watch the failure appear.

# 7.4 DNS Deep
Advanced · **Must-know**

**Definition:** The hierarchical, cache-driven naming system that maps a name to the records a client needs to reach a service, and the set of caching behaviours that make it fast and simultaneously make deployments painful.

**The hierarchy**

```
            .                                   root servers (13 logical, anycast)
            |                                   answer: "ask com. at 192.5.6.30"
         .--|--.                                TLD servers (.com, .net, .org, ...)
            |                                   answer: "ask ns1.example.com at 203.0.113.1"
      -----+------
            |                                   authoritative: the zone's own data
   ns1.example.com  ns2.example.com
            |
       example.com. A 203.0.113.10
```

**Resolution flow, recursive vs iterative**

```
client (stub resolver)
  │  1. check its own cache: hosts file, nscd/systemd-resolved, browser
  │  2. ask the recursive resolver: "give me the A record for api.example.com"
  │       recursive resolver checks ITS cache (respecting TTL)
  │       if miss → iterative queries:
  │         a. root        "who is .com?"                  → referral to .com servers
  │         b. .com        "who is example.com?"           → referral + glue
  │         c. auth        "A for api.example.com?"        → ANSWER (authoritative)
  │         d. cache the answer with its TTL, return it
  │  3. return to client; client caches per its own TTL/stale policy
  ▼
client connects to the IP
```

- **Recursive** means "you give me the final answer, I don't care how". The client-to-resolver query is recursive.
- **Iterative** means "give me the best you have, and I'll follow the referral myself". The resolver-to-authority queries are iterative.
- **Stub** is the client-side code. In Node, `dns.lookup` talks to the OS resolver (so it uses `nsswitch.conf`, `/etc/hosts`, `systemd-resolved`, mDNS), while `dns.resolve4`/`dns.resolve6`/`dns.resolveAny` talk to a DNS server directly over the wire (UDP/TCP port 53) and ignore `/etc/hosts` and NSS.

**`dns.lookup` vs `dns.resolve` — a real interview distinction**

| Aspect | `dns.lookup(name)` | `dns.resolve4(name)` / `resolve6` / `resolveMx` / `resolveTxt` / `resolveCname` |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | calls the OS resolver (getaddrinfo/gethostbyname) | builds a DNS query itself and sends UDP/TCP to a nameserver |
| Honours `/etc/hosts` | yes | no |
| Honours NSS (mDNS, LDAP, container DNS, split-horizon via resolver config) | yes | no |
| Uses search domains | yes (resolver appends `search` list) | no |
| Runs on | the libuv **thread pool** (default 4 threads) | the event loop (async form), no thread pool |
| Order of results | OS-dependent, often IPv6-first | exactly the type requested |
| Typical use | "what address should I dial" | "what records exist for this name" (MX, TXT, SRV, CAA) |
| Consequence | can be slow if the OS resolver is slow; thread pool exhaustion under load | bypasses local overrides, which is usually what you want for service discovery |

The practical trap: in a container with a service mesh sidecar or a split-horizon resolver, `dns.lookup` gets the mesh's answer and `dns.resolve` gets the public answer. Pick deliberately. Also, `dns.lookup` occupying libuv thread-pool threads can starve your app's other thread-pool work (crypto, zlib, fs) if you resolve per request.

**Every record type that matters**

| Type | Holds | Used for | Gotcha |
|---|---|---|---|
| `A` | IPv4 address | the normal case | IPv4-only; nothing about a name is "v4" other than this record existing |
| `AAAA` | IPv6 address | v6 clients | publishing a broken AAAA breaks part of your traffic (see 7.3) |
| `CNAME` | alias to another name | `www` → `example.com`, multi-tenant subdomains | **cannot coexist with any other record type at the same name** (no A, no MX, no TXT) |
| `ALIAS` / `ANAME` | vendor-specific apex alias | pointing `example.com` (apex) at a CDN or load balancer | a non-standard extension, so it's invisible to other resolvers; apex A records cannot be a CNAME by spec (RFC 1034 §3.6.2) because the apex also carries SOA and NS |
| `NS` | nameserver for a zone | delegation, authoritative servers | must match at parent and child; missing glue for in-bailiwick NS makes delegation non-glue and fragile |
| `SOA` | zone metadata: MNAME, RNAME, serial, refresh, retry, expire, minimum | zone transfer, negative caching TTL | the **serial number is how secondaries know to reload** |
| `MX` | mail exchanger + preference | mail routing | lower preference wins; MX without a hostname that has an A record silently fails to deliver |
| `TXT` | free-form strings | SPF, domain verification, BIMI | SPF must be exactly one record; two SPF records is a permanent error |
| `CAA` | which CAs may issue for this domain | constrain issuance | `issue`, `issuewild`, `iodef`; absence means "any CA" |
| `SRV` | service, priority, weight, port, target | service discovery, XMPP, SIP, some gRPC naming | target must have an A/AAAA; priority/weight do host selection |
| `HTTPS` / `SVCB` | service binding: endpoint, ALPN, port, IPv4/IPv6 hints, ECH config | HTTP/3 advertisement, preferred endpoints | RFC 9460; `HTTPS` is the special case with default ALPN h3/h2 and port 443 |
| `PTR` | reverse mapping IP→name | logging, verification, some reputation systems | reverse DNS is a separate zone; PTR does not influence forward resolution |
| `NAPTR` | rewrite rules | legacy SRV bootstrapping | rare in web stacks |
| `DS` / `DNSKEY` / `RRSIG` / `NSEC` | DNSSEC chain of trust | authenticity | see DNSSEC below |
| `CAA`, `URI` | redirect target location | sometimes used for apex redirects | non-standard, use ALIAS or a 301 |

**Caching and TTLs**

TTL is a hint, and different layers honour it differently:

```
browser DNS cache ── OS/SD-resolved cache ── local caching resolver ── authoritative
     (per browser, often ~60s or per OS)
```

- **Browser cache:** Chrome and Firefox maintain their own in-memory DNS caches, typically tens of seconds to a minute, and some entries get special treatment. This is why a laptop that keeps hitting a stale IP while your phone gets the new one is normal.
- **OS cache:** `systemd-resolved` caches and honours the minimum of the record TTL and the local configuration, and negative answers per SOA `minimum`.
- **Resolver cache:** most recursive resolvers cap TTLs at their configured maximum (30s–24h) and may serve stale records under load.
- **Authoritative server:** answers authoritatively, may serve slightly stale data, and **does not** honour a record's TTL for its own authoritative data.
- **The deployment rule: TTL is a floor, not a promise.** Lowering a TTL does not purge existing caches. You must wait at least the *previous* TTL before a change can be relied upon. That is why the standard sequence is: set TTL to 60, wait 60+ seconds (really, wait the old TTL too), change the record, verify, then restore a high TTL.

**Negative caching**

- A resolver caches "no such record" answers too. The duration comes from the **SOA `minimum`** field of the zone (in older practice) or from RFC 2308, which defines the negative-caching TTL as the minimum of the SOA's `MINIMUM` and the SOA's TTL itself.
- Consequence: create a record that doesn't exist yet and clients will get a hard `NXDOMAIN` for up to that window, even after you add the record.
- This is the single most common cause of "the deploy works for me but fails for users for 10 minutes".

**DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT)**
- DoH is DNS inside HTTPS, specified in RFC 8484. DoT is DNS inside TLS, RFC 7858, usually on port 853.
- **Motivation:** integrity and privacy of lookups, and using the same authentication/encryption machinery you already have.
- **Costs:** the client must bootstrap the DoH server's address (usually a hardcoded IP or a separate bootstrap resolution), you cannot rely on local network DNS, split-horizon and internal discovery break unless the DoH resolver is inside the network, and enterprise monitoring of DNS becomes harder.
- **Consequence for engineers:** with DoH, your `/etc/hosts` file may be bypassed entirely, and per-user or per-device DNS policy is harder to enforce. Some platforms (Firefox with TRR enabled, Chrome with the right flags, iOS with a DoH profile) enable it per-app.

**DNSSEC**
- Adds `DNSKEY` (public keys), `RRSIG` (signatures over records), and `DS` (a hash of the child's key, placed in the parent) to create a chain of trust from the root.
- Validators check that a signed answer is signed by the zone's key, that the key is authorised by the DS in the parent, and that the DS is authorised by the root. Any modification breaks the chain.
- **It authenticates, it does not encrypt.** Anyone can still read the queries, and DNSSEC deliberately does not provide confidentiality.
- **Operational reality:** it is deployed at the root and in many TLDs, but end-to-end adoption by registrars and hosting providers is uneven. A broken DS record on a parent makes a whole zone resolve as `SERVFAIL` for validating resolvers while it still works on non-validating ones — a genuinely nasty asymmetry to debug.
- **DS automation:** DS records need to be updated when you rotate keys, and that means an API call to the registrar. This is a recurring operational chore and a common source of outages.

**Split-horizon DNS**

The same name resolves differently depending on where you ask.

```
external:  api.example.com  → 203.0.113.10        (public edge / load balancer)
internal:  api.example.com  → 10.20.30.40         (service directly, or internal LB)
```

Why teams want it: internal traffic avoids hairpin NAT, the public load balancer, and TLS termination hops; internal certificates can be shorter-lived; and staging can shadow production names.

Costs: two systems to keep consistent, and a very common outage — the internal zone still points at a decommissioned service because nobody updated it. Debugging tip: always ask the question from the *other* network, and remember that the resolver you ask determines the answer.

**Why DNS TTL causes deployment pain**

```
t=0    TTL=3600. Deploy: point api.example.com at new LB.
t=0    You curl it. Your resolver has the old A cached. You see the OLD server.
       You "fix" it by flushing your own cache and declaring victory.
t=0+   5,000 other resolvers still hold the old A for up to an hour.
t=3600 everything converges, and for that hour a meaningful
       fraction of traffic hit a server you may have already decommissioned.
```

Better patterns:
- **Blue/green with a stable VIP or a weighted DNS answer** so the switch is a weight change, not a record change.
- **Low TTLs (30–60s) on records that point at load balancers**, and high TTLs on records that are stable (MX, CAA, SPF). TTL should reflect *how often you plan to change the record*, nothing else.
- **Health-check-driven cutover** rather than DNS-driven cutover: keep DNS stable, have the LB drain targets.
- **Never let DNS be the only signal**: a DNS change with no corresponding capacity change is how you get a 502 storm.

**Questions**
1. Explain recursive versus iterative resolution, and who does which.
2. Walk a cold resolution of `api.example.com` to an IP, naming the query type at each step.
3. Why can a `CNAME` not coexist with an `MX` record? What are the workarounds?
4. What is an apex `ALIAS`/`ANAME`, why is `CNAME` illegal at the apex, and what breaks with a vendor-specific apex alias?
5. `dig` returns NOERROR with an empty answer. Explain, and give the deploy sequence that avoids it.
6. What sets the negative-caching TTL, and why does it surprise deployers?
7. You set a TTL from 3600 to 60 and redeploy immediately. What did you actually accomplish?
8. Describe `dns.lookup` vs `dns.resolve4` in Node, including which one uses the libuv thread pool and what breaks if you pick wrong.
9. What is split-horizon DNS, when do you want it, and what is its most common failure?
10. What does DNSSEC protect against, what does it *not* protect against, and how does a bad DS record manifest?
11. Why is the apex a special case for record types, and what does RFC 1034 say?
12. Your app must verify an SPF policy. Which record type and what failure modes do two SPF records or an `include:` loop create?
13. What is `HTTPS`/`SVCB` for, and how does it relate to `Alt-Svc` for HTTP/3?
14. How does a CAA record reduce risk, and what happens if you set `issue` for one CA and then move to another?
15. Explain the delegation and glue problem: what happens if an in-bailiwick nameserver has no glue A record?
16. Why do some apps use `SRV` or service discovery instead of A records for internal routing?
17. Explain DNS rebinding at a protocol level and what control mitigates it.
18. When should you use `resolveAny`/`resolveCname` and what are the practical caveats?

**Model answer, Q7 (senior framing: Context → Decision → Reasoning → Trade-offs → Failure scenario → Alternative):**
> "Context: someone lowered a TTL from an hour to a minute and immediately redeployed, and traffic is still hitting the old targets.
>
> Decision: the correct sequence is a three-step TTL dance, and it's a policy, not a one-off. Step one: lower the TTL and wait. Step two: make the change. Step three: leave the low TTL in place for at least one full previous-TTL period plus a margin, then raise it back.
>
> Reasoning: TTLs are cached independently at the browser, the OS, every recursive resolver in the path, and in some cases the authoritative server's own hidden records. Lowering the TTL only affects answers issued after the change. Every answer already in a cache keeps its original expiry. So the effective convergence time after step two is bounded by the *old* TTL, not the new one, and the client-side caches add more. That's the entire illusion: I changed the future, not the past.
>
> Trade-offs: low TTLs cost query volume and slightly increase the risk of load-balancer churn as resolvers spread across many answers. Very low TTLs also make it easier for an attacker or a misconfiguration to move traffic. So low TTL on a record is a commitment, and I want it justified by a real change cadence.
>
> Failure scenario: a team deploys with a 30-second TTL, rolls back after an incident, and the rollback DNS change also takes 30 seconds to converge — during which a known-bad version is still receiving a share of traffic, so the rollback is partial. I have seen this turn a bad deploy into a bad afternoon. The mitigation is a plan for the bad state, not just the good state: a hard kill switch at the load balancer, or a feature flag, that does not depend on DNS at all.
>
> Alternative: remove DNS from the critical path entirely. Keep a stable hostname pointing at a load balancer and change which backends that balancer considers healthy. That's a health-check-driven cutover, converges in seconds, is observable, and doesn't multiply your DNS load. DNS becomes a stable name, not a deployment mechanism."

**Mistakes:** saying "the browser asks DNS" as one step; thinking TTL changes apply retroactively; using `dns.resolve` when you needed `/etc/hosts` behaviour; assuming a CNAME can have a TTL of its own (the TTL applies to the alias, the target's TTL applies to the answer); forgetting that `dig` uses your local resolver while the browser may use DoH.

**Mini task:** Write a script that, for a given hostname, prints A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, CAA, and HTTPS records, plus the resolved IP's PTR. Then, on a domain you control (or a sandbox you spin up), set a TTL to 60, add a record, and measure how long a *second* resolver you control takes to see it. Do the same for a record you add before it exists (negative caching) and time that too. Write up the two convergence times.
