### 8.4.2 GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Jenkins: mental model comparison

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

#### Definition

All three are **workflow orchestrators**; the mental models differ enough that migrating is a real project, not a translation exercise.

| | **GitHub Actions** | **GitLab CI** | **Jenkins** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit of work | `job` inside a `workflow` | `job` in a `stage` (`.gitlab-ci.yml`) | `stage` containing `step`s, defined in a `Jenkinsfile` |
| Trigger model | events on the repository (push, PR, schedule, `workflow_run`, `repository_dispatch`) | pipeline sources: push, MR, schedule, web/API, child pipelines, parent-child | webhooks + polling; plugins for SCM triggers |
| Composition | **Reusable workflows** (`workflow_call`), composite actions | **includes**, **extends**, child/parent pipelines, components | shared libraries (Groovy), plugins |
| Ecosystem model | marketplace of first/third-party actions, versioned by tag or SHA | built-in catalogue of prebuilt jobs | a plugin ecosystem (hundreds), each a JVM dependency |
| Runner model | GitHub-hosted, or your own ephemeral/self-hosted | GitLab-hosted, or your own runners | your own agents, always |
| Secrets | Org/environment/repo secrets; environments with protection rules | CI/CD variables (project/group/instance), masked/protected variables, environment scopes | credentials store (system, folder, global) + credentials binding |
| Environments | `environment:` with reviewers and URL | environments with deployment approvals and rules | "stages" are not environments; needs Folders/Blue Ocean or plugins |
| Reusable pipelines | `workflow_call` (+ `secrets: inherit`) | `include: component`, `include: local` | shared libraries |
| Merge trains | merge queue | merge trains | depends on multibranch + plugin |
| Matrix | `strategy.matrix` | `parallel:matrix` | Declarative Pipeline `matrix` axis |
| Cache | `actions/cache` + `cache-from/to` in buildx | `cache:` key + policies | `cache()` step (arbitrary) + `stash`/`unstash` |
| Artifacts | `upload-artifact` / `download-artifact` (immutable v4) | `artifacts:` paths (no built-in download across jobs; `needs:artifacts`) | `archiveArtifacts` |
| Approval | environment protection rules | environment approvals | `input` step with `Submitter`, or a plugin |
| Hosting | SaaS only (GHES for on-prem) | SaaS or self-managed | self-managed |
| Cost model | billable minutes per runner | compute minutes | your own servers |

#### Mechanics

**GitHub Actions** is a *workflow file per event* with jobs as a DAG declared by `needs:`, reusable via `workflow_call`, and heavily dependent on the **action marketplace**. The ecosystem's main virtue is composability; its main risk is that **third-party actions are arbitrary code with access to your secrets and token**. Hence SHA pinning (8.4.13). `GITHUB_TOKEN` is per-run, scoped to the repository, and expires with the job — an improvement over long-lived PATs.

**GitLab CI** is a *declarative pipeline file* with a stages/phases model, an extremely large built-in catalogue (`node:test`, `docker:build`, `kubernetes:deploy`, `terraform`, security scanners), first-class **environments** with deployment approvals, **merge trains**, and **pipelines as code** with `include`/`extends`. Its strongest idea for this roadmap is the **child pipeline**: one pipeline per service in a monorepo, each triggered on its own path, orchestrated by a parent pipeline that fans out and gates.

**Jenkins** is a *general-purpose automation server* with a plugin ecosystem and Groovy pipelines. Its strengths are self-hosting anywhere, exceptional flexibility, mature agent/scheduling features, and deep legacy integrations. Its weaknesses are operational burden (you run and upgrade the controller and plugins, including security patches for CVEs in hundreds of plugins), Groovy's failure modes, and a configuration experience that invites drift.

#### Real YAML (the same pipeline in all three)

**GitHub Actions:**

```yaml
name: deploy
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      digest: { description: 'image digest', required: true }

concurrency: { group: deploy-prod, cancel-in-progress: false }

jobs:
  deploy:
    environment: { name: production, url: https://api.acme.com }
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with: { name: manifests, path: out }
      - name: apply
        run: |
          kubectl -n prod set image deploy/orders-api \
            api=${{ inputs.digest || needs.build.outputs.digest }}
          kubectl -n prod rollout status deploy/orders-api --timeout=5m
```

**GitLab CI (with a monorepo child pipeline per service and an environment approval):**

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
workflow:
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "schedule"
    - when: never

stages: [verify, build, deploy]

default:
  image: node:22.11-bookworm
  before_script:
    - corepack enable && corepack prepare pnpm@9.12.3 --activate
    - pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

variables:
  REGISTRY_IMAGE: $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE
  KUBE_NAMESPACE_PROD: prod

# Cache keyed on the lockfile; 'pull' so stale entries never break the build.
.pnpm_cache:
  cache:
    key:
      files: [pnpm-lock.yaml]
      prefix: pnpm
    policy: pull-push
    paths: [.pnpm-store]

# --- reusable template: build + push one service ---
.build_service:
  stage: build
  script:
    - |
      set -euo pipefail
      tag="$(echo "$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG" | tr '/' '-')-$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA"
      docker buildx build --cache-from=type=registry,ref=$REGISTRY_IMAGE/cache \
        --cache-to=type=registry,ref=$REGISTRY_IMAGE/cache,mode=max \
        -f services/$SERVICE/Dockerfile -t $REGISTRY_IMAGE/$SERVICE:$tag \
        --push services/$SERVICE
    - echo "DIGEST=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect $REGISTRY_IMAGE/$SERVICE:$tag --format '{{json .Manifest.Digest}}' | tr -d '"')" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

build:orders-api:
  extends: .build_service
  variables: { SERVICE: orders-api }
  artifacts:
    paths: [dist/]
    expire_in: 1 day

# --- main pipeline fans out to child pipelines ---
deploy-production:
  stage: deploy
  trigger:
    include: ['services/*/ci/.gitlab-ci-deploy.yml']
    strategy: depend
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: manual
      allow_failure: false     # required gate; approval in the UI
  environment:
    name: production
    url: https://api.acme.com
```

```yaml
# services/orders-api/ci/.gitlab-ci-deploy.yml — the child pipeline
stages: [deploy, verify]

deploy:
  stage: deploy
  id_tokens:
    KUBE_ID_TOKEN:
      aud: https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
  script:
    - kubectl -n prod set image deploy/orders-api api=$IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA
    - kubectl -n prod rollout status deploy/orders-api --timeout=5m
  environment: { name: production }
  rules: [{ if: '$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "parent_pipeline" || $TRIGGER_TO_CHILD == "production"' }]

verify:
  stage: verify
  script:
    - curl -fsS https://api.acme.com/healthz/ready
```

**Jenkins Declarative Pipeline:**

```groovy
// Jenkinsfile (shared library: acme.platform)
@Library('acme-platform@v4') _

pipeline {
  agent none
  options {
    timestamps(); ansiColor('xterm')
    buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '60', artifactNumToKeepStr: '20'))
    timeout(time: 45, unit: 'MINUTES')
    skipDefaultCheckout(true)
  }
  environment {
    REGISTRY = 'registry.acme.com'
    KUBE_NAMESPACE = 'prod'
  }
  triggers { cron('H/30 * * * 1-5') }
  parameters {
    choice(name: 'ACTION', choices: ['deploy', 'rollback', 'noop'])
    string(name: 'DIGEST', defaultValue: '', trim: true)
  }
  stages {
    stage('Checkout') {
      steps { checkout scm }
    }
    stage('Build') {
      parallel {
        stage('Unit') {
          agent { label 'linux && docker' }
          steps { sh 'make test-unit' }
        }
        stage('Lint') {
          agent { label 'linux' }
          steps { sh 'make lint && make format-check' }
        }
      }
    }
    stage('Build image') {
      agent { label 'docker && buildkit' }
      steps {
        sh(script: './ci/build-image.sh', maskPasswords: true)
      }
    }
    stage('Deploy staging') {
      agent { label 'k8s' }
      steps { sh 'make deploy ENV=staging' }
      post { always { junit allowEmptyResults: true, testResults: 'reports/**/*.xml' } }
    }
    stage('Deploy prod') {
      when {
        expression { params.ACTION == 'deploy' }
        anyBranch { branch 'main' }
      }
      input {
        message 'Deploy to production?'
        submitter 'release-managers,sre'
        timeout time: 2, unit: 'HOURS'
        ok 'Deploy'
      }
      agent { label 'k8s' }
      steps {
        sh './ci/progressive-delivery.sh canary'
        sh './ci/canary-analysis.sh --window 10m'
        sh './ci/progressive-delivery.sh promote'
      }
      post {
        failure { sh './ci/progressive-delivery.sh rollback' }
      }
    }
  }
  post {
    always {
      junit allowEmptyResults: true, testResults: 'reports/**/*.xml'
      recordIssues enabledForFailure: true, tool: freestyle
      slackSend channel: '#releases', message: "${env.JOB_NAME}#${env.BUILD_NUMBER}: ${currentBuild.result}"
    }
  }
}
```

#### When to choose which

- **GitHub Actions** if code lives on GitHub, you want minimal infrastructure, and you can live with the marketplace security model (mitigated by SHA pinning and reusable workflows). Best for: many small services, fast onboarding, tight PR integration.
- **GitLab CI** if you want environments/approvals/merge trains *and* a big built-in catalogue *and* on-prem possibility in one product. Best for: regulated environments needing approval gates, monorepos with many services.
- **Jenkins** only with a strong reason: unusual infrastructure, an existing plugin you cannot replace, air-gapped or exotic environments, or an organisational commitment to self-hosted CI with a platform team that owns it. Best for: heterogeneous build estates and teams that already have CI expertise.
- **Hybrid** is normal and often right: GitHub Actions for PR/build, an internal orchestrator for the heavy deployment orchestration.

#### Trade-offs

**GitHub Actions**
- Pros: zero ops, excellent PR UX, `GITHUB_TOKEN` short-lived, environment protection, merge queue, massive ecosystem, self-hosted runners possible.
- Cons: marketplace supply chain risk, cost surprises (macOS/Windows multipliers, per-minute billing), less expressive scheduling/matrix control than Jenkins, no first-class "environments" beyond protection rules, self-hosted runners require your own patching.

**GitLab CI**
- Pros: environments with approvals, built-in security templates, merge trains, `rules`, includes/extends, child pipelines, self-managed option, excellent monorepo story.
- Cons: YAML features are quirky (`!reference`, `extends` merge semantics, variable expansion), the built-in catalogue ages unevenly, resource-heavy self-managed deployment, secrets/exposed variables need care.

**Jenkins**
- Pros: total flexibility, any environment, mature distributed agents, huge plugin capability, works with anything.
- Cons: you own patching the controller and every plugin (many CVEs), Groovy CPS quirks make pipelines hard to debug, poor default DX, configuration drift, credential management must be designed, scaling agents is work.

#### Production considerations

- **Pin and scan**: actions/workflows pinned to SHAs; Jenkins plugins pinned in an image build with a scheduled update job; GitLab images rebuilt monthly.
- **Self-hosted runners/agents must be ephemeral** — one job per machine, destroyed after; never long-lived with production credentials.
- **Centralise secrets**: 1Password/Vault/Secrets Manager, injected at runtime as short-lived credentials, never stored in the CI system's secret store if avoidable (GitHub/GitLab cannot read back secrets anyway — design around that).
- **Audit logs** for who approved what; require SSO and 2FA on the CI system.
- **A single "pipeline as code" repository** with conventions enforced by `conftest`/OPA policies in CI.
- **Test your CI system** by rebuilding the controller from scratch quarterly; if that takes a day, you are fragile.

#### Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long-lived self-hosted runner | Compromised via a fork PR | Runner reused across trusted/untrusted code | Ephemeral runners per job |
| Unpinned `uses: third-party@v1` | Supply-chain breach | Mutable tags | Pin to commit SHA; Dependabot for updates |
| Secrets available to fork PRs | Leak | `pull_request_target` misuse | `pull_request`; scoped `if:` on secret-using jobs |
| GitLab `rules` without `when: never` catch-all | Pipelines run when they should not | Missing terminal rule | Add `when: never` and document rules |
| Jenkins `input` left unattended | Deployments stuck for days | Timeout too long or no timeout | Short timeout + escalation |
| Secrets in `image:` labels or cache keys | Leaks in logs | Bad practice | Never; use secrets at runtime |
| One giant pipeline in a monorepo | Slow, opaque failures | No split | Child pipelines per service |

#### Interviewer probes

1. "Compare GitHub Actions and Jenkins for a regulated environment." — Actions is faster to adopt but SaaS-hosted and its action ecosystem is a supply-chain risk; Jenkins is self-hostable and flexible but you own patching and configuration.
2. "How do you run one pipeline per service in a monorepo?" — GitLab child/parent pipelines by path; GitHub Actions with `workflow_call` and a change-detection job; Jenkins multibranch + shared library with a job per module.
3. "What is a merge train / merge queue and why?" — It re-runs tests on the exact post-merge commit, serialising merges so you never merge untested code.
4. "How do you implement a manual approval gate?" — GitHub environment protection rules; GitLab environment approvals with `when: manual`; Jenkins `input` with `submitter`.
5. "How do you move secrets between CI systems safely?" — Never copy the value; re-issue from the secret store to the new system with a short TTL, and verify both systems' access is scoped correctly.
6. "What would make you leave your current CI?" — Slow feedback, missing approval gates, no monorepo support, cost, or audit requirements.

---

### 8.4.3 Build optimization: caching, parallelism, matrix builds, and remote caches

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

#### Definition

Build optimization is **removing work that does not need to be redone**, and **doing independent work in parallel**. Concretely: layer caching, dependency caching, build cache reuse across machines, and matrix fan-out with fail-fast control.

Vocabulary: **cache key**, **restore-keys**, **cache hit/miss**, **layer cache vs build cache**, **`type=gha` vs `type=registry` vs `type=local`**, **max/min mode**, **`--mount=type=cache` (BuildKit)**, **registry cache with `image-manifest=true`**, **self-hosted vs hosted runners**, **runner autoscaling (e.g. Karpenter for k8s runners)**, **matrix `include`/`exclude`**, **`fail-fast`**, **`max-parallel`**, **sharding**, **test splitting**, **flaky-test retry (with quarantine)**.

#### Mechanics

**Docker layer caching.** A layer is cached if every instruction and its inputs are unchanged, in order. That means:
- Copy the **lockfile first**, install dependencies, *then* copy the source. This single change is usually the biggest win in a build.
- Multi-stage builds: the dependency layer survives while the source layer changes.
- BuildKit's `--mount=type=cache` caches *directories inside* a build (e.g. `~/.m2`, `node_modules`, `~/.cache/pip`) without committing them to a layer.

**Remote build caches.**
- `type=gha` — GitHub Actions cache, scoped, ~10 GB per repo, evicted after 7 days of no use. Great for CI-only, not for developers locally.
- `type=registry` — pushes a cache manifest to OCI registries; works for both CI and local Docker, survives cluster changes, can be shared with `image-manifest=true` for multi-platform.
- `type=s3`/`type=azblob`/`type=gcs` — general-purpose, large, good for monorepos.
- **max vs min**: `mode=max` caches all intermediate layers (faster rebuilds, bigger cache); `mode=min` only the final layer (smaller).

**Test sharding.** Split the test set deterministically across runners by hashing test name (`--shard=1/8`). Trade-off: sharding by file count is simpler but load-imbalanced; balance by historical duration.

**Parallelism rules.** Parallelise *independent* work. Do not parallelise setup you share (installing the same dependency tree 8 times wastes more than it saves). Use `fail-fast: false` for test matrices so you learn everything in one run.

#### Real YAML

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
# --- deps stage: cache key is the lockfile only ---
FROM node:22.11-bookworm-slim AS deps
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm,sharing=locked \
    corepack enable && corepack prepare pnpm@9.12.3 --activate
WORKDIR /app
COPY pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm-workspace.yaml package.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/pnpm/store,sharing=locked \
    pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

# --- build stage: only source changes now ---
FROM deps AS build
COPY . .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/turbo \
    pnpm turbo run build --filter=$APP --output=dist \
 && pnpm exec prisma generate

# --- prod stage: minimal, non-root, distroless ---
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs22-debian12:nonroot
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=8080
COPY --from=build --chown=nonroot:nonroot /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build --chown=nonroot:nonroot /app/node_modules ./node_modules
EXPOSE 8080
USER nonroot:nonroot
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=2s --start-period=20s \
  CMD ["/nodejs/bin/node", "-e", "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz/ready').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"]
ENTRYPOINT ["/nodejs/bin/node", "dist/main.js"]
```

```yaml
# GitHub Actions: two caches (restored, not written, in the matrix),
# plus a multi-layer BuildKit cache.
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false                       # learn everything in one run
      max-parallel: 8
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-24.04, ubuntu-24.04-arm]
        node: [20, 22]
        shard: [1, 2, 3, 4]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-24.04
            node: 22
            shard: 1
            experiment: true               # opt into experimental features
        exclude:
          - os: ubuntu-24.04-arm
            node: 20
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with: { version: 9.12.3 }
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}, cache: pnpm }
      - name: Restore Playwright browsers
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/ms-playwright
          key: pw-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('e2e/package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: pw-${{ runner.os }}-
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm --filter ${{ matrix.shard == 1 && '...' || '...' }} test:shard -- --shard ${{ matrix.shard }}/4
        env:
          TEST_SHARD: ${{ matrix.shard }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: test-results-${{ matrix.os }}-${{ matrix.node }}-${{ matrix.shard }}
          path: reports/
          retention-days: 7

  build:
    uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
    with:
      cache-from: |
        type=gha,scope=app-max
        type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:buildcache,mode=max
      cache-to: |
        type=gha,mode=max,scope=app-max
        type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:buildcache,mode=max,image-manifest=true
```

```bash
# Local, sharing the CI cache so developers are fast too.
docker buildx build \
  --cache-from type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:buildcache,mode=max \
  --cache-to   type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:buildcache,mode=max,mode=max \
  -t orders-api:dev .

# Good Dockerfile ordering, the single highest-value rule:
#   COPY package.json pnpm-lock.yaml ./
#   RUN pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
#   COPY . .
#   RUN pnpm build
```

#### When to use vs not

- **Layer cache**: always, with correct ordering. `COPY . .` before install is the most common build-speed bug.
- **`--mount=type=cache`**: when the dependency directory is large (npm/pnpm/maven/gradle/cargo/go build cache) and you rebuild often.
- **Remote registry cache** (`type=registry`): when builds are shared across CI and local machines, or when builds exceed the CI cache size/TTL limits.
- **Matrix**: when the test suite has real cross-platform/version differences or you need sharding to fit a time budget.
- **Not worth it**: small projects where the build is 90s; adding caching complexity for a 3-minute build. Measure before optimising.
- **Sharding vs parallelism**: sharding splits one suite (needed when a single suite exceeds your budget); parallelism runs independent suites (usually better, because failure isolation is clearer).

#### Trade-offs

- **Caches are a correctness risk.** A key that omits a relevant input produces a stale artifact and a phantom green build. Include: OS/arch, toolchain version, lockfile hash, build flags.
- **Cache eviction** surprises you: `type=gha` evicts after 7 days idle and at ~10 GB. The first build after a cold cache is a bad day for your SLO.
- **Caching and reproducibility conflict.** Cached dependency trees can hide lockfile drift; always verify with `--frozen-lockfile` so the cache cannot mask a stale lockfile.
- **Matrix multiplies cost linearly.** Shard by historical duration, cap `max-parallel`, and cancel superseded runs.
- **Self-hosted runners** are faster and cheaper per minute but need autoscaling, image management, and cleanup. Kubernetes + Karpenter gives you scale-from-zero in ~1 minute.
- **`fail-fast: false`** costs time on an already-failing run but gives complete information; `fail-fast: true` saves runner-minutes and slows the feedback for the rest.
- **Cache poisoning**: a PR that populates a shared cache from untrusted code can poison it for `main` if the cache key is not branch-scoped. Use separate scopes per trust level.

#### Production considerations

- **Measure before optimising**: cache hit rate, job duration percentiles, and where time actually goes (install vs build vs test).
- **Runner sizing**: most jobs are I/O- and startup-bound; 4 vCPU beats 16 vCPU for speed and cost. Right-size after measuring.
- **Ephemeral runners** with a pre-warmed image containing toolchains, so the job does not `apt-get install`.
- **Self-hosted runner isolation**: no access to the Docker socket (or a rootless/proxy setup), no host network reach into production, and per-job destruction.
- **Registry cache garbage collection** — cache blobs accumulate; set a retention policy and monitor registry storage.
- **Cache keys reviewed in code review**; treat "why did we get a 4-minute build back to 8 minutes" as a regression.

#### Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `COPY . .` before install | Cache invalidated on every source change | Wrong layer order | Copy lockfile, install, then copy source |
| Cache key missing toolchain version | Mysterious wrong behaviour after upgrades | Key too coarse | Include node/java/go versions |
| Shared cache scope across PRs and main | Cache poisoning | Trust boundary ignored | Scope per branch/trust level |
| Relying on `type=gha` for correctness | Cold cache breaks a weekly build | Cache treated as artifact | Treat cache as an optimisation only |
| 1 vCPU runner for a JVM build | 12-minute builds | Undersized | Measure, right-size, cache |
| Matrix without `fail-fast: false` | First failure hides others | Default is true | Set explicitly |
| Sharding by file count | One shard takes 3× longer | Load imbalance | Shard by historical duration |
| `pnpm install` without `--frozen-lockfile` | Builds that should fail silently pass | Lockfile drift | Always freeze in CI |

#### Interviewer probes

1. "Our builds take 25 minutes. Where do you start?" — Profile: install vs build vs test; check Dockerfile layer ordering; cache hit rate; matrix/sharding; runner size; parallelism; then the *pipeline* order (is the PR pipeline doing deploy work?).
2. "How do you make local builds fast for 50 developers?" — Shared registry cache + BuildKit, a Makefile/`devcontainer`, and remote cache on a pre-warmed base image.
3. "Why did the build get slow overnight?" — Cache eviction (7-day TTL), a lockfile change invalidating everything, a new dependency, or the runner image was updated.
4. "How do you avoid cache poisoning from PRs?" — Separate cache scopes by trust level, never restore PR-populated caches into `main` builds, and prefer `restore` (read-only) in untrusted jobs.
5. "When is a matrix build a bad idea?" — When the matrix is large but the differences don't change outcomes, or when it hides a real incompatibility behind exclusions.
6. "How do you shard Playwright/Jest tests?" — Deterministic hash of test id mod N, balanced by recorded durations, with retry-on-failure only for quarantined tests.

---

### 8.4.4 Testing gates: unit, integration, e2e, and flaky-test quarantine

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

#### Definition

A **testing gate** is a check that blocks progress (merge, deploy, promote) when unmet. The tiers:

| Tier | Scope | Runs on | Target time | Count |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Linting/static** | source | every push | < 30s | hundreds |
| **Unit** | functions in isolation, mocked I/O | every push/PR | < 3 min | thousands |
| **Contract** | interface compatibility between services | PR + main | < 5 min | tens |
| **Integration** | real dependencies (DB, queue) in containers | PR | < 10 min | hundreds |
| **Component** | one service + its dependencies | PR/main | < 10 min | dozens |
| **E2E** | full user journeys through the deployed stack | post-deploy | < 15 min | tens |
| **Load/perf** | throughput/latency under expected traffic | nightly + pre-prod | 10–60 min | few |

**Flaky-test quarantine**: the practice of identifying tests that fail intermittently, moving them out of the blocking set into a *quarantine project* that runs on a schedule with retries and notifications, tracking an owner and an expiry date, and **failing the build if the quarantine grows beyond a budget**. The counter-arguments to blind retry-on-failure are real (see trade-offs).

#### Mechanics

**Integration tests with containers.** Use a throwaway database per run — `testcontainers`, Docker-in-Docker, or Kubernetes Jobs against a namespace-scoped database. The pattern that works: schema + migrations from the *actual* migration files, not a hand-maintained schema, so migration bugs are caught.

**E2E on real deployments.** Deploy to a preview or staging environment, run Playwright/Cypress against it, and tear it down. Requires environment provisioning as part of the pipeline (8.4.8) and stable test data.

**Flake detection.** You need a metric: **flakiness = (unexpected passes + unexpected failures + retries) / total runs**. Track it per test over a rolling window. Sources of flake, in rough order of frequency:
1. Test interdependence / shared state / ordering assumptions
2. Real time, sleeps, and clock skew
3. Network and DNS in the test environment
4. Shared external services (a real feature-flag service, a real third-party sandbox)
5. Resource contention (parallel runners)
6. Race conditions
7. Assertions on ordering, hash iteration, or timestamps
8. Retries masking real bugs

**Quarantine mechanics.** Move the test to a separate suite; keep it running nightly with retries; require an owner and a ticket; add a **quarantine budget** (e.g. max 2% of tests, or zero net-new entries per week) so it cannot become a dumping ground; make the suite fail when the budget is exceeded; review the list weekly.

#### Real YAML

```yaml
  unit:
    name: unit tests + coverage gate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
        with: { version: 9.12.3 }
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          pnpm test -- --coverage --coverage.reporter=json-summary --coverage.reporter=lcov
          node tools/coverage-gate.mjs \
            --report coverage/coverage-summary.json \
            --thresholds '{"lines":80,"branches":70,"functions":80,"statements":80}' \
            --diff-base origin/main          # new/changed code needs higher coverage
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: coverage, path: coverage }

  integration:
    name: integration (postgres, redis, s3)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16.3
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
          POSTGRES_DB: orders_test
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres"
          --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 3s --health-retries 10
        ports: ['5432:5432']
      redis:
        image: redis:7.4-alpine
        ports: ['6379:6379']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "redis-cli ping"
          --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 3s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      # Apply the real migrations so migration bugs are caught here.
      - run: pnpm --filter db prisma migrate deploy
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/orders_test?sslmode=disable
      - run: pnpm --filter api test:integration -- --runInBand
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/orders_test?sslmode=disable
          REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379
          CI: 'true'
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with: { name: integration-artifacts, path: reports/, retention-days: 14 }

  e2e:
    name: e2e (blocking, quarantined excluded)
    needs: [deploy-staging]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: |
          pnpm exec playwright test \
            --grep-invert "@quarantine" \
            --retries 0 \
            --reporter=list,github
        env: { BASE_URL: https://staging.api.acme.com }
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with: { name: playwright-report, path: playwright-report/ }

  quarantine-nightly:
    name: quarantined tests (non-blocking, retried)
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    continue-on-error: true
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pnpm exec playwright test --grep "@quarantine" --retries 3
      - name: quarantine budget check
        run: node tools/quarantine-budget.mjs --max-ratio 0.02 --fail-on-exceed
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        if: failure()
        with:
          script: |
            const owners = require('./quarantine/owners.json');
            const message = `Quarantined tests failing: ${owners.join(', ')} — see nightly run`;
            await github.rest.issues.create({
              owner: context.repo.owner, repo: context.repo.repo,
              title: 'Quarantined test failures', labels: ['flaky'],
              body: message
            });
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/flaky-detector.yml — compute flakiness from the run history
# and open issues for tests whose flake rate crosses a threshold.
name: flaky detector
on:
  schedule: [{ cron: '23 4 * * *' }]
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions: { actions: read, issues: write, contents: read }
jobs:
  detect:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const since = new Date(Date.now() - 14 * 864e5).toISOString();
            const runs = await github.paginate(github.rest.actions.listJobsForWorkflowRun, {
              owner, repo, workflow_id: 'e2e.yml', per_page: 100, filter: 'latest'
            });
            const stats = new Map();
            for (const { jobs } of runs) {
              for (const j of jobs) {
                const s = stats.get(j.name) || { total: 0, failed: 0, flaky: 0 };
                s.total += j.steps ? 1 : 0;
                if (j.conclusion === 'failure') s.failed++;
                if (j.steps?.some(st => st.conclusion === 'failure' && st.outcome === 'flaky')) s.flaky++;
                stats.set(j.name, s);
              }
            }
            const flaky = [...stats.entries()]
              .map(([name, s]) => [name, (s.flaky + s.failed) / Math.max(s.total, 1)])
              .filter(([, r]) => r > 0.05)
              .sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);
            core.setOutput('report', JSON.stringify(flaky, null, 2));
      - name: open issues for new flaky tests
        run: |
          node tools/open-flaky-issues.mjs "$(steps.detect.outputs.report)"
```

**Vitest configuration making ordering and isolation explicit (the actual fix for most flake):**

```ts
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    globals: true,
    // One file per worker process; isolated forks kill cross-file state leakage.
    pool: 'forks',
    poolOptions: { forks: { singleFork: false, minForks: 2, maxForks: 8 } },
    isolate: true,
    sequence: { shuffle: true, concurrent: true },     // shuffle exposes ordering bugs
    setupFiles: ['./test/setup.ts'],
    // Fake timers by default so no test depends on wall-clock time.
    fakeTimers: { toFake: ['setTimeout', 'Date'] },
    restoreMocks: true,
    unstubEnvs: true,
    unstubGlobals: true,
    retry: 0,                                          // blocking suites: no blind retry
    sequenceSetupHooks: 'list',
    coverage: {
      provider: 'v8',
      thresholds: { lines: 80, branches: 70, functions: 80, statements: 80 }
    }
  }
});
```

#### When to use vs not

- **Unit tests for every PR.** Non-negotiable; they are the only tier fast enough to gate merges.
- **Integration tests in the PR pipeline** when the dependency is cheap to provide (containers) and the failure mode is expensive (schema, serialisation, transaction behaviour).
- **E2E post-deploy, not pre-merge.** Running full E2E on every PR is slow and flaky; run a small smoke suite pre-merge and the full suite after deploy.
- **Contract tests** when a consumer depends on a producer's schema; they let you deploy independently.
- **Load tests** nightly and pre-release, never on every PR.
- **Quarantine** only with a budget and an owner. If quarantine is free, it becomes a graveyard that hides real regressions.

#### Trade-offs

- **Retries hide bugs.** A test that fails 1 in 20 runs with 3 retries appears green while shipping a 5% defect rate. Use retries *only* in the quarantine suite, and always report the retry count.
- **Quarantine is a loan, not a fix.** Every day a test is quarantined, less coverage exists. The budget and the weekly review are what make it work.
- **More tiers = more maintenance.** Integration suites with containers are slow and require seed data maintenance; E2E requires stable environments.
- **Diff-based coverage gates** are excellent (only changed code needs coverage) but need care with generated files and moved code.
- **Testcontainers** give real dependencies with no external service, at the cost of startup time (~5–20s per container) and CI resource use.
- **Shuffling and fake timers** increase suite value but can expose tests that were "passing" by luck — a one-time burst of failures that is actually a good thing.
- **Coverage percentage is not quality.** 100% coverage with no assertions is worse than 60% with meaningful invariants.

#### Production considerations

- **Every flaky test is a P1 bug with a timer.** Track flake rate as a metric with an owner; the goal is a monotone decrease.
- **Block merges on the blocking suite only**, and make the quarantine suite visible in the UI so the debt is obvious.
- **Seed data factories** with unique-per-run identifiers; never rely on a fixed fixture ID, never share databases between parallel runs.
- **Test against the real migration path**, real schema, real serialisation — the integration tier is where that is cheap.
- **Contract tests in CI for both producer and consumer**, so an API change fails the producer's PR.
- **Quarantine policy in writing**: owner, ticket, expiry date (e.g. 14 days), and a hard cap.
- **Synthetic monitoring after deploy**: the same journeys as E2E, running from outside the cluster continuously.

#### Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `retries: 2` on the blocking suite | Green builds, real flake in prod | Retry hides bugs | No retries in blocking; quarantine instead |
| Quarantine with no budget | 30% of tests quarantined | No enforcement | Cap ratio; fail when exceeded |
| Shared test database across parallel jobs | Intermittent failures | Parallel writes | Unique schema/database per run |
| Time-based assertions | Fail only at month boundaries | Real `Date.now()` | Inject a clock; fake timers |
| Test order dependence | Passes locally, fails in CI in one order | Shared state | `shuffle: true`, isolated forks |
| Coverage gate at 0% | Gate does nothing | Never set | Threshold + diff-based gate |
| E2E on every PR | 30-minute PR feedback | Wrong tier placement | Smoke suite on PR; full post-deploy |
| No seeds for e2e data | Flaky tests on missing data | Ad-hoc setup | Idempotent seed scripts with retries |

#### Interviewer probes

1. "How do you deal with a flaky test?" — Quarantine it with an owner and a ticket, keep it running nightly with retries, fix it within a bounded time, and enforce a quarantine budget so it cannot grow silently.
2. "Why not just retry flaky tests?" — Because retries convert a 5% failure rate into an invisible 5% defect rate; the test suite stops being a signal.
3. "Which tests run on a PR, and why?" — Lint, unit, and fast integration; E2E after deploy. Feedback latency is the constraint.
4. "How do you make test data?" — Idempotent seed scripts with unique IDs per run, real migrations applied, per-run database or schema.
5. "How do you know your tests are meaningful?" — Mutation testing on critical modules, diff-based coverage, asserting on behaviour rather than implementation, and reviewing tests in the same PR as code.
6. "A test failed 3 times in a week and each time looked like a real bug. Now what?" — The flaky-test-as-bug hypothesis is right; track and reproduce it deterministically, likely shared state, time, or ordering — and fix the cause rather than quarantining.
