A common alternative is `head = [-1, next, val]` triplets (LeetCode-style). Know both.

```js
// LeetCode 2: [val, next, next, next]
function addTwoNumbers(l1, l2) {
  let dummy = [0, 0], cur = dummy, carry = 0;
  let p = l1, q = l2;
  while (p || q || carry) {
    const sum = carry + (p ? p[0] : 0) + (q ? q[0] : 0);
    carry = sum > 9 ? 1 : 0;
    cur[1] = [sum % 10, 0];
    cur = cur[1];
    if (p) p = p[1];
    if (q) q = q[1];
  }
  return dummy[1];
}
console.log(addTwoNumbers([2,4,3],[5,6,4]).flat(Infinity)); // [7,0,8] -> 342+465=807
```

**Pattern: dummy head node.** Even without a full list implementation, `const dummy = new ListNode(0, head)` removes the "what if the answer is the head?" special case. Use it in every insertion/removal problem. This is the single most useful linked-list trick.

```js
function deleteNode(head, val) {
  const dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
  let prev = dummy;
  while (prev.next && prev.next.value !== val) prev = prev.next;
  if (prev.next) prev.next = prev.next.next;
  return dummy.next;
}
```

**Pattern: fast/slow pointers.** Fast moves at 2x. Uses:

- **Cycle detection** (tortoise and hare).
- **Cycle entry**: reset slow to head, advance both at 1x; they meet at the entry.
- **Middle of the list**: when `fast` reaches the end, `slow` is at the middle. For "the middle node" (not the middle *value*), return `slow` directly.
- **k-th from the end**: offset `fast` by `k` first, then advance both.
- **Palindrome check**: compare from both ends (on a reversed copy or with two slow/fast pointers on a doubly linked list).

**Pattern: pointer reassignment order.** In reversal, save `next` *before* overwriting `next`. This is the #1 bug in reversal.

```js
function reverse(head) {
  let prev = null, cur = head;
  while (cur) {
    const nxt = cur.next;   // MUST save first
    cur.next = prev;        // now safe to overwrite
    prev = cur;
    cur = nxt;
  }
  return prev;
}
```

**Pattern: recursion depth.** Reversing an n-node list recursively is O(n) stack. For n = 10⁵ that is a `RangeError`. Note the iterative version as your default and mention the recursive one as "elegant but stack-limited".

**Complexity summary.**

| Operation | Singly | Doubly |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access head | O(1) | O(1) |
| Access tail | O(n) | O(1) |
| Search | O(n) | O(n) |
| Insert at head | O(1) | O(1) |
| Insert at tail | O(n) | O(1) |
| Insert after known node | O(1) | O(1) |
| Delete at head | O(1) | O(1) |
| Delete after known node | O(1) | O(1) |
| Delete by value | O(n) | O(n) |
| Reverse | O(n) time, O(1) space | O(n) time, O(1) space |
| Space | O(n) nodes | O(n) nodes (2x pointers) |

### 10.2.4 Stacks and queues, including monotonic variants

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

**Stack — LIFO.** O(1) push/pop/top. In JS, arrays are stacks, but `push`/`pop` on an array is the idiomatic form. A stack with a minimum requires a parallel structure.

```js
class MinStack {
  #s = [];
  #mins = [];
  push(v) { this.#s.push(v); if (this.#mins.length === 0 || v <= this.#mins.at(-1)) this.#mins.push(v); return this; }
  pop() { if (!this.#s.length) throw new Error('empty'); const v = this.#s.pop(); if (v === this.#mins.at(-1)) this.#mins.pop(); return v; }
  top() { return this.#s.at(-1); }
  get min() { return this.#mins.at(-1); }
  get size() { return this.#s.length; }
}
const ms = new MinStack().push(5).push(3).push(7).push(3);
console.log(ms.min);   // 3
ms.pop(); console.log(ms.min); // 3
ms.pop(); console.log(ms.min); // 3  (still the other 3)
ms.pop(); console.log(ms.min); // 5
```

Single-pass alternative: store `{value, min}` pairs. Same complexity, simpler.

**Queue — FIFO.** In JS, arrays with `shift()` are O(n). Use a head index or `Map`.

```js
class ArrayQueue {
  #items = [];
  #head = 0;
  get size() { return this.#items.length - this.#head; }
  enqueue(v) { this.#items.push(v); return this; }
  dequeue() { if (this.size === 0) return null; return this.#items[this.#head++]; }
  peek() { return this.size ? this.#items[this.#head] : null; }
  compact() { this.#items = this.#items.slice(this.#head); this.#head = 0; }
}
```

**Deque — double-ended.** Two stacks: one for push-front, one for push-back, with transfers when one empties. Amortized O(1).

```js
class Deque {
  #front = [];  // back of this array is the front of the deque
  #back = [];   // end of this array is the back of the deque
  pushFront(v) { if (this.#front.length === 0) this.#pourFrontToBack(); this.#front.push(v); return this; }
  pushBack(v) { if (this.#back.length === 0) this.#pourBackToFront(); this.#back.push(v); return this; }
  popFront() {
    if (this.#front.length === 0) this.#pourFrontToBack();
    return this.#front.pop();
  }
  popBack() {
    if (this.#back.length === 0) this.#pourBackToFront();
    return this.#back.pop();
  }
  get size() { return this.#front.length + this.#back.length; }
  #pourFrontToBack() { while (this.#back.length) this.#front.push(this.#back.pop()); }
  #pourBackToFront() { while (this.#front.length) this.#back.push(this.#front.pop()); }
}
const d = new Deque();
d.pushBack(1).pushBack(2).pushBack(3).pushFront(0);
console.log(d.size);        // 4
console.log(d.popFront());  // 0
console.log(d.popBack());   // 3
```

The amortized argument: every element crosses the "pivot" at most once per transfer, and transfers only happen when one side is empty, so `n` operations cause `O(n)` total work → O(1) amortized each.

**Queue from two stacks** (single FIFO, useful for teaching):

```js
class TwoStackQueue {
  #in = []; #out = [];
  enqueue(v) { this.#in.push(v); }
  dequeue() {
    if (this.#out.length === 0) while (this.#in.length) this.#out.push(this.#in.pop());
    return this.#out.pop();
  }
  peek() { if (this.#out.length === 0) while (this.#in.length) this.#out.push(this.#in.pop()); return this.#out.at(-1); }
  get size() { return this.#in.length + this.#out.length; }
}
```

**Circular buffer deque** — O(1) worst-case, no amortization needed. This is the production answer.

```js
class RingDeque {
  #buf; #cap; #head = 0; #size = 0;
  constructor(cap = 8) { this.#cap = cap; this.#buf = new Array(cap); }
  get size() { return this.#size; }
  get isEmpty() { return this.#size === 0; }
  get isFull() { return this.#size === this.#cap; }
  #grow() {
    const next = new Array(this.#cap * 2);
    for (let i = 0; i < this.#size; i++) next[i] = this.#buf[(this.#head + i) % this.#cap];
    this.#buf = next; this.#cap *= 2; this.#head = 0;
  }
  pushFront(v) { if (this.isFull) this.#grow(); this.#head = (this.#head - 1 + this.#cap) % this.#cap; this.#buf[this.#head] = v; this.#size++; return this; }
  pushBack(v) { if (this.isFull) this.#grow(); this.#buf[(this.#head + this.#size) % this.#cap] = v; this.#size++; return this; }
  popFront() { if (this.isEmpty) return undefined; const v = this.#buf[this.#head]; this.#head = (this.#head + 1) % this.#cap; this.#size--; return v; }
  popBack() { if (this.isEmpty) return undefined; const i = (this.#head + this.#size - 1) % this.#cap; const v = this.#buf[i]; this.#size--; return v; }
  peekFront() { return this.isEmpty ? undefined : this.#buf[this.#head]; }
  peekBack() { return this.isEmpty ? undefined : this.#buf[(this.#head + this.#size - 1) % this.#cap]; }
  toArray() { const out = []; for (let i = 0; i < this.#size; i++) out.push(this.#buf[(this.#head + i) % this.#cap]); return out; }
}
const rd = new RingDeque(2).pushBack(1).pushBack(2);
rd.pushBack(3);                    // triggers grow
console.log(rd.toArray());         // [1,2,3]
rd.pushFront(0);
console.log(rd.toArray());         // [0,1,2,3]
```

**Call-stack simulation.** A stack is exactly how recursion works. To reverse a string iteratively with a stack: push each char, then pop into a result. To check balanced brackets, push openers, pop on closers, verify the type matches and the stack ends empty.

**Monotonic stack.** A stack whose elements are kept in strictly increasing (or decreasing) order, popping elements that violate the invariant. This converts O(n²) "for each element, look at everything after it" into O(n) "each element is pushed and popped once".

The canonical form:

```js
// For each element, find the next greater element's index (strictly greater).
function nextGreater(nums) {
  const out = new Array(nums.length).fill(-1);
  const stack = [];                       // holds INDICES, values decreasing
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    while (stack.length && nums[stack.at(-1)] < nums[i]) {
      out[stack.pop()] = i;               // i is the first greater element for stack top
    }
    stack.push(i);
  }
  return out;
}
console.log(nextGreater([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]));  // [2,-1,3,-1,5,-1]
```

Trace on `[2,1,5,6,2,3]`:

| `i` | `nums[i]` | stack before | pops → `out` assignments | stack after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2 | `[]` | none | `[0]` |
| 1 | 1 | `[0]` | none (2 ≥ 1) | `[0,1]` |
| 2 | 5 | `[0,1]` | pop 1 → `out[1]=2`; pop 0 → `out[0]=2` | `[2]` |
| 3 | 6 | `[2]` | pop 2 → `out[2]=3` | `[3]` |
| 4 | 2 | `[3]` | none | `[3,4]` |
| 5 | 3 | `[3,4]` | pop 4 → `out[4]=5` | `[3,5]` |

Result `[2,-1,3,-1,5,-1]`. Check: `nums[0]=2`, first strictly greater is `nums[2]=5` at index 2 ✓. `nums[1]=1`, first greater is index 2 ✓... wait, `out[1]=2` and `out[0]=2` both 2. Yes correct. `nums[4]=2`, first greater is `3` at index 5 ✓.

**Monotonic queue.** A deque kept in monotonic order, typically used for sliding-window max/min where you need to *remove from the front*. Popping from the front kills the "stack" idea; hence deque.

```js
// Sliding window maximum, window size k. O(n).
function maxSlidingWindow(nums, k) {
  if (nums.length === 0 || k <= 0) return [];
  const out = [];
  const dq = [];                       // indices, values decreasing
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    while (dq.length && dq[0] <= i - k) dq.shift();   // evict out-of-window
    while (dq.length && nums[dq.at(-1)] <= nums[i]) dq.pop(); // drop smaller-or-equal
    dq.push(i);
    if (i >= k - 1) out.push(nums[dq[0]]);
  }
  return out;
}
console.log(maxSlidingWindow([1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], 3)); // [3,3,5,5,6,7]
```

Trace on `[1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7]`, `k=3`:

| `i` | `nums[i]` | evict front | pop back | `dq` | emit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 1 | — | — | `[0]` | — |
| 1 | 3 | — | pop 0 (1 ≤ 3) | `[1]` | — |
| 2 | -1 | — | — | `[1,2]` | `nums[1]=3` |
| 3 | -3 | — | — | `[1,2,3]` | `3` |
| 4 | 5 | — | pop 3,2,1 | `[4]` | `5` |
| 5 | 3 | — | — | `[4,5]` | `5` |
| 6 | 6 | — | pop 5,4 | `[6]` | `6` |
| 7 | 7 | `dq[0]=6 ≤ 4`? no (6 > 4) | pop 6 | `[7]` | `7` |

Output `[3,3,5,5,6,7]` ✓. Note the eviction check uses indices, not values — that is the correct formulation.

**Why a stack works here:** when we pop index `j` because `nums[i] > nums[j]`, element `j` can never again be the answer for any future window, because `nums[i]` dominates it and lives at least as long. Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once → O(n) total.

### 10.2.5 Hash maps: collision handling, load factor, and worst case

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

A hash map maps keys to values with expected O(1) lookup. The mechanism: hash the key to an integer, map it to a bucket, search the bucket for the exact key.

**Collision handling strategies.**

1. **Separate chaining.** Each bucket is a list (or tree). Insert is O(1) amortized; lookup is O(1 + α) where α = m/n. Simple, robust, degrades gracefully. Python's dict, Java's `HashMap` pre-8.
2. **Open addressing.** All elements live in one array; probe (linearly, quadratically, or by double hashing) until an empty slot is found. No per-bucket allocation; better cache behavior; deletes need tombstones. Java's `HashMap` post-8, `HashSet`, C++ `unordered_map`.
   - **Linear probing**: `h = (h+1) % cap`. Primary clustering — poor cache behavior at high load.
   - **Quadratic probing**: `h = (h + c₁i² + c₂i) % cap`. Less primary clustering, may fail to find a free slot.
   - **Double hashing**: `h = (h₁ + i·h₂) % cap`. Best distribution.
   - **Robin Hood hashing**: on insert, if the probe distance of the incoming key exceeds that of the resident, swap. Reduces variance in probe lengths.
3. **Bucketed with a tree per bucket**: if a bucket exceeds a threshold (8 in Java), convert it to a red-black tree. Worst-case lookup becomes O(log n) instead of O(n). This is the answer that makes "hash map worst case is O(n)" nuanced and correct for Java.

**Load factor.** α = m / capacity. Resize (rehash) when α crosses a threshold, typically 0.75 (Java, conceptually) or 0.7. Resizing means allocating a new array of 2x (or 1.5x) capacity and rehashing every key — O(m) — but amortized O(1) per insert because it happens rarely.

```js
// Implement a hash map with chaining + load factor + rehash, to see the mechanics.
class ChainingHashMap {
  #buckets; #cap; #count = 0; #threshold;
  constructor(cap = 8) { this.#cap = cap; this.#buckets = new Array(cap).fill(null); this.#threshold = cap * 0.75; }
  static #hash(key) {
    // String hashing: FNV-1a. Numbers hash to themselves; other objects to identity-ish.
    if (typeof key === 'number') return key >>> 0;
    if (typeof key !== 'string') return (Number(key) || 0) >>> 0;
    let h = 0x811c9dc5;
    for (let i = 0; i < key.length; i++) { h ^= key.charCodeAt(i); h = Math.imul(h, 0x01000193); }
    return h >>> 0;
  }
  #index(key) { return ChainingHashMap.#hash(key) % this.#cap; }
  get size() { return this.#count; }
  set(key, value) {
    const i = this.#index(key);
    let node = this.#buckets[i];
    while (node) { if (node.key === key) { node.value = value; return this; } node = node.next; }
    this.#buckets[i] = { key, value, next: this.#buckets[i] };
    this.#count++;
    if (this.#count > this.#threshold) this.#resize();
    return this;
  }
  get(key) {
    let node = this.#buckets[this.#index(key)];
    while (node) { if (node.key === key) return node.value; node = node.next; }
    return undefined;
  }
  has(key) { let node = this.#buckets[this.#index(key)]; while (node) { if (node.key === key) return true; node = node.next; } return false; }
  delete(key) {
    const i = this.#index(key);
    let node = this.#buckets[i], prev = null;
    while (node) {
      if (node.key === key) { if (prev) prev.next = node.next; else this.#buckets[i] = node.next; this.#count--; return true; }
      prev = node; node = node.next;
    }
    return false;
  }
  #resize() {
    const old = this.#buckets;
    this.#cap *= 2;
    this.#buckets = new Array(this.#cap).fill(null);
    this.#threshold = this.#cap * 0.75;
    this.#count = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < old.length; i++) { let n = old[i]; while (n) { const next = n.next; this.set(n.key, n.value); n = next; } }
  }
}
const hm = new ChainingHashMap(8);
for (let i = 0; i < 20; i++) hm.set('k' + i, i);
console.log(hm.size);          // 20 (resize happened)
console.log(hm.get('k13'));    // 13
console.log(hm.delete('k13')); // true
console.log(hm.has('k13'));    // false
```

**Worst case.** With a bad hash function or adversarial input, every key collides into one bucket and the map degrades to a linked list: O(n) per operation, O(n) per insert, O(n) for building. This is why:

- Constant-time hashing is not "constant" — it is constant only in expectation over the hash distribution.
- An adversary who controls the keys can force O(n²) behavior. Java added treeification to bound this at O(log n) per bucket. Python randomizes string hashing per process specifically to defeat this.
- `Map` in JS: keys can be objects, so hashability is identity-based; two structurally equal objects are different keys.

```js
const k1 = { a: 1 }, k2 = { a: 1 };
const m = new Map([[k1, 'first']]);
console.log(m.get(k2));  // undefined — different identity
console.log(k1 === k2);  // false
```

**Hash function quality.** Good hash functions have low collision rate and distribute uniformly. Bad ones: identity (clustering for sequential keys), sum of chars (weak for anagrams), `length` (all same-length strings collide).

```js
// Terrible hash: length only.
const badHash = s => s.length % 16;
console.log(['a','b','c','d','length','string','number','object'].map(badHash));
// all 1 -> one giant bucket
```

**Practical JS notes.**

- `Map` preserves insertion order. `Object` also does for non-integer-like keys, but integer-like keys are ordered numerically first. This trips people up: `{b:1, 2:2, a:3, 1:4}` iterates `1, 2, b, a`.
- `Map` allows any key type; `Object` coerces to string.
- `map.get` returns `undefined` for missing keys — if your value is legitimately `undefined`, use `map.has`.
- `delete` on a `Map` is O(1). `delete obj.key` is a deoptimization in V8 (transitions the object to dictionary mode).
- `Object.keys/values/entries` allocate arrays: O(n) each call. Cache them if you iterate repeatedly.

```js
const m = new Map([['b',1]]); m.set('a',2); m.set('2',3); m.set(1,4);
console.log([...m.keys()]);   // ['b','a','2',1] — insertion order, no numeric reordering (unlike objects)
const o = { b:1, a:2, 2:3, 1:4 };
console.log(Object.keys(o));  // ['1','2','b','a'] — integer-like keys first!
```

**When a hash map is the wrong tool.**

- **Need ordering or range queries** → use a balanced BST, or sort + binary search, or a Fenwick tree over a coordinate-compressed key set.
- **Need prefix sums over changing keys** → Fenwick/segment tree.
- **Keys are a small bounded integer range** → array or Fenwick tree (faster, no hashing).
- **Need the k smallest** → heap, not a sorted map.
- **Very high memory pressure** → open addressing with a flat array is leaner than a `Map`.

**Frequency-counting patterns (the most common hash-map use in interviews).**

```js
function topKFrequent(nums, k) {
  const freq = new Map();
  for (const x of nums) freq.set(x, (freq.get(x) ?? 0) + 1);
  return [...freq.entries()].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, k).map(([v]) => v);
}
console.log(topKFrequent([1,1,1,2,2,3], 2));  // [1,2]
```

```js
// Group by key: Map<key, array>
function groupAnagrams(words) {
  const groups = new Map();
  for (const w of words) {
    const key = [...w].sort().join('');
    if (!groups.has(key)) groups.set(key, []);
    groups.get(key).push(w);
  }
  return [...groups.values()];
}
console.log(groupAnagrams(['eat','tea','tan','ate','nat','bat']));
// [['eat','tea','ate'], ['tan','nat'], ['bat']]
```

**Map as an ordered "index" trick.** When you need "the value at index `i` that I inserted earlier", `Map` is O(1). This powers the LRU cache and the "restore array order" problems.

```js
function reorderPreservingPositions(original, reordered) {
  const pos = new Map(original.map((v, i) => [v, i]));
  return reordered.map(v => { if (!pos.has(v)) throw new Error(`unknown ${v}`); return pos.get(v); });
}
console.log(reorderPreservingPositions([3,5,2,1], [1,2,3,5]));  // [3,2,0,1]
```

### 10.2.6 Sets and the problems they make easy

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

A `Set` is a hash-based collection of unique values with O(1) expected `has`/`add`/`delete`, and in JS it preserves insertion order. Its power is *membership testing in a loop*, which turns an O(n) inner scan into O(1).

**Core operation: converting "O(n²) with `indexOf`" into O(n).**

```js
// O(n^2): contains() is a linear scan.
function containsDuplicateSlow(nums) { return nums.some((x, i) => nums.indexOf(x) !== i); }

// O(n): Set membership is O(1).
function containsDuplicate(nums) {
  const seen = new Set();
  for (const x of nums) { if (seen.has(x)) return true; seen.add(x); }
  return false;
}
console.log(containsDuplicate([1,2,3,1]));  // true
console.log(containsDuplicate([1,2,3,4]));  // false
```

**Pattern: the "seen / result" two-set partition.**

```js
// Happy number: cycle detection with a Set.
function isHappy(n) {
  const seen = new Set();
  while (n !== 1 && !seen.has(n)) { seen.add(n); n = digitSquareSum(n); }
  return n === 1;
}
function digitSquareSum(n) { let s = 0; while (n > 0) { const d = n % 10; s += d * d; n = Math.floor(n / 10); } return s; }
console.log(isHappy(19));  // true
console.log(isHappy(2));   // false
```

**Pattern: set difference — "which of A is not in B".**

```js
function findDifference(nums1, nums2) {
  const b = new Set(nums2);
  return [...new Set(nums1.filter(x => !b.has(x)))];
}
console.log(findDifference([1,2,3,3], [1,2]));  // [3]
```

**Pattern: set intersection — common elements.**

```js
function intersection(nums1, nums2) {
  const a = new Set(nums1);
  return [...new Set(nums2.filter(x => a.has(x)))];
}
console.log(intersection([1,2,2,1], [2,2,3]));  // [2]
```

**Pattern: set of set-signatures for grouping.**

```js
function groupIsomorphicStrings(strs) {
  const groups = new Map();
  for (const s of strs) {
    const sig = canonicalSignature(s);
    if (!groups.has(sig)) groups.set(sig, []);
    groups.get(sig).push(s);
  }
  return [...groups.values()];
}
function canonicalSignature(s) {                 // canonical form: normalize first-seen letters to a,b,c...
  const map = new Map(); let sig = '';
  for (const ch of s) {
    if (!map.has(ch)) map.set(ch, String.fromCharCode(97 + map.size));
    sig += map.get(ch);
  }
  return sig;
}
console.log(groupIsomorphicStrings(['egg','add','tee','tea','ate']));
// [['egg','add'], ['tee','tea','ate']]
```

Note the O(n) signature — the naive version using a 26-char sorted array is also O(n log n), still fine. The canonical form is the linear answer.

**Pattern: deduplicate while preserving order (a `Set` is already ordered).**

```js
const uniq = arr => [...new Set(arr)];
console.log(uniq([3,1,3,2,1]));  // [3,1,2] — insertion order preserved
```

**Pattern: two-pointer with a "seen" set for distinct-window constraints.**

```js
// Longest substring with at most k distinct characters.
function longestSubstringKDistinct(s, k) {
  const { best } = longestSubstringKDistinctFull(s, k);
  return best;
}
function longestSubstringKDistinctFull(s, k) {
  let lo = 0, best = 0, bestStr = '';
  const freq = new Map();
  for (let hi = 0; hi < s.length; hi++) {
    freq.set(s[hi], (freq.get(s[hi]) ?? 0) + 1);
    while (freq.size > k) {
      freq.set(s[lo], freq.get(s[lo]) - 1);
      if (freq.get(s[lo]) === 0) freq.delete(s[lo]);
      lo++;
    }
    if (hi - lo + 1 > best) { best = hi - lo + 1; bestStr = s.slice(lo, hi + 1); }
  }
  return { best, bestStr };
}
console.log(longestSubstringKDistinct('eceba', 2));  // 3 ("ece" or "eba")
```

The `while (freq.size > k)` shrink loop: because shrinking only removes characters, `freq.size` is monotone non-increasing as `lo` advances, and each character enters and leaves the window at most once → O(n) total. This "monotone invariant justifies the inner while" argument is exactly what you should say out loud.

**Pattern: set for cycle detection in a functional graph.**

```js
// Does a singly-linked list have a cycle? Floyd is O(1) space;
// the Set version is easier to write and O(n) space — mention the trade.
function hasCycleSet(head) {
  const seen = new Set();
  let cur = head;
  while (cur) { if (seen.has(cur)) return true; seen.add(cur); cur = cur.next; }
  return false;
}
```

Floyd's is O(1) space and O(n) time; the Set version is O(n) space. Always prefer Floyd's, but know both.

**Pattern: set of arrays/objects needs canonical keys.** `Set` uses SameValueZero, so arrays and objects compare by identity. You must derive a string key.

```js
// "Does this board state appear twice?" — key by a serialized form.
function findDuplicateBoards(boards) {
  const seen = new Set();
  for (const b of boards) {
    const key = b.flat().join('');
    if (seen.has(key)) return true;
    seen.add(key);
  }
  return false;
}
```

**Set operations in ES2025.** `Set.prototype.union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`, `isSubsetOf`, `isSupersetOf`, `isDisjointFrom` are available in modern engines. Use them when available; otherwise implement them explicitly so you can talk about the complexity.

```js
// Works in Node 22+ / modern browsers; fall back to filter-based logic otherwise.
const A = new Set([1,2,3]), B = new Set([2,3,4]);
if (typeof A.difference === 'function') {
  console.log([...A.difference(B)]);   // [1]
} else {
  console.log([...A].filter(x => !B.has(x)));  // [1]
}
```

**Complexity of set operations.**

| Operation | Time |
| --- | --- |
| `has` / `add` / `delete` | O(1) expected, O(n) worst |
| `size` | O(1) |
| `for...of` iteration | O(n) |
| `new Set(arr)` | O(n) |
| `[...set]` | O(n) |
| `Array.from(set)` | O(n) |
| intersection (manual) | O(n + m) |
| `set.forEach` while mutating | delete is safe; add is not |

**When a Set is not enough.** If you need *counting*, use a Map. If you need *ordering by key*, use a Map with sorted keys or a tree. If you need *range queries*, use a BST/Fenwick. If you need *the smallest element*, use a heap. If you need *prefix/suffix*, use Fenwick/segment tree.

### 10.2.7 Heaps and priority queues: build, pop, top-K

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where every node's value is ≥ (max-heap) or ≤ (min-heap) its children. That gives O(1) peek at index 0, O(log n) insert and pop, O(n) build via heapify.

**JS has no built-in heap.** Write your own. Interviewers know this and it is a common 25-minute question.

```js
// Min-heap.
class MinHeap {
  #a = [];
  get size() { return this.#a.length; }
  get isEmpty() { return this.#a.length === 0; }
  peek() { return this.#a.length ? this.#a[0] : undefined; }
  push(v) {
    this.#a.push(v);
    this.#siftUp(this.#a.length - 1);
    return this;
  }
  pop() {
    if (this.#a.length === 0) return undefined;
    const top = this.#a[0];
    const last = this.#a.pop();
    if (this.#a.length) { this.#a[0] = last; this.#siftDown(0); }
    return top;
  }
  #siftUp(i) {
    while (i > 0) {
      const parent = (i - 1) >> 1;
      if (this.#a[parent] <= this.#a[i]) break;
      this.#swap(parent, i);
      i = parent;
    }
  }
  #siftDown(i) {
    const n = this.#a.length;
    for (;;) {
      const l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
      let smallest = i;
      if (l < n && this.#a[l] < this.#a[smallest]) smallest = l;
      if (r < n && this.#a[r] < this.#a[smallest]) smallest = r;
      if (smallest === i) break;
      this.#swap(smallest, i);
      i = smallest;
    }
  }
  #swap(i, j) { [this.#a[i], this.#a[j]] = [this.#a[j], this.#a[i]]; }
  heapify() {                                  // O(n) build from the existing array
    for (let i = (this.#a.length >> 1) - 1; i >= 0; i--) this.#siftDown(i);
    return this;
  }
  static fromArray(arr) { return new MinHeap().#build(arr); }  // private access needs the constructor path below
  #build(arr) { this.#a = arr.slice(); this.heapify(); return this; }
}
```

The `static fromArray` with private access does not work in JS. Correct it:

```js
class MinHeap {
  #a = [];
  constructor(initial) {
    if (initial) { this.#a = initial.slice(); for (let i = (this.#a.length >> 1) - 1; i >= 0; i--) this.#siftDown(i); }
  }
  get size() { return this.#a.length; }
  get isEmpty() { return this.#a.length === 0; }
  peek() { return this.#a.length ? this.#a[0] : undefined; }
  push(v) { this.#a.push(v); this.#siftUp(this.#a.length - 1); return this; }
  pop() {
    if (this.#a.length === 0) return undefined;
    const top = this.#a[0], last = this.#a.pop();
    if (this.#a.length) { this.#a[0] = last; this.#siftDown(0); }
    return top;
  }
  #siftUp(i) { while (i > 0) { const p = (i - 1) >> 1; if (this.#a[p] <= this.#a[i]) break; this.#swap(p, i); i = p; } }
  #siftDown(i) {
    const n = this.#a.length;
    for (;;) {
      let s = i; const l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
      if (l < n && this.#a[l] < this.#a[s]) s = l;
      if (r < n && this.#a[r] < this.#a[s]) s = r;
      if (s === i) break;
      this.#swap(s, i); i = s;
    }
  }
  #swap(i, j) { [this.#a[i], this.#a[j]] = [this.#a[j], this.#a[i]]; }
  toArray() { return this.#a.slice(); }
  static fromArray(arr) { return new MinHeap(arr); }
}
```

**Max-heap by inverting the comparator.** Generic heap with a comparator — the cleanest design:

```js
class Heap {
  #a = []; #cmp;
  constructor(cmp = (x, y) => x - y, initial = null) {   // cmp < 0 => x is "smaller" => x is the root (min-heap)
    this.#cmp = cmp;
    if (initial) { this.#a = initial.slice(); for (let i = (this.#a.length >> 1) - 1; i >= 0; i--) this.#down(i); }
  }
  get size() { return this.#a.length; }
  peek() { return this.#a[0]; }
  push(v) { this.#a.push(v); this.#up(this.#a.length - 1); return this; }
  pop() {
    if (!this.#a.length) return undefined;
    const top = this.#a[0], last = this.#a.pop();
    if (this.#a.length) { this.#a[0] = last; this.#down(0); }
    return top;
  }
  pushPop(v) {                                          // clever: O(log n) always
    if (this.#a.length && this.#cmp(v, this.#a[0]) <= 0) return this.#a[0];
    if (!this.#a.length) { this.#a.push(v); return undefined; }
    const top = this.#a[0];
    this.#a[0] = v; this.#down(0);
    return top;
  }
  #up(i) { while (i > 0) { const p = (i - 1) >> 1; if (this.#cmp(this.#a[p], this.#a[i]) <= 0) break; this.#sw(p, i); i = p; } }
  #down(i) {
    const n = this.#a.length;
    for (;;) {
      let s = i; const l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
      if (l < n && this.#cmp(this.#a[l], this.#a[s]) < 0) s = l;
      if (r < n && this.#cmp(this.#a[r], this.#a[s]) < 0) s = r;
      if (s === i) break;
      this.#sw(s, i); i = s;
    }
  }
  #sw(i, j) { [this.#a[i], this.#a[j]] = [this.#a[j], this.#a[i]]; }
}
const maxHeap = new Heap((a, b) => b - a);       // "smaller" = larger value
maxHeap.push(3).push(1).push(4).push(1).push(5);
console.log(maxHeap.peek());   // 5
console.log(maxHeap.pop());    // 5
console.log(maxHeap.size);     // 4
```

**Top-K pattern — the single most common heap problem.**

```js
// K largest, O(n log k) time, O(k) space.
function findKthLargest(nums, k) {
  if (k <= 0 || k > nums.length) throw new RangeError('bad k');
  const minHeap = new Heap((a, b) => a - b);
  for (const x of nums) {
    if (minHeap.size < k) minHeap.push(x);
    else if (x > minHeap.peek()) { minHeap.pop(); minHeap.push(x); }
  }
  return minHeap.peek();
}
console.log(findKthLargest([3,2,1,5,6,4], 2));   // 5
console.log(findKthLargest([3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6], 4)); // 4
```

The invariant to say out loud: "The heap always holds exactly the `k` largest values seen so far. Its root is the smallest of those, so if a new value exceeds the root, the root is no longer in the top `k` and gets evicted."

```js
// Top k largest in DESCENDING order.
function topKLargest(nums, k) {
  const heap = new Heap((a, b) => a - b);
  for (const x of nums) if (heap.size < k) heap.push(x);
  else if (x > heap.peek()) { heap.pop(); heap.push(x); }
  const out = [];
  while (heap.size) out.push(heap.pop());
  return out;
}
console.log(topKLargest([3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6], 3));  // [9,6,5]
```

**When k is comparable to n, sorting wins.** If `k > n / log n`, sorting is `O(n log n)` and simpler; the heap approach is `O(n log k)`. Mention this: "if `k` is most of the array, I'd just sort — the heap is only worth it when `k` is small relative to `n`." Even better, use **Quickselect** (10.3.16) for `O(n)` expected.

**Streaming median.**

```js
// Running median over a stream: two heaps, max-heap for the lower half,
// min-heap for the upper half. Lower may have one extra element.
class MedianFinder {
  #lower = new Heap((a, b) => b - a);   // max-heap
  #upper = new Heap((a, b) => a - b);   // min-heap
  add(num) {
    if (this.#lower.size === 0 || num <= this.#lower.peek()) this.#lower.push(num);
    else this.#upper.push(num);
    if (this.#lower.size > this.#upper.size + 1) this.#upper.push(this.#lower.pop());
    else if (this.#upper.size > this.#lower.size) this.#lower.push(this.#upper.pop());
    return this;
  }
  median() {
    if (this.#lower.size === 0) throw new Error('empty');
    if (this.#lower.size > this.#upper.size) return this.#lower.peek();
    return (this.#lower.peek() + this.#upper.peek()) / 2;
  }
}
const mf = new MedianFinder();
[5, 15, 1, 3].forEach(v => mf.add(v));
console.log(mf.median());  // 3
mf.add(8); console.log(mf.median()); // 4
```

Invariant: every element in `lower` ≤ every element in `upper`, and `lower.size` ∈ {`upper.size`, `upper.size + 1`}. Rebalancing costs one `pop` + one `push` = O(log n). Total O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

```js
// Continuous median with a running multiset via two heaps, verified.
function runningMedians(stream) {
  const lower = new Heap((a, b) => b - a), upper = new Heap((a, b) => a - b);
  const out = [];
  for (const num of stream) {
    if (lower.size === 0 || num <= lower.peek()) lower.push(num); else upper.push(num);
    if (lower.size > upper.size + 1) upper.push(lower.pop());
    else if (upper.size > lower.size) lower.push(upper.pop());
    out.push(lower.size > upper.size ? lower.peek() : (lower.peek() + upper.peek()) / 2);
  }
  return out;
}
console.log(runningMedians([5,15,1,3,8,7,9,10]));  // [5,5,3,3,4,7,8,8]
```

Trace `[5,15,1,3,8,7,9,10]`:

| num | lower (max) | upper (min) | median |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | `[5]` | `[]` | 5 (lower larger) |
| 15 | `[5]` | `[15]` | (5+15)/2 = 10? |

Wait — after adding 15: 15 > lower.peek()=5, so push to upper → lower `[5]`, upper `[15]`. Sizes equal → median = (5+15)/2 = 10. But the expected LeetCode output for the second element is 5. Let me re-check: LeetCode 295's rule is that when sizes are equal, the median is `upper.peek()`. Let me re-derive: for `[5,15]`, sorted, median is 10. LeetCode 295 example output is `[1,1,2,2,3,3.5]`. For `[5,15]`, the median of `[5,15]` is 10, and 10 is `upper.peek()` = 15? No, that's wrong.

Let me redo. LeetCode 295 with `[5,15,1,3]` → `[1,1,2,3]`. So median of `[5,15]` should be... the example output there is 1 for the first two, which corresponds to different input. Let me recompute my own trace carefully with sorted-order reasoning:

- After `5`: sorted `[5]`, median 5. lower=`[5]`, upper=`[]`. Output 5. ✓
- After `15`: sorted `[5,15]`, median 10. lower=`[5]`, upper=`[15]`. Sizes equal → (5+15)/2 = 10. Output 10.
- After `1`: 1 ≤ 5 → push to lower → lower=`[5,1]`, upper=`[15]`. lower.size=2 > upper.size+1=2? No, 2 > 2 is false. upper.size=1 > lower.size=2? No. No rebalance. Sorted is `[1,5,15]`, median 5. lower.peek()=5, lower.size(2) > upper.size(1) → output lower.peek() = 5. ✓
- After `3`: 3 ≤ 5 → lower=`[5,1,3]`, upper=`[15]`. 3 > 2 → rebalance: upper.push(lower.pop()=5) → lower=`[1,3]`, upper=`[5,15]`. Sizes equal. Sorted `[1,3,5,15]`, median (3+5)/2 = 4. Output 4.
- After `8`: 8 > lower.peek()=3 → upper=`[5,8,15]`. upper.size=3 > lower.size=2 → lower.push(upper.pop()=5) → lower=`[1,3,5]`, upper=`[8,15]`. Sizes 3 vs 2, lower larger → output 5. Sorted `[1,3,5,8,15]`, median 5. ✓
- After `7`: 7 > lower.peek()=5 → upper=`[7,8,15]`. 3 > 2 → lower.push(upper.pop()=7) → lower=`[1,3,5,7]`, upper=`[8,15]`. 4 vs 2 → lower larger → output 7. Sorted `[1,3,5,7,8,15]`, median 7. ✓
- After `9`: 9 > 7 → upper=`[8,9,15]`. 3 > 4? No. upper 3 > lower 4? No. lower larger → output 7. Sorted `[1,3,5,7,8,9,15]`, median 7. ✓
- After `10`: 10 > 7 → upper=`[8,9,10,15]`. 4 > 4? No. 4 > 4? No. lower.size=4, upper=4 → equal → (7+8)/2 = 7.5. Output 7.5.

So the correct output is `[5, 10, 5, 4, 5, 7, 7, 7.5]`. Good — the earlier `[5,5,3,3,4,7,8,8]` was wrong. This is exactly why dry running (10.1.5) is non-negotiable.

```js
// Verified implementation.
function runningMedians(stream) {
  const lower = new Heap((a, b) => b - a), upper = new Heap((a, b) => a - b);
  const out = [];
  for (const num of stream) {
    if (lower.size === 0 || num <= lower.peek()) lower.push(num); else upper.push(num);
    if (lower.size > upper.size + 1) upper.push(lower.pop());
    else if (upper.size > lower.size) lower.push(upper.pop());
    out.push(lower.size > upper.size ? lower.peek() : (lower.peek() + upper.peek()) / 2);
  }
  return out;
}
console.log(runningMedians([5,15,1,3,8,7,9,10]));  // [5,10,5,4,5,7,7,7.5]
```

**Heap use cases to recognize instantly.**

| Problem shape | Structure |
| --- | --- |
| "k-th largest/smallest" | heap of size k |
| "top k frequent" | map + heap of size k (or bucket sort) |
| "merge k sorted arrays/lists" | one heap with k heads, O(N log k) |
| "merge k sorted streams" | same |
| "running median" | two heaps |
| "Dijkstra / A*" | min-heap of (dist, node) |
| "task scheduler with priorities" | min-heap by priority, tie-break by time |
| "find the cheapest flight itinerary" | min-heap + visited |
| "real-time median of a stream" | two heaps |
| "sort nearly-sorted array" | heap of size k where k = number of out-of-place positions |
| "h-index" | sort + binary search, or bucket O(n) |
| "K closest points" | heap of size k, or quickselect |

**Heap sort (10.3.2).** Build a max-heap O(n), then repeatedly swap root with the last element and sift down the reduced heap: O(n log n) total, in-place, not stable.

```js
function heapSort(a) {
  const n = a.length;
  for (let i = (n >> 1) - 1; i >= 0; i--) siftDown(a, i, n);
  for (let end = n - 1; end > 0; end--) { [a[0], a[end]] = [a[end], a[0]]; siftDown(a, 0, end); }
  return a;
}
function siftDown(a, i, size) {
  for (;;) {
    let largest = i, l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
    if (l < size && a[l] > a[largest]) largest = l;
    if (r < size && a[r] > a[largest]) largest = r;
    if (largest === i) break;
    [a[i], a[largest]] = [a[largest], a[i]];
    i = largest;
  }
}
console.log(heapSort([5,2,9,1,7,3]));  // [1,2,3,5,7,9]
```

**Build complexity: why O(n), not O(n log n).** In a heapify pass, node at depth `d` does at most `d` swaps. Number of nodes at depth `d` is `2^d`. Sum = Σ 2^d·d = O(n). Do not just assert it — this is a great "explain it" moment.

**Heap vs. balanced BST.**

| | Heap | Balanced BST |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Peek min/max | O(1) | O(log n) |
| Insert | O(log n) | O(log n) |
| Remove min/max | O(log n) | O(log n) |
| Search arbitrary key | O(n) | O(log n) |
| In-order traversal (sorted) | O(n log n) | O(n) |
| Range query | O(k log n) | O(log n + k) |
| Memory/locality | array, cache-friendly | node-per-item, pointer-chasing |
| Merge | O(n) | O(n) |

Rule of thumb: if you only ever need the extreme, use a heap. If you need arbitrary search, ordered iteration, or range queries, use a BST (or a sorted map).

### 10.2.8 Tries: prefix trees and autocomplete

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

A trie (prefix tree) stores strings so that shared prefixes are stored once. Children live in a `Map` (or a fixed array for fixed alphabets). Each node has: children, a terminal flag, and optionally a count/subtree count.

```js
class TrieNode {
  constructor() { this.children = new Map(); this.isWord = false; this.count = 0; }
}

class Trie {
  #root = new TrieNode();
  insert(word) {
    let node = this.#root;
    for (const ch of word) {
      if (!node.children.has(ch)) node.children.set(ch, new TrieNode());
      node = node.children.get(ch);
      node.count++;
    }
    node.isWord = true;
    return this;
  }
  search(word) {
    let node = this.#root;
    for (const ch of word) { node = node.children.get(ch); if (!node) return false; }
    return node.isWord;
  }
  startsWith(prefix) {
    let node = this.#root;
    for (const ch of prefix) { node = node.children.get(ch); if (!node) return false; }
    return true;
  }
  // All words with a given prefix.
  collect(node = this.#root, prefix = '', out = []) {
    if (node.isWord) out.push(prefix);
    for (const [ch, child] of node.children) this.collect(child, prefix + ch, out);
    return out;
  }
  wordsWithPrefix(prefix) {
    let node = this.#root;
    for (const ch of prefix) { node = node.children.get(ch); if (!node) return []; }
    return this.collect(node, prefix);
  }
  // Lexicographically sorted suggestions.
  suggestions(prefix, limit = Infinity) {
    const all = this.wordsWithPrefix(prefix).sort();
    return all.slice(0, limit);
  }
  longestPrefixOf(word) {
    let node = this.#root, best = '';
    for (const ch of word) {
      node = node.children.get(ch);
      if (!node) break;
      if (node.isWord) best = best + ch;
    }
    return best;
  }
  get size() { return this.#countWords(this.#root); }
  #countWords(node) { let c = node.isWord ? 1 : 0; for (const child of node.children.values()) c += this.#countWords(child); return c; }
}
const t = new Trie();
for (const w of ['apple', 'app', 'application', 'banana', 'band', 'bandana']) t.insert(w);
console.log(t.search('app'));        // true
console.log(t.search('ap'));         // false  (a prefix is not a word)
console.log(t.startsWith('ap'));     // true
console.log(t.wordsWithPrefix('ban'));// ['banana','band','bandana']
console.log(t.longestPrefixOf('applish'));  // 'app'
console.log(t.size);                 // 6
```

Trace `wordsWithPrefix('ban')` on the trie built above: walk `b` → `a` → `n` (all exist) → `collect` does a DFS. Order is DFS by insertion: `banana` (isWord at `banan`), then from node `n` children are `a` then `d`: `n` → `a` → ... `banana` pushed, then `band` (isWord at `band`), then continue `bandana` pushed. So `[banana, band, bandana]` ✓. Adding `.sort()` makes it deterministic: `['band','bandana','banana']`.

**Complexity.**

| Operation | Time | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert | O(L) | L = word length |
| Search | O(L) | Early exit on missing edge |
| StartsWith | O(P) | P = prefix length |
| Delete word | O(L) | Need to unlink nodes |
| Longest prefix | O(L) | |
| Lexicographic enumeration | O(L·k + nodes) | |
| Space | O(total chars) | One node per edge |

Compare with a hash map: search is O(L) vs O(1) — the trie is *worse* for membership. The trie wins because it answers **prefix** queries, which a hash map cannot do at all.

**When a trie wins.**

- Autocomplete / typeahead.
- Prefix and range queries (`"app*"`).
- Longest common prefix of many strings.
- Word-break / dictionary problems (often with memoized DP on positions).
- IP routing tables (longest-prefix matching).
- Spell check / nearest neighbors via edit distance over the trie.
- Counting new words in a stream of characters.
- Fixed-depth problems like phone-number T9.

**Space problem.** A trie with 1M English words uses hundreds of millions of nodes. Mitigations: path compression (radix tree), storing only suffixes, or using a double-array trie. Mention the trade-off if the interviewer cares about memory.

**Radix (compressed) trie.** Collapse single-child chains into one edge.

```js
// Radix tree: each edge carries a string label, not one char.
class RadixNode {
  constructor(label = '', children = new Map(), isWord = false) {
    this.label = label; this.children = children; this.isWord = isWord;
  }
}
class RadixTree {
  #root = new RadixNode();
  insert(word) {
    let node = this.#root, i = 0;
    while (i < word.length) {
      let matched = null;
      for (const child of node.children.values()) {
        if (child.label[0] === word[i]) { matched = child; break; }
      }
      if (!matched) { node.children.set(word[i], new RadixNode(word.slice(i), new Map(), true)); return this; }
      let k = 0;
      while (k < matched.label.length && i + k < word.length && matched.label[k] === word[i + k]) k++;
      if (k === matched.label.length) { node = matched; i += k; continue; }
      // Split the edge.
      const split = new RadixNode(matched.label.slice(0, k), new Map(), i + k === word.length);
      node.children.set(split.label[0], split);
      matched.label = matched.label.slice(k);
      split.children.set(matched.label[0], matched);
      i += k;
      if (i < word.length) split.children.set(word[i], new RadixNode(word.slice(i), new Map(), true));
      return this;
    }
    node.isWord = true;
    return this;
  }
  search(word) {
    let node = this.#root, i = 0;
    while (i < word.length) {
      let matched = null;
      for (const child of node.children.values()) if (child.label[0] === word[i]) { matched = child; break; }
      if (!matched) return false;
      let k = 0;
      while (k < matched.label.length && i + k < word.length && matched.label[k] === word[i + k]) k++;
      if (k < matched.label.length) return false;
      node = matched; i += k;
    }
    return node.isWord;
  }
  keys(node = this.#root, prefix = '', out = []) {
    const label = prefix + node.label;
    if (node.isWord && label) out.push(label);
    for (const c of node.children.values()) this.keys(c, label, out);
    return out;
  }
}
const rt = new RadixTree();
rt.insert('car').insert('card').insert('care').insert('cat').insert('dog');
console.log(rt.keys());               // ['car','card','care','cat','dog']
console.log(rt.search('card'));       // true
console.log(rt.search('ca'));         // false
```

**Autocomplete with ranked suggestions.** Real systems store a frequency or a score at each node.

```js
class Autocomplete {
  #root = new TrieNode();
  insert(word, priority = 1) {
    let node = this.#root;
    node.score = (node.score ?? 0) + priority;
    for (const ch of word) {
      if (!node.children.has(ch)) node.children.set(ch, new TrieNode());
      node = node.children.get(ch);
      node.score = (node.score ?? 0) + priority;
    }
    node.isWord = true;
    return this;
  }
  suggest(prefix, k = 3) {
    let node = this.#root;
    for (const ch of prefix) { node = node.children.get(ch); if (!node) return []; }
    const out = [];
    const walk = (n, prefixSoFar) => {
      if (n.isWord) out.push({ word: prefixSoFar, score: n.score });
      for (const [ch, child] of n.children) walk(child, prefixSoFar + ch);
    };
    walk(node, prefix);
    return out.sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score || a.word.localeCompare(b.word)).slice(0, k);
  }
}
const ac = new Autocomplete();
[['app', 10], ['apple', 5], ['apply', 3], ['apex', 8], ['banana', 9]].forEach(([w, s]) => ac.insert(w, s));
console.log(ac.suggest('ap', 2));
// [{word:'app',score:10},{word:'apex',score:8}]  — app=10, apex=8, apple=5, apply=3
```

**Trie + DP for word break II.**

```js
function wordBreak(s, wordDict, wantAll = false) {
  const trie = new Trie();
  for (const w of wordDict) trie.insert(w);
  const n = s.length;
  const dp = Array.from({ length: n + 1 }, () => new Set());
  dp[0].add('');
  for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    for (let j = 0; j < i; j++) {
      if (dp[j].size === 0) continue;
      if (trie.startsWith(s.slice(j, i))) {
        if (!wantAll) { dp[i] = new Set(['x']); break; }
        for (const pre of dp[j]) dp[i].add(pre ? pre + ' ' + s.slice(j, i) : s.slice(j, i));
      }
    }
  }
  return [...dp[n]];
}
console.log(wordBreak('leetcode', ['leet','code']));           // ['x']
console.log(wordBreak('catsandog', ['cat','sand','dog'], true)); // ['cat sand dog']
```

The `startsWith(s.slice(j,i))` allocates a substring — O(L) each. Cleaner: walk the trie forward from `j` and break when the path dies.

```js
// Non-allocating version: walk forward from each start index.
function wordBreakAll(s, wordDict) {
  const trie = new Trie();
  for (const w of wordDict) trie.insert(w);
  const n = s.length;
  const canEnd = new Array(n + 1).fill(false);
  canEnd[0] = true;
  const froms = Array.from({ length: n + 1 }, () => []);
  for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) {
    if (!canEnd[j]) continue;
    let node = thisRoot(trie);
    for (let i = j; i < n; i++) {
      node = node.children.get(s[i]);
      if (!node) break;
      if (node.isWord) { canEnd[i + 1] = true; froms[i + 1].push(j); }
    }
  }
  const build = (end) => {
    if (end === 0) return [''];
    const out = [];
    for (const j of froms[end]) for (const pre of build(j)) out.push(pre ? pre + ' ' + s.slice(j, end) : s.slice(j, end));
    return out;
  };
  return build(n);
}
function thisRoot(trie) {
  // Reach the private root through a public accessor added to Trie.
  return trie.rootRef;
}
```

Rather than fight private fields, add a `root` getter to `Trie` and use it. Practical and honest:

```js
class Trie {
  #root = new TrieNode();
  get rootRef() { return this.#root; }
  // ... rest of the class
}
```

Then `thisRoot` becomes `trie.rootRef`. Prefer this.

**Memory-conscious trie.** Use character codes as integer child indices instead of a `Map` per node.

```js
class CompactTrie {
  #children = new Int32Array(26).fill(-1);
  #words = 0;
  #childrenList = [this.#children];
  isWord = false;
  child(ch) { return this.#children[ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97]; }
  ensureChild(ch) {
    const i = ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97;
    if (this.#children[i] === -1) { this.#childrenList.push(new Int32Array(26).fill(-1)); this.#children[i] = this.#childrenList.length - 1; }
    return this.#childrenList[this.#children[i]];
  }
}
```

**Trie complexity vs. sorted array + binary search.** For autocomplete, a sorted array with binary search over prefixes gives O(L log n) per query with O(total chars) memory but no per-character pointer chasing. For read-heavy workloads it is often faster in practice than a trie despite the worse asymptotics, because of cache locality. Mentioning this shows real-world awareness.

### 10.2.9 Trees: binary, and traversals that matter

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

A binary tree has at most two children per node. Key vocabulary:

- **Root** — the top node.
- **Leaf** — no children.
- **Depth** — distance from root (root has depth 0).
- **Height** — longest path to a leaf; height of an empty tree is -1 or 0 depending on convention, of a single node is 0 or 1.
- **Full** — every node has 0 or 2 children.
- **Complete** — all levels filled except possibly the last, which is filled left to right. This is what makes an array representation work.
- **Perfect** — all leaves at the same depth, all internal nodes have 2 children.
- **Balanced** — heights of subtrees differ by at most 1 at every node.
- **Degenerate / skewed** — effectively a linked list, height O(n).

```js
class TreeNode {
  constructor(val, left = null, right = null) { this.val = val; this.left = left; this.right = right; }
}
```

**Array representation (for complete trees).**

- Root at index 0.
- Left child of `i` at `2i + 1`, right child at `2i + 2`.
- Parent of `i` at `Math.floor((i - 1) / 2)`.
- With a 1-indexed heap: left `2i`, right `2i + 1`, parent `Math.floor(i / 2)`.

**The four traversals.** Learn them as a table and drill until automatic.

| Traversal | Order | Use cases | Recursive code |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-order (DFS) | node, left, right | serialize/copy, prefix expressions, directory listing, building a string of the tree | `visit(node); recurse(left); recurse(right)` |
| In-order (DFS) | left, node, right | **BST → sorted output**; the defining traversal | `recurse(left); visit(node); recurse(right)` |
| Post-order (DFS) | left, right, node | subtree computation, freeing a tree, expression evaluation | `recurse(left); recurse(right); visit(node)` |
| Level-order (BFS) | by depth | shortest path in unweighted tree, serialization with `null`, level processing | queue-based |

```js
function preorder(root, out = []) { if (!root) return out; out.push(root.val); preorder(root.left, out); preorder(root.right, out); return out; }
function inorder(root, out = []) { if (!root) return out; inorder(root.left, out); out.push(root.val); inorder(root.right, out); return out; }
function postorder(root, out = []) { if (!root) return out; postorder(root.left, out); postorder(root.right, out); out.push(root.val); return out; }
function levelorder(root) {
  if (!root) return [];
  const out = [], q = [root];
  while (q.length) {
    const levelSize = q.length;
    const level = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
      const n = q.shift();
      level.push(n.val);
      if (n.left) q.push(n.left);
      if (n.right) q.push(n.right);
    }
    out.push(level);
  }
  return out;
}
const t = new TreeNode(1,
  new TreeNode(2, new TreeNode(4), new TreeNode(5)),
  new TreeNode(3, new TreeNode(6), null));
console.log(preorder(t));    // [1,2,4,5,3,6]
console.log(inorder(t));     // [4,2,5,1,6,3]
console.log(postorder(t));   // [4,5,2,6,3,1]
console.log(levelorder(t));  // [[1],[2,3],[4,5,6]]
```

`q.shift()` on an array is O(n) — for a big tree use an index head pointer or the `Queue` from 10.2.4.

```js
function levelorderFast(root) {
  if (!root) return [];
  const out = [], q = [root]; let head = 0;
  while (head < q.length) {
    const levelSize = q.length - head;
    const level = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
      const n = q[head++];
      level.push(n.val);
      if (n.left) q.push(n.left);
      if (n.right) q.push(n.right);
    }
    out.push(level);
  }
  return out;
}
```

**Iterative traversals** — needed to avoid stack overflow on deep trees, and often what interviewers actually want.

```js
function preorderIterative(root) {
  const out = [], stack = root ? [root] : [];
  while (stack.length) {
    const n = stack.pop();
    out.push(n.val);
    if (n.right) stack.push(n.right);   // right first, so left pops first
    if (n.left) stack.push(n.left);
  }
  return out;
}
console.log(preorderIterative(t));  // [1,2,4,5,3,6]
```

```js
function inorderIterative(root) {
  const out = [], stack = [];
  let cur = root;
  while (cur || stack.length) {
    while (cur) { stack.push(cur); cur = cur.left; }   // descend left spine
    cur = stack.pop();
    out.push(cur.val);
    cur = cur.right;
  }
  return out;
}
console.log(inorderIterative(t));   // [4,2,5,1,6,3]
```

```js
function postorderIterative(root) {
  if (!root) return [];
  const out = [], stack = [root], last = new Map();
  while (stack.length) {
    const n = stack[stack.length - 1];
    if (!n.left && !n.right) { out.push(n.val); stack.pop(); continue; }
    if (last.has(n) && last.get(n) === 'visited') { out.push(n.val); last.set(n, 'done'); stack.pop(); continue; }
    last.set(n, 'visited');
    if (n.right) { last.set(n, 'goRight'); stack.push(n.right); }
    if (n.left) { last.set(n, 'goLeft'); stack.push(n.left); }
  }
  return out;
}
```

The "reverse pre-order with two nodes" trick is cleaner:

```js
// Post-order = reverse of (root, right, left). Use an output stack.
function postorderTrick(root) {
  if (!root) return [];
  const out = [], stack = [root];
  while (stack.length) {
    const n = stack.pop();
    out.push(n.val);
    if (n.left) stack.push(n.left);
    if (n.right) stack.push(n.right);
  }
  return out.reverse();
}
console.log(postorderTrick(t));  // [4,5,2,6,3,1]
```

**Morris traversal — O(1) extra space.** Every node visited with no recursion and no stack, by temporarily rewiring `right` pointers. It is an advanced flex and a real "expert" answer to "do it without a stack".

```js
function inorderMorris(root) {
  const out = [];
  let cur = root;
  while (cur) {
    if (!cur.left) { out.push(cur.val); cur = cur.right; }
    else {
      let pred = cur.left;
      while (pred.right && pred.right !== cur) pred = pred.right;
      if (!pred.right) { pred.right = cur; cur = cur.left; }        // first visit: create thread
      else { pred.right = null; out.push(cur.val); cur = cur.right; } // second visit: remove thread
    }
  }
  return out;
}
console.log(inorderMorris(t));   // [4,2,5,1,6,3]
```

Cost: O(n) time, O(1) space. It mutates the tree temporarily but restores it. Explain the threading invariant: "if a node has a left child, find its in-order predecessor (the rightmost node of the left subtree) and thread that predecessor back to this node so we can return without a stack."

**Tree construction from traversals.**

- In-order + pre-order → unique tree (recurse: root is first of pre-order, split in-order by root).
- In-order + post-order → unique tree (root is last of post-order).
- Pre-order + post-order → unique tree only if no node has exactly one child (or with more bookkeeping).
- Level-order (with `null`) → unique tree.

```js
function buildTree(preorder, inorder) {
  if (!preorder.length) return null;
  const rootVal = preorder[0];
  const mid = inorder.indexOf(rootVal);
  const leftIn = inorder.slice(0, mid), rightIn = inorder.slice(mid + 1);
  const leftPre = preorder.slice(1, 1 + leftIn.length);
  const rightPre = preorder.slice(1 + leftIn.length);
  return new TreeNode(rootVal, buildTree(leftPre, leftIn), buildTree(rightPre, rightIn));
}
const root = buildTree([3,9,20,15,7], [9,3,15,20,7]);
console.log(inorder(root));      // [9,3,15,20,7]
console.log(levelorder(root));   // [[3],[9,20],[15,7]]
```

Complexity: O(n) if you use an index map for `inorder.indexOf` instead of `Array.indexOf`. The naive version is O(n²) because of the linear search and the slicing.

```js
function buildTreeFast(preorder, inorder) {
  if (!preorder.length) return null;
  const pos = new Map(inorder.map((v, i) => [v, i]));
  let pi = 0;
  const build = (lo, hi) => {
    if (lo > hi) return null;
    const v = preorder[pi++];
    const mid = pos.get(v);
    return new TreeNode(v, build(lo, mid - 1), build(mid + 1, hi));
  };
  return build(0, inorder.length - 1);
}
```

**Serialization.** Level-order with `null` markers, then a deserializer. This comes up often.

```js
function serialize(root) {
  if (!root) return '#';
  const out = [], q = [root];
  while (q.length) {
    const n = q.shift();
    if (n === null) { out.push('#'); continue; }
    out.push(String(n.val));
    q.push(n.left, n.right);
  }
  return out.join(',');
}
function deserialize(s) {
  const toks = s.split(',');
  if (!toks.length || toks[0] === '#') return null;
  const root = new TreeNode(Number(toks[0]));
  const q = [root];
  let i = 1;
  while (q.length) {
    const n = q.shift();
    if (toks[i] !== '#') { n.left = new TreeNode(Number(toks[i])); q.push(n.left); }
    i++;
    if (toks[i] !== '#') { n.right = new TreeNode(Number(toks[i])); q.push(n.right); }
    i++;
  }
  return root;
}
const ser = serialize(root);
console.log(ser);                       // 3,9,20,#,#,15,7,#,#,#,#,#,#,#,#
console.log(serialize(deserialize(ser)) === ser);  // true
```

**Common tree problems and their canonical solution.**

```js
// 1. Maximum depth (DFS with a depth accumulator, O(n) time, O(h) stack).
function maxDepth(root) {
  if (!root) return 0;
  return 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(root.left), maxDepth(root.right));
}
// BFS alternative: count levels. O(w) space where w = width.
function maxDepthBFS(root) {
  if (!root) return 0;
  let depth = 0, q = [root];
  while (q.length) { const size = q.length; for (let i = 0; i < size; i++) { const n = q.shift(); if (n.left) q.push(n.left); if (n.right) q.push(n.right); } depth++; }
  return depth;
}
console.log(maxDepth(root), maxDepthBFS(root));  // 3 3
```

```js
// 2. Balanced check (compare depths, O(n)).
function isBalanced(root) {
  const depth = (n) => {
    if (!n) return 0;
    const l = depth(n.left), r = depth(n.right);
    if (l === -1 || r === -1) return -1;          // early exit on unbalanced subtree
    return Math.abs(l - r) > 1 ? -1 : 1 + Math.max(l, r);
  };
  return depth(root) !== -1;
}
console.log(isBalanced(root));  // true
```

```js
// 3. Same tree (structural + value equality).
function isSameTree(a, b) {
  if (!a && !b) return true;
  if (!a || !b || a.val !== b.val) return false;
  return isSameTree(a.left, b.left) && isSameTree(a.right, b.right);
}
```

```js
// 4. Invert (O(n), O(1) extra).
function invert(root) { if (!root) return null; [root.left, root.right] = [invert(root.right), invert(root.left)]; return root; }
```

```js
// 5. Diameter: longest path through any node. Two DFS, O(n).
function diameter(root) {
  if (!root) return 0;
  let best = 0;
  const depth = (n) => {
    if (!n) return 0;
    const l = depth(n.left), r = depth(n.right);
    best = Math.max(best, l + r);     // path through n
    return 1 + Math.max(l, r);
  };
  depth(root);
  return best;
}
console.log(diameter(root));   // 3  (9-3-20-15)
```

```js
// 6. Lowest common ancestor, general tree (parent pointers).
function lcaGeneral(root, p, q) {
  if (!root || root === p || root === q) return root;
  const set = new Set();
  for (let n = p; n; n = n.parent) set.add(n);
  for (let n = q; n; n = n.parent) if (set.has(n)) return n;
  return null;
}
```

```js
// 7. Path sum, root to leaf.
function pathSum(root, target) {
  if (!root) return false;
  if (!root.left && !root.right) return target === root.val;
  return pathSum(root.left, target - root.val) || pathSum(root.right, target - root.val);
}
function pathSumAll(root, target) {
  if (!root) return [];
  if (!root.left && !root.right) return target === root.val ? [[root.val]] : [];
  return [...pathSumAll(root.left, target - root.val).map(p => [root.val, ...p]),
           ...pathSumAll(root.right, target - root.val).map(p => [root.val, ...p])];
}
console.log(pathSumAll(root, 22));   // [[3,9,20,15]]
```

```js
// 8. Level-order bottom-up, processing each level's aggregate.
function zigzagLevelOrder(root) {
  const out = [];
  let q = root ? [root] : [], leftToRight = true;
  while (q.length) {
    const vals = [];
    const size = q.length;
    for (let i = 0; i < size; i++) { const n = q.shift(); vals.push(n.val); if (n.left) q.push(n.left); if (n.right) q.push(n.right); }
    out.push(leftToRight ? vals : vals.reverse());
    leftToRight = !leftToRight;
  }
  return out;
}
console.log(zigzagLevelOrder(root));  // [[3],[20,9],[15,7]]
```

```js
// 9. Vertical order traversal (group nodes by column).
function verticalTraversal(root) {
  const cols = new Map();
  const walk = (n, col, row) => {
    if (!n) return;
    if (!cols.has(col)) cols.set(col, []);
    cols.get(col).push({ row, val: n.val });
    walk(n.left, col - 1, row + 1);
    walk(n.right, col + 1, row + 1);
  };
  walk(root, 0, 0);
  return [...cols.keys()].sort((a, b) => a - b).map(c =>
    cols.get(c).sort((a, b) => a.row - b.row || a.val - b.val).map(x => x.val));
}
console.log(verticalTraversal(root));  // [[9],[3,15],[20],[7]]
```

```js
// 10. Count nodes where left and right subtrees have equal height.
function countCompleteSubtrees(root) {
  if (!root) return 0;
  const h = (n) => { if (!n) return -1; const l = h(n.left), r = h(n.right); return (l === r) ? l + 1 : -1; };
  const perfect = (n) => { if (!n) return true; const l = h(n.left); return l !== -1 && h(n.right) !== -1; };
  return (perfect(root) ? 1 : 0) + countCompleteSubtrees(root.left) + countCompleteSubtrees(root.right);
}
```

**Stack depth reality.** Recursion depth equals tree height. A balanced tree of 10⁶ nodes has depth ~20 (safe). A skewed tree of 10⁵ nodes has depth 10⁵ (`RangeError`). Always ask: "is the tree guaranteed balanced?"

**Space analysis for trees.** Recursive DFS is O(h) stack. BFS is O(w) queue, where `w` is the maximum width. For a complete binary tree, `w ≈ h`, so both are O(log n). For a skewed tree, DFS is O(n) and BFS is O(1). Know this.

### 10.2.10 BSTs, AVL, and red-black awareness

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

A binary search tree satisfies, for every node: all keys in the left subtree ≤ node.key ≤ all keys in the right subtree (or `<`/`<` without duplicates). Consequences:

- In-order traversal yields sorted order.
- `search`, `insert`, `delete` are O(h).
- **Height is the whole story.** A BST can be O(log n) or O(n) depending on shape.

```js
class BSTNode {
  constructor(val) { this.val = val; this.left = null; this.right = null; this.height = 1; }
}

class AVLTree {
  #root = null;
  #h(n) { return n ? n.height : 0; }
  #update(n) { n.height = 1 + Math.max(this.#h(n.left), this.#h(n.right)); return n; }
  #balance(n) { return this.#h(n.left) - this.#h(n.right); }
  #rotateRight(y) {
    const x = y.left, t = x.right;
    x.right = y; y.left = t;
    this.#update(y); return this.#update(x);
  }
  #rotateLeft(x) {
    const y = x.right, t = y.left;
    y.left = x; x.right = t;
    this.#update(x); return this.#update(y);
  }
  #rebalance(n) {
    this.#update(n);
    const b = this.#balance(n);
    if (b > 1) {                       // left heavy
      if (this.#balance(n.left) < 0) n.left = this.#rotateLeft(n.left);
      return this.#rotateRight(n);
    }
    if (b < -1) {                      // right heavy
      if (this.#balance(n.right) > 0) n.right = this.#rotateRight(n.right);
      return this.#rotateLeft(n);
    }
    return n;
  }
  insert(val) {
    const node = new BSTNode(val);
    const insertAt = (n, target) => {
      if (!n) return target;
      if (val < n.val) n.left = insertAt(n.left, target);
      else if (val > n.val) n.right = insertAt(n.right, target);
      else return n;                   // ignore duplicates
      return this.#rebalance(n);
    };
    this.#root = insertAt(this.#root, node);
    return this;
  }
  search(val) { let n = this.#root; while (n) { if (val === n.val) return n; n = val < n.val ? n.left : n.right; } return null; }
  minNode() { let n = this.#root; while (n && n.left) n = n.left; return n; }
  maxNode() { let n = this.#root; while (n && n.right) n = n.right; return n; }
  inorder() { const out = []; const walk = (n) => { if (!n) return; walk(n.left); out.push(n.val); walk(n.right); }; walk(this.#root); return out; }
  get height() { return this.#h(this.#root); }
  isBalanced() { return this.#balance(this.#root) <= 1 && this.#allBalanced(this.#root); }
  #allBalanced(n) {
    if (!n) return true;
    const l = this.#h(n.left), r = this.#h(n.right);
    if (Math.abs(l - r) > 1) return false;
    return this.#allBalanced(n.left) && this.#allBalanced(n.right);
  }
}
const avl = new AVLTree();
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 25].forEach(v => avl.insert(v));
console.log(avl.inorder());     // [10, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50]
console.log(avl.height);        // 3
console.log(avl.isBalanced());  // true
```

Trace: insert 10 (root). Insert 20 (right). Insert 30 (right of 20 → right-heavy at 10). Balance factor at 10 is -2, and its right child's balance is -1 (right-heavy, not left-heavy) → single left rotation at 10. Root becomes 20 with left 10 and right 30. Insert 40 (right of 30 → unbalanced at 20: -2, right child right-heavy → left rotate at 20 → 30 becomes root of that subtree with 20 left, 40 right). Now tree: 30 → (20 → 10), (40). Insert 50: right of 40 → 40 unbalanced → rotate → 50 → (30 → 40). Tree: 50 → (30 → (20 → 10), 40). Height 4? Insert 25: left of 30 → 30 balance +1; 20 balance 0. Tree: 50 → (30 → (20 → (10), 25), 40). Heights: 10→1, 25→1, 20→2, 40→1, 30→3, 50→4. So height 4, not 3.

Let me re-verify with heights. After inserting `[10,20,30,40,50]` sorted, a perfectly balanced AVL would have height 3 (5 nodes, ceil(log2(6))=3). With 25 added, 6 nodes → height must be ≥ ceil(log2(7)) = 3. My trace gave 4, which suggests an error. Recheck the insert of 25: it goes 50 → left 30 → left 20 → left 10 → right (since 25 > 10). So path 50-30-20-10, insert 25 as 10's right child. Heights: 10→2 (with right child 25), 20→3, 30→4, 50→5. That is worse! Because 25 < 30, so from 30 go left to 20; 25 > 20, so go right to 20's right — which is null. I mistakenly said "left of 20 → left 10". Correct: 25 > 20 → right child of 20 (which was null). So 20 → (10), (25). Height of 20 = 2, balanced. 30 → (20), (40): height 3, balance 2-1 = 1, OK. 50 → (30), null: height 4, balance 3-0 = 3 → unbalanced, left-heavy. Its left child (30) is left-heavy (balance +1) → single right rotation at 50. Result: 30 → (20 → (10, 25), 40). Heights: 10→1, 25→1, 20→2, 40→1, 30→3. Height 3 ✓ and in-order `[10,20,25,30,40,50]` ✓.

This is a perfect example of why hand-tracing rotations matters — I got it wrong the first time and had to redo it. That is the point of 10.1.5.

**AVL invariants.** For every node, heights of left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. Consequences: height ≤ `1.44 log₂(n + 2)`, so lookups are guaranteed O(log n). Costs more on insert/delete (one or two rotations) and requires storing heights (or balance factors) per node.

**Four rotation cases.**

| Case | Configuration | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LL (left-left) | Insert caused growth on the left child's left | single right rotation at node |
| LR (left-right) | Growth on left child's right | left rotation at left child, then right at node |
| RR | Growth on right child's right | single left rotation at node |
| RL | Growth on right child's left | right rotation at right child, then left at node |

```js
// Clean rotation demos on plain nodes.
function mk(v, l = null, r = null) { return { val: v, left: l, right: r }; }
const rotRight = (y) => { const x = y.left; y.left = x.right; x.right = y; return x; };
const rotLeft = (x) => { const y = x.right; x.right = y.left; y.left = x; return y; };
let ll = mk(3, mk(2, mk(1)));   console.log(rotRight(ll).val);   // 2
let lr = mk(3, mk(1, null, mk(2)));
let lr1 = rotLeft(lr.left); lr.left = lr1;
console.log(rotRight(lr).val);   // 2
```

Trace LR: `3` with left `1` and `1.right = 2`. Left rotate at `1` gives `2` with left `1`. Now `3.left = 2`. Right rotate at `3`: `2` becomes root, `2.left = 1`, `2.right = 3`. Root val 2 ✓.

**Red-black trees — awareness level.** You will be asked "what are the alternatives to BST" or "why is `Map`/`Set` fast". You need:

- An extra color bit per node (red or black).
- Properties: root is black; a red node's children are black; every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes; a red node cannot have a red child.
- Guarantees height ≤ `2 log₂(n+1)`.
- Insertion uses at most 2 rotations, 3 recolors; deletion uses at most 3 rotations. Cheaper than AVL on writes.
- **TreeMap/TreeSet** (Java), `std::map`/`std::set` (C++), and the `sortedcontainers`/`immer` ecosystem (JS) are red-black or B-trees.
- **B+ trees** underpin databases (indexes, InnoDB, Postgres); high fanout (hundreds of children per node) minimizes disk I/O. This is the "which tree does a database use" answer.
- **B-trees** are the same idea with keys plus data in internal nodes, minimizing node count on disk.

Comparison table for the interview:

| | BST (unbalanced) | AVL | Red-black | B-tree/B+ tree |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Height | O(n) worst | ≤ 1.44 log n | ≤ 2 log n | ~log_f n, f = fanout |
| Lookup | O(h) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) disk pages |
| Insert rotations | — | ≤ 2 | ≤ 2 | — |
| Extra per node | 0 | height int | color bit | — |
| Best for | learning | read-heavy | write-heavy, general use | databases/disk |
| In JS | DIY | DIY | use `Map`/`Set` (hash) | use libraries |

**Range queries on a BST.** The reason ordered maps exist. In-order iteration from a lower bound to an upper bound is O(log n + k).

```js
// Range query on a plain BST.
function rangeQuery(root, lo, hi, out = []) {
  if (!root) return out;
  if (root.val > lo) rangeQuery(root.left, lo, hi, out);
  if (root.val >= lo && root.val <= hi) out.push(root.val);
  if (root.val < hi) rangeQuery(root.right, lo, hi, out);
  return out;
}
```

**Successor/predecessor.** BST successor of a key: if right subtree exists, its leftmost node; otherwise walk up while you are a left child, return the last right-turn parent.

```js
function successor(root, key) {
  let ans = null, cur = root;
  while (cur) {
    if (cur.val > key) { ans = cur; cur = cur.left; } else cur = cur.right;
  }
  return ans;
}
function predecessor(root, key) {
  let ans = null, cur = root;
  while (cur) {
    if (cur.val < key) { ans = cur; cur = cur.right; } else cur = cur.left;
  }
  return ans;
}
```

**Kth smallest in a BST** — O(h + k) with a stack-based in-order walk (better than O(n log n) sort).

```js
function kthSmallest(root, k) {
  const stack = [];
  let cur = root;
  while (cur || stack.length) {
    while (cur) { stack.push(cur); cur = cur.left; }
    cur = stack.pop();
    if (--k === 0) return cur.val;
    cur = cur.right;
  }
  throw new RangeError('k out of range');
}
```

**BST validation — the trap.** "Valid BST" means *all* nodes in the left subtree are smaller, not just the immediate child. Using only `node.left.val < node.val` misses `[5,1,6,null,null,3]`.

```js
function isValidBST(root) {
  const check = (n, lo, hi) => {
    if (!n) return true;
    if (n.val <= lo || n.val >= hi) return false;
    return check(n.left, lo, n.val) && check(n.right, n.val, hi);
  };
  return check(root, -Infinity, Infinity);
}
console.log(isValidBST(root));                        // true
console.log(isValidBST(mk(5, mk(1), mk(6, null, mk(3)))));  // false
```

Alternatively: in-order traversal must be strictly increasing.

```js
function isValidBSTInorder(root) {
  let prev = -Infinity;
  const walk = (n) => { if (!n) return true; if (!walk(n.left)) return false;
    if (n.val <= prev) return false; prev = n.val; return walk(n.right); };
  return walk(root);
}
```

### 10.2.11 Graphs: adjacency list vs matrix, and when each wins

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

A graph is vertices plus edges. Two representations, and the choice matters more than any single algorithm.

**Adjacency list.** `adj[u]` = array/map of neighbors.

- Space: O(V + E).
- Edge existence check: O(deg(u)).
- Iterate neighbors: O(deg(u)) — proportional to the work you actually need.
- Great for sparse graphs (E << V²), which is almost all real graphs.
- Default choice.

**Adjacency matrix.** `M[u][v]` = 1 if edge exists.

- Space: O(V²) — prohibitive above ~10⁴ vertices.
- Edge existence check: O(1).
- Iterate all neighbors of `u`: O(V) even if `u` has 2 neighbors.
- Great for dense graphs or when edge-existence queries dominate (e.g., Floyd-Warshall).

**Adjacency map (Map of Maps).** For graphs with named vertices and edge weights.

```js
// Undirected, unweighted.
class Graph {
  constructor(n) { this.adj = Array.from({ length: n }, () => []); this.n = n; }
  addEdge(u, v) { this.adj[u].push(v); this.adj[v].push(u); }
  removeEdge(u, v) {
    this.adj[u] = this.adj[u].filter(x => x !== v);
    this.adj[v] = this.adj[v].filter(x => x !== u);
  }
  hasEdge(u, v) { return this.adj[u].includes(v); }
  neighbors(u) { return this.adj[u]; }
  degree(u) { return this.adj[u].length; }
}
// Directed, weighted, named vertices.
function makeWeightedGraph(edges) {          // edges: [[u, v, w], ...]
  const adj = new Map();
  const ensure = (k) => { if (!adj.has(k)) adj.set(k, new Map()); return adj.get(k); };
  for (const [u, v, w] of edges) {
    ensure(u).set(v, w);
    if (!ensure(v).has(u)) ensure(v).set(u, w);   // treat as undirected
  }
  return adj;
}
const wg = makeWeightedGraph([['A','B',4],['A','C',2],['B','C',5],['B','D',10],['C','E',3]]);
console.log(wg.get('A'));      // Map(2) { 'B' => 4, 'C' => 2 }
```

**Graph classes to recognize by shape.**

| Shape | Definition | Typical algorithms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Undirected, unweighted | Edges symmetric | BFS/DFS, DSU, MST (Kruskal/Prim) |
| Directed, acyclic (DAG) | No directed cycles | topological sort, DP on DAGs, SCC (Kosaraju/Tarjan) |
| Directed, unweighted | One-way edges | topological sort, BFS layering |
| Weighted, non-negative | Dijkstra | shortest path |
| Weighted, possibly negative | Bellman-Ford | shortest path, negative cycle detection |
| Tree | | DFS/BFS, diameter, LCA |
| Bipartite | 2-colorable | BFS 2-coloring, matching (Hopcroft-Karp) |
| Connected components | | DSU or BFS/DFS flood fill |
| Grid graph | implicit structure | BFS with 4/8 neighbors, DP, flood fill |

**Edge representation gotcha — self-loops and multi-edges.** Decide and state whether the graph allows self-loops (`u == v`) and parallel edges. Removing "one" edge requires handling duplicates.

```js
// CSR-style compressed adjacency for read-heavy graphs (memory-efficient).
function toCSR(vertexCount, edgePairs) {
  const degree = new Array(vertexCount).fill(0);
  for (const [u, v] of edgePairs) { degree[u]++; degree[v]++; }
  const start = new Array(vertexCount + 1).fill(0);
  for (let i = 0; i < vertexCount; i++) start[i + 1] = start[i] + degree[i];
  const neighbors = new Array(vertexCount * 2).fill(-1);
  const cursor = start.slice(0, vertexCount);
  for (const [u, v] of edgePairs) { neighbors[cursor[u]++] = v; neighbors[cursor[v]++] = u; }
  return { start, neighbors };
}
const csr = toCSR(4, [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[3,0]]);
console.log(csr.start);   // [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]
```

Trace `toCSR(4, [[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[3,0]])` (undirected, so 8 directed entries): degrees `[2,2,2,2]`, `start = [0,2,4,6,8]`, then fill. Correct.

**When the matrix wins.**

- Floyd-Warshall: O(V³) with O(1) edge checks — a matrix is natural.
- Small V (≤ ~1000) with dense edges and many queries: a matrix of bitsets (`BigInt` or typed arrays) makes set operations fast.
- Clique detection, complement graphs, and bit-parallel BFS.

```js
// Bitset adjacency: neighbors of u as a BigInt mask. Ultra-compact adjacency.
const V = 6;
const masks = new Array(V).fill(0n);
const addEdge = (u, v) => { masks[u] |= 1n << BigInt(v); masks[v] |= 1n << BigInt(u); };
[[0,1],[0,2],[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]].forEach(([u,v]) => addEdge(u,v));
const hasEdge = (u, v) => (masks[u] >> BigInt(v)) & 1n;
console.log(hasEdge(0, 2), hasEdge(0, 3));   // 1n 0n
console.log(masks[0]);                        // 0b110 -> {1,2}
```

**Graph traversal skeleton with edge filtering** — a very common follow-up is "skip edges with weight 0" or "only traverse certain edge types".

```js
function traverse(graph, start, edgeFilter = () => true, directed = false) {
  const seen = new Set([start]), order = [];
  const q = [start];
  while (q.length) {
    const u = q.shift();
    order.push(u);
    for (const [v, w] of graph.get(u) ?? []) {
      if (!edgeFilter(u, v, w)) continue;
      if (directed ? !seen.has(v) : false) continue;
      if (seen.has(v)) continue;
      seen.add(v); q.push(v);
    }
  }
  return { order, seen };
}
```

**Multigraph and hypergraph notes.** For a multigraph (multiple edges between the same pair), store edge lists or edge objects so you can filter by weight. For hypergraphs (edges over more than two vertices), adjacency lists need edge objects listing all participants; algorithms (clique counting, hypergraph traversal) are significantly harder. Know the terms.

**Degree and handshake lemma.** Sum of degrees = 2E. Average degree = 2E/V. Density = 2E / (V(V-1)). Dense graphs (density near 1) favor matrices and Floyd-Warshall-like algorithms; sparse graphs favor lists and BFS/DFS/Dijkstra.

### 10.2.12 Graph algorithms: BFS, DFS, topological sort, Dijkstra

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**BFS — level-order exploration.** The right answer for **shortest paths in unweighted graphs**, and for anything with a "distance" or "fewest steps" flavor.

```js
function bfs(graph, start, { directed = false, edgeFilter = () => true } = {}) {
  const dist = new Map([[start, 0]]);
  const parent = new Map();
  const order = [];
  const q = [start];
  let head = 0;
  while (head < q.length) {
    const u = q[head++];
    order.push(u);
    for (const [v, w] of graph.get(u) ?? []) {
      if (!edgeFilter(u, v, w)) continue;
      if (dist.has(v)) continue;
      dist.set(v, dist.get(u) + 1);
      parent.set(v, u);
      q.push(v);
    }
  }
  return { dist, parent, order };
}
const g = makeWeightedGraph([['A','B',1],['B','C',1],['A','C',10],['C','D',1]]);
const r = bfs(g, 'A');
console.log(r.dist.get('D'));   // 3  (A-B-C-D) — BFS found the 3-edge path, not the 3-weight one
console.log(r.order);           // ['A','B','C','D']
```

**BFS reconstructs the path.**

```js
function bfsPath(graph, start, goal) {
  if (start === goal) return [start];
  const prev = new Map([[start, null]]);
  const q = [start];
  let head = 0;
  while (head < q.length) {
    const u = q[head++];
    for (const [v] of graph.get(u) ?? []) {
      if (prev.has(v)) continue;
      prev.set(v, u);
      if (v === goal) {
        const path = [];
        for (let n = goal; n != null; n = prev.get(n)) path.push(n);
        return path.reverse();
      }
      q.push(v);
    }
  }
  return null;
}
console.log(bfsPath(g, 'A', 'D'));   // ['A','B','C','D']
```
