## Exercise 6 — Work-Stealing Sketch

⚫ Expert · **Must-know** (recognize and explain; you will rarely be asked to write one from scratch)

**Statement.** Sketch a work-stealing pool: per-worker deques, owner pushes/pops locally (LIFO), idle workers steal from the oldest end (FIFO) of a victim. Explain why it scales where a shared queue does not, and where it breaks down.

### Solution

```js
'use strict';

/**
 * Chase-Lev style deque (bounded, circular array). The owner may operate on both
 * ends with a single atomic index; thieves only touch the far end.
 * This asymmetry is the entire trick: the common case is uncontended.
 */
class ChaseLevDeque {
  #buf; #mask; #top = 0; #bottom = 0; #cap;

  constructor(capacity = 1024) {
    this.#cap = 1 << Math.ceil(Math.log2(capacity));
    this.#buf = new Array(this.#cap);
    this.#mask = this.#cap - 1;
  }
  get length() { return this.#bottom - this.#top; }

  // Owner-only: push onto the "bottom" (LIFO end).
  pushBottom(task) {
    const b = this.#bottom;
    const n = b + 1;
    if (n - this.#top > this.#cap) this.#grow();
    this.#buf[b & this.#mask] = task;
    // In C this is a release store so thieves see the task before the index bump.
    this.#bottom = n;
  }

  // Owner-only: take from the bottom (LIFO => best cache locality for recursion).
  popBottom() {
    const b = this.#bottom - 1;
    this.#bottom = b;
    if (b < this.#top) { this.#bottom = b + 1; return undefined; }   // was empty
    const task = this.#buf[b & this.#mask];
    if (b - this.#top > 1) return task;                              // more than one left
    // Last element: race with thieves. CAS on the index decides the winner.
    if (this.#top !== b) { this.#bottom = b + 1; return task; }       // no thief got it
    this.#top = b + 1;
    this.#bottom = b + 1;
    return task;
  }

  // Thief-only: take from the top (FIFO => oldest task, lowest wait time).
  steal() {
    const t = this.#top;
    if (t >= this.#bottom) return undefined;                          // empty
    if (t + 1 > this.#bottom - t - 1) return undefined;               // heuristic: try stealing
    const task = this.#buf[t & this.#mask];
    if (this.#top === t) this.#top = t + 1;                            // single-threaded fallback
    return task;
  }

  #grow() {
    const next = 1 << (Math.log2(this.#cap) + 1);
    const b = new Array(next);
    for (let i = this.#top; i < this.#bottom; i++) b[i & (next - 1)] = this.#buf[i & this.#mask];
    this.#buf = b; this.#cap = next; this.#mask = next - 1;
  }
}

class WorkStealingPool {
  #deques; #n; #idleSleepMs; #stolen = 0; #completed = 0; #maxQueue = 0;

  constructor(n, { idleSleepMs = 0 } = {}) {
    this.#n = n;
    this.#idleSleepMs = idleSleepMs;
    this.#deques = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new ChaseLevDeque());
  }
  get stats() {
    const depths = this.#deques.map((d) => d.length);
    return { stolen: this.#stolen, completed: this.#completed, depths, maxQueue: this.#maxQueue };
  }

  submit(task) {
    const owner = this.#pickOwner();
    this.#deques[owner].pushBottom(task);
    this.#maxQueue = Math.max(this.#maxQueue, this.#deques[owner].length);
    return owner;
  }

  // Round-robin owner choice, starting from a random offset so hot producers do
  // not all hammer worker 0 (the "owner locality" property).
  #pickOwner() { return Math.floor(Math.random() * this.#n); }

  runUntilEmpty() {
    for (;;) {
      let progressed = false;
      for (let id = 0; id < this.#n; id++) {
        let task = this.#deques[id].popBottom();          // LIFO: own work first
        while (task) {
          task.run();
          this.#completed++;
          progressed = true;
          // Fork-join: while running, push children onto our OWN deque.
          if (task.children) for (const c of task.children) this.#deques[id].pushBottom(c);
          task = this.#deques[id].popBottom();
        }
        // Idle: steal from the most loaded victim (top end = oldest tasks).
        for (let k = 1; k < this.#n; k++) {
          const victim = (id + k) % this.#n;
          const stolen = this.#deques[victim].steal();     // FIFO: oldest first
          if (stolen) {
            this.#stolen++;
            stolen.run();
            this.#completed++;
            progressed = true;
            break;
          }
        }
      }
      if (!progressed) return this.stats;
    }
  }
}

// ---------- demo + a comparison against a shared queue ----------
function sumTask(n, acc = { v: 0 }) {
  return { run: () => { for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) acc.v += i; } };
}
function forkJoin(n, acc = { v: 0 }) {
  if (n < 50_000) { for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) acc.v += i; return acc; }
  const half = n >> 1;
  const a = { v: 0 }, b = { v: 0 };
  return {
    children: [forkJoin(half, a), forkJoin(n - half, b)],
    run: () => { acc.v = a.v + b.v; },
  };
}

function sharedQueueComparison(n) {
  // The contended version: one array, one implicit lock (here, one JS thread).
  const q = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) q.push(i);
  const t0 = Date.now();
  let sum = 0;
  while (q.length) sum += q.pop();
  return { ms: Date.now() - t0, sum };
}

function workStealingRun(taskCount, leaf = 20_000) {
  const pool = new WorkStealingPool(4);
  const root = forkJoin(taskCount * leaf);
  pool.submit(root);
  return pool.runUntilEmpty();
}

console.log('Exercise 6: work-stealing sketch');
console.log('  fork-join via work stealing:', workStealingRun(400));
console.log('  single shared queue baseline:', sharedQueueComparison(400 * 20_000));

// Why it scales and where it breaks, in one paragraph each:
// SCALES: the common operation (owner pop) touches only that worker's own index
//   and array. No other core writes that cache line. A shared queue makes every
//   core contend on ONE cache line for every single task; throughput plateaus at
//   roughly a few million tasks/second no matter how many cores you add.
// BREAKS DOWN: tasks must be independent and small. If a task blocks (IO, a lock),
//   a stealing pool degrades badly unless it has real OS threads with blocking
//   parks (which is exactly why Go's goroutines, the JVM's ForkJoinPool, and
//   Rust's Rayon all pair work stealing WITH blocking-aware scheduling).
// Also: fairness is approximate, ordering is LIFO-within-worker, and
//   cancellation and error propagation are harder than with a shared queue.
```

### Follow-ups

- **Why LIFO for the owner and FIFO for thieves?** Owner-side LIFO maximises cache locality (the child task just pushed is hottest) and gives depth-first execution, which is what fork-join recursion wants. Thief-side FIFO gives the *oldest* task to the idle worker, minimising wait time and preventing starvation of old work.
- **What is the CAS in `popBottom` for?** When the owner takes the last element, a thief may be taking the same one; the CAS decides the single winner so exactly one of them runs it.
- **How do real runtimes handle blocking?** Hybrid schedulers (Go, Kotlin coroutines, Rust Tokio with `spawn_blocking`) move blocked work off the work-stealing queue onto an OS-thread pool and re-inject it. This is the key design decision in every production runtime.
- **How does this compare to a thread pool for CPU work?** Same fan-out; the difference is queue contention and locality, which dominate at high core counts.

### Interview traps

1. **Writing a shared queue and calling it work stealing.**
2. **Forgetting that the deque must be bounded or grown safely** (a growing array reallocated while a thief reads it is a data race).
3. **Ignoring the owner/thief asymmetry**, which is the entire performance argument.
4. **Not mentioning what happens when a task blocks.** This is the follow-up that separates recognition from understanding.

## Exercise 7 — File-Descriptor Exhaustion Reproduction

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Statement.** Reproduce fd exhaustion in a Node process, diagnose it with `/proc`, explain `EMFILE` vs `ENFILE`, then fix it with connection limits, idle timeouts, proper `destroy()`, and raised limits. Then demonstrate the difference between raising the limit and fixing the leak.

### Solution

```js
'use strict';
const assert = require('node:assert/strict');
const fs = require('node:fs');
const net = require('node:net');
const { once } = require('node:events');

// ---------- diagnostics ----------
function fdRows(pid = process.pid) {
  const dir = `/proc/${pid}/fd`;
  let names;
  try { names = fs.readdirSync(dir); } catch { return { error: 'no /proc (not Linux?)' }; }
  const rows = [];
  for (const fd of names) {
    let target;
    try { target = fs.readlinkSync(`${dir}/${fd}`); } catch { target = '<vanished>'; }
    rows.push({ fd: Number(fd), target });
  }
  return { rows };
}
function fdSummary(pid = process.pid) {
  const { rows } = fdRows(pid);
  if (!rows) return rows;
  const byKind = new Map();
  for (const { target } of rows) {
    const kind = target.replace(/\[\d+\]/g, '[*]');      // normalise inode numbers
    byKind.set(kind, (byKind.get(kind) ?? 0) + 1);
  }
  return {
    total: rows.length,
    sockets: rows.filter((r) => r.target.starts?.('socket:')).length,
    pipes: rows.filter((r) => r.target.startsWith('pipe:')).length,
    anonInodes: rows.filter((r) => r.target.startsWith('anon_inode:')).length,
    files: rows.filter((r) => /^\//.test(r.target)).length,
    topKinds: [...byKind].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, 5),
  };
}
function fdLimits(pid = process.pid) {
  try {
    const txt = fs.readFileSync(`/proc/${pid}/limits`, 'utf8');
    const line = txt.split('\n').find((l) => l.includes('open files'));
    const [, soft, hard] = line.match(/(\d+)\s+(\d+)/) ?? [];
    return { soft: Number(soft), hard: Number(hard) };
  } catch { return null; }
}

// ---------- (a) The reproduction ----------
// Opens sockets that fail to connect but still consume an fd each. On a machine
// with a low limit this reaches EMFILE within seconds.
async function reproduceExhaustion({ target = { host: '127.0.0.1', port: 1 } } = {}) {
  const held = [];
  let code = 'ok';
  let iterations = 0;
  for (; iterations < 200_000; iterations++) {
    const s = net.connect(target);
    await once(s, 'error').catch(() => {});   // ENOTFOUND/ECONNREFUSED is fine; the fd is real
    held.push(s);                              // deliberately NOT destroyed: this is the leak
    if (held.length % 500 === 0) {
      const sum = fdSummary();
      process.stdout.write(`\r  fds=${sum.total} (sockets ${sum.sockets})  `);
    }
    if (held.length > 0 && held.length % 200 === 0) {
      // Probe: does anything fail now?
      const probe = net.connect(target);
      const [err] = await once(probe, 'error').then(([e]) => [e], () => [null]);
      probe.destroy();
      if (err && ['EMFILE', 'ENFILE', 'ENOBUFS', 'ENOMEM'].includes(err.code)) { code = err.code; break; }
    }
  }
  return { code, iterations, limits: fdLimits(), summary: fdSummary() };
}

// ---------- (b) The production-grade server ----------
class GuardedServer {
  #server; #sockets = new Set(); #limit; #idleMs; #handshakeMs;
  constructor({ limit = 1024, idleTimeoutMs = 30_000, handshakeMs = 5000, port = 0 } = {}) {
    this.#limit = limit;
    this.#idleMs = idleTimeoutMs;
    this.#handshakeMs = handshakeMs;
    this.#server = net.createServer((s) => this.#onConnection(s));
    this.port = port;
    this.metrics = { accepted: 0, rejected: 0, closedByIdle: 0, closedByPeer: 0, peak: 0 };
  }

  #onConnection(socket) {
    if (this.#sockets.size >= this.#limit) {
      this.metrics.rejected++;
      socket.end('HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n');
      socket.destroy();                                  // MUST destroy, not just end
      return;
    }
    this.metrics.accepted++;
    this.#sockets.add(socket);
    this.metrics.peak = Math.max(this.metrics.peak, this.#sockets.size);

    // (1) Handshake deadline: a client that connects and sends nothing still holds an fd.
    const handshake = setTimeout(() => socket.destroy(), this.#handshakeMs);
    // (2) Idle timeout: the single most effective fd defence.
    const idle = setTimeout(() => { this.metrics.closedByIdle++; socket.destroy(); }, this.#idleMs);

    const refresh = () => { clearTimeout(idle); idle.refresh?.() ?? armIdle(); };
    function armIdle() { return setTimeout(() => { socket.destroy(); }, 0); }

    socket.on('data', () => { clearTimeout(idle); this.#respawnIdle(socket); });
    socket.once('close', () => {
      clearTimeout(handshake); clearTimeout(idle);
      this.#sockets.delete(socket);
    });
    socket.on('error', () => socket.destroy());
    void refresh;
  }
  #respawnIdle(socket) { /* setTimeout().refresh() on Node 10.2+ keeps this simple */ }

  listen() {
    return new Promise((res) => this.#server.listen(this.port, '127.0.0.1', () => res(this.#server.address())));
  }
  async close({ graceMs = 1000 } = {}) {
    await new Promise((res) => this.#server.close(res));
    const deadline = Date.now() + graceMs;
    while (this.#sockets.size && Date.now() < deadline) {
      for (const s of this.#sockets) s.destroy();
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 10));
    }
    return this.metrics;
  }
}

// ---------- (c) Proving the fix: leak vs limit-raising ----------
async function compareLeakVsLimit() {
  const soft = fdLimits()?.soft ?? 1024;

  // Case 1: leak one fd per request (never destroy). Steady state climbs forever.
  const leaking = [];
  const sample = async (label, fn, n) => {
    const before = fdSummary().total;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { const s = fn(); leaking.push(s); }
    const after = fdSummary().total;
    console.log(`  ${label}: ${before} -> ${after} fds (${n} iterations)`);
    return after - before;
  };

  const a = await sample('leaking server,  300 conns', () => net.connect({ host: '127.0.0.1', port: 1 }), 300);
  const b = await sample('leaking server,  600 conns', () => net.connect({ host: '127.0.0.1', port: 1 }), 300);

  // Case 2: destroy every socket. Steady state is flat.
  for (const s of leaking) s.destroy();
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));
  const before = fdSummary().total;
  for (let i = 0; i < 1200; i++) { const s = net.connect({ host: '127.0.0.1', port: 1 }); s.on('error', () => {}); s.destroy(); }
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50));
  const after = fdSummary().total;
  console.log(`  destroying server, 1200 conns: ${before} -> ${after} fds (flat == no leak)`);

  console.log(`  limits: soft=${soft}; raising it would only have delayed the crash.`);
  assert.ok(a > 0 && b > 0, 'the leaking pattern consumes fds monotonically');
  assert.ok(Math.abs(after - before) <= 5, 'the destroying pattern is flat');
}

// ---------- (d) Finding the leak in code review ----------
function auditFdLifecycle() {
  const checks = [
    ['every socket has destroy() on the error path', 'else EMFILE under load'],
    ['idle + handshake timeouts are set', 'else slow-loris exhausts fds'],
    ['no listener accumulation on a long-lived emitter', 'else sockets leak one per connection'],
    ['child_process uses stdio: ignore/inherit or closes all pipes', 'else 3 fds per child'],
    ['AbortController is passed to every fetch/stream', 'else in-flight requests hold sockets'],
    ['response bodies are consumed or destroyed', 'else http.IncomingMessage holds its socket'],
    ['fs watch recursion is bounded (inotify watches)', 'else ENOSPC from max_user_watches'],
    ['ulimit -n is raised in the deployment, not only in dev', 'else production EMFILE at 1024'],
  ];
  return checks.map(([check, consequence]) => ({ check, consequence }));
}

// ---------- run ----------
(async () => {
  if (!fs.existsSync('/proc/self/fd')) {
    console.log('Exercise 7: skipped (no /proc; run in a Linux container)');
    return;
  }
  console.log('  limits before:', fdLimits());
  console.log('  summary before:', fdSummary().total, 'fds');

  console.log('  --- the fix, first (so the test process does not wedge) ---');
  await compareLeakVsLimit();

  console.log('  --- the reproduction (bounded so it cannot run away) ---');
  const r = await reproduceExhaustion();
  console.log(`\n  reproduction: code=${r.code} after ${r.iterations} attempts`);
  console.log(`  limits: ${JSON.stringify(r.limits)}`);
  console.log(`  summary: ${JSON.stringify(r.summary)}`);
  assert.ok(['EMFILE', 'ENFILE', 'ok'].includes(r.code));

  console.log('  --- the guarded server under a burst ---');
  const srv = new GuardedServer({ limit: 50, idleTimeoutMs: 200, handshakeMs: 100 });
  const addr = await srv.listen();
  const conns = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 200; i++) {
    const s = net.connect(addr);
    s.on('error', () => {});
    conns.push(s);
  }
  await new Promise((r2) => setTimeout(r2, 100));
  console.log(`  peak concurrent sockets: ${srv.metrics.peak} (limit ${50})`);
  console.log(`  metrics: ${JSON.stringify(srv.metrics)}`);
  assert.ok(srv.metrics.peak <= 50, 'the limit was enforced');
  console.log(`  after idle timeout, live sockets: ${srv.metrics.peak} -> ${await new Promise((res) => {
    setTimeout(() => res(srv.metrics.peak), 300);
  })}`);
  await srv.close();
  conns.forEach((c) => c.destroy());

  console.log('  audit checklist:');
  for (const { check, consequence } of auditFdLifecycle()) console.log(`    - ${check}  (${consequence})`);

  console.log('Exercise 7: demonstrated');
})();
```

### Follow-ups

- **How do you raise the limit in production?** `LimitNOFILE=` in a systemd unit, `nofile` in `limits.conf`, `--ulimit nofile=` for Docker. Soft limit raises are instant; hard limit raises need privileges.
- **What about `ENFILE`?** System-wide (`fs.file-max`). Same symptoms, different layer; the fix is on the node, not in your process.
- **What about ephemeral ports?** `EADDRNOTAVAIL` and `TIME_WAIT` exhaustion for short-lived outbound connections. Fix with keep-alive and connection reuse.
- **How do you monitor it?** Count `/proc/self/fd` on an interval and alert on the *slope*, not the absolute value.

### Interview traps

1. **Raising `ulimit` and calling it a fix.** It is a mitigation; the leak is the bug.
2. **`end()` without `destroy()`** and expecting the fd to be released immediately.
3. **No idle timeout** on a server that accepts arbitrary clients.
4. **Confusing EMFILE (per-process) with ENFILE (system-wide).**
5. **Forgetting `child_process` pipes.**

---

## Exercise 8 — Memory-Ordering Visibility Demo

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Statement.** Demonstrate the store-buffer visibility problem with `SharedArrayBuffer` + `Atomics`, show that `load`/`store` pairs do not give atomicity, show the correct publish/acquire-release pattern, and show why plain (non-`Atomics`) `SharedArrayBuffer` access is a data race that the engine may optimise around.

### Solution

```js
'use strict';
const assert = require('node:assert/strict');
const { Worker, isMainThread, workerData, parentPort } = require('node:worker_threads');
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

/**
 * Flag layout in a SharedArrayBuffer:
 *   [0] data      (Int32)  -- the payload
 *   [1] ready     (Int32)  -- the synchronisation flag
 *   [2..N) shard slots for the sharded comparison
 */

if (!isMainThread && workerData?.role === 'publisher') {
  const f = new Int32Array(workerData.sab);
  if (workerData.mode === 'ordered') {
    Atomics.store(f, 1, 42);            // release semantics: data before flag
    Atomics.store(f, 0, 1);             // ready
  } else if (workerData.mode === 'unordered') {
    Atomics.store(f, 0, 1);             // ready FIRST -- the bug
    Atomics.store(f, 1, 42);            // data
  }
  parentPort.postMessage('published');
  return;
}

if (!isMainThread && workerData?.role === 'consumer') {
  const f = new Int32Array(workerData.sab);
  const deadline = Date.now() + 2000;
  let spins = 0;
  // Wait for ready, then read data.
  while (Atomics.load(f, 0) === 0) {
    if (++spins % 1e6 === 0 && Date.now() > deadline) {
      parentPort.postMessage({ status: 'timeout', spins });
      return;
    }
  }
  const data = Atomics.load(f, 1);
  parentPort.postMessage({
    status: data === 42 ? 'ok' : 'TORN_READ',
    data,
    spins,
  });
  return;
}

// ---------- 1. The naive publish (ready before data) ----------
async function naivePublish() {
  const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(Int32Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT * 2);
  const pub = new Worker(__filename, { workerData: { role: 'publisher', sab, mode: 'unordered' } });
  const con = new Worker(__filename, { workerData: { role: 'consumer', sab } });
  const [r] = await Promise.all([once(con), once(pub)]);
  pub.terminate(); con.terminate();
  console.log(`  naive publish  -> ${JSON.stringify(r)}`);
  return r;
}

// ---------- 2. The correct publish (data before flag) ----------
async function correctPublish() {
  const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(Int32Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT * 2);
  const pub = new Worker(__filename, { workerData: { role: 'publisher', sab, mode: 'ordered' } });
  const con = new Worker(__filename, { workerData: { role: 'consumer', sab } });
  const [r] = await Promise.all([once(con), once(pub)]);
  pub.terminate(); con.terminate();
  console.log(`  correct publish-> ${JSON.stringify(r)}`);
  return r;
}

// ---------- 3. load/store pair is NOT an atomic RMW ----------
async function showNonAtomicPair(nWorkers = 4, iters = 300_000) {
  const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(Int32Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT);
  const view = new Int32Array(sab);
  const run = (mode) => Promise.all(Array.from({ length: nWorkers }, () => new Promise((res, rej) => {
    const w = new Worker(__filename, { workerData: { role: 'rmw', sab, mode, iters } });
    w.once('message', res); w.once('error', rej);
  })));
  await run('loadstore');  const racy = view[0];
  await run('add');       const atomic = view[0];
  console.log(`  load+store pair-> ${racy} / ${nWorkers * iters}  (lost ${nWorkers * iters - racy})`);
  console.log(`  Atomics.add    -> ${atomic} / ${nWorkers * iters}`);
  assert.equal(atomic, nWorkers * iters, 'atomic RMW is exact');
  assert.ok(racy < nWorkers * iters, 'the load/store pair lost updates');
  return { racy, atomic };
}

// ---------- 4. Plain (non-Atomics) access is a data race ----------
// There is no way to "detect" this from JS, which is the point: the language
// gives you no guarantee, and the engine may hoist or elide. The only correct
// discipline is: every access to shared memory goes through Atomics.
function plainAccessIsUndefined() {
  const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(8);
  const typed = new Int32Array(sab);
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(sab);
  // Both views alias the same 8 bytes. Writing through one and reading through
  // the other with non-atomic ops is a data race: you may read torn/stale data.
  typed[0] = 0x00010000;
  const lo = bytes[0], hi = bytes[1];
  return { typedValue: typed[0], lo, hi, aliased: lo === 0 && hi === 1 };
}

// ---------- 5. Seq-cst fences: the "always safe" pattern ----------
// Atomics.load/store in the JS memory model are sequentially consistent, so a
// seq-cst store after a seq-cst store guarantees the consumer sees the first
// value if it sees the second. If your platform ever needed weaker ordering,
// you would reach for Atomics.fence (not universally available) or embed the
// critical section in a native addon with explicit acquire/release semantics.
async function demonstrateFence() {
  const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(Int32Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT * 3);
  const f = new Int32Array(sab);
  f[0] = 0; f[1] = 0; f[2] = 0;                 // plain init before any sharing: fine
  Atomics.store(f, 2, 1);                        // "shared" flag set LAST, after init
  // Everything above this line is guaranteed visible to anyone who sees flag==1.
  Atomics.store(f, 1, 7);
  const seen = Atomics.load(f, 2);
  const data = Atomics.load(f, 1);
  const ok = seen === 1 && data === 7;
  console.log(`  safe publication -> flag=${seen} data=${data} ok=${ok}`);
  assert.equal(ok, true);
}

// ---------- 6. The lock-free ring buffer, built correctly ----------
// Useful because it forces every correctness question in this section at once.
class LockFreeRingBuffer {
  #buf; #cap; #mask; #head = 0; #tail = 0;
  constructor(capacity = 64) {
    this.#cap = 1 << Math.ceil(Math.log2(capacity));
    this.#mask = this.#cap - 1;
    this.#buf = new ArrayBuffer(this.#cap * Int32Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT);
    this.#buf = new Int32Array(this.#buf);
  }
  get size() { return (this.#head - this.#tail) & this.#mask; }
  push(v) {
    const h = this.#head;
    const next = (h + 1) & this.#mask;
    if (next === Atomics.load(this.#tailView, 0)) return false;  // full
    Atomics.store(this.#buf, h, v);
    Atomics.store(this.#headView, 0, next);                        // release: buf[h] before head
    this.#head = next;
    return true;
  }
  pop() {
    const t = Atomics.load(this.#tailView, 0);
    if (t === this.#head) return undefined;                         // empty
    const v = Atomics.load(this.#buf, t);                          // acquire: sees buf[t]
    Atomics.store(this.#tailView, 0, (t + 1) & this.#mask);        // release
    this.#tail = (t + 1) & this.#mask;
    return v;
  }
}

function once(emitter) {
  return new Promise((res) => emitter.once('message', res));
}

// ---------- tests ----------
(async () => {
  console.log('  --- visibility ---');
  const naive = await naivePublish();
  const correct = await correctPublish();
  assert.equal(correct.status, 'ok');
  // naive may appear to work on x86 (TSO); the point is that you cannot rely on it.
  console.log(`  naive result is ${naive.status} on this machine; it is still UB by construction`);

  console.log('  --- atomicity ---');
  await showNonAtomicPair();

  console.log('  --- aliasing ---');
  console.log('  plain aliased access:', plainAccessIsUndefined());

  console.log('  --- fences ---');
  await demonstrateFence();

  console.log('Exercise 8: demonstrated');
})();

if (!isMainThread && workerData?.role === 'rmw') {
  const view = new Int32Array(workerData.sab);
  if (workerData.mode === 'loadstore') {
    for (let i = 0; i < workerData.iters; i++) {
      const c = Atomics.load(view, 0);
      Atomics.store(view, 0, c + 1);
    }
  } else {
    for (let i = 0; i < workerData.iters; i++) Atomics.add(view, 0, 1);
  }
  parentPort.postMessage('done');
}
```

### Follow-ups

- **What if I need acquire/release rather than seq-cst?** In Java, `final` fields plus `volatile`; in C11/C++20, `memory_order_acquire`/`memory_order_release`. In JS, `Atomics` is seq-cst only, which is why shared-memory algorithms in JS are simple and slower.
- **Why can't you take a JS lock and hold it across `Atomics.wait`?** Because `Atomics.wait` parks the whole thread; the lock cannot be released, and in Node it blocks the event loop.
- **How do you crash-safe share memory between processes?** `SharedArrayBuffer` does not cross processes. Use `mmap` via a native addon, `SharedArrayBuffer` inside one process only, or `Atomics` over a shared file mapped with `MAP_SHARED`.
- **What is a seqlock?** A seqlock lets readers proceed without a lock while writers bump a sequence counter; readers re-read if the counter changed. It needs careful memory ordering and is the classic answer to "read-heavy, write-rare, and reads must be consistent".

### Interview traps

1. **Believing `Atomics.load` + `Atomics.store` is an atomic RMW.** It is not.
2. **Accessing `SharedArrayBuffer` with plain indexing.** Data race, and the engine may optimise around it.
3. **Publishing the flag before the data.**
4. **Using `Atomics.wait` on the Node main thread** (blocks the event loop) or the browser main thread (forbidden).
5. **Forgetting `SharedArrayBuffer` needs cross-origin isolation in browsers.**

---
# 10.4-10.5 TRACE/OUTPUT DRILLS (15)

Each drill gives you a short concurrent program and asks **which outputs are possible, which are impossible, and why**. The answer must include the interleaving that produces each possible outcome. This is the skill that separate's "I can write the code" from "I understand what the code does".

The rule for every drill: **list the interleavings, do not guess from intuition.**

---

## Trace 1 — `await` interleaving, three tasks

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

```js
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
const log = [];
async function A() { log.push('A1'); await sleep(0); log.push('A2'); }
async function B() { log.push('B1'); await sleep(0); log.push('B2'); }
async function C() { log.push('C1'); await sleep(0); log.push('C2'); }
(async () => {
  A(); B(); C();
  log.push('main');
  await sleep(10);
  console.log(log.join(' '));
})();
```

**Possible output:**

```
A1 B1 C1 main A2 B2 C2
```

**Impossible:** any output where `A2` precedes `A1`; any output where `main` appears after `A1`; any output with only two of `A1 B1 C1`.

**Why:** the synchronous prefix `A(); B(); C();` runs to completion of each synchronous prefix before the first suspension. `sleep(0)` schedules a timer, so all three timers are queued in call order, and the `microtask`/`timer` phase runs them FIFO. `main` is pushed synchronously after `A(); B(); C();`, i.e. after `A1 B1 C1`. This drill is the foundation of everything else: **a single-threaded event loop with FIFO timers is deterministic; concurrency becomes nondeterministic only when you add real threads, real IO, or explicit scheduling.**

---

## Trace 2 — the lost update, in two tasks

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

```js
let counter = 0;
async function inc() { const c = counter; await sleep(0); counter = c + 1; }
(async () => {
  await Promise.all([inc(), inc()]);
  console.log(counter);
})();
```

**Possible output:** `1` or `2`.

**Impossible:** `0`, `3`, or anything else.

**Interleavings:**

| # | Order | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | read(0) [A] · read(0) [B] · write(1) [A] · write(1) [B] | `1` (lost update) |
| 2 | read(0) [A] · write(1) [A] · read(1) [B] · write(2) [B] | `2` |

**Why:** the read-then-write pair straddles a suspension point, so it is not atomic. `sleep(0)` is a *minimum* delay; both tasks are scheduled as timers and the first one's timer runs first, but if the second task's read happened before the first's write (which is what happens here, because both tasks park before either resumes) you lose an update. **Non-determinism: the output is not guaranteed, so any test asserting a single value is a bad test.**

---

## Trace 3 — check-then-act on a cache

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

```js
const cache = new Map();
let loads = 0;
async function get(k) {
  if (cache.has(k)) return cache.get(k);
  await sleep(0);              // the "expensive fetch"
  loads++;
  cache.set(k, 'v');
  return 'v';
}
(async () => {
  await Promise.all([get('a'), get('a'), get('a')]);
  console.log(loads);
})();
```

**Possible output:** `1` or `3`. Never `2`. Never `0`.

**Interleavings:**

| # | Order | loads |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | all three `has()` checks pass before any `set()` | `3` |
| 2 | call 1 sets before calls 2 and 3 check | `1` |
| 3 | call 1 sets before call 2 checks, but call 3 checked earlier | `2` |

**Fix (and the important part):** an in-flight promise map. Note this only works because the `#inflight.set()` is *synchronous* relative to the check; add an `await` between the check and the `set` and the coalescing map itself races.

```js
const inflight = new Map();
async function get(k) {
  if (cache.has(k)) return cache.get(k);
  if (inflight.has(k)) return inflight.get(k);
  const p = (async () => { await sleep(0); loads++; cache.set(k, 'v'); return 'v'; })();
  inflight.set(k, p);
  try { return await p; } finally { inflight.delete(k); }
}
// loads === 1, deterministically.
```

---

## Trace 4 — Promise combinator ordering

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

```js
const out = [];
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
async function work(name, ms, value) { await sleep(ms); out.push(name); return value; }
(async () => {
  const p1 = work('slow', 20, 1);
  const p2 = work('fast', 0, 2);
  out.push('sync');
  Promise.all([p1, p2]).then(([a, b]) => out.push(`all:${a}${b}`));
  await sleep(5);
  out.push('mid');
})();
setTimeout(() => console.log(out.join(' ')), 100);
```

**Output (deterministic):**

```
sync fast mid slow all:12
```

**Why:** `work('slow')` and `work('fast')` both start synchronously and push nothing; `out.push('sync')` happens immediately. `fast` resolves first (0 ms timer), `slow` at 20 ms. `await sleep(5)` yields, so `mid` is pushed at ~5 ms, before `slow` at 20 ms. `Promise.all` resolves after both, pushing `all:12`. Note `Promise.all` preserves **input order** in its result (`[1, 2]`), even though `slow` completed first — a distinction that is free marks in an interview.

---

## Trace 5 — `Promise.all` vs `allSettled` under failure

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

```js
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
const log = [];
async function task(name, ms, fail) {
  try { await sleep(ms); if (fail) throw new Error(name); log.push(`ok:${name}`); return name; }
  catch (e) { log.push(`err:${name}`); throw e; }
}
(async () => {
  await Promise.allSettled([task('a', 5, false), task('b', 1, true), task('c', 10, false)]);
  console.log('allSettled:', log.join(' '));
  log.length = 0;
  await Promise.all([task('d', 5, false), task('e', 1, true), task('f', 10, false)]);
  console.log('all:', log.join(' '));
})();
```

**Output:**

```
allSettled: err:b ok:a ok:c
all: err:e ok:d
```

**Why:** `allSettled` waits for every promise and never rejects, so you see all three outcomes in completion order. `all` rejects as soon as `b`/`e` fails, but the other two tasks keep running; the `await Promise.all` throws, so only the log entries written before the throw are visible (`err:e` then `ok:d`, which completed 4 ms later). **The crucial insight: `Promise.all` rejecting does not cancel the other work.** If you need cancellation, you need `AbortController`.

---

## Trace 6 — semaphore fairness under release

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

```js
class Sem {
  #n; #waiters = [];
  constructor(n) { this.#n = n; }
  async acquire() { if (this.#n > 0) { this.#n--; return; } await new Promise((r) => this.#waiters.push(r)); this.#n--; }
  release() { const w = this.#waiters.shift(); if (w) w(); else this.#n++; }
}
(async () => {
  const s = new Sem(1);
  const order = [];
  await s.acquire();                                  // main holds the only permit
  const ps = [1, 2, 3, 4].map((i) => s.acquire().then(() => order.push(i)));
  await sleep(0);
  s.release(); s.release(); s.release(); s.release();
  await Promise.all(ps);
  console.log(order.join(','));
})();
```

**Output:** `1,2,3,4` — deterministic, because `release` uses `shift()` (FIFO) and each release wakes exactly one waiter.

**What if `release` used `this.#waiters.pop()`?** Output: `4,3,2,1` — still deterministic, but LIFO (last-in-first-out), which means the first waiter can starve under sustained load.

**What if `release` woke all waiters?** Output is nondeterministic: all four proceed to `this.#n--`, and the counter goes negative, so subsequent `acquire` calls succeed spuriously — a classic semaphore bug (the "wake-all" bug that Java's `Condition`/`Semaphore` implementations avoid by transferring permits instead of signalling).

---

## Trace 7 — producer/consumer with capacity 1

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

```js
const log = [];
class Q {
  #items = []; #waiters = [];
  async push(v) { while (this.#items.length >= 1) await new Promise((r) => this.#waiters.push(r)); this.#items.push(v); log.push(`push ${v}`); this.#waiters.shift()?.(); }
  async pop() { while (!this.#items.length) await new Promise((r) => this.#waiters.push(r)); const v = this.#items.shift(); log.push(`pop ${v}`); this.#waiters.shift()?.(); return v; }
}
(async () => {
  const q = new Q();
  const consume = (async () => { for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { const v = await q.pop(); log.push(`got ${v}`); } })();
  for (const v of [1, 2, 3]) await q.push(v);
  await consume;
  console.log(log.join(' | '));
})();
```

**Output (one legal ordering):**

```
push 1 | pop 1 | got 1 | push 2 | pop 2 | got 2 | push 3 | pop 3 | got 3
```

**Other legal orderings:**

```
push 1 | pop 1 | push 2 | pop 2 | got 1 | got 2 | push 3 | pop 3 | got 3
```

**Impossible:** any ordering where a `pop` of 3 precedes a `push` of 3; any ordering with two `pop`s before two `push`es (capacity 1 forbids it); any ordering where `push 2` precedes `pop 1` (the queue is full until 1 is removed).

**Key observation:** the `while` loops are mandatory. If you use `if`, a woken waiter that finds the slot taken again will proceed anyway and blow the capacity invariant.

---

## Trace 8 — the two-thread deadlock, traced

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

```js
const log = [];
async function T1(A, B) { await A.acquire(); log.push('T1 has A'); await B.acquire(); log.push('T1 has B'); await B.release(); await A.release(); }
async function T2(A, B) { await B.acquire(); log.push('T2 has B'); await A.acquire(); log.push('T2 has A'); await A.release(); await B.release(); }
(async () => {
  const A = { locked: false, acquire() { if (!this.locked) { this.locked = true; return Promise.resolve(); } return new Promise(() => {}); }, release() { this.locked = false; } };
  const B = { ...A };
  Promise.allSettled([T1(A, B), T2(A, B)]);
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100));
  console.log(JSON.stringify(log));
})();
```

**Output:** `["T1 has A","T2 has B"]`

**Impossible:** any output containing `"T1 has B"` or `"T2 has A"`; the program never completes and never throws.

**Why:** `T1` takes `A` first (synchronously), then parks on `B`. `T2` takes `B` first, then parks on `A`. Both log lines appear because both acquires succeed before either suspension. Neither can proceed. **This is a deadlock, and no amount of extra time changes the log — which is why the reproduction must be raced with a timeout.**

---

## Trace 9 — `Promise.all` with a deadlock inside

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

```js
async function needsMutex(m, x, v) { await m.acquire(); try { return x + v; } finally { m.release(); } }
(async () => {
  const m = { locked: false, waiters: [],
    async acquire() { if (!this.locked) { this.locked = true; return; } const p = new Promise((r) => this.waiters.push(r)); await p; },
    release() { this.locked = false; this.waiters.shift()?.(); } };
  const a = needsMutex(m, 1, 1);
  const b = needsMutex(m, 2, 2);
  // A third task releases a permit that nobody is waiting for yet.
  setTimeout(() => m.release(), 50);
  console.log(await Promise.race([Promise.all([a, b]).then((r) => r.join('+')), new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r('TIMEOUT'), 500))]));
})();
```

**Output:** `TIMEOUT`.

**Why this is the interesting version:** `Promise.race` saves you from a hang, but the underlying deadlock is real. `a` holds the permit; `b` parks. The stray `release()` at 50 ms hands the permit to `b`, `b` completes and releases (which increments nothing because `release` woke a waiter directly), then `a` completes. Actually, `a` already completed. So `Promise.all` resolves... unless `release` is called while `b` is parked and `b`'s `release()` then finds no waiter and sets `locked = false`, allowing `a`'s path to re-acquire. **The correct reading: this program is order-dependent and fragile; the only safe statement is that any mutex implementation must transfer permits, not toggle a boolean, and every acquire must have a matching release on all paths.** Write the test to expose the bug, not to depend on it.

---

## Trace 10 — thread-pool rejection vs caller-runs

🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

```js
class Pool {
  #max; #queue; #busy = 0; #lat = [];
  constructor(max, cap) { this.#max = max; this.#cap = cap; this.#queue = []; }
  async run(fn, id) {
    const t0 = Date.now();
    if (this.#busy < this.#max) { this.#busy++; try { return await fn(); } finally { this.#busy--; } }
    if (this.#queue.length < this.#cap) { this.#queue.push(() => fn()); this.#lat.push(Date.now() - t0); return new Promise(() => {}); }
    // reject: fall through to caller-runs
    this.#lat.push(Date.now() - t0);
    return fn();
  }
}
```

**Questions:** which caller sees the shortest latency? The one admitted directly (no queue). Which sees the longest? The one that queued first. What is the maximum number of tasks executing concurrently under caller-runs? **`max + number of rejected callers` — unbounded.** Under `abort`, the answer is `max`, with rejections instead.

**The trace that matters:** with `max=2, cap=2` and 10 tasks of 10 ms: tasks 1-2 run immediately (0 ms queue wait), tasks 3-4 queue (≈10-20 ms wait), tasks 5-10 either reject (client retries, latency becomes 0 + retry + backoff, and the *system* is less loaded) or run in the caller (0 ms queue wait for *them*, but the submitting request now takes 10 ms extra). **Caller-runs improves the p50 and destroys the tail of the pool while protecting the pool's throughput.**

---

## Trace 11 — mutex acquisition order decides the answer

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

```js
async function transfer(m, from, to, amount) {
  const [fa, fb] = [from, to].sort();
  await m[fa].acquire();
  await m[fb].acquire();
  try { from.balance -= amount; to.balance += amount; return true; } finally { await m[fb].release(); await m[fa].release(); }
}
```

**Question:** does global ordering (`sort()`) eliminate deadlock here? **Yes.** Every path acquires `m[a]` before `m[b]`, so no cycle exists, regardless of the direction of the transfer.

**What breaks it?** Any code path that skips the `sort()`, or a function called while holding a lock that acquires locks internally in a different order. **The trace drill is: for each function, list the set of locks it can hold and the set it acquires, and verify the partial order is acyclic.** A topological sort of the lock-acquisition graph is a one-time CI check you can write.

---

## Trace 12 — `Atomics` cache-line contention

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

```js
// Version A: 4 Workers, all hammering index 0 of one Int32Array.
for (let i = 0; i < 300000; i++) Atomics.add(view, 0, 1);
// Version B: 4 Workers, worker t owns index t+1 exclusively.
const mine = view[t+1]; let local = 0;
for (let i = 0; i < 300000; i++) local++;
Atomics.store(view, t+1, local);
```

**Question:** both are correct. Which is faster, and by how much? **Version B, often 5-50x on real hardware.**

**Why, at the cache-line level:** a 64-byte cache line holds 16 `Int32`s. Index 0..15 all live on the same line. Every `Atomics.add` requires *exclusive* ownership of that line, so each of the 1.2M stores forces a coherence transaction to the owning core. Version B touches 4 distinct lines, each owned exclusively by one core for the whole loop, with **zero** coherence traffic after the first access.

**The generalisable rule:** shared-memory counters must be **sharded by owner and summed at the end**, not hammered atomically. `LongAdder` in Java, per-thread counters + merge in Python, and striped counters in any metrics library all exist because of this.

---

## Trace 13 — the visibility bug on a strong vs weak architecture

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

```
Thread P:  data = 42;   ready = true;
Thread C:  while (!ready) {}  print(data);
```

**On x86-64 (TSO):** stores are not reordered with other stores, and loads are not reordered with older loads, but a *load* may pass an older *store*. Here both operations in P are stores and both in C are loads, so TSO guarantees C sees `ready == true` only after `data == 42` is globally visible. **This program works.**

**On ARM64 / RISC-V (weak ordering):** each store may sit in a store buffer independently. C can observe `ready == true` while `data` is still buffered. C prints garbage (whatever `data` initialised to). **This program is broken.**

**The fix, on any architecture:** make `ready` `volatile` / use release-store on `ready` and acquire-load on the read, or use a mutex, or (in JS) route both through `Atomics`.

**The interview lesson:** "it works on my machine" is a memory-model bug. x86's total-store-order made an entire generation of Java programs correct by accident, until JSR-133 codified it in 2004 — and the ARM server transition made a decade of those bugs visible.

---

## Trace 14 — `Atomics.wait` / `notify` wake-up counting

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

```js
// Slot layout: [0] = data, [1] = sequence number
producer: Atomics.store(view, 0, v); Atomics.add(view, 1, 1); Atomics.notify(view, 1);
consumer: while (Atomics.load(view, 1) === lastSeen) Atomics.wait(view, 1, lastSeen);
```

**Question:** can the consumer miss a notification? **Yes, if the producer's increment happens between the consumer's `load` and its `wait`.** `Atomics.wait` compares the value at the index to the expected value and only sleeps if they are *equal*. So:

| Consumer | Producer | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `load(seq)` reads 5 | `add(seq)` → 6, `notify` | `wait(view,1,5)` sees 6 ≠ 5, returns `'not-equal'` immediately. **No lost wakeup.** |

That comparison is exactly why the API takes an *expected value*. A `wait`-without-compare design would lose wakeups; the value argument is the fix.

**What still bites:** if the consumer processes the item, updates `lastSeen`, and then loops and `load`s again *before* the producer's next increment, everything is fine. But if the consumer ever uses a *different* index for `wait` than for the check, you have recreated the lost-wakeup bug. And in Node, `Atomics.wait` on the main thread blocks the entire event loop — which is why `Atomics.waitAsync` (or a `MessagePort`) is the right tool there.

---

## Trace 15 — event-loop starvation

🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

```js
const log = [];
const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));
async function slowLoop() { for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { log.push(`loop${i}`); } }
async function timers() { await sleep(0); log.push('timer'); }
(async () => {
  timers();      // starts, parks on setTimeout(0)
  timers();      // parks again
  timers();      // parks again
  log.push('before-loop');
  await slowLoop();      // synchronous, no awaits: blocks the loop
  log.push('after-loop');
})();
setTimeout(() => console.log(log.join(' ')), 10);
```

**Output (deterministic):**

```
before-loop loop0 loop1 loop2 loop3 loop4 after-loop timer timer timer
```

**The lesson:** all three timers were *scheduled* before the loop ran, but none of their callbacks could execute until the loop returned to the event loop. The synchronous `slowLoop` runs to completion, then the timers fire in scheduling order. **Adding `await` inside the loop would interleave, and that is exactly the (misleading) technique people use to "make async work non-blocking". It does not raise throughput; it just makes the loop yield.**

---
# 10.4-10.5 DEBUGGING SCENARIOS (10)

Each scenario: **symptoms**, **evidence you should gather**, **root cause**, **the fix**, and **the class of bug**. The discipline being trained is *symptom → hypothesis → evidence → fix*, in that order, with the temptation to skip evidence called out explicitly.

---

## Scenario 1 — Latency p50 fine, p99 catastrophic

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** A Node API serving a Postgres-backed endpoint. Median 40 ms. p99 alternates between 60 ms and 4 s. Error rate near zero. CPU 45%. No deploys correlate.

**Wrong first moves:** "the database is slow" (it is not, on average), "add caching" (does not address the tail), "increase the pool size" (will make it worse).

**Evidence to gather, in order:**
1. **Histogram, not average.** `p50=40, p95=55, p99=4000`. Averages hide this.
2. **Per-hop latency**, correlated with the request id. Which hop is slow at p99?
3. **Connection-pool wait histogram.** If a large fraction of requests wait >100 ms for a connection, the pool is the queue.
4. **Pool utilisation time series.** If it plateaus at exactly `max`, the pool is saturated.
5. **Slow-query log** for that window. Likely: an unindexed query that the planner only picks when statistics go stale.
6. **`pg_stat_activity`** — connection count per state, and long-running queries.

**Root cause.** Two interacting things: pool size of 10 against a Postgres instance whose effective capacity is 8 concurrent queries, plus a query that occasionally takes 2 s (a `seq scan` chosen after autovacuum updated statistics). Queueing theory says a utilisation of 0.8 already produces long waits, and a 2 s service time at 0.8 utilisation produces a multi-second p99 with almost no errors.

**Fix.**
- Size the pool to Postgres capacity minus headroom (typically `cores * 2 + effective_spindle_count`, capped well below `max_connections`).
- `SET statement_timeout` per connection so a pathological query fails instead of holding a connection for 2 s.
- Add the missing index; verify with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.
- Cap queueing: `tryAcquire` with a timeout, return 503 + `Retry-After`. Unbounded queueing is what turned a slow query into a latency incident.

**Class:** queueing + tail-latency amplification. The bug is *not* the slow query; the bug is allowing a slow query to become a long queue.

---

## Scenario 2 — "It only happens in production"

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** A counter is correct in staging and drifts in production. Rate is proportional to concurrency. Resetting the counter "fixes" it for a while.

**Evidence.**
1. Compare the drift rate to the number of active Worker threads: if the drift is proportional to concurrency, you have a race.
2. Look at the code path: is there a `SharedArrayBuffer` or `Atomics` anywhere near the counter?
3. `Atomics.load` / `Atomics.store` pairs instead of `Atomics.add`.
4. Cache-line sharding: is one counter hammered by all Workers?

**Root cause.** A read-modify-write split across `Atomics.load` and `Atomics.store` — individually atomic, jointly not. Staging has one Worker, so the window never opens.

**Fix.** `Atomics.add`, or (better) per-worker shards summed at read time, which is also faster.

**Class:** data race masked by low concurrency. Always reproduce with concurrency, never with a single thread.

---

## Scenario 3 — The process hangs on deploy

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** `SIGTERM` sent; the process logs "shutting down" and never exits. The orchestrator waits 30 s then sends `SIGKILL`. In-flight requests are lost. This happens ~1 deploy in 5.

**Evidence.**
1. `lsof -p <pid>` or `/proc/<pid>/fd` count *after* the shutdown signal: fds stay open.
2. `ps -L -p <pid>` thread count: Worker threads or libuv pool threads still alive.
3. `AsyncResource`/`async_hooks` dump: which async ids are still referenced?
4. Does the code `await server.close()` before or after draining the Worker pool? If it closes the pool first, in-flight requests never finish and `server.close()` never resolves (it waits for existing connections).

**Root cause.** Shutdown ordering plus unreferenced resources. Typical: (a) `server.close()` is called but keep-alive connections are still open, so the callback never fires; (b) a Worker pool is terminated before the HTTP server stops accepting; (c) a `setInterval` is never cleared; (d) a Redis/DB client is never closed and holds a socket.

**Fix — the canonical order:**
```
1. Mark not-ready: remove from load balancer, keep serving.
2. Stop accepting new connections (but keep existing ones alive).
3. Stop the intake to queues; drain in-flight with a deadline.
4. Close the DB/Redis clients.
5. Clear all intervals/timers.
6. Terminate Worker pools; await exit.
7. server.close() + destroy remaining sockets after the grace period.
8. process.exit(0) as the last resort, with a logged reason.
```

**Class:** lifecycle/ordering bug. Concurrency bugs are frequently just "who finishes first" bugs.

---

## Scenario 4 — CPU at 95%, throughput flat

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** After adding a Worker pool of 32 to an 8-core box, throughput did not improve and p99 got worse. CPU is pegged.

**Evidence.**
1. `pidstat -w 1`: **involuntary context switches** are enormous; voluntary ones are small. This is the smoking gun.
2. `pidstat -u 1`: system time is a large fraction of CPU (kernel time = switching + cache-coherence overhead).
3. `perf stat`: cache misses per instruction is high.
4. `perf c2c` or a false-sharing report: multiple threads writing adjacent cache lines.

**Root cause.** Two compounding causes. (a) Oversubscription: 32 runnable CPU-bound threads on 8 cores, so most of the time is spent preempting and re-warming caches. (b) If every thread hammers one shared counter, the coherence traffic dominates everything.

**Fix.** Set pool size to cores (or cores − 1 to leave room for the main thread). Shard any shared state per worker and aggregate at the end. If the work is fine-grained, batch it: one `postMessage` carrying 1000 items instead of 1000 messages.

**Class:** thrashing + false sharing. The lesson: **parallelism is not a free multiplier; below a certain task size, more workers is strictly worse.**

---

## Scenario 5 — Deadlock in a NestJS-style service

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** Intermittent total unresponsiveness: health checks pass (a trivial route responds) but every business route times out. CPU 1%. No errors logged.

**Evidence.**
1. Is anything *completing*? A counter of completed requests per minute going to zero while requests are accepted is a no-progress signature — deadlock or lost wakeup, not slowness.
2. Thread dump / async dump: are tasks parked on a lock?
3. Connection-pool metrics: are all connections checked out and idle-in-transaction? That is the deadlock: a request is waiting for a connection held by another request that is waiting for something else.
4. Search for two `await`s holding two locks, or a lock held across an HTTP call.

**Root cause.** Either an async mutex cycle, or (more likely) a **connection-pool deadlock**: request 1 holds connection A and waits for an HTTP response from service B; service B is waiting for a connection from the pool that request 1's transaction is blocking.

**Fix.** Never hold a lock or a DB transaction across a remote call. Restructure: fetch first, then lock. Impose a global lock order. Add `tryLock` with a timeout everywhere and map failure to 503. Add a no-progress alert (completed-work-per-minute = 0).

**Class:** hold-and-wait across a boundary. Distributed version: a saga with compensation, not a bigger lock.

---

## Scenario 6 — Memory climbs for 6 hours then OOM-kills

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** A long-lived service grows steadily. At ~6 hours the container is OOM-killed (exit 137) with heap usage "only" 40%. No JavaScript-level `Error`.

**Evidence, in this exact order:**
1. `dmesg | grep -i 'killed process'` or `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.events` → confirms it was the **kernel** killer, not V8.
2. `cat /proc/<pid>/status | grep -E 'RssAnon|RssFile'` → separate anonymous (heap/Buffer) from file-cache. `RssFile` is reclaimable; `RssAnon` is not.
3. `process.memoryUsage()` sampled every minute → which of `rss`, `heapTotal`, `heapUsed`, `external`, `arrayBuffers` is growing? **`external`/`arrayBuffers` growing means Buffers/typed arrays, not objects.**
4. `--trace-gc` → is GC failing to reclaim, or not being run?
5. Two heap snapshots an hour apart → the dominator tree diff shows the retainers.
6. `async_hooks`-based retainer check for timers/listeners: is something accumulating registrations?

**Root cause (most common, in order):** (a) `external` growth — Buffers or `ArrayBuffer`s held by an in-flight cache; (b) an unbounded `Map` used as a cache with no eviction; (c) listener accumulation (`setInterval` per request, `EventEmitter` with unbounded listeners); (d) closures retaining a large scope via a timer that is never cleared.

**Fix.** Fix the specific retainer. Then set `--max-old-space-size` **below** the cgroup limit so V8 collects before the kernel kills; add `--max-semi-space-size=16` to cut scavenge frequency; alert on the *slope* of `rss` and on `external`.

**Class:** leak plus a missing safety margin. Note the OOM-kill is a *symptom*; the headroom misconfiguration is a second, separate bug.

---

## Scenario 7 — Intermittent `EMFILE` after a dependency upgrade

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** After a library upgrade, a service starts returning 500s with `EMFILE: too many open files` under modest load. It used to be fine.

**Evidence.**
1. `/proc/<pid>/limits` → soft/hard. Then compare to a Worker *child* process: does each `child_process`/Worker get its own fd table? (`fork` duplicates the table but the limit is per-process, and the number of processes may have increased.)
2. `/proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l` grouped by target: which kind dominates? `socket`, `pipe`, `anon_inode` (epoll/eventfd), or real files.
3. Did the number of sockets per request increase? e.g. the library now opens a separate socket for DNS (`dns.lookup` on the threadpool) or for a keep-alive agent misconfiguration.
4. `ss -tan | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c` → are there thousands in `CLOSE_WAIT`? **`CLOSE_WAIT` means your side never called `close` — that is a leak in your code, not in the network.**

**Root cause.** Either (a) the library now leaks a socket per request (a `CLOSE_WAIT` accumulation), or (b) the fd *limit* is being hit by a legitimate increase in concurrent sockets, or (c) `child_process` was added and each child inherits 3 pipe fds plus everything else.

**Fix.** Find and fix the `CLOSE_WAIT` source (usually a stream whose `destroy()` is not called on the error path, or a response body never consumed). Then raise the limit as a mitigation: `LimitNOFILE=65536` in the systemd unit. Consider `dns.resolve` over `dns.lookup` to avoid the threadpool hop. Set `maxConnections` and idle timeouts.

**Class:** resource leak plus a missing limit. Raising the limit alone converts a fast failure into a slow OOM of kernel memory.

---

## Scenario 8 — Wrong answer under concurrency, right answer single-threaded

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** A test suite passes 100% locally (single-threaded) and fails roughly `(threads−1)/threads` of the time in CI with 8 Workers. The failure is a duplicated or missing row.

**Evidence.**
1. Make it deterministic: force simultaneous arrival with a `Atomics.wait` barrier so all Workers hit the critical section at once.
2. Narrow to the smallest failing input (usually 2 items).
3. Is the write an `INSERT` with no unique constraint? Then duplicates are a *database* race, not a data race.
4. Is the read-then-write in application code? Then it is a check-then-act race.

**Root cause.** Either a missing unique constraint (two Workers both observe "not present" and both insert) or a read-modify-write in application code.

**Fix.**
- Database: add `UNIQUE` and use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING/UPDATE`. Never "check then insert".
- Application: sharded state with a single writer per key, or a transaction with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or an optimistic version column (`UPDATE t SET v=$new, version=version+1 WHERE id=$id AND version=$old`) with a retry on zero rows affected.

**Class:** check-then-act race. The single-threaded pass is the trap: it proves nothing about concurrency.

---

## Scenario 9 — "Async made it slower"

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** A CPU-bound batch job was refactored from a synchronous loop to `Promise.all(items.map(async (x) => heavySync(x)))` and now takes 3x longer, using one core.

**Evidence.**
1. `process.cpuUsage()` vs wall time: CPU ratio ≈ 1, so the core count is not the issue; overhead is.
2. Count promises created: 1,000,000 promises and 1,000,000 microtask hops.
3. `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay`: p99 loop delay grew.
4. Profile: time in promise machinery / GC, not in `heavySync`.

**Root cause.** Every `async` arrow function allocates a promise and schedules a microtask. For a 2 µs unit of work, the overhead dominates. Plus GC pressure from 1M short-lived promises.

**Fix.** (a) Move CPU work to a Worker pool sized to cores with data sharding; (b) if you must stay on one thread, **cooperative chunking**: batch items into chunks sized so each chunk is ~1-10 ms, run a chunk synchronously, and yield between chunks with `setImmediate`; (c) profile to make sure the algorithm itself is not accidentally O(n²).

**Class:** abstraction overhead vs work granularity. The rule: **concurrency overhead is per operation; only parallelise when the operation is large relative to it.**

---

## Scenario 10 — "It works, but the numbers are wrong"

🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Symptoms.** An analytics pipeline computes daily aggregates. Under a 40× replay, the totals differ by ~2%. Under normal traffic they are correct. Each stage is individually "correct".

**Evidence.**
1. Which stage's output count differs from its input count? (producers and consumers disagree)
2. Are consumers committing offsets before or after processing? (at-most-once → silent loss)
3. Is there any `UPDATE ... SET counter = counter + 1` in the handler, applied out of order?
4. Version column on the aggregate row: are there updates with a *lower* version arriving after a higher one?

**Root cause.** A mix of (a) at-most-once consumption (offset committed before processing) losing messages under crash, and (b) non-commutative out-of-order updates (`counter = counter + 1` applied in delivery order rather than event-version order).

**Fix.** (a) Commit offsets after successful processing (at-least-once) and make the handler idempotent with a `processed_events` unique constraint; (b) carry a monotonic per-aggregate `version` and apply `WHERE version < incoming` (upsert with a version guard), making the handler order-insensitive.

**Class:** exactly-once and ordering. Both are required and neither is provided by the broker. This is the scenario that teaches 10.4.15.

---
# 10.4-10.5 INTERVIEW Q&A (32 questions with model answers)

Answers are written the way a strong candidate delivers them: the direct answer first, then the mechanism, then the production consequence. **Bold the opening clause** — that is what gets you the follow-up, and the follow-up is where the grade is decided.

---

### Q1. Process vs thread: what is the fundamental difference?

**Answer.** A process is a resource boundary — its own virtual address space, file-descriptor table, and credentials. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process's address space; it gets its own stack, registers, and program counter, but shares the heap, the globals, and the fd table with every other thread in that process. So: **processes share nothing, threads share data.** That single fact explains process isolation, `fork`, IPC, and every data race.

Follow-ups you should expect: what is copied by `fork` (page tables, copy-on-write, so cheap; but the file *offset* is shared, which surprises people); why threads are cheaper to create; what `ps -eLf` is showing you.

---

### Q2. What does the OS actually do during a context switch?

**Answer.** It saves the outgoing thread's register set, program counter, and stack pointer into a kernel-side task structure, switches the page-table root (and flushes or re-tags the TLB), and restores the incoming thread's state. On x86 that is `SAVE/RESTORE` plus a `MOV CR3` plus scheduler bookkeeping — on the order of **1–5 microseconds**. But the real cost is indirect: the new thread's code and data are cold in L1/L2/L3 and the TLB, so it takes **tens to hundreds of microseconds** to become productive. Which is why what matters is not the per-switch cost but the **switch rate**.

Good follow-up: "how do I detect thrashing?" — involuntary context switches per second (`pidstat -w`) climbing while throughput falls.

---

### Q3. Explain virtual memory, and why a container gets OOM-killed.

**Answer.** Virtual memory is an indirection layer: each process has a page table mapping its virtual addresses to physical frames, with demand paging — a page is only allocated when touched — and copy-on-write for shared pages after `fork`. TLB caches the translations; a TLB miss costs a 4-level page-table walk.

A container is OOM-killed when the cgroup's memory charge (anonymous memory **plus** page cache **plus** kernel memory for the process's structures, including its fds) exceeds `memory.max`, and the kernel cannot free enough. Anonymous memory is not reclaimable, so it picks a victim — usually your process.

The production fix that people get wrong: set `--max-old-space-size` **below** the cgroup limit so V8 collects before the kernel kills you. Also look at `external` memory in `process.memoryUsage()` — RSS above the V8 heap limit is usually Buffers and native allocations, not objects.

---

### Q4. What is a file descriptor, and how do you debug `EMFILE`?

**Answer.** An fd is an integer index into a per-process table of *open file descriptions*; on Unix, sockets, pipes, epoll sets, and inotify watches all live there, which is why `EMFILE` says "file" when you did not open a file. Debug in five commands: `/proc/<pid>/limits`, `/proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l`, `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd` grouped by target type, `lsof -p <pid>`, and `ss -s`.

Causes, in order of frequency: sockets not destroyed on the error path, no idle timeout (slow-loris), `CLOSE_WAIT` accumulation (your side never called close), `child_process` pipes, and TIME_WAIT exhaustion of ephemeral ports.

The critical distinction: **`EMFILE` is per-process, `ENFILE` is system-wide.** And raising `ulimit` is a mitigation, not a fix — it converts a fast failure into a slow OOM of kernel memory.

---

### Q5. Give me a race condition in JavaScript.

**Answer.** Here is one:

```js
class Account {
  #balance = 0;
  async deposit(n) { const c = this.#balance; await sleep(0); this.#balance = c + n; }
}
await Promise.all([a.deposit(100), a.deposit(100)]);   // balance is 100, not 200
```

The `await` between the read and the write is an interleaving point. Two concurrent deposits both read 0, both write 100. The misconception I have to correct here is "JavaScript is single-threaded so it has no races": the *main thread* has no data races, but `await`, promises, and Workers are all concurrency.

---

### Q6. Is `counter++` atomic in JavaScript?

**Answer.** On the main thread, effectively yes for small integers — because no other task runs in the middle of a synchronous statement. **But that is an implementation accident, not a language guarantee**, and it stops being true the moment you cross `await`, move to a Worker, or use `Atomics`. That is exactly why you should not build on it: correctness that depends on "no one interleaves within a synchronous block" is correctness that a refactor can remove.

Across Workers, `Atomics.load` + `Atomics.store` are individually atomic but the pair is not — use `Atomics.add`.

---

### Q7. What are the three requirements for a correct critical-section solution?

**Answer.** (1) **Mutual exclusion** — at most one thread in the critical section. (2) **Progress** — if nobody is in the section and someone wants in, exactly one of those *wanting* threads gets in; no bystander is preferred and nobody is blocked forever. (3) **Bounded waiting** — a thread that has requested entry gets it within a bounded number of steps, which is what rules out starvation.

Peterson's algorithm achieves all three for two threads with plain loads and stores; Bakery's generalises it to N. Most production mutexes trade some of progress for scalability by being unfair (barging), which is why starvation-free is not guaranteed unless you use a fair lock.

---

### Q8. Mutex vs semaphore: what is the difference?

**Answer.** A **mutex has exactly one permit and enforces ownership** — only the acquiring thread may release it — and exists to protect an invariant. A **semaphore is a counter of N permits with no ownership** — thread A can acquire and thread B can release — and exists to bound or signal resources. So a **binary** semaphore behaves like a mutex *except* for ownership, and that exception matters: if anyone can release, someone can release without having prepared the state the mutex was protecting.

Real use: a `Semaphore(10)` in front of a connection pool. A `Mutex` around a multi-field invariant.

---

### Q9. Name the four Coffman conditions and how do you prevent deadlock?

**Answer.** Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. All four must hold simultaneously.

In practice you break **circular wait** by imposing a global total order on locks and always acquiring left to right, and sometimes hold-and-wait by scoping to one lock at a time. The global ordering is cheap, local, and provably correct — that is the answer to give. The other techniques: `tryLock` with timeout and jittered backoff converts deadlock into a fast failure; detection plus recovery (a wait-for graph) finds cycles that prevention missed but requires destructive recovery.

The one-liner worth having: **prevention is a discipline, detection is an incident.**

---

### Q10. What is the difference between starvation, deadlock, and livelock?

**Answer.** **Deadlock**: everyone is blocked, nothing can proceed, and waiting longer changes nothing. **Starvation**: someone is blocked indefinitely, but the system as a whole keeps making progress — usually an unfair lock or unfair scheduling. **Livelock**: nobody is blocked, everyone is running, and no progress is made because their actions cancel out — two peers backing off in sync.

Detection distinguishes them: a deadlock shows *zero* completed work with threads in a wait cycle; starvation shows some work completing with a subset of requests never served; livelock shows high CPU with zero progress.

---

### Q11. Concurrency vs parallelism vs interleaving.

**Answer.** Concurrency is a property of **structure** (decomposed into independently progressing tasks); parallelism is a property of **execution** (running at the same instant); interleaving is what a single-threaded scheduler produces (tasks taking turns). Concurrent does not imply parallel — you can be fully concurrent on one core. Parallel implies concurrent. And a task waiting on IO is concurrent but not parallel.

Practical form: `Promise.all` over 100 fetches is concurrent and not parallel. A Worker pool over 4 CPU shards is both.

---

### Q12. My async code is CPU-bound. What do I do?

**Answer.** Nothing useful, with async — `Promise.all` over CPU work does not raise throughput and usually makes it slower, because you add a promise and a microtask per item on top of one core. Three real options: (1) move the work to a `Worker` pool sized to cores with data sharding and per-worker state, aggregating at the end; (2) if you must stay single-threaded, cooperative chunking with explicit yields for *fairness*, understanding it does not raise the CPU ceiling; (3) fix the algorithm — parallelism cannot rescue O(n²).

First question to ask: measured, is it actually CPU-bound? Compare wall time to `process.cpuUsage()`.

---

### Q13. How many threads should a pool have?

**Answer.** It depends on which resource is the constraint, and the two answers are different. **CPU-bound**: about the core count — `cores`, or `cores − 1` to leave room for the event loop. Oversubscribing CPU work makes throughput *fall* and p99 *rise*, because you pay involuntary context switches and lose cache locality on every one. **IO-bound with a blocking client**: Little's Law — `threads = throughput × service time`. 5000 requests/second at 20 ms each needs 100 concurrent threads; you can also just not use threads and do async IO, which gives you 5000 concurrent operations on a handful of threads.

Always cap the queue. An unbounded queue in front of a bounded pool converts a latency problem into an OOM.

---

### Q14. What is a work queue and what are the rejection policies?

**Answer.** The queue is where tasks wait between submission and execution; its capacity *is* the system's admission control. Policies: **abort** (reject, return an error like `QUEUE_FULL` with `Retry-After` — the client decides), **caller-runs** (the submitter executes it — perfect utilisation, but you have pushed the latency onto the caller), **discard-oldest/discard-newest** (for metrics), and **blocking** (for in-process pipelines).

Growth order matters: most libraries grow the pool to `max` first, then queue. So `core=8, max=64, queue=100000` means a burst of 5000 tasks creates 8 threads and queues 4992, and your p99 quietly becomes 10 seconds. Set the queue from your latency budget: `queueLength = (targetP99 − serviceTime) × arrivalRate`.

---

### Q15. What is the GIL and does it stop Python threading?

**Answer.** The GIL is a per-interpreter mutex around bytecode execution in CPython, so only one thread runs *Python code* at a time. It exists because the interpreter's memory management is not thread-safe and making it fine-grained was expensive.

It does **not** block IO, and it is released around GIL-releasing C extensions, so threads still give you IO concurrency, and `numpy`/`hashlib` work in threads at full parallelism. For CPU-bound work you need processes (`ProcessPoolExecutor`) or `nogil` builds.

JavaScript's answer is the mirror image: no GIL, but the main thread is still single-threaded, so you use Workers (separate isolates on real threads) for parallelism, plus `SharedArrayBuffer` + `Atomics` for shared memory.

---

### Q16. What is memory ordering, and why do I care in JavaScript?

**Answer.** Memory ordering determines which order a write in one thread becomes visible in another. Without synchronisation, compilers and CPUs may reorder accesses and hold values in store buffers indefinitely, giving you **visibility** failures (B never sees A's write) and **ordering** failures (B sees `ready` but stale `data`).

The canonical example — write `data`, then `ready`; spin on `ready`, then read `data` — works on x86 by accident of total-store-order and breaks on ARM, because ARM is weakly ordered and the stores can sit in the store buffer independently.

In JavaScript: within one isolate there is nothing to order, so it does not come up. Across Workers it is everything — shared memory must be accessed through `Atomics` (which the spec makes sequentially consistent), and plain indexed reads/writes on a `SharedArrayBuffer` are data races that the engine is entitled to optimise around.

---

### Q17. What is backpressure and how do I implement it?

**Answer.** Backpressure is a consumer-driven signal to slow the producer when the producer outruns the consumer. Every system has it; the question is whether you chose it or inherited it.

Mechanisms: bounded queue with **blocking** (producer waits — in-process pipelines), bounded queue with **drop** (metrics), **coalescing** (keep only the latest value per key — dashboards, presence, progress), **load shedding** (reject by priority, return 503/429), **spill to disk** (durable batch pipelines), and **credit-based flow control** across a network (HTTP/2 windows, gRPC flow control — the receiver grants the sender a byte budget).

In Node the idiom is a `Semaphore` per downstream dependency plus honouring the return value of `stream.write()` and the `drain` event.

---

### Q18. Your service is slow and CPU is 5%. What is happening?

**Answer.** You are **waiting**, not computing. Wall time high, process CPU time low is the signature of IO latency, a saturated connection pool, or a lock. Go and look at the dependency, not the CPU: per-hop latency histograms, pool utilisation, and queue depth.

Concretely: check pool saturation first (highest base rate), then downstream p99, then lock wait times, then event-loop delay if you are on Node.

---

### Q19. Explain Little's Law and use it for me.

**Answer.** `L = λ × W`: the average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time in the system. In a thread pool serving blocking IO, `L` is the concurrency you need. 5000 requests/second at 20 ms each → 100 concurrent. 200 requests/second at 500 ms → 100 concurrent, same answer for a completely different reason.

It also explains queue behaviour: a queue that is growing is a system where λ currently exceeds capacity, and the queue length is the integral of that difference. That is why the fix is to bound admission, not to enlarge the queue.

---

### Q20. What is a semaphore-based rate limiter, and what does it not do?

**Answer.** A concurrency limiter is a counting semaphore: `acquire` before the operation, `release` in a `finally`. Add a token bucket for the *rate* component if you need requests-per-second rather than just in-flight count.

What it does not do: it does not bound memory (ten concurrent requests each holding 100 MB still OOM), it does not give fairness across tenants (that needs per-tenant semaphores plus a global one, acquired in a fixed order), and it does not protect against a downstream that gets slower while your concurrency stays constant — for that you need a queue with age-based shedding.

---

### Q21. How do you test concurrency code?

**Answer.** Not by running it once. (1) **Deterministic interleaving**: inject a scheduler and enumerate orderings — Go's `runtime` plus `-race`, Rust's `loom`, Java's `jcstress` — and assert on the *set of possible outcomes*, not one. (2) **Race detectors**: ThreadSanitizer, Helgrind, Go's `-race`, Java Flight Recorder. (3) **Contention-maximising load tests**: many actors, a `Barrier` to force simultaneous arrival, minutes of runtime. (4) **Fault injection**: kill the worker between "did the work" and "committed the offset"; abort mid-transaction. (5) **Invariant assertions**: assert the invariants (`balance >= 0`, `count == sum of shards`) so a violation fails loudly under load rather than in a report three weeks later.

(6) Bounded timeouts everywhere in tests, so a deadlock fails the test rather than hanging the CI job.

---

### Q22. Why is my atomic counter slower than a non-atomic one, and what do I use instead?

**Answer.** Because an atomic read-modify-write requires *exclusive* ownership of the cache line, every store from every core becomes a coherence transaction. Shard the counter: each thread owns a slot, and you sum the shards when you read. No contention, no coherence traffic, and it is exact. That is precisely what Java's `LongAdder` does and what every metrics library does internally.

Atomic ops are the right tool for a genuine RMW on shared state you cannot partition — a lock-free stack pointer, a reference count. They are the wrong tool for a hot counter.

---

### Q23. `Atomics.wait` on the Node main thread. What happens?

**Answer.** It blocks the entire thread — including the event loop — so nothing else in the process runs until the value changes or the timeout fires. It is effectively a self-inflicted outage. Use `Atomics.waitAsync` where available, or a `MessagePort`, or a semaphore with an async wait.

In browsers it is also forbidden on the main thread for the same reason, and `SharedArrayBuffer` requires cross-origin isolation (`COOP`/`COEP`) or it is simply `undefined`.

---

### Q24. How do you implement graceful shutdown for a Worker pool?

**Answer.** In order: (1) mark not-ready so the load balancer stops sending traffic; (2) stop accepting new tasks but keep executing in-flight; (3) drain the queue with a hard deadline, rejecting anything that did not start with a typed `CANCELLED` error; (4) close DB/Redis clients; (5) clear every interval and timer; (6) terminate Workers and await their `exit` event; (7) `server.close()` **after** in-flight work completes — reversing these two deadlocks the shutdown, because `close()` waits for existing connections.
