| Good on exact terms, poor on paraphrase | Vectors only, no lexical leg | Hybrid search |
| Great on paraphrase, poor on error codes | Sanitisation stripped codes, or no lexical leg | Preserve codes; hybrid search |
| Perfect offline, poor in production | Eval set not representative | Cluster production queries; measure coverage |
| Degrades over time | Index stale | Incremental indexing (13.4.10) |
| Degrades after a deploy | Prompt or model change | Regression suite; recipe-level rollback |
| Same query, different answer each time | No caching, no pinning, nondeterministic sampling | Cache; lower temperature; pin model |
| Answer from an old policy | Deletions not propagated | Soft-delete propagation + index sweep |
| Correct answer from an irrelevant-looking chunk | Chunk contains the fact but not in isolation | Breadcrumb prefixes; parent expansion |

**The debugging procedure.** Always walk the pipeline in order, and stop at the first broken stage.

```ts
export async function debugRagQuery(query: string, tenantId: string): Promise<RagDebugReport> {
  const stages: any[] = [];

  // 1. Retrieval candidates
  const dense = await vectorSearch(toVector(query), tenantId, 50);
  const lexical = await lexicalSearch(query, tenantId, 50);
  stages.push({ stage: "candidates", dense: dense.length, lexical: lexical.length,
    denseTop: dense.slice(0, 5).map((h) => ({ id: h.id, score: h.score, preview: preview(h.meta.text) })) });

  // 2. Fusion
  const fused = reciprocalRankFusion([
    { name: "dense", hits: dense, weight: 1 },
    { name: "lexical", hits: lexical, weight: 1 },
  ]);
  stages.push({ stage: "fused", n: fused.length,
    onlyInDense: fused.filter((f) => f.source === "dense").length,
    onlyInLexical: fused.filter((f) => f.source === "lexical").length });

  // 3. Rerank
  const { hits, diagnostics } = await retrieveWithRerank(query, tenantId,
    { lexicalK: 50, denseK: 50, finalK: 8, rerank: reranker });
  stages.push({ stage: "rerank", diagnostics });

  // 4. Assembly
  const asm = assembleByBudget(hits, remainingBudget(budget), tokenizer);
  stages.push({ stage: "assembly", usedTokens: asm.usedTokens,
    excludedByBudget: asm.excluded.length, included: asm.included.map((h) => h.id) });

  // 5. Generation
  const res = await generate(query, asm.included, recipe);
  stages.push({ stage: "generation", stopReason: res.stopReason,
    outputTokens: res.usage.outputTokens });

  // 6. Verification
  const ground = await scoreGroundedness(textOf(res.content), sourceMap(asm.included), judge);
  stages.push({ stage: "verify", unsupportedClaims: ground.unsupported.length,
    unresolvedCitations: ground.unsupported.filter((u) => !u.bestSourceId).length });

  return { query, stages, verdict: diagnose(stages) };
}

function diagnose(stages: any[]): string {
  const [c, f, r, a, g, v] = stages;
  if (r.diagnostics.finalIds.length === 0) return "RETRIEVAL_EMPTY: no candidates survived filtering";
  if (c.dense === 0 && c.lexical === 0) return "INDEX_EMPTY: filters likely too restrictive";
  if (v.unsupportedClaims > 0 && a.excludedByBudget > 0)
    return "ASSEMBLY_TRUNCATED: relevant chunk likely dropped by budget";
  if (f.onlyInLexical > f.onlyInDense * 3) return "LEXICAL_DOMINANT: consider hybrid weights";
  if (v.unsupportedClaims > 0 && r.diagnostics.reranked) return "GENERATION_HALLUCINATION: evidence was present";
  if (g.stopReason === "max_tokens") return "TRUNCATION: raise budget or chunk the task";
  return "UNKNOWN: inspect stages";
}
```

**The three highest-yield debugging techniques.**
1. **Show the prompt.** Literally paste the assembled prompt for the failing case. Half of all "the
   model is dumb" reports dissolve here.
2. **Swap stages.** Replace retrieval with "the one chunk you know is right." If the answer is still
   wrong, it is a generation or prompt problem, not retrieval.
3. **Check the chunk, not the document.** Read the actual retrieved chunk text. Frequently the fact is
   absent because chunking cut it out.

**When to use / when not to.** Use this procedure whenever you have a *specific* reported failure with
a stored request. For aggregate quality monitoring, use the dashboards and sampling from 13.8 instead â€”
you cannot debug 400 failures individually.

**Trade-offs.** Rich debug tooling costs storage (storing full prompts and retrieved chunk text) and
engineering time. Mitigate by sampling: keep full prompt snapshots for 1% of traffic plus 100% of
flagged failures, and keep chunk text references (ids) for everything so it can be rehydrated.

**Production considerations.**
- One-click "explain this answer" in your internal tooling. It pays for itself in the first week.
- Store the retrieved chunk ids *and* the assembled prompt hash on every request.
- When users report a bad answer (a feedback button), capture the full debug report automatically.
- Watch for failure modes that change shape over time: index rot, prompt drift, and model updates all
  look like "it used to work better."

**Common mistakes.**
- Debugging by re-running the query and getting a different answer (nondeterminism masquerading as a
  bug).
- Blaming the model when the right chunk was retrieved but never included in the prompt.
- Not storing chunk text with the trace, so you cannot reconstruct what the model saw.
- Fixing retrieval for a query type that represents 0.1% of traffic.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "A user says the answer was wrong. Walk me through your debugging process."
- "How do you tell whether a bad answer is retrieval or generation?"

---

### 13.4.10 Data freshness and incremental indexing

ðŸ”Ÿ Advanced Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** Freshness is the guarantee that the index reflects the source of truth within a stated
window. It is an SLO ("p95 staleness under 15 minutes for changed documents, under 1 hour for new
documents") and it requires an explicit change-propagation design.

**Mechanics â€” the ingestion pipeline with change tracking.**

```ts
export interface IngestJob {
  source: SourceRef;
  sourceVersion: string;      // etag, hash, or updated_at from the source
  mode: "full" | "incremental";
}

export async function ingest(job: IngestJob): Promise<IngestReport> {
  const existing = await db.query(
    `SELECT source_version, indexed_at FROM document_sources WHERE source = $1`, [job.source.id]);
  if (existing.rows[0] && existing.rows[0].source_version === job.sourceVersion) {
    return { status: "skipped", reason: "unchanged" };
  }

  const docs = await fetchChangedDocuments(job.source, job.sourceVersion);
  const report: IngestReport = { status: "ok", added: 0, updated: 0, deleted: 0, unchanged: 0 };

  for (const doc of docs) {
    const contentHash = sha256(doc.text);
    const prev = await db.query(
      `SELECT id, content_hash, chunker_ver, embed_model FROM documents
        WHERE source = $1 AND external_id = $2`, [job.source.id, doc.externalId]);

    if (prev.rows.length === 0) {
      await indexDocument({ ...doc, contentHash, mode: "insert" });
      report.added++;
      continue;
    }
    const p = prev.rows[0];
    if (p.content_hash === contentHash) { report.unchanged++; continue; }

    // Content changed. Re-chunk and re-embed, but reuse embeddings for unchanged chunks
    // when the chunk text is byte-identical.
    const { chunks, reusedEmbeddingIds } = await chunkAndDiff(doc, p);
    const toEmbed = chunks.filter((c) => !c.textHashes.has(p.id));
    const vecs = toEmbed.length > 0 ? await embedder.embed(toEmbed.map((c) => c.text), "document") : [];

    await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
      await tx.query(`UPDATE documents SET content_hash = $1, updated_at = now() WHERE id = $2`,
        [contentHash, p.id]);
      // Soft-delete old chunks; they become visible to vacuum, not to search.
      await tx.query(`UPDATE chunks SET deleted_at = now() WHERE doc_id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`, [p.id]);
      await insertChunks(tx, p.id, chunks, vecs);
    });
    report.updated++;
  }

  // Hard-delete handling: sources that removed documents must propagate.
  const seen = new Set(docs.map((d) => d.externalId));
  const stale = await db.query(
    `SELECT id, external_id FROM documents WHERE source = $1`, [job.source.id]);
  for (const s of stale.rows) {
    if (seen.has(s.external_id)) continue;
    await softDeleteDocumentTree(s.id);      // documents AND chunks AND parent nodes
    report.deleted++;
  }

  await db.query(
    `UPDATE document_sources SET source_version = $1, indexed_at = now() WHERE source = $2`,
    [job.sourceVersion, job.source.id]);
  return report;
}
```

**Soft delete and vacuum.** Never hard-delete chunks you may still need to debug; mark them and exclude
them from search. But tombstones degrade ANN quality and waste space, so run a periodic sweep that
physically removes rows deleted more than N days ago, ideally during low traffic.

```sql
-- Vacuum: remove tombstones older than 7 days, in bounded batches.
WITH dead AS (
  SELECT id FROM chunks WHERE deleted_at < now() - interval '7 days' LIMIT 5000
)
DELETE FROM chunks c USING dead WHERE c.id = dead.id;
```

**Trigger strategies.**
- **Webhook / event-driven:** fastest, but you must handle missed and duplicated events. Keep a
  periodic reconciliation sweep regardless, because webhooks are always lossy.
- **Polling on change tokens:** simple and reliable for sources with an `updated_at` or etag. Poll at
  a frequency matching your staleness SLO.
- **Full reindex on a schedule:** the safety net. Weekly or nightly for critical corpora.

**Chunk-level diffing.** Re-embedding an entire document on every keystroke-save is expensive. Compute
chunk text hashes and reuse the stored vector for any chunk whose text is byte-identical. For a 200-chunk
document where 3 chunks changed, that is 3 embeddings instead of 200.

```ts
export async function chunkAndDiff(
  doc: SourceDocument, prev: DocumentRow,
): Promise<{ chunks: ChunkDraft[]; reusedEmbeddingIds: Set<string> }> {
  const chunks = buildChunks(doc, CHUNKER_CONFIG);   // current version
  const prevChunks = await db.query(
    `SELECT id, text_hash, embedding FROM chunks WHERE doc_id = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL`, [prev.id]);
  const prevByHash = new Map(prevChunks.rows.map((r) => [r.text_hash, r]));

  const reused = new Set<string>();
  const drafts: ChunkDraft[] = chunks.map((c) => {
    const h = sha256(c.text);
    const p = prevByHash.get(h);
    if (p) { reused.add(p.id); prevByHash.delete(h); }
    return { ...c, textHash: h, reuseId: p?.id };
  });
  // Unmatched previous chunks are gone: their ids stay in `reused` and must not be re-inserted.
  return { chunks: drafts, reusedEmbeddingIds: reused };
}
```

**Handling embedding-model or chunker-version change.** This is a full reindex. Do it as a **dual-index
migration**, never a drop-and-rebuild:

```
1. Create chunks_v2 alongside chunks_v1.
2. Backfill in the background, prioritized by query traffic (hot documents first).
3. Shadow-query: run both indexes for real traffic, log recall differences on labelled queries.
4. Cut over reads at a config flag.
5. Keep v1 warm for one rollback window, then drop.
```

**When to use / when not to.** Any corpus that changes while users read it needs a freshness design. If
your corpus is a versioned artifact â€” a documentation snapshot, a release, a quarterly filing â€” you can
use immutable snapshots and a pointer swap, which is far simpler and gives perfect consistency for
as-of questions.

**Trade-offs.** Freshness costs write throughput, index churn, and dual-write complexity during
migrations. Aggressive freshness (continuous reindex) can dominate your embedding bill; lazy freshness
(weekly) is cheap and occasionally embarrassingly wrong. The SLO should reflect what your users
actually need: a policy document needs hours; a changelog needs seconds.

**Production considerations.**
- Expose index freshness in your own status dashboard alongside the model provider's status.
- Alert on ingestion failures and on `staleness_p95` breaching the SLO.
- Make ingestion idempotent â€” jobs retry, events duplicate, and the pipeline must survive both.
- Serialize ingestion per source with a lock so two runs cannot interleave deletes and inserts.
- Chunk-level diffing is the single biggest ingest cost optimization; implement it early.

**Common mistakes.**
- Only reindexing on a schedule and never reacting to deletes, so removed policies remain answerable.
- Re-embedding everything on every change.
- Dropping and rebuilding the index in place during a deploy, with no rollback.
- Trusting webhooks alone, with no reconciliation sweep, and drifting further out of sync every week.
- Forgetting that soft-deleted documents still appear in *search results UI* if you filter only in the
  vector query and not in the metadata query.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "How do you keep a RAG index fresh?"
- "What happens to your index when you change the embedding model?"
- "How do you handle a document being deleted?"

---

---
## 13.5 Tool and Function Calling

### 13.5.1 The contract: name, description, JSON schema

ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** Tool calling is how a model requests that *your* code do something. The model never
executes anything; it emits a structured request naming a tool and providing arguments, and your server
decides whether to run it. The tool definition **is** the API surface you are designing.

**Mechanics.** Three fields, each doing a specific job:

1. **Name.** A verb-noun identifier, stable across prompt versions. Models match names to descriptions
   far more reliably than humans expect; renaming a tool is a breaking change to behaviour, not just
   to code. Prefer one clear name over two overlapping ones â€” ambiguity between similar tools is the
   top cause of wrong-tool selection.
2. **Description.** The model's *only* documentation. It must say what the tool does, when to use it,
   when **not** to use it, what each argument means including units and formats, and what the return
   value is. This is the highest-leverage text in your entire system.
3. **Input schema.** A JSON Schema for the arguments, with `required`, `additionalProperties: false`,
   enums, and descriptions on every property. The schema is both documentation (the model reads the
   `description` fields) and, where supported, a decoding constraint.

```ts
export interface ToolSpec {
  name: string;
  description: string;
  input_schema: Record<string, unknown>;
  // Optional, your own metadata â€” never sent to the model.
  meta?: {
    destructive?: boolean;
    requiresApproval?: boolean;
    idempotent?: boolean;
    scopes: string[];              // authz scopes the CALLER must hold
    costClass?: "free" | "cheap" | "expensive";
    timeoutMs?: number;
  };
}

export const searchOrders: ToolSpec = {
  name: "search_orders",
  description: [
    "Search the current customer's orders by status, date range, or free-text query.",
    "Use this when the user asks about their own orders, shipments, or order status.",
    "Returns up to 25 orders, newest first, as {id, status, placedAt, totalCents, itemCount}.",
    "If the user asks about pricing or plan features rather than specific orders, use list_plans instead.",
    "Never use this to search the product catalogue; use search_catalog for that.",
  ].join(" "),
  input_schema: {
    type: "object",
    additionalProperties: false,
    required: ["query"],
    properties: {
      query: {
        type: "string",
        description:
          "Free-text search terms, e.g. 'sneakers', or a status like 'pending'. May be empty string to list all orders.",
      },
      status: {
        type: "string",
        enum: ["pending", "paid", "shipped", "delivered", "cancelled", "refunded"],
        description: "Optional exact status filter. Omit to search across all statuses.",
      },
      placedAfter: {
        type: "string",
        description: "ISO-8601 date, inclusive lower bound, e.g. '2026-01-15'. Omit for no lower bound.",
      },
      placedBefore: {
        type: "string",
        description: "ISO-8601 date, exclusive upper bound. Omit for no upper bound.",
      },
      limit: {
        type: "integer",
        minimum: 1,
        maximum: 25,
        description: "Maximum results to return. Defaults to 10. Hard cap 25.",
      },
    },
  },
  meta: {
    destructive: false,
    requiresApproval: false,
    idempotent: true,
    scopes: ["orders:read"],
    costClass: "cheap",
    timeoutMs: 3_000,
  },
};
```

**Output shape for tool results.** Return a compact, structured, *already-formatted* result. The model
reads tool output and either reuses it or summarizes it, so verbose JSON wastes tokens and invites
misreading. Return exactly the fields needed, plus a stable `ok` discriminator, and cap size.

```ts
export function formatToolResult(ok: boolean, data: unknown, err?: { code: string; message: string }): string {
  const payload = ok
    ? { ok: true, data: truncateDeep(data, MAX_RESULT_CHARS) }
    : { ok: false, error: { code: err?.code ?? "unknown", message: err?.message ?? "tool failed" } };
  return JSON.stringify(payload);
}
```

Errors are results, not exceptions. An error tool result lets the model recover ("the date was invalid,
let me retry") instead of aborting the whole turn.

**When to use / when not to.** Use tool calling when the model needs information you have (a database,
an internal API, live state) or the ability to take an action with side effects. Do not use it when a
deterministic function call would do â€” putting a tool around `add(a, b)` adds latency, tokens, and a
failure mode for nothing. Keep the tool count small: past roughly 15â€“20 tools in a single request,
selection accuracy degrades sharply. Split into multiple tool groups selected by a router.

**Trade-offs.** Tools cost prompt tokens (schemas are usually a few hundred to a couple thousand tokens
each) on **every** request. Schema strictness improves argument quality but makes the model fail
harder on unusual inputs. Descriptions cost tokens too, and verbose descriptions compete with each
other for the model's attention.

**Production considerations.**
- Version tool schemas alongside prompts; a schema change alters model behaviour.
- Validate arguments against the schema **server-side** before executing, even when the provider claims
  to enforce it. Never trust the model's arithmetic, ranges, or enum values.
- Bound every result. A tool returning 2MB of JSON will blow the context and cost.
- Tool definitions must be part of the cached prefix (13.7.2) or you pay for them on every turn.

**Common mistakes.**
- Vague descriptions ("Gets data") with no units or format hints.
- Two tools whose descriptions overlap, so the model picks wrong.
- No `additionalProperties: false`, letting the model invent parameters you then reject.
- Returning raw database rows with internal fields and IDs you did not intend to expose.
- Throwing on tool failure instead of returning an error result.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "How do you write a good tool description?"
- "How do you decide how many tools to expose?"
- "What do you do when the model passes invalid arguments?"

---

### 13.5.2 Tool selection accuracy and description engineering

ðŸ”´ Advanced Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** Tool selection accuracy is the probability the model picks the right tool given the
request. It is measurable with a labelled set, and it is improved primarily by **description
engineering**, not by model upgrades.

**Mechanics â€” the levers, in order of impact.**

**1. Disambiguate boundaries explicitly.** State what each tool is for *and* what to use instead. Models
choose by contrast.

```
- search_orders: Use for the customer's own orders. NOT for product availability â€” use search_catalog.
- search_catalog: Use for products, stock, and pricing. NOT for a customer's order history.
```

**2. One tool per concept.** If you have `get_user` and `get_user_with_orders`, you have created a
choice. Prefer one tool with an optional `include` parameter.

**3. Put argument constraints in the description.** Models respect prose constraints surprisingly well:
"Date must be ISO-8601. Do not pass relative dates like 'last month'."

**4. Include the shape of the return value.** It reduces hallucinated assumptions about what comes back.

**5. Name the trigger conditions.** "Use when the user says 'refund', 'return', or 'money back'."

**6. Reduce the tool count via routing.** Two-stage dispatch: a cheap classifier picks a tool group,
then only that group's tools are exposed.

```ts
export interface ToolGroup { id: string; label: string; tools: ToolSpec[]; examples: string[]; }

export async function selectToolGroup(
  userText: string, groups: ToolGroup[], classifier: ModelFn,
): Promise<ToolGroup> {
  const catalogue = groups
    .map((g) => `<group id="${g.id}" examples="${escapeAttr(g.examples.join(" | "))}">\n${g.label}\n</group>`)
    .join("\n");
  const res = await classifier({
    model: FAST_MODEL,
    maxOutputTokens: 40,
    temperature: 0,
    responseSchema: {
      type: "object",
      additionalProperties: false,
      required: ["group"],
      properties: { group: { type: "string", enum: groups.map((g) => g.id) } },
    },
    messages: [
      {
        role: "system",
        content:
          "Route the request to exactly one tool group. Output the group id only.\n\n" +
          "GROUPS\n" + catalogue,
      },
      { role: "user", content: userText },
    ],
  });
  const parsed = JSON.parse(textOf(res.content));
  return groups.find((g) => g.id === parsed.group) ?? groups[0];
}
```

**Measuring selection accuracy.** Build a labelled set: for each of 100â€“200 realistic requests, the tool
a human says *should* be called (and the arguments). Then measure:

```ts
export interface ToolSelectionCase {
  id: string;
  userText: string;
  history?: ChatMessage[];
  expectedTool: string;
  expectedArgs?: Record<string, unknown>;
  forbiddenTools?: string[];   // tools that would cause harm or cost if chosen
}

export interface SelectionReport {
  accuracy: number;
  toolAccuracy: number;         // right tool
  argAccuracy: number;          // right tool AND right args
  confusion: Record<string, Record<string, number>>;
  forbiddenChosen: number;      // must be zero
}

export async function evaluateSelection(
  cases: ToolSelectionCase[], run: (c: ToolSelectionCase) => Promise<{ tool: string; args: unknown }>,
): Promise<SelectionReport> {
  const confusion: SelectionReport["confusion"] = {};
  let toolOk = 0, argOk = 0, forbidden = 0;

  for (const c of cases) {
    const got = await run(c);
    confusion[c.expectedTool] ??= {};
    confusion[c.expectedTool][got.tool] = (confusion[c.expectedTool][got.tool] ?? 0) + 1;
    if (got.tool === c.expectedTool) {
      toolOk++;
      if (c.expectedArgs === undefined || deepEqual(got.args, c.expectedArgs)) argOk++;
    }
    if (c.forbiddenTools?.includes(got.tool)) forbidden++;
  }

  const n = cases.length;
  return {
    accuracy: toolOk / n,
    toolAccuracy: toolOk / n,
    argAccuracy: argOk / n,
    confusion,
    forbiddenChosen: forbidden,
  };
}
```

**Reading the confusion matrix.** Errors are rarely random. Typical patterns: `search_orders` and
`get_order` confused (fix: merge or sharpen boundaries); `search_orders` chosen for product questions
(fix: add the contrast line); a rare tool never chosen (fix: add trigger words to its description);
`no_tool` cases where the model invents a call (fix: add an explicit "if none apply, respond directly").

**Description A/B testing.** Because descriptions are just prompt text, treat them as experiments. Run
the selection eval against candidate descriptions, gate on accuracy and on `forbiddenChosen`, and
record the winner in the prompt changelog.

**When to use / when not to.** Always measure on more than a handful of tools â€” selection accuracy
degrades non-linearly as the tool set grows. If you have under five well-differentiated tools, careful
descriptions are usually enough and you do not need routing. Add routing when you exceed ~15 tools or
when accuracy is high on the common cases but poor on the long tail.

**Trade-offs.** Every sentence of description costs tokens on every request, including turns where the
tool is irrelevant. Explicit contrast lines are worth it; full prose documentation is not. Routing adds
a model call and a failure mode (wrong group) in exchange for a much smaller tool list.

**Production considerations.**
- Keep the selection eval in CI when you change any description or add a tool.
- Track `tool_call_rate`, `unknown_tool_rate`, `invalid_args_rate`, and `no_op_tool_rate` (tool called
  and result ignored) in production. A rising no-op rate means descriptions or the prompt are off.
- Log every tool selection with its request text so new confusions are discoverable from real traffic.
- Version descriptions and keep the eval labels in sync.

**Common mistakes.**
- Judging tool quality by whether it "works when called" rather than whether it gets called.
- Adding tools without adding eval cases.
- Making descriptions long and abstract instead of short and operational.
- Not measuring argument accuracy separately from tool accuracy â€” a right tool with wrong arguments is
  usually still a bug.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "How do you improve tool-calling accuracy?"
- "How many tools is too many?"
- "How do you test tool selection?"

---

### 13.5.3 Parallel tool calls and orchestration

ðŸ”´ Advanced Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** Models can request several tool calls in one turn (parallel calls), and they can be
driven across multiple turns (sequential orchestration). The orchestration layer is deterministic code
you own; the model only ever *proposes* the next action.

**Mechanics â€” the loop.** The invariant that keeps agentic systems safe and debuggable: **the loop is
your code.** You decide the tools, the iteration cap, the authorization, the timeouts, and when to
stop. The model only emits the next action.

```ts
export interface AgentStep {
  index: number;
  modelOutput: ModelResponse;
  toolCalls: { id: string; name: string; input: unknown }[];
  toolResults: { toolUseId: string; content: string; isError: boolean }[];
  usage: Usage;
  latencyMs: number;
}

export interface AgentResult {
  steps: AgentStep[];
  finalText: string;
  stop: "end_turn" | "max_steps" | "budget_exceeded" | "cancelled" | "no_progress";
  totalUsage: Usage;
  transcript: ChatMessage[];
}

export async function runAgentLoop(
  initial: ChatMessage[],
  tools: ToolRegistry,
  opts: {
    system: string;
    maxSteps?: number;
    maxToolCalls?: number;
    deadlineMs?: number;
    signal?: AbortSignal;
    onEvent?: (e: AgentEvent) => void;
  },
): Promise<AgentResult> {
  const maxSteps = opts.maxSteps ?? 8;
  const maxToolCalls = opts.maxToolCalls ?? 24;
  const transcript: ChatMessage[] = [
    { role: "system", content: opts.system },
    ...initial,
  ];
  const steps: AgentStep[] = [];
  let toolCallCount = 0;
  let totalUsage: Usage = { inputTokens: 0, outputTokens: 0, cachedInputTokens: 0 };
  const toolSignatures: string[] = [];

  for (let i = 0; i < maxSteps; i++) {
    if (opts.signal?.aborted) return finish("cancelled");
    const res = await client.complete({
      model: MODEL, maxOutputTokens: 1500, messages: transcript,
      tools: tools.specs(), toolChoice: { type: "auto" },
    }, { signal: opts.signal, timeoutMs: opts.deadlineMs ?? 90_000 });

    totalUsage = addUsage(totalUsage, res.usage);
    const toolUses = res.content.filter(isToolUse);

    const step: AgentStep = {
      index: i, modelOutput: res, toolCalls: [], toolResults: [],
      usage: res.usage, latencyMs: 0,
    };

    if (toolUses.length === 0) {
      steps.push(step);
      return { steps, finalText: textOf(res.content), stop: "end_turn", totalUsage, transcript };
    }

    toolCallCount += toolUses.length;
    if (toolCallCount > maxToolCalls) return finish("budget_exceeded");

    // Loop detection: identical tool+args twice in a row means we are stuck.
    const sig = toolUses.map((t) => `${t.name}:${stableStringify(t.input)}`).sort().join("|");
    toolSignatures.push(sig);
    if (i > 0 && toolSignatures[i] === toolSignatures[i - 1]) return finish("no_progress");

    // Execute tool calls. Independent calls run concurrently; dependent ones cannot.
    const executions = await executeToolCalls(toolUses, tools, {
      signal: opts.signal,
      onEvent: opts.onEvent,
      // Never execute a tool the loop has not seen and authorized.
      maxConcurrency: 6,
    });

    for (const e of executions) {
      step.toolCalls.push({ id: e.id, name: e.name, input: e.input });
      step.toolResults.push({ toolUseId: e.id, content: e.content, isError: e.isError });
      opts.onEvent?.({ type: "tool_result", name: e.name, ok: !e.isError });
    }
    steps.push(step);

    // Append assistant turn (with tool_use blocks) then the tool results.
    transcript.push({ role: "assistant", content: res.content });
    transcript.push({ role: "tool", content: executions.map((e) => ({
      type: "tool_result", tool_use_id: e.id, content: e.content, is_error: e.isError,
    })) });
  }
  return finish("max_steps");

  function finish(stop: AgentResult["stop"]): AgentResult {
    const last = steps[steps.length - 1];
    return {
      steps,
      finalText: last ? textOf(last.modelOutput.content) : "",
      stop, totalUsage, transcript,
    };
  }
}
```

**Parallel versus sequential.** If the model emits multiple tool uses in one turn, they are
*intentionally* independent â€” the model has already decided it needs both. Execute them concurrently
with a concurrency cap, but be careful: "independent" means the model thinks so, not that they are.
`transfer_funds` and `check_balance` emitted together are a real hazard if the model expected the
balance first. Mitigations: mark mutating tools as non-parallelizable in metadata; serialize tools with
a side-effect lock per resource; and require approval for destructive tools regardless.

```ts
export const PARALLEL_POLICY: Record<string, { parallelizable: boolean; lockKey?: (input: any) => string }> = {
  search_orders: { parallelizable: true },
  search_catalog: { parallelizable: true },
  get_order: { parallelizable: true },
  check_balance: { parallelizable: true },
  transfer_funds: { parallelizable: false, lockKey: (i) => `account:${i.accountId}` },
  cancel_order: { parallelizable: false, lockKey: (i) => `order:${i.orderId}` },
};

export async function executeToolCalls(
  calls: { id: string; name: string; input: unknown }[],
  registry: ToolRegistry,
  opts: { signal?: AbortSignal; maxConcurrency: number; onEvent?: (e: AgentEvent) => void },
): Promise<ToolExecution[]> {
  const lock = new KeyedMutex();
  const groups: ToolExecution[][] = [];
  let parallel: ToolExecution[] = [];

  for (const c of calls) {
    const policy = PARALLEL_POLICY[c.name] ?? { parallelizable: false };
    if (policy.parallelizable) { parallel.push(invoke(c)); continue; }
    if (parallel.length) { groups.push(parallel); parallel = []; }
    const k = policy.lockKey ? policy.lockKey(c.input) : `tool:${c.name}`;
    groups.push([lock.runExclusive(k, () => invoke(c))]);
  }
  if (parallel.length) groups.push(parallel);

  const out: ToolExecution[] = [];
  for (const g of groups) {
    out.push(...(await Promise.all(
      g.map((p) => limit(() => p, opts.maxConcurrency, opts.signal)),
    )));
  }
  return out;

  async function invoke(c: { id: string; name: string; input: unknown }): Promise<ToolExecution> {
    const tool = registry.get(c.name);
    if (!tool) {
      return { id: c.id, name: c.name, input: c.input, isError: true,
        content: formatToolResult(false, null, { code: "unknown_tool",
          message: `No tool named ${c.name}. Available: ${registry.names().join(", ")}` }) };
    }
    const parsed = tool.schema.safeParse(c.input);
    if (!parsed.success) {
      return { id: c.id, name: c.name, input: c.input, isError: true,
        content: formatToolResult(false, null, { code: "invalid_arguments",
          message: parsed.error.issues.map((i) => `${i.path.join(".")}: ${i.message}`).join("; ") }) };
    }
    try {
      opts.onEvent?.({ type: "tool_start", name: c.name });
      const result = await tool.run(parsed.data, { signal: opts.signal });
      return { id: c.id, name: c.name, input: c.input, isError: false,
        content: formatToolResult(true, result) };
    } catch (e) {
      return { id: c.id, name: c.name, input: c.input, isError: true,
        content: formatToolResult(false, null, { code: "tool_error", message: publicMessage(e) }) };
    }
  }
}
```

**Orchestration patterns worth knowing.**
- **Chain:** deterministic sequence of model calls, each consuming the last one's output. Far more
  reliable than a free-running loop.
- **Router:** classify, then dispatch to a specialized handler.
- **Parallel map-reduce:** fan a task across N sub-calls, then a synthesis call.
- **Evaluator-optimizer:** generate, critique, regenerate, bounded iterations.
- **Human checkpoint:** pause the loop for approval (13.6.7).

Prefer all of these to "let the agent figure it out." Each is testable; a free-running loop is not.

**When to use / when not to.** Use parallel calls when the model naturally requests several reads. Use
explicit orchestration patterns instead of a loop whenever you can name the steps in advance. Run a free
loop only when the task genuinely requires open-ended exploration, and then cap it hard.

**Trade-offs.** Concurrency multiplies load on your downstream systems; a loop with 24 tool calls can
produce 24 database queries. Tool results bloat the context, so a long loop degrades both quality and
cost. Iterations multiply latency: an 8-step loop with a 2s per-call model is 16s minimum.

**Production considerations.**
- Hard caps on steps, tool calls, wall-clock time, and total tokens. All four, enforced by the loop.
- Per-tool timeouts, shorter than the loop's overall deadline.
- Emit an event per tool start/finish so the UI can show progress; a silent 30-second wait is a bad
  experience.
- Idempotency keys on mutating tools, because retries and resumed loops will re-issue calls.
- Record the full transcript of every loop for debugging and for eval.

**Common mistakes.**
- No step cap, so the model loops until the budget is gone.
- Executing all tool calls blindly in parallel, including mutating ones.
- Not detecting repeated identical calls, burning tokens forever.
- Truncating tool results so aggressively the model cannot use them.
- Not streaming progress, so the UI appears frozen.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "Walk me through your tool-calling loop."
- "How do you prevent infinite loops?"
- "When is parallel tool execution unsafe?"

---

---
### 13.5.4 Server-side execution and authorization

ðŸ”´ Advanced Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** Tool execution happens in **your** server process, under **your** identity model, with
**your** database connection. The authorization decision must be made from the authenticated user's
identity and the tool's declared requirements â€” never from anything the model produced or requested.

**Mechanics â€” the authorization model.**

Every tool declares, in your own metadata, what it needs. The executor checks the *caller's* claims
against that declaration, on every call, with no caching across identity changes.

```ts
export interface CallerIdentity {
  userId: string;
  tenantId: string;
  scopes: Set<string>;
  roles: string[];
  resourceConstraints?: Record<string, unknown>;   // e.g. { region: "eu-west" }
  authzVersion: number;
}

export interface AuthzDecision {
  allowed: boolean;
  reason?: string;
  scopedInput?: unknown;    // input rewritten to enforce tenant/resource boundaries
}

export async function authorizeToolCall(
  caller: CallerIdentity,
  tool: ToolSpec,
  input: unknown,
): Promise<AuthzDecision> {
  const required = tool.meta?.scopes ?? [];
  for (const scope of required) {
    if (!caller.scopes.has(scope) && !hasRole(caller, scope)) {
      return { allowed: false, reason: `missing scope ${scope}` };
    }
  }
  // Tenant scoping: the model must never be able to name another tenant.
  if (tool.meta?.requiresTenantScope !== false) {
    const claimedTenant = (input as any)?.tenantId;
    if (claimedTenant !== undefined && claimedTenant !== caller.tenantId) {
      return { allowed: false, reason: "tenant mismatch" };
    }
    input = { ...(input as object), tenantId: caller.tenantId };
  }
  return { allowed: true, scopedInput: input };
}
```

**Enforce the tenant in the query, not in the prompt.** The reliable pattern is to inject the tenant
into the database query itself, so even a bug in the tool cannot cross the boundary.

```ts
// The tool NEVER accepts a tenantId from the model. It uses the server-side identity.
export const getInvoiceTool = defineTool({
  name: "get_invoice",
  description: "Fetch one invoice for the current customer by invoice number, e.g. 'INV-004821'.",
  schema: z.object({ invoiceNumber: z.string().regex(/^INV-\d{6}$/) }),
  meta: { scopes: ["invoices:read"], idempotent: true, destructive: false },
  async run(args, ctx) {
    // ctx.caller is set by the executor from the authenticated request, never from the model.
    return db.one(
      `SELECT invoice_number, total_cents, currency, status, issued_at
         FROM invoices
        WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND invoice_number = $2`,
      [ctx.caller.tenantId, args.invoiceNumber],
    );
  },
});
```

**Deny by default.** A tool not explicitly registered has no handler and returns `unknown_tool`. There
is no "generic HTTP fetch" tool, no "run SQL" tool, no "read this file path" tool in a system where the
model supplies those values â€” each is an arbitrary-read primitive. If you need file access, expose a
tool that reads only from an allow-listed set of document ids the caller is authorized for.

**Guard against confused-deputy and prompt-injected intent.** The model can be induced to call a tool
with arguments the *user* would not have been allowed to specify. Defenses:
- Re-derive authorization from the request identity on every call.
- Never let the model supply identity-bearing arguments (`userId`, `tenantId`, `role`, `price`,
  `permissions`).
- For high-value parameters, confirm with the user rather than trusting the model (13.5.5).
- Log every tool call with caller identity, arguments, and decision, in an immutable audit log.

```ts
export async function auditToolCall(entry: {
  caller: CallerIdentity; tool: string; input: unknown; decision: AuthzDecision;
  result?: string; conversationId: string; messageId: string;
}) {
  await auditLog.append({
    ...entry,
    at: new Date().toISOString(),
    // Redact secrets/PII from the audit payload while keeping the decision trail.
    input: redact(entry.input),
  });
}
```

**Sandbox the tool code itself.** Tool implementations run in the same process as your API by default.
Anything that executes third-party or model-supplied content (parsing a document, rendering markdown,
running a query the model built) belongs in a separate, sandboxed process with no credentials and a
filesystem jail. See 13.6.6.

**When to use / when not to.** Always. Authorization is not optional for any tool that reads or writes
data. The question is only how much you trust the arguments: read-only, tenant-scoped tools can be
straightforward; anything cross-tenant, financial, permission-changing, or externally visible needs
explicit scoping, audit, and often a confirmation step.

**Trade-offs.** Per-call authorization checks add latency (usually sub-millisecond for a cached
decision, more for a remote policy engine). Never authorize the *loop* once and then trust every
subsequent call â€” the loop can run for many steps, across many different arguments, and identity can
change (token expiry, role change mid-loop).

**Production considerations.**
- Scopes are additive and checked per call; make the default-deny path the easy one to write.
- Re-check authorization inside long loops on a TTL if the loop can exceed token lifetime.
- Separate the *audit* log from the *application* log; audits must be append-only and retained.
- Redact PII and secrets from tool arguments before logging, but log enough to reconstruct the decision.
- Have a "break glass" path for operators, with its own audit and alerting.

**Common mistakes.**
- Trusting `tenantId` or `userId` supplied in tool arguments.
- Checking authorization once when the loop starts.
- A generic file-read or HTTP-fetch tool with model-supplied paths or URLs (SSRF and arbitrary read).
- Not auditing refusals â€” the interesting attacks are the ones that were denied.
- Tool implementations that use a service account with broader access than any user has.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "How do you prevent a prompt injection from making a tool read another tenant's data?"
- "Where do you check authorization in a tool-calling loop?"
- "What tools would you never expose to a model?"

---

### 13.5.5 Confirmation for destructive actions

ðŸ”´ Advanced Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** Confirmation is an explicit, human, informed consent step between the model's *intent*
and the *effect* of an irreversible or high-impact action. It converts a probabilistic decision into a
deterministic one.

**Mechanics â€” which actions need it.** Classify by reversibility and blast radius:

| Class | Examples | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read-only | search, get, list | No confirmation |
| Reversible write | create draft, add to cart, schedule | No confirmation, but announce it |
| Irreversible, bounded | send email, publish post, close ticket | Confirm, with a clear preview |
| Irreversible, financial | charge card, transfer funds, issue refund | Confirm with explicit amount, plus a hard limit |
| Irreversible, security-sensitive | delete account, rotate keys, change permissions, disable MFA | Confirm with re-authentication; often restrict to non-model paths entirely |
| Bulk/bulk-destructive | delete 500 records, mass email | Confirm with counts and a scoped preview; prefer a reversible staging action |

**The confirmation contract.** The model proposes; the *system* renders the confirmation, not the model.
The model must never generate the confirmation text, because a prompt-injected model can generate
anything.

```ts
export interface ActionProposal {
  proposalId: string;
  conversationId: string;
  toolName: string;
  args: Record<string, unknown>;
  /** Rendered by your server from a template + the validated args. Never model-authored. */
  confirmation: ConfirmationView;
  expiresAt: string;
  risk: RiskClassification;
}

export type RiskClassification = {
  level: "none" | "reversible" | "irreversible" | "financial" | "security";
  blastRadius: number;
  requiresReauth: boolean;
  requiresMfa: boolean;
};

export function classifyRisk(tool: ToolSpec, args: unknown): RiskClassification {
  const meta = tool.meta ?? {};
  const estimatedAffected = (args as any)?.orderIds?.length ?? (args as any)?.all ? Infinity : 1;
  const financial = tool.name.includes("transfer") || tool.name.includes("refund")
    || tool.name.includes("charge") || typeof (args as any)?.amountCents === "number";

  if (meta.requiresMfa || tool.name === "delete_account" || tool.name === "rotate_api_keys") {
    return { level: "security", blastRadius: Infinity, requiresReauth: true, requiresMfa: true };
  }
  if (financial) {
    return { level: "financial", blastRadius: estimatedAffected, requiresReauth: true, requiresMfa: false };
  }
  if (meta.destructive) {
    return { level: "irreversible", blastRadius: estimatedAffected, requiresReauth: false, requiresMfa: false };
  }
  if (meta.requiresApproval) {
    return { level: "irreversible", blastRadius: estimatedAffected, requiresReauth: false, requiresMfa: false };
  }
  return { level: "none", blastRadius: estimatedAffected, requiresReauth: false, requiresMfa: false };
}

export function renderConfirmation(tool: ToolSpec, args: unknown, caller: CallerIdentity): ConfirmationView {
  switch (tool.name) {
    case "transfer_funds":
      return {
        kind: "financial",
        title: "Confirm transfer",
        lines: [
          `Amount: ${formatMoney((args as any).amountCents, (args as any).currency)}`,
          `To account: ${maskAccount((args as any).destinationAccount)}`,
          `From: ${maskAccount((args as any).sourceAccount)}`,
        ],
        confirmLabel: `Transfer ${formatMoney((args as any).amountCents, (args as any).currency)}`,
        destructive: true,
      };
    case "cancel_order":
      return {
        kind: "destructive",
        title: "Confirm cancellation",
        lines: [
          `Order: ${(args as any).orderId}`,
          `This cannot be undone. Return window: ${(args as any).returnWindow ?? "unknown"}.`,
        ],
        confirmLabel: "Cancel order",
        destructive: true,
      };
    default:
      return {
        kind: "generic",
        title: `Confirm: ${humanize(tool.name)}`,
        lines: summarizeArgs(args),
        confirmLabel: "Yes, do it",
        destructive: Boolean(tool.meta?.destructive),
      };
  }
}
```

**The approve/deny protocol.** The proposal is a server-side record with a TTL. Approval must be bound
to a **hash of the exact arguments**, so a user cannot approve `transfer $10` and have the system
execute `transfer $10000`. This matters: the loop can be re-entered, the model can produce different
arguments on the next turn, and the UI might be stale.

```ts
export async function approveProposal(
  proposalId: string, approver: CallerIdentity, argsHashFromClient: string,
): Promise<ToolExecution> {
  const row = await db.one(
    `SELECT * FROM action_proposals WHERE id = $1 AND conversation_id = $2`, [proposalId, approver.conversationId]);
  if (!row) throw new ProposalNotFound();
  if (new Date(row.expires_at) < new Date()) throw new ProposalExpired();
  if (row.status !== "pending") throw new ProposalAlreadyResolved(row.status);
  if (row.approver_user_id !== null && row.approver_user_id !== approver.userId) {
    throw new WrongApprover();     // four-eyes: a different user must approve
  }
  if (row.args_hash !== argsHashFromClient) {
    throw new ArgumentsChangedSinceApproval();   // critical integrity check
  }
  if (row.risk.requiresReauth && !await recentAuth(approver, 5 * 60_000)) throw new ReauthRequired();

  // Atomic transition so two approvals cannot both execute.
  const claimed = await db.query(
    `UPDATE action_proposals SET status = 'executing', approver_user_id = $2, approved_at = now()
      WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'pending' RETURNING *`, [proposalId, approver.userId]);
  if (claimed.rowCount === 0) throw new ProposalAlreadyResolved("executing");

  const args = decryptArgs(row.args_encrypted);
  return executeTool(row.tool_name, args, { caller: approver, idempotencyKey: row.id });
}
```

**Announce reversible actions too.** For non-destructive writes, surface a clear "Done: I added X to
your cart" line. Silence after a tool call makes users nervous and drives redundant retries.

**When to use / when not to.** Confirm anything irreversible, financial, or security-relevant. Do not
confirm read-only actions (it destroys trust in confirmations and users will click through). Prefer
**making the action reversible** over adding a confirmation: soft deletes, drafts, and staged changes
are better UX than a dialog. For very high-frequency low-value actions (adding an item to a cart),
confirmation fatigue is real â€” design for reversibility instead.

**Trade-offs.** Confirmations add a round trip and a UI surface, and they are a well-known target for
click-through habits: users who always click "confirm" have no confirmation at all. Mitigations: make
the confirmation show *specific* values (amounts, counts, names) rather than a generic prompt; require
re-authentication for financial and security actions; support a bounded "trust for this session"
allowance with a hard cap.

**Production considerations.**
- Proposals expire (5â€“15 minutes) and are single-use.
- Bind approval to an argument hash and use an atomic status transition.
- Support four-eyes for high-value actions in enterprise deployments.
- Log every proposal, approval, denial, and execution in the audit log with the approver's identity.
- Never let the model auto-approve. There must be no code path where a tool with
  `requiresApproval: true` executes without a human decision.

**Common mistakes.**
- Rendering the confirmation text from model output.
- Approving by proposal id without checking the arguments have not changed.
- No expiry, so an old proposal gets executed hours later in an unrelated context.
- Confirming everything, training users to click through.
- Non-atomic approval, so double-clicking executes twice.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "How do you handle a destructive tool call?"
- "Why hash the arguments on approval?"
- "How do you prevent click-through fatigue?"

---

### 13.5.6 MCP and tool interop awareness

âš« Expert

**Definition.** The Model Context Protocol is an open protocol for exposing tools, resources, and
prompts to model applications over a standard transport, so that tool definitions can be written once
and consumed by many clients. It is the interop layer for tools.

**Mechanics â€” the model in the protocol.** A **server** exposes primitives:
- **Tools**: callable functions with a name, description, and input schema (model-controlled).
- **Resources**: readable content addressed by URI (application-controlled; the client decides what to
  attach).
- **Prompts**: reusable, parameterized prompt templates surfaced by the client.

A **host** (the application) discovers servers, lists their primitives, and decides which to expose to
the model. Crucially, the *client* still owns authorization, confirmation, and sandboxing â€” a protocol
server is a capability provider, not a trust boundary.

```ts
// Minimal client-side view of a connected tool provider.
export interface ToolProvider {
  id: string;
  transport: "stdio" | "http";
  listTools(): Promise<{ name: string; description: string; inputSchema: unknown }[]>;
  callTool(name: string, args: unknown, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<{ content: unknown; isError?: boolean }>;
  listResources(): Promise<{ uri: string; name: string; mimeType?: string }[]>;
  readResource(uri: string): Promise<{ contents: unknown }>;
}

// Turning a provider's tools into your own ToolSpec, with your own policy applied.
export async function ingestProvider(provider: ToolProvider, policy: ProviderPolicy): Promise<ToolSpec[]> {
  const raw = await provider.listTools();
  return raw
    .filter((t) => policy.allowlist.includes(t.name))
    .map((t) => ({
      name: namespace(provider.id, t.name),           // prevent collisions across providers
      description: prefixWithPolicy(t.description, policy),
      input_schema: t.inputSchema as Record<string, unknown>,
      meta: {
        destructive: policy.destructiveNames.includes(t.name),
        requiresApproval: policy.approvalNames.includes(t.name),
        idempotent: false,                              // unknown: do not assume
        scopes: policy.scopesFor(t.name) ?? [],         // your scopes, not theirs
        costClass: "free",
      },
    }));
}

// Namespacing matters: two providers both offering "search" would otherwise be ambiguous.
export const namespace = (providerId: string, toolName: string) => `${providerId}__${toolName}`;
```

**What interop does and does not give you.** It gives you: a standard discovery format, a standard
transport, and the ability to swap tool backends without changing your agent. It does **not** give you
a security boundary, consistent error semantics, schema stability, or idempotency. A third-party
provider's `delete_everything` is still your responsibility to gate.

**Practical stance.** Know the protocol and its shape; adopt it where it reduces integration cost
(especially for local tools and internal services with heterogeneous consumers); do not treat it as a
substitute for your own tool layer. Your agent still needs its own registry, policy, authorization,
confirmation, sandbox, and audit â€” because those depend on your users and your data, not on the
protocol.

**When to use / when not to.** Use it when you have several tool backends and want one integration
surface, when you want third parties to extend your product, or when your team already standardizes on
it. Skip it if you have a handful of internal tools and one client: an in-process typed registry is
simpler and safer.

**Trade-offs.** Interop lowers integration friction and raises the supply-chain surface. Every connected
provider is third-party code you are choosing to trust with a slot in your model's tool list, which
directly degrades selection accuracy (13.5.2) and expands the injection surface.

**Production considerations.**
- Allowlist providers and tools explicitly; never auto-connect a discovered server.
- Namespace tool names to avoid collisions and to make provenance obvious in audit logs.
- Apply your own authorization; a provider's permission model is not yours.
- Add timeouts and result-size caps per provider, since they are remote by definition.
- Track per-provider latency and error rate separately so one bad provider does not poison the loop.

**Common mistakes.**
- Treating a connected provider as trusted.
- Merging all provider tools into one flat namespace.
- Assuming provider tools are idempotent.
- No per-provider timeout, so one hangs the whole loop.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "What problem does a tool protocol actually solve?"
- "If you connect a third-party tool provider, what do you add around it?"

---

---
## 13.6 Agents Basics

### 13.6.1 What an agent loop actually is

ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** An agent is a **control loop you own** in which a model repeatedly chooses actions,
your code executes them, and the results are fed back until the model stops or a limit is reached. The
model proposes; your code disposes.

**Mechanics.** The anatomy is always the same five parts:

1. **Goal / stopping condition.** What "done" means. Usually the model emitting a final text response,
   but often a deterministic check (an expected record exists, a test passes).
2. **State.** The message transcript plus any scratch state the loop maintains (plan, accumulated
   results, budget counters).
3. **Action space.** The tools, each with schemas (13.5).
4. **Policy.** The model, plus the prompt that frames the goal, the constraints, and the tool guidance.
5. **Guardrails.** Step caps, tool-call caps, timeouts, token budgets, authorization, confirmation,
   loop detection, and a hard abort.

The loop from 13.5.3 is the canonical implementation. What distinguishes a *good* agent from a naive
one is almost entirely items 1 and 5.

```ts
export interface AgentDefinition<T> {
  name: string;
  goal: string;                                  // the success condition, in testable terms
  tools: ToolSpec[];
  systemPrompt: string;
  limits: { maxSteps: number; maxToolCalls: number; maxWallClockMs: number; maxTokens: number };
  /** Deterministic completion check. Beats trusting the model's "I'm done". */
  isComplete(state: AgentState): boolean;
  /** Deterministic progress check for loop detection and for the "no progress" exit. */
  progressFingerprint(state: AgentState): string;
  onStep?(step: AgentStep): void;
  verifyFinal?: (result: AgentResult) => Promise<Verification>;
}
```

**State must be inspectable.** The single most valuable debugging affordance in agent systems is a full,
replayable state dump per step: the exact messages, the tool args, the results, the token counts, and
the timestamps.

```ts
export interface AgentState {
  conversationId: string;
  runId: string;
  messages: ChatMessage[];
  plan: string[];
  stepIndex: number;
  toolCallCount: number;
  usage: Usage;
  startedAt: number;
  artifacts: Record<string, unknown>;      // durable outputs, not just chat text
}

export function dumpState(state: AgentState): AgentTrace {
  return {
    runId: state.runId,
    steps: state.messages.map((m, i) => ({
      i, role: m.role, bytes: JSON.stringify(m).length,
      blocks: blockSummary(m),
      toolCalls: (Array.isArray(m.content) ? m.content : []).filter(isToolUse)
        .map((b: any) => ({ name: b.name, args: b.input })),
    })),
    usage: state.usage,
    elapsedMs: Date.now() - state.startedAt,
  };
}
```

**Context management inside a loop.** A long loop's transcript becomes the dominant cost. Techniques:
truncate old tool results to a summary while keeping the recent window intact; keep the plan and
artifacts in a structured system-message block that is regenerated each step rather than appended to;
and drop tool results that are no longer relevant to the remaining plan.

**When to use / when not to.** Use an agent when the task requires an unknown number of steps whose
sequence depends on intermediate results â€” investigation, debugging across a codebase, multi-system
data collection, open-ended research. Do not use one when you can name the steps: write the pipeline.

**Trade-offs.** Agents maximize flexibility and minimize predictability. They are harder to test (the
hard part is testable, the loop is not), harder to bound in cost, harder to explain to a user, and
their failure modes are combinatorial. They are also much more impressive in a demo than in
production, which is exactly where they should be treated with suspicion.

**Production considerations.**
- Every agent needs a **deterministic fallback**: if the loop fails, do the bounded thing (a single
  well-crafted call) and say so.
- Log the trace per step with full token accounting, and cap the stored trace size.
- Support resuming a failed run from the last good step, with the side effects already applied.
- Version the agent definition (prompt + tools + limits) as one identifier.

**Common mistakes.**
- No `isComplete`, so the model declares success on its own terms.
- No loop detection, so it retries the same failing call.
- Treating the transcript as the only state, so nothing durable survives a crash.
- Unbounded step count tied only to token budget, which is too large a unit.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "What is an agent, in your own words?"
- "How do you know when to stop the loop?"

---

### 13.6.2 When an agent is the wrong architecture

ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** The most valuable agent skill is restraint. Agents are the default answer for a class
of problems that mostly has a better answer: a deterministic pipeline.

**Mechanics â€” the decision test.** Ask: **do I know the sequence of steps?**

- **Yes, and it doesn't depend on data** â†’ write the pipeline. Cheaper, faster, testable, debuggable.
- **Yes, but data-dependent** â†’ write a pipeline with branches, or a router + handlers. Still not an
  agent.
- **No, and I know the *shape* of the exploration** â†’ a bounded agent with a small tool set, or an
  explicit plan-then-execute two-phase design.
- **No, and the space is genuinely open** â†’ an agent, with hard limits and human checkpoints.

**Concrete cases where agents lose.**

| Problem | Agent | Better |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Summarize this week's support tickets by theme" | 15 tool calls, 60s, $0.30, no guarantee of coverage | One SQL query + one summarization call |
| "Extract invoice fields from this PDF" | Agent loops trying parsers | Deterministic parse + one extraction call + one repair |
| "Reset my password and email me" | Agent with an email tool | One endpoint, one template |
| "Find all code paths touching billing" | Agent explores for minutes | A language-server index query, then a summary call |
| "Answer questions from our docs" | Agent | RAG (13.4) |
| "Migrate 40 API endpoints to v2" | Agent per endpoint | Deterministic codemod + agent only for the residue |

**Structural arguments against agents.**
1. **You cannot test them.** You can test the tools and the prompt; the emergent behaviour needs
   statistical evaluation.
2. **They cannot be held to an SLA.** Latency and cost are variable and unbounded in practice.
3. **The failure surface is combinatorial.** More steps means more possible bad states; each new tool
   multiplies the space.
4. **The security surface is larger.** Every tool is a capability; every capability is a prompt-injection
   target.
5. **Users cannot predict them.** A deterministic flow can be designed and documented; an agent's
   behaviour must be explained in disclaimers.
6. **Debugging cost is superlinear.** One bad turn in step 7 is much harder to diagnose than a bad line of
   code.

**The hybrid that usually wins.** Deterministic skeleton, model at the points of genuine ambiguity:

```ts
export async function resolveTicket(ticketId: string): Promise<Resolution> {
  // 1. Deterministic data gathering. No model involved.
  const [ticket, history, account] = await Promise.all([
    fetchTicket(ticketId), fetchHistory(ticketId), fetchAccount(ticketId),
  ]);

  // 2. One classification call to pick the routing lane.
  const route = await classify(ticket, ROUTE_LABELS);          // schema-constrained

  // 3. Deterministic action per lane, with the model used only for language.
  switch (route.category) {
    case "billing_duplicate":
      return refundIfEligible(account, route.evidence);        // rules, not a model
    case "bug_report":
      return fileTicketWithLLMSummary(ticket, route.evidence);
    case "needs_human":
      return escalate(ticket, route.reason);
  }
}
```

This is "agentic" in the loose sense â€” it perceives, decides, and acts â€” but every step is bounded,
testable, and auditable. Reserve the free-running loop for the small residue that genuinely needs it.

**When to use / when not to.** Default to pipelines and routers. Introduce an agent only when you have
measured that a fixed sequence cannot handle the input distribution, and even then, narrow the tool
set aggressively and cap the steps. Ask "what's the simplest architecture that handles 95% of traffic,
and what handles the other 5%?"

**Trade-offs.** Pipelines need you to anticipate cases; agents absorb novelty. Pipelines degrade
gracefully (a wrong branch is a bug you can find); agents degrade unpredictably. If your domain is
stable and your inputs are structured, pipelines win decisively.

**Production considerations.**
- Track what fraction of requests take the "agent" path. If it grows, you probably have an
  under-specified pipeline, not a need for more autonomy.
- Instrument the fallback rate: how often does the bounded path handle it? That number is your
  automation ceiling.
- Document the blast radius of every tool an agent can reach, and re-review it whenever tools change.

**Common mistakes.**
- Building an agent because the problem felt "AI-shaped."
- No measurable reason for autonomy.
- Exposing a broad tool set when three well-designed tools would do.
- Treating agent failures as model failures when they are architecture failures.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "When would you *not* use an agent?"
- "How do you decide between a pipeline and an agent?"
- "Tell me about a time you replaced an agent with something simpler."

---

### 13.6.3 Planning, memory, and tool use patterns

ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** Three patterns that make agent behaviour less erratic: **planning** (decide the steps
before acting), **memory** (persist what matters beyond the transcript), and **tool use discipline**
(minimal, purposeful action).

**Mechanics â€” planning.**

Two shapes:

**Plan-then-execute (two-phase).** A first call produces a numbered plan; the loop then executes it,
allowing replanning only on explicit failure. Most predictable, and the plan is inspectable by a human
before any action is taken.

```ts
export interface Plan {
  goal: string;
  assumptions: string[];
  steps: { id: string; description: string; toolHint?: string; dependsOn: string[] }[];
  risks: string[];
  doneWhen: string[];
}

export async function makePlan(goal: string, toolNames: string[], ctx: string): Promise<Plan> {
  const res = await client.complete({
    model: STRONG_MODEL,
    maxOutputTokens: 1200,
    temperature: 0.2,
    responseSchema: PLAN_SCHEMA,
    messages: [{
      role: "system",
      content:
        "Produce a concrete execution plan. Keep it under 8 steps. Every step must name the tool it " +
        "will use or state that none is needed. Declare what 'done' looks like. Do not execute anything.",
    }, { role: "user", content: `GOAL\n${goal}\n\nCONTEXT\n${ctx}\n\nTOOLS\n${toolNames.join(", ")}` }],
  });
  if (res.stopReason === "max_tokens") throw new PlanTruncated();
  return PlanSchema.parse(JSON.parse(textOf(res.content)));
}

export function planIsExecutable(plan: Plan, tools: ToolRegistry): string[] {
  const problems: string[] = [];
  const ids = new Set(plan.steps.map((s) => s.id));
  for (const s of plan.steps) {
    for (const d of s.dependsOn) if (!ids.has(d)) problems.push(`step ${s.id} depends on unknown ${d}`);
    if (s.toolHint && !tools.has(s.toolHint)) problems.push(`step ${s.id} names unknown tool ${s.toolHint}`);
  }
  if (plan.steps.length > 12) problems.push("plan too long");
  return problems;
}
```

**Reactive planning (plan in the loop).** The agent keeps a short plan in the transcript and updates it
each step. Cheaper (no extra call), but plans drift and the model may ignore its own plan. If you use
this, put the plan in a structured block that is *regenerated* server-side each step, not appended to
by the model.

**Mechanics â€” memory.** Distinguish four things, because conflating them is the classic agent mistake:

| Memory | Scope | Storage | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Working memory | One loop | Transcript | Immediate reasoning |
| Scratch/artifacts | One run | DB row (JSON) | Durable outputs: fetched rows, computed results |
| Episodic memory | Cross-session | Vector store / table | "Last time the user asked about X, we did Y" |
| Semantic memory | Cross-session | Curated store | Facts about the user, org, or domain, with provenance |

```ts
export interface Scratchpad {
  runId: string;
  facts: { key: string; value: unknown; source: string; at: number }[];
  artifacts: Record<string, unknown>;
  unresolved: string[];
}

export function remember(sp: Scratchpad, key: string, value: unknown, source: string) {
  const i = sp.facts.findIndex((f) => f.key === key);
  const rec = { key, value, source, at: Date.now() };
  if (i >= 0) sp.facts[i] = rec; else sp.facts.push(rec);
}

export function renderScratchpad(sp: Scratchpad, maxChars = 1500): string {
  const lines = sp.facts.map((f) => `- ${f.key} = ${JSON.stringify(f.value)} (from ${f.source})`);
  if (sp.unresolved.length) lines.push(`- UNRESOLVED: ${sp.unresolved.join("; ")}`);
  const out = lines.join("\n");
  return out.length <= maxChars ? out : out.slice(0, maxChars) + "\n- [truncated]";
}
```

Episodic and semantic memory need care: **provenance and TTL**. A fact learned from a user utterance is
a claim, not a truth; store who said it and when, and expire or re-verify it. Unbounded memory without
provenance is how agents confidently propagate their own earlier mistakes.

**Mechanics â€” tool use discipline.** The best agents use *fewer* tools per task than you would expect.
Patterns:
- **Read before write.** Always fetch current state before mutating; compare against what the model
  believes.
- **Batch reads.** Prefer one tool that returns a summary over ten that return rows.
- **No exploratory writes.** Writes are hard to undo; reads are not.
- **Prefer deterministic tools.** A `compute_refund_eligibility(accountId)` tool beats asking the model
  to reason about rules you already have in code.
- **One tool per turn** unless you are confident the calls are independent and read-only.

**When to use / when not to.** Plan-then-execute for anything with side effects, anything a human must
approve, and anything long enough that a mid-course correction is expensive. Reactive planning for
short, exploratory, read-only loops. Artifacts for anything longer than one turn â€” if you need the data
later, do not leave it only in the transcript.

**Trade-offs.** Planning costs an extra call and can be confidently wrong; a bad plan wastes every
subsequent step. Mitigate by validating the plan structurally (`planIsExecutable`) and by showing it to
a human before execution when stakes are high. Memory costs storage and can go stale or become
self-reinforcing.

**Production considerations.**
- Persist the scratchpad so a crashed run can resume.
- Bound memory size and apply a recency/importance policy; unbounded memory eventually exceeds the
  context.
- Include `doneWhen` in the prompt so the model has an explicit success criterion.
- Track replan count as a metric: high replanning means the plan was bad or the environment is
  surprising.

**Common mistakes.**
- Plans that name steps with no tool, producing narration instead of work.
- Treating remembered facts as authoritative.
- Memory growing without bound until the context is useless.
- Not persisting artifacts, so a resumed run has to redo expensive reads.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "How do you keep an agent from going in circles?"
- "What kinds of memory does an agent need, and where does each live?"

---

### 13.6.4 Multi-agent systems and why they usually are not worth it

ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** Multi-agent systems split work across several agents with distinct roles and possibly
distinct contexts, coordinated by a supervisor or by each other. The pitch is parallelism, specialization,
and context isolation. The bill is coordination overhead, non-determinism multiplying, and debugging
difficulty going up sharply.

**Mechanics â€” the three architectures.**

**Supervisor.** A lead agent decomposes and delegates to specialists, then synthesizes. Simple to reason
about; the supervisor becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

**Peer / handoff.** Agents pass control to each other. Works for genuinely different domains (billing vs.
technical) but requires an explicit routing decision, and misrouting wastes a whole sub-run.

**Parallel fan-out.** N agents each work a slice, then a synthesizer merges. This is the only pattern
with a solid justification â€” because the work is genuinely independent and the merge is a single
deterministic-ish step. Even here, prefer fanning out *deterministic* workers with a model at the merge.

```ts
export interface SubtaskSpec {
  id: string;
  instruction: string;
  toolSubset: string[];         // least privilege per subtask
  maxSteps: number;
  outputSchema: Record<string, unknown>;
}

export async function fanOutAndMerge<T>(
  goal: string,
  subtasks: SubtaskSpec[],
  merge: (goal: string, results: { id: string; output: unknown; ok: boolean }[]) => Promise<T>,
  opts: { concurrency: number; signal?: AbortSignal; onPartial?: (r: unknown) => void },
): Promise<{ merged: T; subtaskResults: SubtaskResult[] }> {
  const results = await mapLimit(subtasks, opts.concurrency, async (st) => {
    const r = await runSubagent(st, { signal: opts.signal });
    opts.onPartial?.(r);
    return r;
  }, opts.signal);

  const merged = await merge(goal, results);
  return { merged, subtaskResults: results };
}
```

**Why they usually lose â€” the honest accounting.**

1. **Context is not actually isolated in a way that pays.** Each subagent needs the goal, the relevant
   background, and its own output contract. That overhead is comparable to just telling one agent.
2. **Error rates compound.** If each subagent succeeds 85% of the time and you need all six, the
   workflow succeeds about 32% of the time. Multi-agent systems multiply tail failures.
3. **Cost multiplies.** Each subagent re-reads the system prompt, the goal, and often the same
   documents. The "specialization savings" rarely cover it.
4. **Debugging becomes archaeology.** A wrong output has six possible origins, five of which are
   nondeterministic.
5. **Coordination is a prompt problem.** Routing, handoff, and merge prompts are themselves prompts that
   need versioning and evals â€” you have multiplied your surface area.
6. **Parallelism does not help when the bottleneck is the model provider.** Fan-out is bounded by your
   rate limits, and you pay concurrency limits for it.
7. **Shared state is a race.** Subagents writing to shared scratch state produce nondeterministic
   behaviour that is nearly impossible to reproduce.

**When they do earn their keep.**
- Genuinely independent parallel work (reviewing 50 files, researching 20 vendors) where a deterministic
  orchestrator drives per-item model calls.
- Context isolation for genuinely large corpora: one subagent per document, each with its own context
  window, merging to a citation-backed synthesis. This is the strongest real use case.
- Different permission scopes: a research agent with read-only web tools and a separate executor with
  write tools, so the untrusted-content agent can never act.
- Independent verification: a separate critic agent that did not see the generator's reasoning.

**When to use / when not to.** If you cannot name the specific coordination problem you are solving and
the specific cost you will save, do not build it. Start with one agent and a good tool set; introduce a
second agent only when you have measured a concrete failure that one agent structurally cannot handle.

**Trade-offs.** You trade a lot of predictability and simplicity for a modest gain in parallelism and
specialization. The trade is favourable only when sub-tasks are truly independent and the merge is
robust. Otherwise you have built a distributed system with nondeterministic workers, which is the hardest
kind of system to operate.

**Production considerations.**
- Cap subagents (3â€“5) and total tool calls across the whole system.
- Give each subagent least-privilege tools; never give every subagent every tool.
- Make merges deterministic where possible: schema-validate each subagent output, then let a model
  synthesize from *validated* structures rather than free text.
- Record the full dependency graph of the run for debugging.
- Set a global (not per-subagent) budget.

**Common mistakes.**
- Six agents where one would do.
- Shared mutable scratch state across parallel subagents.
- Unvalidated free-text outputs fed into a merge prompt.
- Per-subagent budgets that multiply into an unbounded system budget.
- No graph recorded, so a wrong result cannot be attributed.

**Interviewer probes.**
- "When would you use multiple agents?"
- "Why do multi-agent systems often disappoint?"
- "How would you debug a multi-agent failure?"

---

---
### 13.6.5 Guardrails: input, output, and action

ðŸ”´ Advanced Â· **Must-know**

**Definition.** Guardrails are deterministic (or model-based) checks placed **before**, **around**, and
**after** the model to constrain what it can be told, what it can say, and what it can do. They are the
difference between "we hope the prompt holds" and "the system cannot do the wrong thing."

**Mechanics â€” three planes.**

**Input guardrails** protect the model from hostile or malformed input.
- Length and shape limits (max characters, max images, max attachments, nesting depth).
- Content classification: prompt injection, jailbreak patterns, encoded payloads (base64 blobs, hex,
  zero-width characters), and instruction-shaped text in retrieved documents.
- Strip invisible and control characters; normalize Unicode; collapse homoglyph confusion where it
  matters.
- **Trust labelling:** mark every content source with its provenance so the prompt can treat untrusted
  content as data.
- **Retrieval-side:** if a retrieved document contains injection attempts, drop or quarantine the chunk.

```ts
export interface InputVerdict {
  allow: boolean;
  reason?: string;
  sanitized: string;
  flags: string[];
  trustLabel: "trusted_system" | "trusted_app" | "untrusted_user" | "untrusted_external";
}

const INJECTION_PATTERNS: RegExp[] = [
  /ignore\s+(all\s+)?(previous|prior|above)\s+instructions/i,
  /disregard\s+(your|the)\s+(system\s+)?(prompt|instructions|rules)/i,
  /you\s+are\s+now\s+/i,
  /\b(reveal|print|show|repeat|output)\s+(your|the)\s+(system\s+)?(prompt|instructions)/i,
  /<\/?(system|assistant|human)\b/i,
  /\{\{.*\}\}/,                                   // template injection
];

export function screenInput(raw: string, opts: { maxChars: number; trust: InputVerdict["trustLabel"] }): InputVerdict {
  const flags: string[] = [];
  let s = raw.normalize("NFKC");

  // Strip zero-width and bidi control characters used to hide instructions.
  const cleaned = s.replace(/[\u200B-\u200F\u202A-\u202E\u2060-\u2064\uFEFF]/g, "");
  if (cleaned !== s) flags.push("invisible_chars_removed");
  s = cleaned;

  if (s.length > opts.maxChars) { flags.push("truncated"); s = s.slice(0, opts.maxChars); }

  for (const re of INJECTION_PATTERNS) if (re.test(s)) flags.push(`injection_pattern:${re.source.slice(0, 24)}`);

  // Long high-entropy blobs are a common exfiltration channel.
  if (/[A-Za-z0-9+/]{200,}={0,2}/.test(s)) flags.push("large_encoded_blob");

  const severity = flags.some((f) => f.startsWith("injection_pattern")) ? "block_or_quote" : "allow";
  return {
    allow: severity === "allow",
    reason: severity === "block_or_quote" ? "possible prompt injection" : undefined,
    sanitized: severity === "block_or_quote" ? quoteAsData(s) : s,
    flags,
    trustLabel: opts.trust,
  };
}

// Quoting is a soft mitigation that preserves usefulness without pretending to be a boundary.
function quoteAsData(s: string): string {
  return `[untrusted content, quoted verbatim]\n<<<DATA\n${s}\nDATA>>>`;
}
```

**Output guardrails** protect users and downstream systems from the model.
- Schema validation on everything structured (13.2.4).
- PII/secret detection and redaction before logging or persisting.
- Toxicity and policy classification for user-facing surfaces (with an appeal path).
- **Sanitization of rendered output:** markdown with no raw HTML, safe link protocols only, no
  `javascript:` URLs, no data-URI exfiltration, code blocks rendered as text.
- Refusal handling and safe fallbacks (13.3.5).
- Domain-specific validators: no invented identifiers, no claims outside evidence, no pricing not in
  the source.

```ts
export function sanitizeModelHtml(md: string): string {
  // Convert to safe HTML with a strict allowlist. Never pass model output through a raw HTML sink.
  const html = mdToHtml(md, {
    allowedTags: ["p", "br", "strong", "em", "ul", "ol", "li", "code", "pre", "h1", "h2", "h3", "a", "blockquote", "table", "thead", "tbody", "tr", "th", "td"],
    allowedAttributes: { a: ["href", "title"] },
    allowedSchemes: ["http", "https", "mailto"],
    transformTags: { a: (tag, attrs) => {
      const href = attrs.href ?? "";
      if (!/^(https?:|mailto:)/i.test(href)) return { tagName: "span", attribs: {} };
      return { tagName: "a", attribs: { href, rel: "noopener noreferrer nofollow", target: "_blank" } };
    }},
  });
  return html;
}

export async function screenOutput(text: string, policy: OutputPolicy): Promise<OutputVerdict> {
  const flags: string[] = [];
  let out = text;

  const pii = detectPII(out);
  if (pii.found && policy.redactPII) {
    out = pii.redact(out);
    flags.push(`pii_redacted:${pii.kinds.join(",")}`);
  }
  if (looksLikeSecret(out)) flags.push("possible_secret_in_output");

  if (policy.requireGrounding) {
```
