modes; two production incidents handled with written blameless postmortems and a preventive change
you shipped; one design doc that changed a team's direction, including the political work to adopt
it; two engineers visibly levelled up; an SLO for a service you own with an error budget gating
deploys; and a written retrospective on your last two quarters including what you stopped doing.

---

### X.4.4 Staff: cross-team influence, org-wide design, strategy

**The bar**: you affect systems you do not own, teams you do not manage, and a horizon measured in
years. You are evaluated on leverage — how much other people's throughput and quality improve
because you exist — and on whether the organisation is pointed at the right problem.

**What must have**

- **Org-wide architecture**: multi-region, multi-team data and service boundaries, and the
  organisational constraints (team ownership, on-call, compliance) that determine which technical
  options are even available.
- **Strategy as a written artefact**: a multi-year technical bet tied to revenue, cost, or risk, with
  milestones and *kill criteria*.
- **Decision frameworks**: reusable ways of thinking that others apply to new problems — not one-off
  opinions. The test is whether a team uses your doc as a template without you.
- **Influence without authority**: aligning teams that do not report to you, resolving genuine
  conflicts of interest, and being able to say "no" upward with evidence.
- **Compounding leverage**: you have grown seniors who are now growing others. Your success is their
  promotion.
- **Risk literacy**: knowing which org-wide risks deserve retirement now (compliance, the migration,
  the incident class, the vendor lock-in) and which can wait.
- **Organisational design**: team boundaries, role design, hiring calibration, the level bar.

**What the interviews actually test**

- **Scope decomposition**: given a slow org, produce a portfolio of bets with sequencing and a
  narrative about why the order matters.
- **Disagreement resolution**: two teams' proposals conflict; you must find a decision both can live
  with, and articulate the principle behind it.
- **Long-horizon judgement**: a technology migration three years out — what do you commit to now, and
  what do you deliberately defer?
- **Self-awareness about failure**: what org-wide bet did you get wrong, and what did it cost, and
  what did you change about how you bet?

**Concrete differences from senior**

| Dimension | Senior | Staff |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Optimisation horizon | one to two quarters | one to three years |
| Change mechanism | you design it well and people follow the design | you build the decision framework and the coalition |
| Blast radius of a bad call | a system | several teams and possibly a migration |
| Primary output | designs and reviews | strategies, RFCs, decision records, and grown people |
| Success measure | the system works | other teams are faster and better, and the bet paid off |

**Anti-patterns**: architecture for its own sake; meetings as the deliverable; becoming the approval
bottleneck everyone routes through; depth without breadth, becoming the person who knows one system
perfectly; strategy that is really a technology preference in a longer document.

**Evidence to build in year one**: one cross-team architectural change (something three teams had to
coordinate — it will take longer, and that is the job); a decision framework others reuse; technical
strategy tied to a business metric; leaders grown into seniors whom you actively work on and take
credit for; an org-level risk retired; and hiring and team design where you set the level bar.

---

### X.4.5 What each level is actually measured on

**A concrete rubric, so you can self-assess**

| Dimension | Junior | Mid | Senior | Staff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scope of decisions | Within the task | Within the feature | Within the system | Across systems and goals |
| Problem framing | Accepts the problem as stated | Asks a clarifying question | Reframes the problem and says why | Reframes the portfolio and the goal |
| Design | Follows an existing pattern | Chooses a pattern | Argues for a pattern and a cost | Sets a standard others follow |
| Implementation | Correct, readable | Correct, tested, reviewable | Tested, instrumented, rollback-safe | Leaves the codebase better than found |
| Failure | Fixes the bug | Prevents the class | Designs so the class cannot recur | Designs the org to see it sooner |
| Communication | Answers in the thread | Writes the plan | Writes the doc that unblocks a team | Aligns organisations around a direction |
| Influence | Answers questions | Reviews a PR well | Raises the level of a team | Raises the level of several teams |
| Judgement under ambiguity | Asks for a spec | Writes a small spec | Makes the call and documents it | Makes the call that changes the game |
| Operational ownership | Runs it locally | Deploys it | Owns it in production, page and all | Owns the platform others own things on |
| Hiring | Passes their bar | Raises the bar | Gets others hired well | Builds the hiring system |
| Self-improvement | Learns quickly | Deliberately practises | Teaches deliberately | Raises the team's capability system |

**The same three questions, asked differently**

- *"Why did you do it that way?"* — Junior: "that is the tutorial pattern." Mid: "X is constrained
  by Y." Senior: "Z cost more than we could justify, and here is the condition under which I would
  switch." Staff: "We chose a portfolio posture of optimising for reversibility, and here is how I
  know it worked."
- *"What happens if this breaks?"* — Junior: "we fix it." Mid: "tests and monitoring." Senior:
  "fails closed, pages the on-call, runbook at this link, rollback takes four minutes, and I have
  run it." Staff: "blast radius bounded by tenant, we degrade to the last-known-good path, and the
  error budget tells us whether we ship the next thing."
- *"How do you know it worked?"* — Junior: "the tests pass." Mid: "metrics moved." Senior: "the
  SLO held and the error budget did not spend." Staff: "the predicted outcome is the measured
  outcome, and the ones we got wrong are written down."

**Common to every level**: communication, ownership, and judgement. The level changes how much
ambiguity each absorbs. A junior who communicates clearly and asks good questions is hired faster
than a mid who is silent and correct.

**Signals you are being considered for the next level**: you are invited to *design* reviews rather
than attend; you are asked "how would you do this" rather than "can you do this"; people outside your
team ask you questions; you are asked to review a design document; you are asked to represent the
team externally. If you want the next level, the fastest route is usually not more individual
output — it is taking ownership of something whose outcome you could not previously influence, and
carrying it visibly.

---

### X.4.6 Promotional evidence: what to do in year one at each level

Promotion is not a conversation you have; it is a body of evidence you accumulate and can point at.
Assume you were hired at the level named.

**Junior — year one evidence**

| Evidence | Why it counts | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5–8 shipped features, small to medium | Delivery reliability | Volunteer for the ticket nobody wants; ship it fully including tests and docs |
| One feature improved after feedback | Coachability | Ask for the review, take one piece seriously, show the diff |
| A bug found before it shipped | Quality instinct | Read other people's PRs; say "this breaks if" once you are sure |
| A growth narrative with specifics | Velocity | Keep a private log: what you did not know in month 1 versus month 12, with evidence |
| Questions that improve the team | Contribution | A one-page note on a repeated mistake, shared without ego |
| A side project | Sustained effort | One thing, finished, with a README |
| Asking for help early and well | Communication | "I'm stuck on X; here is what I tried; here is my hypothesis" — practise it |

Anti-evidence: shipping volume without quality; visibility instead of usefulness; avoiding ambiguity;
learning alone because asking felt slow.

**Mid — year one evidence**

| Evidence | Why it counts | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2–3 features owned end to end | Ownership | Volunteer for the feature with messy requirements and cross-team dependencies |
| A design doc that changed a plan | Technical judgement | Write it before you start; circulate, take the disagreement, revise, cite the decision |
| A production incident you handled | Operational judgement | Volunteer to be first responder once; write the timeline afterwards |
| Test coverage that catches real bugs | Quality | A regression test for every bug you fix; count them |
| Two code reviews that taught something | Leverage | Comments that explain why, not what; track who thanked you |
| A performance or cost improvement with a number | Measurement | Profile something, fix it, report before and after |
| A decision others disagreed with | Ability to act | Take a stance with reasons, write the risk down, check the outcome |
| Mentored someone through something hard | Multiplier | Pair on their worst task; do not take over |

Anti-evidence: the person who always says yes; avoiding design discussions; hoarding context;
technical excellence in a project nobody uses.

**Senior — year one evidence**

| Evidence | Why it counts | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A system you redesigned with a measured outcome | Architectural impact | Propose it, quantify the baseline, ship incrementally, publish the numbers |
| SLOs and an error budget you own | Operational maturity | Add them to a service nobody was measuring; tie release policy to the budget |
| A blameless postmortem that changed practice | Learning culture | Write it, run the review, ship the preventive change, then say so |
| Cross-team technical alignment | Influence | Get two teams to agree a contract or standard; write down why |
| 2–3 engineers visibly levelled up | Multiplication | Take someone through a design decision, a presentation, a review, a failure |
| Removed something | Judgement | Kill a service, a flag, a dependency, a process; write the postmortem on the deletion |
| A recurring incident class eliminated | Systemic thinking | Find the pattern across three incidents and fix the class |
| Standards followed without enforcement | Leverage | A template, a checklist, a lint rule, a paved road people choose |
| A written retrospective you acted on | Self-awareness | Quarterly, with specifics, including what you stopped doing |

Anti-evidence: heroics; being the single point of failure; redesigns as identity; influence that is
just proximity to decision-makers.

**Staff — year one evidence**

| Evidence | Why it counts | How to build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A cross-team architectural change | Org-level scope | Something three teams had to coordinate; it takes longer and that is the job |
| A migration of teams or systems | Sustained change management | Years-long, so year one is the first committed slice plus the coalition |
| A decision framework others reuse | Abstraction | The doc that becomes the template for other decisions |
| Strategy aligned to business goals | Strategy | A multi-year bet tied to revenue, cost, or risk, with milestones and kill criteria |
| Leaders grown into seniors | Compounding leverage | Their promotion is yours; work on it actively and take credit for them |
| An org-level risk retired | Risk awareness | The compliance programme, the migration, the incident class, the vendor lock-in |
| Hiring and team design at scale | Org construction | Role design, interview calibration, the level bar you defined |
| A written history of trade-offs | Institutional memory | Decisions age badly; the document explaining why is worth more than the decision |
| Measured leverage: teams faster | The strategy worked | Cycle time, deploy frequency, incident rate, on-call load — before and after |

Anti-evidence: architecture for its own sake; meetings as the deliverable; becoming the person
everyone routes approvals through; depth without breadth.

**The mechanism that actually works at every level**

1. **Pick a problem that hurts everyone** — not your problem, everyone's.
2. **Write the current state with numbers.** Baseline.
3. **Write the plan, including what you will delete.** Budget the deletion.
4. **Ship the smallest slice that proves the direction.** One team, one service, one week.
5. **Show the numbers changed.** This is the evidence; without it you have a story.
6. **Tell the story before you are asked.** A one-page write-up circulated to your manager with the
   evidence attached converts many conversations into one. Do it quarterly.
7. **Ask for the level when the evidence is there.** Promotion is a data question, and most
   managers are waiting for you to make the case with specifics.

And one rule across all four levels: **the evidence must survive your memory.** Write it down while
it is fresh. A promotion conversation reconstructed from memory in March is a conversation about
what you vaguely remember.

# TRACK SELECTION SELF-ASSESSMENT

Answer every question closed-book and timed. Score each item **0** (cannot attempt), **1** (roughly
right, cannot go deeper), **2** (correct, with specifics), **3** (correct, with the trade-off, the
failure mode, and when you would choose differently).

Record four numbers per section: score, time, confidence (1–5), and stability (same answer on a
week-later re-test?). **Confidence below score is the most valuable signal in the instrument** — it
is where you will be caught in an interview.

## Part 2 — The questions

**A. JavaScript & TypeScript**

1. Execution order of a synchronous statement, a promise `then`, and `setTimeout(0)`? Why?
2. What is a closure, and a real bug it causes in a loop?
3. What is `this` in an arrow function inside a class method, and why?
4. Module scope, block scope, and function scope — with a `var`/`let`/`const` example.
5. `==` versus `===` versus `Object.is` versus `??`, including `0` and `""`.
6. Why can `typeof null` not be fixed, and how do you check for null safely?
7. `flatMap` versus `map().flat()` — what does only the first do?
8. Shallow versus deep copy, and when a spread is a bug.
9. What is a memoised selector and what invalidates it?
10. `unknown` over `any`, and `never` in a switch default?
11. Interface versus type alias, for unions and generics?
12. Variance: why is `Array<Dog>` not `Array<Animal>`, but a function taking `Dog` fits one taking
    `Animal`?
13. What does `readonly` guarantee at compile time and not at runtime?
14. When does TypeScript let you lie, and how do you catch it in CI?

**B. Browser & CSS**

15. Walk through typing a URL to first paint.
16. What is the critical rendering path and which resources block it?
17. Box model, `box-sizing`, and the two common layout bugs.
18. `grid` versus `flexbox`, and what each does that the other does not.
19. What causes layout shift, and four ways to prevent it?
20. How do you honour `prefers-reduced-motion` and `prefers-color-scheme`?
21. What is `content-visibility` for, and what must it be paired with?
22. What is a stacking context, and one bug an unwanted one causes?
23. `localStorage` versus `sessionStorage` versus cookies versus IndexedDB?
24. How do you stop a third-party script hurting your performance budget?

**C. HTTP & APIs**

25. `401` versus `403` versus `404` — in intent, not in code.
26. `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `If-None-Match`, and a conditional request end to end.
27. What does `Vary` do, and what breaks without it?
28. CORS: what the preflight is, when it happens, and what it protects.
29. `PUT` versus `PATCH`, and what each must be?
30. What is idempotency, and how do you implement it for a client retry?
31. What belongs in a `429` response?
32. Offset versus keyset pagination, and when each is right.
33. What is an idempotent `PUT` in practice, and why is HTTP defined that way?
34. How do you version an API without breaking clients?

**D. Databases & SQL**

35. Read a query plan: what do rows, loops, and `rows=1` tell you?
36. When is an index not used? Five reasons.
37. Composite index column order, and how it interacts with `WHERE` and `ORDER BY`.
38. What does N+1 look like, and what are three fixes?
39. Isolation levels, and the anomaly each permits.
40. `EXPLAIN` versus `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, and estimated versus actual rows.
41. What problem does a partial index solve?
42. How do you paginate a table being written to while you paginate it?
43. What does `ON DELETE CASCADE` cost, and when would you avoid it?
44. Design users, posts, tags, and post_tags with the constraints that make invalid states
    impossible.

**E. Backend & reliability**

45. Your retry policy, and why naive retry is harmful.
46. Timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads — what does each stop?
47. How do you survive a third-party API dying mid-flow?
48. A race condition you have hit, and how you proved it.
49. How do you handle connection pool exhaustion?
50. Idempotent consumer design, and where must the idempotency record live?
51. Graceful shutdown, and what happens without it during a deploy.
52. How do you debug a production issue with only logs and a database?
53. What is a deadlock, and two ways to avoid it?
54. How do you make a long-running job resumable after a crash?

**F. Frontend & React**

55. Why did this component re-render? Answer precisely.
56. What does `useEffect` dependency comparison actually compare, and the trap?
57. Why keys in lists, and what goes wrong with an array index?
58. When are `useMemo` and `useCallback` a pessimisation?
59. Server state versus client state, and why duplicating server state causes bugs.
60. Optimistic updates — implementation and every failure case.
61. Controlled versus uncontrolled input, and what it changes about validation.
62. How do you prevent a form double-submit?
63. Hydration mismatch: cause, symptom, three fixes.
64. What is an error boundary, and what can it not catch?

**G. System design**

65. Design a URL shortener: data model, key generation, redirects, abuse.
66. Design a rate limiter: algorithm, state location, and behaviour when the state store fails.
67. Design a notification system for likes and comments, with fan-out and dedupe.
68. Design a read-heavy catalogue at 10k QPS with a daily sale spike.
69. Design a job queue that survives worker death and duplicate delivery.
70. Design a multi-tenant analytics dashboard with strict isolation.
71. Design a 5 GB file upload path with resume and virus scanning.
72. Design a session store that survives a regional failover.
73. Design search over 100M documents with typo tolerance.
74. For any of 65–73: what changes at 100×, and what breaks first?

**H. Testing & DevOps**

75. What should a unit test assert, and never assert?
76. When is a test suite a liability, and what do you do about it?
77. What do you mock, and what do you deliberately not mock?
78. Test pyramid proportions, and when integration beats unit tests.
79. Why is a flaky test worse than a missing test?
80. A multi-stage Docker build, and why layer order matters.
81. What belongs in a CI pipeline, in what order, and what can a PR skip?
82. How do you roll back, and how do you know you need to?
83. `/healthz` versus `/readyz`, and what breaks if you confuse them.
84. How do you run a migration with no downtime during a rolling deploy?

**I. Security**

85. How should passwords be stored, and why is a fast hash wrong?
86. CSRF and two defences.
87. Preventing SQL injection, including dynamic identifiers.
88. Storing a third-party API secret.
89. SSRF and how to prevent it.
90. Token rotation with reuse detection — what attack does it catch?
91. Preventing IDOR, and why hiding the ID is not a defence.
92. What does a content security policy actually prevent?
93. Keeping secrets out of a container image, and how you prove it.
94. Your first-day actions after a credential leak.

**J. DSA**

95. Two-sum with a hash map — the trade-off versus sorting.
96. Merge N sorted lists — when is a heap better than repeated pairwise merging?
97. LRU cache with O(1) `get` and `put`; name two implementations.
98. Longest substring without repeating characters — two approaches and the trade-off.
99. Course schedule (topological sort) — what does a cycle mean for your system?
100. Merge overlapping intervals — why does sorting first make it easy?
101. Binary tree level order — BFS versus DFS, and the recursion risk.
102. Subarray sum equals k with the prefix-sum insight.
103. Coin change — greedy fails on which coins, and what proves it?
104. Design `TicTacToe` with minimax: complexity and pruning.

## Part 3 — Track mapping

**Step 1**: compute per-section percentages and rank them.

**Step 2**: read your profile shape.

| Shape | Track | Where to focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A and B high, D and E low | 🟢 Frontend-leaning (X.3.1) | D, E to working knowledge; keep A and B sharp |
| D and E high, F low | 🔴 Backend-leaning (X.3.2) | F to working knowledge; A stays critical |
| A, C, D, F all mid-high, none above 85% | Balanced full stack (X.3.3) | Highest section becomes your T-depth |
| F, C, I, H high, G mid, high shipping velocity | Startup generalist (X.3.4) | G is the growth edge; I is the differentiator |
| Everything mid, nothing below 60% | Choose by the pleasure test (X.3.5 Step 2) | Breadth now, depth later |
| I or H below 40% | Any track, but fix this first | A security or operability gap is a hard blocker |

**Step 3**: pick a target *level*, not just a track, using J, G, and E as the signal.

| Signal | Level |
| --- | --- |
| J under 40%, G under 40%, I or H under 40% | Junior. Do not interview for mid yet |
| J 40–70%, G 50–75%, D 60%+ with reasoning | Mid |
| J 70%+, G 70%+, E 75%+, you can talk about failures and trade-offs | Senior |
| J and G both 85%+, plus cross-team technical leadership in the last year | Staff |

**Step 4**: write the plan. For each of your bottom two sections write the exact thing you cannot
do, the artifact that proves it closed, and the week it happens. Then take the relevant path from
X.2: 2-week, 8-week, 6-month, or 12-month.

---

## Part 4 — Interpretation and traps

- **High score, low confidence is a warning, not a strength** — you are pattern-matching. Fix with
  closed-book re-tests a week apart.
- **A low DSA score does not mean junior.** Some strong seniors are slow at DSA. Check what the
  target loop actually weighs.
- **High G score with slow time is fragile.** Two minutes per problem means recalling a template;
  interrogate yourself with "what would change if this constraint changed?".
- **Section I below 40% is a blocker.** Re-do it before any other study, at any level.
- **Re-test in four weeks.** The trend is the measurement; keep the first one and compare honestly.
- **Never take this with notes open.** It measures recognition, not what you need.

# PROJECT SCORING RUBRICS

A reusable rubric per stage so you grade a build before an interviewer does. Use it strictly, and
twice — once mid-build, once after you think you are done.

**How to use**: 0–4 per dimension, no halves (they invite negotiation with yourself). Score each
dimension before looking at any example answer. A 0 or 1 is a rewrite, not a fix; two 1s means stop
and rebuild. Re-score after 48 hours away — fatigue hides gaps.

| Score | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Absent or wrong |
| 1 | Present, but only at the tutorial level |
| 2 | Correct and conventional; a reviewer would approve |
| 3 | Correct, non-obvious choices, each justifiable |
| 4 | Production-shaped, measured, with limits and a next evolution named |

---

## X.1.1 Responsive portfolio

| Dimension | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Semantic HTML | div soup | some landmarks | semantic, ordered, alt text | full semantics, skip link, named landmarks | plus a documented audit and a screen-reader pass |
| CSS architecture | inline styles, `!important` | works, duplicated | tokens, no magic numbers | primitives, zero leakage | a system a stranger can use |
| Responsive craft | fixed px, breaks | media queries work | fluid units, clean 320→2560 | content-driven breakpoints | a resize matrix with real content |
| JS architecture | inline handlers, globals | one file, globals | ES modules, small functions | store + router + views, tree-shaken | typed with `tsc --noEmit` |
| Performance | slow | assets unoptimised | hashed assets, lazy images | Lighthouse 100 mobile, critical CSS inlined | metric-adjusted fonts, budget in CI |
| Accessibility | none | alt text | keyboard reachable | axe clean, focus managed | reduced motion honoured, live regions used |
| Deployment | localhost | host button | domain, HTTPS, headers | CI deploy, headers committed | documented cache strategy, status check |
| Documentation | none | install steps | README with live URL | decision log, screenshot, trade-offs | plus "what I would change" |

**Probes**: Why inline critical CSS? Why `clamp()`? What is your JS budget and what would you
remove? How did you verify no theme flash?

## Cross-project rubric — every project

| Dimension | A 2 looks like | A 4 looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deployability | runs on your machine | a real URL, real env config, a monitored restart, a rehearsed rollback |
| Code quality | readable | readable, small modules, no dead code, consistent naming, no `TODO` left |
| Tests | happy paths | a suite that would catch your next bug, with explainable coverage |
| Security | no obvious hole | threat model, least privilege, no secrets in code, dependency risk reviewed |
| Observability | print statements | logs, metrics, traces, and a dashboard that answers a question |
| Documentation | how to run it | architecture, decision log, trade-offs, "what I would change" |
| Performance | works | measured baseline, documented improvement, a budget that fails a regression |
| Data model | ad hoc | modelled, constrained, with migrations you can reason about |
| Failure handling | errors thrown | timeouts, retries, idempotency, degraded modes, user-visible error states |
| Communication | none | a 90-second pitch, three deep-dive decisions, one thing you would change |

**The three-question self-test before any interview**

1. Which decision in this project would you defend hardest, and what is its cost?
2. Which part is weakest, and what is the first thing you would do about it?
3. If this had ten times the traffic, what breaks first, and how would you know?

If all three answers are specific and honest, the project is doing its job. If any answer is
"probably" or "it should be fine", you have a reading assignment, not a project.

# LEARNING PATH DAY-BY-DAY SCHEDULES

Hour-by-hour tables for the 2-week path, weekly day-patterns for the 8-week path, and the 6-month
and 12-month periods in weekly form. Every row is an output, not a topic; a row with no output does
not belong in a plan.

Notation: **E1** evening block 1 (90 min, highest quality), **E2** evening block 2 (60 min,
interleaved practice), **SA/SB** Saturday morning/afternoon, **SU** Sunday morning (2.5h), **Rest**
deliberately nothing.

Rules applying to every table: every session ends with a written artifact; every Sunday review is
closed-book and re-plans the week; never skip twice (a missed session is not a missed week); the
hardest topic goes in the highest-quality block; a day that produced nothing gets a 20-minute floor
session rather than a longer one, because the streak matters more than the length.

---

## The 2-week path — day by day (full-time sprint)

Assumes unemployed or on leave. Three blocks a day: **M** morning (3h), **A** afternoon (3h),
**E** evening (2h).

| Day | M | A | E | E2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Inventory | Self-diagnostic: 60 questions from X.2.5, closed-book, timed | Re-read the READMEs and code of your last three projects | Write your 90-second project pitch in full | Recruiter prep: why this company, why this role, salary, notice |
| 2 JS | Event loop, microtasks vs macrotasks, `setTimeout` vs promises | Scope, closures, `this`, prototypes, modules | Flashcards: 60 on JS fundamentals | Re-answer every miss out loud; list the five you still cannot explain |
| 3 HTTP | Request lifecycle, TLS handshake shape, HTTP/1.1→2→3 | Caching: `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `If-None-Match`, `Vary`, CDN | Cookies, sessions, tokens, `SameSite`, CSRF, CORS preflight | Six rapid-fire HTTP questions, timed |
| 4 SQL | Joins, group by, subqueries, window functions, CTEs | Indexes, composite order, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, partial indexes | Transactions, isolation levels with a concrete anomaly each | Diagnose an N+1; rewrite it with keyset pagination |
| 5 Design I | Caching, CDN, invalidation, stampede protection | Stateless services, load balancing, sticky vs hash | Databases: relational vs document vs KV vs search; access patterns | Design: URL shortener, 45 min, whiteboard |
| 6 Design II | Queues, delivery guarantees, idempotent consumers, DLQs | Consistency, replication, read-after-write, quorum reads | Failure: timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, backoff | Design: rate limiter, 45 min, plus the Redis-down answer |
| 7 Rest | Light closed-book review of days 1–6, no new material | — | — | 25 questions from `INTERVIEW Q&A`, out loud, timed |
| 8 Framework | Your primary framework's rendering model, or the request lifecycle | The five most common bugs in your stack and why they happen | Routing, data fetching, caching, error states; do the refactor you were avoiding | Six DSA problems, medium, narrated |
| 9 Project | Walk your strongest project end to end, request to database | The 15 questions a hostile interviewer would ask | Your three best trade-off stories, each with its cost | Refine the pitch; rehearse with a timer until it is exactly 90s |
| 10 DSA | Four problems: graphs, two pointers, sliding window | Four problems: hash maps, heaps, trees | DP foundations: four problems | Redo your worst problem alone, clean |
| 11 Mock | 45-min system design + 30-min coding, with a human if possible | Debrief in writing: strengths, dodges, guesses | Repair the two biggest gaps from the debrief | Company research: product, stack, blog, the job post's nouns |
| 12 Design depth | Two design problems, each with "what changes at 100× and 1000×" | Second mock: behavioural + technical, with a human | Six STAR stories: conflict, failure, ambiguity, feedback, impact, disagreement | Review the 30 weakest flashcards |
| 13 Environment | Screen share, audio, camera, lighting, second monitor, hotspot — verified twice | — | Questions to ask them, written and ordered; then fix one thing you are ashamed of in your code | Three easy/medium problems, timed at 20 minutes |
| 14 Consolidation | 60-minute light review of the 30 most fragile items only | Read your notes and decision log end to end | Logistics verified twice; no new material; early night | — |

**Per-day outputs at a glance**: day 1 a scored diagnostic and a one-page architecture diagram; day 2
20 checked predicted outputs; day 3 a labelled packet-lifecycle diagram; day 4 fifteen runnable
queries plus three before/after plans; days 5–6 two whiteboard designs with scaling notes; day 7
25 recorded answers; day 8 a render/request diagram and six narrated solutions; day 9 a written
deep-dive plus 15 hostile answers; day 10 fourteen narrated solutions; day 11 a recorded mock and a
written debrief; day 12 two written scale-ups and six STAR stories; day 13 six questions and three
timed solutions; day 14 confirmation you can defend everything you wrote.

**2-week deliverables checklist**

- [ ] Diagnostic scored, with per-area percentages
- [ ] One-page architecture diagram of your strongest project
- [ ] 90-second pitch rehearsed to 90 seconds
- [ ] 8 design problems whiteboarded with scaling notes
- [ ] 40+ DSA problems narrated, 25+ without hints
- [ ] 2 mocks with a human, both recorded and debriefed in writing
- [ ] 6 STAR stories written
- [ ] Environment verified twice

Fixed shape every week: Mon–Thu evenings (2.5h each), Fri deliverable day (3h), Sat rest or 1h

# INTERVIEW Q&A (25 questions with model answers)

Twenty-five questions with the kind of answer that lands. Each shows the *structure* — the moves
that make it work — because structure transfers and content does not.

Read once, close the document, answer from memory, then check. That cycle beats reading ten times.

**The six moves in almost every strong answer below**

1. **State the constraint first** — names, numbers, limits — because they anchor everything after.
2. **Name the trade-off explicitly**; an answer claiming a choice is free is guessing, not thinking.
3. **Show the failure mode** and how you would know it is happening.
4. **Give a second option and why you rejected it** — proves you chose rather than defaulted.
5. **Quantify.** "Slower" is not an answer; "two extra round trips, ~80ms at p95" is.
6. **Say what would change your mind.** Nearly free, and the clearest seniority signal.

---

## Q1. Walk me through what happens when a user types a URL and presses enter. 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

**Model answer** (assuming `https://example.com/dashboard`)

1. **Parse and cache.** The browser checks its own caches, then the OS resolver, then DNS. `HTTPS` is
   in the HSTS preload list or a prior response, so it goes straight to TLS rather than redirecting.
2. **TLS handshake.** TCP three-way handshake, then TLS: client hello, server certificate,
   verification against the certificate store, key exchange, and session resumption via a ticket if
   one exists. This is expensive, and it is why connection reuse and session tickets matter.
3. **HTTP request.** Under HTTP/2 or /3 the browser may coalesce requests on one connection. The
   request carries cookies, `Accept`, `Accept-Encoding`, `User-Agent`, and conditional headers.
4. **DNS to edge.** Typically a CDN anycast address; TLS terminates at the edge, which serves from
   cache or forwards.
5. **Origin.** The CDN forwards to an origin, usually a load balancer, which picks a target by
   least-connections or least-response-time, with health checks removing dead instances.
6. **Application.** Middleware in a fixed order: `helmet` → CORS → request id → body parse → auth
   → rate limit → route → error handler.
7. **Data.** The handler calls a service, which calls a repository: one query, one pooled connection,
   cached if appropriate.
8. **Response.** Status, headers (`Cache-Control`, `Vary`, security headers, cookies), and a body,
   with compression negotiated via `Accept-Encoding`.
9. **Rendering.** HTML parses; render-blocking CSS and parser-blocking JS are handled; first
   contentful paint; then hydration, then async chunks.
10. **Sub-resources and feedback.** Images, fonts, deferred JS; hydration makes it interactive; an
    SPA route change then needs no network round trip.

**What makes it land**: the ordering, the two independent costs (TLS and hydration), and the edge.
**Follow-up trap**: "where would you measure first?" — LCP split by TTFB versus resource load, using
field data, not your laptop.

---

## Q2. Explain the JavaScript event loop, microtasks, and why `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs last. 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

JavaScript has one call stack and queues of work. The loop: take the next macrotask, run it to
completion — draining the entire microtask queue after each task and after each microtask — render,
then repeat.

- **Macrotasks**: `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, I/O, UI events, `MessageChannel`, `postMessage`.
- **Microtasks**: promise `then`/`catch`/`finally`, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`.

So `setTimeout(() => log(1), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => log(2)); log(3)` prints `3, 2, 1`:
`log(3)` is synchronous, `log(2)` runs when the stack empties (before the next macrotask), and
`log(1)` waits for a fresh tick. The delay is not magic — `setTimeout(…, 0)` enters a task queue, and
nested timeouts are clamped to ~4ms after five levels.

**Where this bites in production**

- A microtask that never resolves — an `await` loop over a huge array, an unbounded promise chain —
  starves rendering entirely. That is a frozen page, not a stack overflow.
- Rendering happens *between* macrotasks, so work in one long macrotask blocks paint while work split
  across tasks lets the browser render in between. That is the real argument for chunking loops with
  `setTimeout` or `scheduler.yield()`.
- `await` yields to the *microtask* queue, not the event loop. An `await`-driven heavy loop still
  freezes the UI.

**Trap question**: "does `await` let the browser paint?" No — it resumes on a microtask. You need a
macrotask or `scheduler.yield()`.

---

## Q3. `useEffect` dependencies: what is compared, and what is the trap? 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

The dependency array is compared element-wise with `Object.is` between renders. A length change always
re-runs. No array means every render; an empty array means once after first render. The traps:

1. **Stale closures.** `[]` closes over the first render's values forever. Fix: include what you read —
   or better, stop reading it. Use the functional updater (`setState(prev => …)`), a `useRef` for a
   value that should not retrigger, or move the read into the event handler.
2. **Objects and functions in the array.** `[{a: 1}]` is a new object each render, so the effect
   re-runs every render. Memoise it, destructure the primitives you read, or compute inside.
3. **Development double-invocation.** StrictMode intentionally mounts, unmounts, and remounts in
   development; a non-idempotent effect or a missing cleanup shows it. Fix: make every effect idempotent
   and clean it up properly, because production also remounts on Suspense boundaries and navigations.
4. **Effects that fetch on mount.** Every caller must then guard. Prefer a data-fetching library that
   owns caching, or move the fetch to a route loader.

**Design principle**: an effect synchronises with something outside React. If it synchronises React
state with other React state, you have the wrong tool — do it during render or in a handler. Every
effect you delete is a class of bug you do not have.

---

## Q4. When is an index not used? Give five reasons. 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

1. **A function or expression on the column.** `WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-01-01'` cannot use a
   plain index. Fix: an expression index, or rewrite to a sargable range
   `created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-02'`.
2. **Implicit type conversion.** `WHERE user_id = '42'` on an `int` column may cast the column. Match
   the parameter type.
3. **A leading wildcard.** `LIKE '%son'` cannot use a B-tree. Fix: trigram or full-text index, or an
   exact prefix.
4. **The query returns a large fraction of rows.** At 40% a sequential scan is cheaper than index
   lookups plus heap fetches; the planner is right, and "fixing" it makes it slower.
5. **A union branch whose type does not match the indexed column.** The planner may take the branch
   without the index.
6. **(Bonus) Stale statistics.** After a bulk load, `ANALYZE` has not run and estimates are wrong — a
   common cause of a "suddenly slow" query.

**How to answer it well**: pull up `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and *show* one. "The planner chose a
seq scan because it expected 40% of the table" is the answer; naming one cause alone is half.

---

## Q5. Design a rate limiter. 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

Two phases: the algorithm, and the state.

**Algorithm — token bucket.** Tokens accrue at rate `r`/second up to a burst capacity `b`; each
request spends one; empty means reject with `429` and a `Retry-After` equal to the time until one
token exists. It allows a controlled burst and enforces a long-run average. **Rejected: fixed
window** — one counter per `floor(now/60)`, cheap but allows a 2× burst across the boundary (60/min
becomes 120 in two seconds straddling it). **Also rejected: sliding window log** — exact, but stores
an entry per request, so 600k entries/minute at 10k QPS. **Sliding window counter** (current plus
previous, weighted by progress into the window) is the pragmatic exact-ish option.

**State.** Redis, because the limit must hold across instances — and via a Lua script, because two
`INCR`s are not atomic and that is the detail people miss.

```lua
-- KEYS[1]=bucket  ARGV[1]=capacity  ARGV[2]=refill/s  ARGV[3]=now(ms)
local d = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(d[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local ts = tonumber(d[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + (tonumber(ARGV[3]) - ts) / 1000 * tonumber(ARGV[2]))
local allowed = tokens >= 1
if allowed then tokens = tokens - 1 end
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', ARGV[3])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(tonumber(ARGV[1]) / tonumber(ARGV[2])) * 2 + 60)
return { allowed, tostring(tokens) }
```

**Headers**: `RateLimit-Limit`, `-Remaining`, `-Reset`, and on rejection `Retry-After`.

**When Redis is down** — the question they actually want. Fail open (availability) or fail closed
(protection). For a public API, fail open with a fallback in-process limiter, imperfect across
instances but far better than nothing; for login or payments, fail closed. State the choice per route
class and monitor it, because a silent fail-open is a vulnerability.

**Layering**: a cheap per-instance limiter, Redis for the shared limit, and per-tenant or per-user
quotas so one noisy tenant cannot exhaust the global pool. Concurrency semaphores, not just request
rates, for expensive endpoints.

---

## Q6. Explain refresh token rotation with reuse detection. 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

A 15-minute access token plus a long-lived refresh token in an `httpOnly` cookie. The access token
can live in memory; the refresh token must not be readable by JavaScript.

**Rotation.** Every refresh issues a new refresh token and revokes the old one; the chain shares a
`family_id`. The old row gets `revoked_at` and `replaced_by`, and the new row is inserted — same
transaction, old row locked with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`.

**Storage.** Only a hash. SHA-256 is right for a 256-bit random token; Argon2 is unnecessary because
this is not a low-entropy password.

**Reuse detection.** A refresh whose hash matches an already-revoked row means theft or a client bug;
the response is identical either way — `401` and revoke the entire `family_id`. That single rule
converts a silent, indefinite compromise into a detected, contained one.

**Why it matters.** Without rotation, a stolen refresh token is valid for its whole 30-day lifetime
and the legitimate user sees nothing. With rotation, the attacker and the user race, and whichever
uses the old token second triggers the alarm.

**Related attacks**

- *Replay from clock skew or a duplicated tab.* Rotation plus the transaction handles it; the cost is
  a family-revocation false positive, which you must handle by logging the user out rather than
  silently. Some systems allow a few seconds of grace with a `previous_token_id` pointer.
- *Theft via XSS.* Why refresh lives in an `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookie and the access
  token stays in memory rather than `localStorage`.
- *CSRF against refresh.* `SameSite` plus a CSRF token.

**Storage choice**: opaque random tokens with a server-side DB read (revocable) versus self-contained
signed JWTs (no read, but revocation needs a denylist, which reintroduces the read). For most systems
opaque + DB is the simpler correct answer. Say out loud that this costs one write per refresh and a
false-positive path you must handle — both worth it.

---

## Q7. Explain the N+1 problem and three fixes. 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

Fetch 100 posts, then loop and fetch each author: 101 queries for one page. It is the most common ORM
trap and usually invisible in development because per-query latency is low and the dataset is small.
Three real fixes:

1. **Eager load / join.** `findMany({ include: { author: true } })` generates a join or a second
   batched query. **Verify the generated SQL** — that is the actual skill; read the query log.
2. **Batch.** Extract ids, run one `WHERE id IN (…)`, join in memory with a `Map`. Works without an
   ORM and is the safest general fix.
3. **DataLoader / a batching layer.** For graph traversal it batches all loads for one event-loop tick
   into one query and caches per request, so a repeated lookup is free.

**Anti-fix worth naming**: a naive cross-request in-memory cache. Correct, but it hides the problem
and becomes a correctness bug the moment a value changes.

**How to detect it**: assert query counts in tests. A test that fetches 100 posts and asserts fewer
than five queries is a permanent guard. That — not "I know about N+1" — is the answer that impresses.

---

## Q8. What is idempotency, and where must it hold? 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

Performing an operation N times has the same effect as once. With at-least-once delivery, duplicates
will happen, and the alternative is charging someone twice or sending two emails. Where it must hold,
easiest to hardest:

1. **The API boundary.** A client-supplied key persisted with a unique constraint. First request
   inserts; a retry gets a conflict and you return the *original response*, not an error. Essential
   for anything a client will retry.
2. **Your handlers.** A job that runs twice must not send two emails: record the effect in the same
   transaction as the effect itself, keyed by an idempotency key, and return early on conflict.
3. **The external call.** Pass a key to the provider (Stripe returns the original object on replay).
   Where a provider offers no idempotency, use a natural key — your id in their reference field, with a
   search before create.
4. **At-least-once consumers.** `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` plus a unique constraint on the natural key.

**Where it does not matter**: pure reads, and idempotent-by-nature operations. `POST /cart/items` with
`quantity: +1` is inherently non-idempotent; `PUT /items/5/quantity: 3` is not.

**The traps**: "I use transactions, so I am idempotent" — transactions give atomicity, not
idempotency. And "I check if it exists first" is a race: two concurrent requests both see nothing. The
protection must be a database constraint, not a check.

---

## Q9. How do you run a schema migration with no downtime? 🔴 Advanced · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

Run migrations as a separate one-off step *before* the new version serves traffic, guarded by an
advisory lock, and make every migration backward-compatible with the version still running. That
second half is what makes a rolling deploy safe, and it is the half people forget.

**Expand / contract across three deploys**

1. **Expand.** Add the new column nullable with no constraint — safe, since old code ignores it.
   Dual-write from the new code. Backfill in small batches:
   `UPDATE … WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM t WHERE new_col IS NULL LIMIT 500)` in a loop with a sleep.
   Add `NOT NULL` as `CHECK … NOT VALID` then `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT`, which takes a weaker lock.
2. **Migrate.** New code reads the new column. Rollback stays possible because the old column is still
   written.
3. **Contract.** After the old code is fully retired, stop dual-writing and drop the old column in a
   later deploy. **Never rename in one step** — a rename is a drop plus an add to old code, so a
   rolling deploy leaves replicas unable to read the table.

**Operational details**: `SET lock_timeout = '3s'` on every migration so one that cannot get the lock
fails fast instead of queueing behind a long transaction and blocking the table; never add a column
with a *volatile* default on a large table (`DEFAULT now()` still rewrites; only non-volatile constants
avoid it); `NOT NULL` with no default always scans, so add nullable, backfill, validate;
`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` so index builds do not take a write lock (it cannot run in a transaction
and can leave an invalid index behind, so check and clean up). Rollback is not always possible: when
you choose forward-only, write the compensating SQL *before* shipping. "This migration is
forward-only; here is the compensating statement" is a senior answer.

---

## Q10. Explain `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` output and how you read it. 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

`EXPLAIN` shows the plan. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` executes and shows it with real timings and row counts, so
never run it on a mutation outside a transaction you can roll back. Read in this order:

1. **Estimated versus actual rows** per node, and the ratio. A 100× divergence means stale statistics
   or a predicate the planner did not model — `ANALYZE` may fix it, or the planner needs help.
2. **The loop.** A nested loop re-executes the inner side per outer row. `actual rows=1` inside an
   outer node of 500,000 is 500,000 index lookups.
3. **`loops=`.** Per-loop cost times the loop count is the real cost. `time=0.05 rows=1 loops=900000`
   is 45 seconds, and this is where people are surprised.
4. **`Buffers: shared hit=… read=…`.** Reads are disk, hits are cache. High reads on a hot query mean
   the working set exceeds `shared_buffers`.
5. **Sort spills** — `Sort Method: external merge` means it went to disk: fix the index or `work_mem`
   rather than raising `work_mem` globally.
6. **Node type.** `Seq Scan` is not automatically bad on a small table. `Index Only Scan` is the target
   for read-heavy paths and needs a current visibility map or it still visits the heap.

**Order of operations**: `EXPLAIN` first (cheap, no execution), confirm the plan, then
`EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on a copy or in a transaction. Fix one thing, re-measure. Never change
three indexes at once.

---

## Q11. Explain retries and why naive retries are harmful. 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

A naive retry is "try three times on failure". It fails for three reasons: **not all failures are
retryable** (a 400 never succeeds; retrying a validation error is pure waste — retry only 429, 502,
503, 504, and connection errors, and only when the operation is idempotent or carries an idempotency
key); **retry storms** (when a dependency degrades, every client retries at once, and the retries
arrive just as it is recovering and knock it over again — this is how a 30-second blip becomes a
20-minute outage); and **no jitter** (without it, clients that failed together retry together in
lockstep, forever).

**The correct policy**

- **Exponential backoff with full jitter**: `sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))`. Full
  jitter is what AWS recommends and it works; equal jitter is a reasonable compromise if you need a
  floor.
- **Cap** the delay (30s) and attempts (3–5), and give up explicitly.
- **A retry budget** — allow retries only while retry volume stays below a percentage of total
  requests; beyond that, fail fast. This is what actually stops a storm.
- **Deadline propagation.** A caller with 500ms left should not retry a 200ms operation twice. Send a
  `Deadline` header or equivalent.
- **A circuit breaker**: after a failure threshold, fail fast for a window, then probe with a single
  request. This protects both sides from work that cannot succeed.
- **An idempotency key** on anything non-idempotent.

**What shows depth**: retries are a *load* decision, not error handling. The question is not "should I
retry" but "am I allowed to add load to a system that is already struggling".

---

## Q12. How do you debug a production issue with only logs? 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

A method, not a vibe:

1. **Establish scope.** All users, one tenant, one region, one endpoint, one version? Find a failing
   request id and search on it. If you cannot correlate, that is the finding — add correlation ids.
2. **Get a baseline.** Error rate, p50/p95/p99, throughput, per-endpoint breakdown, saturation. A
   problem you cannot scope is usually a change: what deployed, what config moved, which dependency
   shifted behaviour.
3. **Form a falsifiable hypothesis.** "The 502s started at 14:02, when the upstream certificate
   rotated" is testable; "something is wrong" is not.
4. **Narrow with data.** Does it correlate with a version, tenant, region, status, flag, payload shape,
   or a particular country (timezones)?
5. **Bisect in time.** Correlate the first error with deploys, config changes, status pages, and traffic
   shape. `git bisect` the deploy range if it looks like code.
6. **Reproduce locally** with production-shaped data volumes — and say so honestly when a race needing
   10k concurrent requests will not reproduce locally.
7. **Mitigate first, diagnose second.** Roll back, disable a flag, shed load, fail over. The incident is
   not over until users are unblocked; root-causing during an outage is a privilege, not a duty.
8. **Then write it up.** Timeline, impact, root cause, contributing factors, and the specific preventive
   change you shipped. Blameless — the target is the system, not the person.

**What makes it land**: mitigate-before-diagnose, honesty about what logs cannot tell you, and the
escalation to metrics, traces, and a synthetic check when logs run out. **Trap**: "you have a race
condition and only logs" — logs cannot order events across machines; you need clock discipline, a
correlation id, and ideally distributed tracing. Naming that limitation is the senior part.

---

## Q13. Explain database isolation levels with a concrete anomaly for each. 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know**

**Model answer**

Four anomalies, each assumed to arise from a transaction that reads then writes:

- **Dirty read** — reading uncommitted data. B reads A's uncommitted write; A rolls back; B acted on
  data that never existed. Postgres Read Committed does not permit this; MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ
  does not either.
- **Non-repeatable read** — the same row read twice returns different values because another
  transaction committed between. **Read Committed permits this**, and that is what it means: each
  statement gets a fresh snapshot.
- **Phantom read** — a range query returns different row *sets* because rows were inserted. Postgres
  snapshot isolation does not permit phantoms within a statement, but two `SELECT count(*)` calls in one
  Read Committed transaction can differ. SERIALIZABLE prevents it.
- **Write skew** — two transactions read overlapping data, take different decisions, and both commit,
  breaking a joint invariant. Two on-call doctors each check "at least one is on shift", both see one,
  both go on break. Snapshot isolation permits it; SERIALIZABLE prevents it by aborting one with a
  serialization failure, which must be retried.

| Level | Dirty | Non-repeatable | Phantom | Write skew |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Read Uncommitted | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| Read Committed | no | **yes** | yes | yes |
| Repeatable Read | no | no | mostly | yes |
| Serializable | no | no | no | no |

**Where SERIALIZABLE hurts**: it aborts transactions, so you must retry on `40001`/`40P01`, and it
reduces concurrency. Prefer `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` for the common case and reserve SERIALIZABLE for
invariants that genuinely cannot be locked. Two safe patterns worth naming: the `FOR UPDATE` row lock,
and inserting a row with a unique constraint to claim a resource.

---

## How to use the Q&A section

1. **Read once, fully.** Do not take line-by-line notes; you will not retain them.
2. **Answer every question from memory the next day.** Mark each: fluent, partial, blank.
3. **Record yourself on the blanks.** Speaking a half-answer surfaces gaps far faster than rereading.
4. **Work the follow-ups.** For each question, write two follow-ups an interviewer could ask and
   answer those. That is where interviews actually live.
5. **Re-do it in a week, cold.** Stability matters more than first-attempt quality.
6. **Then adapt, do not memorise.** The numbers here are placeholders — use your own project, scale,
   and decisions. A recited model answer is detectable in ninety seconds, and it wastes a good
   interview.

---

# RAPID-FIRE (40)

Forty short questions with sharp answers. Ten a day, out loud, under thirty seconds each. Speed
matters: these arrive in a burst, and hesitation reads as not knowing rather than as care.

**Practise**: read the question, answer immediately and out loud, then check. Score **2** (correct,
under 30s), **1** (correct but slow), **0** (blank or hedged). Any 1 is a rereading assignment; any
0 is a re-teach; confident-and-wrong is the worst case — trace the specific fact rather than
re-reading the topic.

Difficulty: 🟢 Beginner · **Must-know** · 🟡 Intermediate · **Must-know** ·
🔴 Advanced · **Must-know** · ⚫ Expert

---

## JavaScript and TypeScript

**1. 🟢** What does `typeof null` return, and why can it not be fixed?
`"object"`. Values were originally tagged with a type and the null pointer's tag was `0`, which is
also the object tag — `Object(null)` returns `{}` for the same historical reason. Check with
`x === null`.

**2. 🟢** `==` versus `===` for `null`, `undefined`, `0`, `""`?
`===` compares type and value; `==` coerces, with nasty cases: `null == undefined` is true,
`null == 0` is false, `"" == 0` is true, and `NaN == NaN` is false. Use `===` plus explicit checks.

**3. 🟡** What does `Object.is` do that `===` does not?
Handles `NaN` (equal to itself) and distinguishes `+0` from `-0`. It is what `===` conceptually
should be.

**4. 🟢** Ways to copy an object, and what is shallow about each?
Spread, `Object.assign`, `structuredClone`. The first two are one level deep, so a nested object is
shared and mutating `copy.a.b` changes the original. `structuredClone` is deep and handles cycles,
Dates, and Maps, but throws on functions and DOM nodes.

**5. 🟡** What is a closure, and name a bug it causes?
A function plus its surrounding lexical environment. The classic bug: `var` in a `for` loop, where
every closure shares one binding, so all handlers see the final value. `let` per iteration fixes it
because each iteration gets its own binding.

**6. 🟡** What is the temporal dead zone?
The window between entering a scope and the `let`/`const` declaration being evaluated, where access
throws a `ReferenceError` instead of returning `undefined`. `var` has no TDZ — it is hoisted and
initialised to `undefined`.

**7. 🟢** What is hoisting?
Declarations are processed before execution: `var` and `function` declarations are hoisted and
available at the top of scope; `let`, `const`, and `class` are hoisted but stay in the TDZ until
their declaration runs.

**8. 🟡** Microtasks versus macrotasks?
Microtasks (promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`) drain completely before the next
macrotask. Macrotasks (`setTimeout`, I/O, events) run one at a time with the microtask queue drained
after each. Rendering happens between macrotasks, which is why an `await` loop still freezes the UI.

**9. 🟡** What is `requestIdleCallback`, and when is it the wrong tool?
Work during browser idle time with a deadline. Wrong for anything user-visible or time-sensitive:
idle time is not guaranteed and a busy page may never yield. Use it for analytics and prefetching.

**10. 🔴** `WeakMap` and `WeakSet` — what for, and why can you not iterate a `WeakMap`?
They hold references weakly, so keys can be collected — that is how you attach metadata to an object
without preventing collection, which a `Map` would turn into a real leak. They are not iterable
precisely because collection timing is nondeterministic. Keys must be objects.

**11. 🟡** What does `unknown` buy you over `any`?
It accepts anything on assignment but nothing can be used from it without narrowing, forcing a check.
`any` disables checking for the whole expression; `unknown` is the type-safe "anything".

**12. 🔴** Why is `Array<Dog>` not assignable to `Array<Animal>`, but a function taking `Dog` fits one
taking `Animal`?
Arrays are invariant because the type system protects writes: pushing a `Cat` into an `Array<Dog>`
reference would break it. Function *parameters* are contravariant — a function handling any `Animal`
can stand in for one handling only `Dog`, because everything you might pass it is a `Dog`.

**13. 🟡** What does `satisfies` do that an annotation does not?
It checks the value against a type without widening it; an annotation widens and discards the literal
shape. It is the difference between `{ id: 1 }` being inferred literally and being baked in.

**14. ⚫** Conditional types and `infer`, with a real use?
They let a type depend on another type. `type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T` — the
basis of most library utility types, and how you write a typed `deepReadonly`.

**15. 🟡** What does a discriminated union give you, and what is `never` for in the default branch?
It lets the compiler know which fields exist on which variant — `payload.at` is only accessible after
narrowing on `type`. The `never` default makes a switch that misses a variant a compile error, so
adding a variant surfaces every unhandled case.

---

## Browser and CSS

**16. 🟢** The three causes of layout shift?
An image or iframe without reserved dimensions, a font swap that changes metrics, and content injected
above existing content. Fix with `width`/`height` or `aspect-ratio`, a metric-adjusted fallback font
via `size-adjust`, and reserved space for anything async.

**17. 🟢** `grid` versus `flexbox`?
Grid is two-dimensional and for page structure — you define tracks and place items into cells. Flexbox
is one-dimensional, for a row or column along one axis. They compose: a grid page whose header is a
flex container is normal and good.

**18. 🟡** The box model?
Content, padding, border, margin, controlled by `box-sizing: border-box` (the sensible default). The
common bug is forgetting it, so padding and border add to a width you thought was fixed.

**19. 🟡** What is a stacking context, and name a bug it causes?
Any positioned element with `z-index` other than `auto`, an opacity below 1, a transform, a `filter`,
`will-change`, `contain: paint`, or a fixed element creates one. Inside it, `z-index` is scoped, so a
`z-index: 9999` header can end up *behind* a lower-indexed element outside the context. Fix by
flattening unnecessary contexts.

**20. 🟡** What is `content-visibility: auto` for, and what must it be paired with?
It skips rendering and layout for offscreen content. Pair it with `contain-intrinsic-size`, or the
scrollbar jumps around as content is measured.

**21. 🟢** How do you respect reduced motion?
`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` to disable transitions and animations, and check it in JS
with `matchMedia` before anything imperative. Also stop scroll-triggered animation loops entirely —
motion that ignores the preference is an accessibility failure, not a preference failure.

**22. 🟡** What is `will-change` for, and what is the cost?
It hints that a property will change so the browser prepares a layer. The cost is GPU memory per
layer, and long-lived hints cause memory bloat. Use it shortly before the change and remove it after.

**23. 🟡** `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, cookies, IndexedDB?
`localStorage` is synchronous, string-only, origin-scoped, persists forever, and blocks the main
thread — fine for a theme, wrong for anything large. `sessionStorage` is the same but per tab.
Cookies are sent with requests (small size limit) and can be `HttpOnly`/`Secure`/`SameSite`, which is
why auth tokens go there. IndexedDB is asynchronous, structured, and large — for offline data and blobs.

**24. 🔴** The three longest tasks you would look for in a trace, and the fix for each?
Long tasks from synchronous JS or a huge layout/paint — chunk with `scheduler.yield()` and reduce DOM
work. Layout thrashing from interleaved layout reads and writes — batch reads then writes. A long
script from a large bundle — split and defer.

---

## HTTP and APIs

**25. 🟢** `401` versus `403` versus `404`?
`401`: I do not know who you are; here is how to authenticate. `403`: I know exactly who you are and
you may not do this. `404`: I will not tell you whether it exists — which avoids leaking existence to
an unauthorised caller.

**26. 🟡** What is a CORS preflight, and when does it happen?
For a non-simple request — anything but GET/HEAD/POST with simple headers and a simple content type —
the browser sends `OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method` and headers, and the server must
answer with `Access-Control-Allow-*`. It does not happen for simple requests, so those are sent before
you know they will be blocked. CORS protects the *response* from scripts; it does not prevent a form
post.

**27. 🟡** What does `Vary` do?
It tells caches the response depends on a request header, so they store per-header variants. Omit
`Vary: Accept-Encoding` on a compressed response and you serve gzipped bytes to a client that cannot
decompress them. Also `Vary: Origin` for per-origin API responses.

**28. 🟡** `PUT` versus `PATCH`, and what must each be?
`PUT` replaces the resource at a known URI and **must** be idempotent — the same request ten times
leaves the same state. `PATCH` applies a partial modification and need not be idempotent. If a resource
has no meaningful URI, `PUT` to `/articles` with a client-generated id in the body stays idempotent.

**29. 🟡** What belongs in a `429` response?
A `Retry-After` header plus `RateLimit-Limit`, `-Remaining`, `-Reset`, and optionally a JSON body with
the same information and a machine-readable code. Consistent codes across endpoints matter more than
exact field names.

**30. 🔴** When is `OFFSET` pagination wrong?
When the table is being written to: inserts before your offset shift everything, so you skip and
repeat records. When the offset is deep, because the database still walks the skipped rows. Keyset
pagination fixes all three, at the cost of no random page access, and needs a stable, indexed, unique
sort key.

---

## Databases

**31. 🟢** What does a partial index do, and why is it useful?
It indexes only rows matching a predicate — `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. Smaller, cheaper, more
specific than a full index, and often matched exactly by the query predicate so no filter step is
needed. A unique partial index also enforces uniqueness on a subset, which is how soft deletes are
handled.

**32. 🟡** Why might a composite index on `(a, b)` not be used for a query filtering only on `b`?
Leading-column rule: the index is sorted by `a` first, so rows with a given `b` are scattered across
the whole index. Reorder the columns to match the query or add an index on `b`.

**33. 🟡** What is an index-only scan, and what prevents it?
The index contains everything the query needs, so the heap is never visited. It requires a current
visibility map (recent vacuum) or Postgres still checks the heap for visibility. Covering indexes with
`INCLUDE` columns make it possible.

**34. 🟡** What is a deadlock, and how do you avoid it?
Two transactions holding locks the other needs. Avoid with consistent lock ordering across the
codebase, short transactions, a single atomic statement instead of read-then-write, and catching the
deadlock error to retry — Postgres detects and kills one automatically.

**35. 🔴** What is write skew, and how do you prevent it?
Two transactions each read overlapping state, take different decisions, and both commit, breaking a
joint invariant. Prevent with `SERIALIZABLE` (retry on `40001`), with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the rows
read, or by claiming the resource with a unique-constraint insert.

**36. ⚫** What does `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` tell you that `EXPLAIN` does not?
Actual row counts and timings, plus buffer reads and hits. It executes the query, so never run it on
a mutation outside a rollback-able transaction. Buffers reveal disk versus cache, and `loops` times rows
reveals a nested-loop blow-up.

---

## Reliability, testing, and operations

**37. 🟡** What must `/healthz` and `/readyz` do differently?
`/healthz` is liveness: is the process alive? It must **not** check dependencies, or a database blip
restarts every pod at once and turns a blip into an outage. `/readyz` is readiness: can this instance
serve traffic? It checks dependencies, so a degraded database removes the pod from the load balancer
without killing it.

**38. 🔴** Why does layer order in a Dockerfile matter to the build cache?
Each layer is a diff of the previous filesystem. Copy the lockfile and install before copying source,
and the dependency layer is cached for every commit that does not change dependencies. Reverse the
order and you reinstall on every code change.

**39. 🟡** What is the difference between a flaky test and a missing test?
A flaky test teaches you to ignore red, which is strictly worse than no test because it erodes the
signal for the whole suite. Causes: real timing dependencies, shared state between tests, ordering
assumptions, reliance on the network or the clock. Fix the cause, quarantine with an owner and a
deadline, and never simply re-run in CI.

**40. 🔴** What is an error budget, and how does it change what you ship?
The allowed unreliability: `(1 − SLO) × period`. 99.9% over 30 days is about 43 minutes. With budget
left, you ship faster and take more risk; with it spent, you stop feature work and fix reliability.
The point is making the trade-off explicit, so reliability stops losing every argument by default.

---

## Bonus 15 — mixed, for a final drill

**B1. 🟢** Cookie versus `localStorage` for an auth token?
A cookie is sent automatically and can be `HttpOnly` (invisible to JavaScript), `Secure`, and
`SameSite`, so it is protected from the most common theft path. `localStorage` is readable by any
script on the page, so one XSS exfiltrates the token. Cookies have a small size limit and ride along
on every matching request.

**B2. 🟢** `401` versus `403` in code, and why the logging distinction matters?
`401` means "authenticate" and should include `WWW-Authenticate`; `403` means "not allowed". Log them
differently: a 401 spike usually means expired credentials or a broken client, while a 403 spike
usually means a permissions bug or an attack.

**B3. 🟡** What is idempotent about HTTP `GET`, and why is that not a guarantee about your API?
The specification requires GET to be safe — no side effects — which makes it idempotent in theory.
But a badly built endpoint increments a counter in a GET handler. The spec constraint is on server
behaviour, and only holds if you honour it.

**B4. 🟡** N+1 in one sentence, and one fix.
One logical operation issues one query per result row; fix with an eager join or a batched `IN`
query.

**B5. 🟡** What does a database constraint buy you that application validation does not?
Enforcement under concurrency and across every writer, including a buggy script and a manual `psql`
session. Validation in application code is advisory; `UNIQUE` is not.

**B6. 🟡** What is a race condition, and the general fix?
Two operations interleave so the outcome depends on timing. The general fix is a lock, a unique
constraint, or a single atomic statement — not application-level check-then-act.

**B7. 🟡** What does `500` versus `503` tell an operator?
`503` is "temporarily unavailable, retry with backoff" and should carry `Retry-After`. `500` is "we
have a bug". Telling a client to retry a 500 is usually wrong; retrying a 503 is usually right.

**B8. 🔴** What is cache stampede, and how do you prevent it?
Many requests for one key miss together, the origin is hammered, and it falls over. Prevent with
request coalescing (one refresh, everyone waits), a short stale-while-revalidate window, jittered
TTLs, and a lock on the miss path.

**B9. 🔴** What is a thundering herd, and where else does it appear?
The same problem elsewhere: cache expiry, a service restart clearing all connections at once, a token
expiring for all clients simultaneously, or a scheduled job running on every instance. Fixes: jitter,
coordination, and graceful drain.

**B10. 🟡** What is a connection pool, and why does exhaustion cascade?
A bounded set of reusable database connections. A slow query holds a connection, so concurrency rises,
the queue grows, latency rises, and more queries hold connections longer. Bound the pool, set a short
acquisition timeout so requests fail fast rather than queue, and fix the slow query.

**B11. 🔴** What does eventual consistency mean from the user's perspective, and what is the
alternative?
The write is not visible everywhere immediately, so a user who writes and immediately reads a
different node sees stale data. Alternatives: read your own writes from the primary, use a
read-your-writes session token, or accept staleness and design the UI not to contradict itself — do
not show a modal that a background refresh immediately contradicts.

**B12. 🟡** `EXCEPT` versus `INTERSECT`, and when do you use them?
Set operators on compatible result sets: `UNION`, `UNION ALL` (keeps duplicates, often much faster),
`INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`. Use `EXCEPT` for a set-difference anti-join; `NOT IN` with a nullable column is a
trap, because one `NULL` makes the whole predicate unknown.

**B13. 🔴** What is a saga, and how does it differ from a distributed transaction?
A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, so no global lock or two-phase commit is
needed. Each step has a rollback. The trade-off is no isolation — intermediate states are visible — so
you need idempotency, a reliable compensator, and a way to resume from a crash mid-saga.

**B14. ⚫** What is a CRDT, and when is it worth the complexity?
A data structure whose merges are commutative, associative, and idempotent, so replicas converge
without coordination. Worth it for genuinely collaborative editing, counters, and sets. Not worth it
for most products: large complexity, larger payloads, subtle semantics, and it does not solve intent —
two users deleting the same text is still a product decision.

**B15. 🔴** What is backpressure, and name three places it appears?
Resisting overload by making the queue upstream finite and slowing producers. It appears in a bounded
queue between services, a `bufferedAmount` threshold on a WebSocket, and a connection pool with a short
acquisition timeout. Without it, latency grows until everything times out and the failure moves from
slow to broken.

## Scoring yourself

| Score | Meaning | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2, under 30s | Ready | Move on |
| 1, correct but slow | Known, not owned | Rehearse once more; it comes fast under pressure |
| 0 or hedged | Not known | Re-teach, then return tomorrow |
| Confident and wrong | Worst case | Trace the specific fact; do not re-read the whole topic |

Run the set twice. The gap between the two runs is your real learning rate. If it is small, you are
done with this set; if it is large, keep going.

# CROSS-CUTTING FINAL READINESS CHECKLIST

One gate for the whole roadmap, top to bottom. Every box must be genuinely ticked — "mostly" is
unticked. Score the ticks: **0–35** not ready, start at X.2.4 or X.2.1; **36–60** ready for a junior
loop with gaps you can talk about; **61–80** ready for a solid mid loop; **81–100** ready for
mid/senior loops, where the remaining work is depth and interview polish.

---

## 1. Foundations you cannot be interviewed on

- [ ] I can explain the event loop, microtasks versus macrotasks, and where promises land.
- [ ] I know what `typeof null` returns and why.
- [ ] I can explain closures and name a bug they cause.
- [ ] I understand `this` in methods, arrow functions, and callbacks.
- [ ] I can say what hoisting is and what the temporal dead zone is.
- [ ] I can explain shallow versus deep copy, and when a spread is a bug.
- [ ] I know `unknown` over `any`, and what `readonly` does not guarantee.
- [ ] I can explain what a discriminated union buys and how `never` works in a switch.
- [ ] I know the box model, `box-sizing`, and why they cause bugs.
- [ ] I can choose between grid and flexbox and explain why.
- [ ] I know what causes layout shift and how to prevent it.
- [ ] I can honour `prefers-reduced-motion` and `prefers-color-scheme`.
- [ ] I can explain `localStorage`, cookies, `sessionStorage`, and IndexedDB trade-offs.
- [ ] I can explain what a CSP actually stops.

## 2. HTTP and API design

- [ ] I can walk the journey from typing a URL to first paint, in order.
- [ ] I know `401` versus `403` versus `404`, including the security reasoning for `404`.
- [ ] I can explain a conditional request with `ETag` and `If-None-Match` end to end.
- [ ] I know what `Cache-Control: no-store` is for and when I need it.
- [ ] I can explain `Vary` and one bug it prevents.
- [ ] I can explain the CORS preflight, when it happens, and what it does not stop.
- [ ] I know `PUT` versus `PATCH` and the idempotency requirement of each.
- [ ] I can define idempotency and name where it must hold in my system.
- [ ] I know what belongs in a `429` response.
- [ ] I can explain when `OFFSET` pagination is wrong and what replaces it.
- [ ] I can describe versioning an API without breaking clients.
- [ ] I can write one error contract (problem details) used everywhere.

## 3. Data

- [ ] I can read `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and know what estimated-versus-actual means.
- [ ] I can give five reasons an index is not used, with a real example.
- [ ] I understand composite index column order and its interaction with `WHERE`/`ORDER BY`.
- [ ] I can diagnose and fix an N+1, and I have a test that catches one.
- [ ] I can explain each isolation level and the concrete anomaly it permits.
- [ ] I can explain a partial index and when it beats a full one.
- [ ] I can design a schema that makes invalid states impossible.
- [ ] I know when a unique constraint beats application validation, and why.
- [ ] I can implement keyset pagination with a signed cursor.
- [ ] I can explain connection pooling and how exhaustion cascades.

## 4. Reliability and operations

- [ ] I can explain timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and what each stops.
- [ ] I can write a retry policy with backoff, full jitter, a cap, and a budget.
- [ ] I know what idempotent consumer design is and where the record must live.
- [ ] I can run a schema migration with no downtime via expand/contract.
- [ ] I can distinguish `/healthz` from `/readyz` and explain the failure mode of confusing them.
- [ ] I can implement graceful shutdown and explain what happens without it during a deploy.
- [ ] I can debug a production issue with only logs, and know what logs cannot tell me.
- [ ] I can describe a real incident with a timeline and a preventive change.
- [ ] I can build a multi-stage Dockerfile, non-root, digest-pinned.
- [ ] I can write CI with parallel gates, concurrency groups, and coverage thresholds.
- [ ] I can rehearse a rollback and describe the trigger that would make me do it.
- [ ] I know which metrics are correct and that labels must not include user or URL.

## 5. Frontend depth (skip if backend-leaning; invert section 6)

- [ ] I can say precisely why a component re-rendered.
- [ ] I know what `useEffect` compares, and can name the stale-closure trap.
- [ ] I understand keys and what an array index breaks.
- [ ] I know when `useMemo` and `useCallback` are a pessimisation.
- [ ] I can separate server state from client state and say why duplicating causes bugs.
- [ ] I can implement optimistic updates and handle every failure case.
